On the eve of the Philippine Revolution in 1896 it was one of eight provinces placed under martial law for rebelling against Spain, and it is represented on the Flag of the Philippines by one of the eight rays of the sun.

Japanese planes bombed Clark Field on 8 December 1941, which began the invasion of the province. After the Second World War the Hukbalahap rebels fought government forces from 1946 to 1954. Under a 1947 agreement the United States held Clark Air Base until November 1991, when the Philippine Senate rejected a renewal. In June 1991 the eruption of Mount Pinatubo had buried towns and villages under lahar floods.

During the People Power revolution, 20,000 people blocked the Bamban Bridge on 25 February to stop loyalist troops reaching Manila, and the Marcos family was flown from Clark to exile in Hawaii. The former base became the Clark Special Economic Zone, created in 1993.

Pampanga has 19 municipalities and three cities. Its people are the Kapampangans, who speak Kapampangan, one of the Central Luzon languages, and the province is predominantly Roman Catholic. Farming and fishing are the main industries, with rice, corn, sugarcane and tilapia as major products. San Fernando is known for the handcrafted lanterns called parols made each Christmas season. Clark International Airport serves the province.
pamphylia: Pamphylia lay in the south of Asia Minor between Lycia and Cilicia, extending from the Mediterranean to Mount Taurus, all within the modern Antalya province of Turkey. Pisidia bounded it on the north. It was a country of small extent, with a coastline of only about 120 km and a breadth of about 50 km. Under Roman administration the term was extended to include Pisidia and the whole tract up to the frontiers of Phrygia and Lycaonia. The name comes from the Greek for of mingled tribes or races, and Herodotus derived it from a Dorian tribe, the Pamphyloi.

Herodotus and Strabo record that the Pamphylians descended from Greeks who came with Calchas and Amphilochos after the Trojan War. Some modern scholars suggest that they migrated from Arcadia and the Peloponnese in the 12th century BCE. Britannica describes them as a mixture of aboriginal inhabitants, immigrant Cilicians and Greeks. In the Late Bronze Age the region lay on the western edge of the Hittite sphere of influence. In the historical era the population spoke Pamphylian, an idiosyncratic dialect of Greek that was seemingly influenced by neighbouring Anatolian languages and shares features with Arcadian and Cypriot.

After Cyrus defeated Croesus, Pamphylia passed to the Persian Empire, and Darius placed it in his first tax-district with Lycia, Ionia and others. Between 468 and 465 BCE the Athenians under Cimon defeated the Persians at the Eurymedon and added Pamphylia to the Delian League.

Persia retook it near the end of the Peloponnesian War, and after Alexander the Great defeated Darius III it passed back to Greek rule. After the defeat of Antiochus III in 190 BCE it was annexed by the Romans to the dominions of Eumenes of Pergamum. Some of its people then joined the Pisidians and Cilicians in piracy, with Side as the chief slave market of these raiders. After the death of Amyntas, king of Galatia, it became a district of a Roman province.

Its archaeological sites include Perga, Aspendos, Side, Sillyon and Etenna. At Aspendos a Roman bridge over the Eurymedon was reconstructed by the Seljuks and follows a zigzag course over the river. Notable Pamphylians include the mathematician Apollonius of Perga, the benefactress Plancia Magna of Perga and the historian Philip of Side.
pamplona: Pamplona lies at about 450 metres above sea level in a rounded valley, the Basin of Pamplona, on the flood plain of the Arga river, a tributary of the Ebro. The basin links the mountainous north of Navarre with the Ebro valley, and its position at a crossroads has served as a commercial link between those very different parts of the region. The historical centre stands on the left bank of the Arga.

Early settlement there goes back to the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age. In the winter of 75 to 74 BCE the area served as a camp for the Roman general Pompey in the war against Sertorius, and he is considered the founder of Pompaelo. Later research found that it was already the chief town of the Vascones, who called it Iruña, meaning the city. During the Visigothic period it became an episcopal see, and a staging ground for the Christianization of the area. The Franks raided it in 541.

From the 11th century economic recovery revived urban life, and the pilgrimages to Santiago de Compostela renewed commercial and cultural exchange with Christian Europe. In the 12th century two new boroughs, San Cernín and San Nicolás, were added to the original nucleus, the Navarrería, and the population there was swelled by Occitan merchants and artisans. Charles III decreed the union of the three places under a single municipality in 1423.

After the Castilian conquest of Navarre in 1512, Pamplona remained the capital of the semi-autonomous kingdom, which kept its own institutions and laws, but it became a Castilian-Spanish outpost. In 1513 King Ferdinand V ordered the demolition of the medieval castle and the city's monasteries and the building of a new castle nearby. Its southern walls were destroyed only in 1915.

Pamplona is the capital of the Chartered Community of Navarre. Its Gothic cathedral, of the 14th century, has an outstanding cloister, and the citadel and three of the four sides of the city walls survive. The city is known for the running of the bulls during the San Fermín festival, held each year from 6 to 14 July and brought to literary renown by Ernest Hemingway's novel The Sun Also Rises of 1926.
pan-africanism: Pan-Africanism aims to strengthen solidarity among all indigenous peoples of Africa and all peoples of African descent. It is said to originate in the struggles of sub-Saharan Africans against enslavement and colonization, from resistance on slave ships to plantation uprisings and the Back to Africa movements of the 19th century. Its core belief is that African people, on the continent and in the diaspora, share a common history and a common destiny.

The end of the 19th century produced an intercontinental political movement, alongside numerous slave insurrections in the New World, of which the Haitian Revolution is the best known. Ethiopianism gave a religious form to the same outlook. In London the Sons of Africa, addressed by Quobna Ottobah Cugoano in 1791, wrote letters to Granville Sharp, William Pitt and King George III.

Modern Pan-Africanism began around the start of the 20th century, led first by people of the diaspora. Henry Sylvester Williams, a barrister, established the African Association around 1897 and called the First Pan-African Conference, held in London's Westminster Hall in 1900, to protest the seizure of colonial lands and racial discrimination. The Pan-African Congress series followed, with meetings in Paris in 1919, London in 1921 and 1923, New York in 1927 and Manchester in 1945, pressing the cause of decolonisation.

Ghana's independence in March 1957 made Kwame Nkrumah its first prime minister and president, and he became a leading advocate of the unity of independent Africa and of regional integration for the whole continent. Under him Pan-Africanism moved beyond a movement of black Africa to a political discourse of regional unity. Pan-African thought influenced the founding of the Organisation of African Unity in 1963, since succeeded by the African Union. Most newly independent states opposed Nkrumah's wish for political union because they saw it as a threat to their sovereignty, and Félix Houphouët-Boigny was a staunch opponent.

The movement has produced many organisations and symbols, among them Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association, which adopted the red, black and green flag on 13 August 1920 in New York, and Robert Sobukwe's Pan Africanist Congress in apartheid South Africa. Flags in Malawi, Kenya and South Sudan draw on those colours, while green, yellow and red come from Ethiopia's 1897 flag. Women such as Amy Jacques Garvey and Claudia Jones were prominent, although scholarship has given them little attention. Critics, among them the journalist Philip Ochieng in 1971, have called it a movement of a self-interested educated elite that did not concern ordinary Africans.
pan-arabism: Pan-Arabism, in Arabic al-waḥda al-ʿarabiyyah or Arab unity, calls for the unification of all Arab peoples in a single nation-state from the Atlantic Ocean to the Arabian Sea. It is closely tied to Arab nationalism, which holds that the Arabs form one nation. Its origins are often traced to the Nahda, the Arab awakening of the late 19th century in the Arab regions of the Ottoman Empire. Jurji Zaydan, a Levantine Christian émigré in Egypt, argued that Arabic-speaking regions from the Maghreb to the Persian Gulf form one people whose linguistic bond outweighs religious and territorial ones.

As a political project it was first pressed by Sharif Hussein ibn Ali of Mecca, who sought a unified Arab state in the Mashreq. The Hussein-McMahon Correspondence of 1915 and 1916 produced a promise by the United Kingdom of support if the Arabs revolted, but the Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916 divided parts of the region between the United Kingdom and France. A more formal ideology appeared in the 1930s among Syrian thinkers, and Michel Aflaq and Zaki al-Arsuzi helped found the Arab Ba'ath Party.

Abdullah I of Jordan hoped to unite Syria, Palestine and Jordan as Greater Syria, and distrust of this plan helped lead to the founding of the Arab League in 1945. Egypt had shown little interest in pan-Arabism before the 1950s. Under Gamal Abdel Nasser, Arab nationalism and Arab socialism became state policy. The United Arab Republic of Egypt and Syria, formed in 1958 on the initiative of Syrian leaders, was the first merger of two independent Arab states. It was a unitary state, which critics saw as a small country annexed by a larger one, and it ended in 1961 when Syrian army officers staged a coup and withdrew.

Other attempts followed. The Arab Federation of Jordan and Iraq, also founded in 1958, collapsed after six months. The United Arab States, a confederation with Yemen, dissolved in 1961. The union of seven emirates as the United Arab Emirates and of North and South Yemen are rare cases of actual unification.

The decline of pan-Arabism is attributed to pan-Islamism, sectarian and social differences, rivalry among Arab leaders and military defeat. Israel's victory in the 1967 Six-Day War and the failure of Egypt and Syria to generate economic growth damaged its credibility. By the mid-1970s, according to The Continuum Political Encyclopedia of the Middle East, the idea of Arab unity had become less apparent in Arab politics, though it remained a goal for the masses. By the late 1980s it was eclipsed by nationalist and Islamist ideologies.
pan-islamism: Pan-Islamism advocates the unity of Muslims under one Islamic state, often a caliphate or an international organisation with Islamic principles. It differs from pan-Arabism by focusing on religion rather than ethnicity, and it takes the ummah, the Muslim community, as the focus of allegiance. Classical scholars such as al-Mawardi and al-Ghazali discussed the ummah in a political sense, and the ideology draws on the early Islam of Muhammad and the Rashidun Caliphate. Many scholars see its doctrines in earlier states such as Islamic Iberia and the Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires.

In the 18th century reformers such as Shah Wali Allah of Delhi, Muhammad Ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab and Uthman dan Fodio called for puritanical renewal. They are regarded as precursors of modern pan-Islamism, but their influence stayed local, in South Asia, Arabia and West Africa, since they did not call for an international Islamic entity.

In the last quarter of the 19th century Sultan Abdul Hamid II promoted pan-Islamism in the Ottoman Empire, after Ottomanism, to prevent secession movements among the empire's Muslim peoples. The movement's major thinkers were Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, Muhammad Abduh and Rashid Rida, who opposed European penetration of Muslim lands. Afghani feared that nationalism would divide Muslims and sought the replacement of rulers subservient to foreigners by strong patriotic ones. His student Abduh preferred gradual reform through education and distanced himself from Afghani's political path.

Rida believed unity required restoring a caliphate that applied the Sharia, and in the 1920s he set out his doctrine in al-Khilafa aw al-Imama al-'Uzma. His journal Al-Manar promoted Islamic revival and anti-British revolt. Lothrop Stoddard noted in 1921 that the pan-Islamic press had grown from about 200 journals in 1900 to over 1000 by 1914.

After the abolition of the caliphate in 1924, pan-Islamism mobilised traditionalist and reform movements alike. After the Second World War, Arab nationalist parties such as the Ba'ath and Nasserist parties took power in Egypt, Libya, Iraq and Syria, and Islamists faced repression. Sayyid Qutb was imprisoned and later executed, and Nasser took control of the mosques. After the Arab defeat in the Six-Day War, pan-Islamism regained ground against pan-Arabism. Nasser dropped his opposition to a pan-Islamic platform, and the first summit of Muslim heads of state met at Rabat in 1969, leading to the Organisation of Islamic Conference.

During the Cold War Saudi Arabia and allied states led the pan-Islamist effort against communism. The Iranian Revolution of 1979 and the Afghan mujahideen's success against the Soviet Union in 1989 raised the popularity of Islamists. Sunni thinkers such as Abul Ala Maududi embraced a new caliphate, while Ruhollah Khomeini envisaged a united Islamic state led by a Shia scholar of law.
panama-canal: The idea of a canal across the Isthmus of Panama dates back to 1513, when the Spanish conquistador Vasco Núñez de Balboa first crossed the isthmus and noted the possibility in his journal. The earliest proposal for action dates to 1534, when the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V ordered a survey for a route through the Americas to ease the voyage of ships between Spain and Peru. In 1668 the English physician and philosopher Sir Thomas Browne proposed the isthmus as the most convenient place for such a canal.

The French diplomat Ferdinand de Lesseps, who had built the Suez Canal, and the engineer Philippe Bunau-Varilla led the French attempt, begun in 1881. A concession from the Colombian government, obtained in 1878 and valid for 99 years, allowed the company to dig and exploit a canal. The French stopped in 1889 because investors lost confidence after engineering problems and a high death rate among workers. The United States took control of the canal property on 4 May 1904, inheriting a depleted workforce and a mass of equipment, much of it in poor condition.

The canal is an artificial waterway 82 kilometres long that connects the Caribbean Sea with the Pacific Ocean at the narrowest point of the isthmus. Because of the shape of the isthmus its general direction from the Atlantic to the Pacific is from north-west to south-east. Locks at each end lift ships up to Gatun Lake, an artificial lake 26 metres above sea level, created in 1913 by damming the Chagres River; locks at the other end lower them again. At its creation Gatun Lake was the largest human-made lake in the world. The original locks are 33.5 metres wide and admit ships of the Panamax size. A third, wider set of locks, built between 2007 and 2016, takes larger vessels.

The United States built the canal under the Isthmian Canal Commission, which also controlled the Panama Canal Zone. In 1907 Stevens resigned as chief engineer and President Theodore Roosevelt appointed Major George Washington Goethals of the US Army Corps of Engineers, who finished the work in 1914, two years ahead of the target date. The canal opened on 15 August 1914.

It shortened voyages between the oceans and spared ships the long and hazardous route around the southern tip of South America. Traffic rose from about 1,000 ships in 1914 to 14,702 vessels in 2008. The United States kept control of the canal and the Panama Canal Zone until the Torrijos–Carter Treaties of 1977 provided for its handover to Panama. After a period of joint American and Panamanian control, the Panamanian government took over in 1999, and the canal is now run by the Panama Canal Authority.
panama-city: Pedro Arias Dávila, also called Pedrarias, founded the city on 15 August 1519. Within a few years it became a launching point for the exploration and conquest of Peru, and the expeditions that conquered the Inca Empire set out from it in 1532. It was also a transit point for the gold and silver sent back to Spain through the isthmus, on a route that led to the fairs of Nombre de Dios and Portobelo.

On 28 January 1671 the privateer Henry Morgan attacked the city with a band of 1,400 men, looted it and set it on fire. The ruins, known as Panamá Viejo, still stand and are now a World Heritage Site. The city was rebuilt on a peninsula about 8 kilometres to the southwest, the site now called the Casco Viejo, which was planned as a walled city against further pirate attacks.

The Panama Railroad ran fully from 1855, and between 1848 and 1869 about 375,000 people crossed the isthmus from the Atlantic to the Pacific and 225,000 in the other direction, which brought the city prosperity. Panama declared independence from Colombia on 3 November 1903. The Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty of that year gave the United States a strip of land ten miles wide for a canal, and the canal was completed in 1914. William Gorgas, the chief sanitary officer, ordered the fumigation of homes and the cleansing of water, and yellow fever was eradicated by November 1905. Tension over the Canal Zone broke out on 9 January 1964, remembered as Martyrs' Day, and in 1999 the United States transferred full control of the canal to Panama.

Panama City is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Panama, at the Pacific entrance of the Panama Canal. About 410,354 people live in the city proper and over a million in the Panamá District. It is the country's political and administrative centre and a hub of banking and commerce. Panamá Viejo and the Casco Viejo, which UNESCO designated a World Heritage Site in 2003, hold the city's colonial past, and the old quarter mixes Spanish colonial, French, Antillean and art deco buildings.
pancho-villa: Villa told conflicting stories about his early life. According to most sources he was born on 5 June 1878 as José Doroteo Arango Arámbula, the eldest of five children of a sharecropper, Agustín Arango, and Micaela Arámbula. He grew up on the Rancho de la Coyotada, one of the largest haciendas in Durango, and had little schooling beyond basic literacy. He worked as a sharecropper, muleskinner, butcher, bricklayer and foreman for a US railway company. His dictated memoirs say that he became a hill-country thief after killing a hacienda owner who had raped his sister; the record shows that on 22 September 1894 he shot the man in the foot.

Villa joined the rebellion that Francisco Madero called in 1910 against President Porfirio Díaz, after Abraham González reached out to him in Chihuahua, and Madero promoted him to colonel. After Madero was murdered in the coup of February 1913, Villa joined Venustiano Carranza's Constitutionalist Army against Victoriano Huerta. That year local commanders elected him provisional governor of Chihuahua against Carranza's wishes, and he carried out a significant land reform, confiscating estates and expelling their owners. In 1914 Carranza diverted him from a direct advance on Mexico City, and Carranza's army entered the capital first in August.

After Huerta's fall, Villa and Emiliano Zapata allied against Carranza after the Convention of Aguascalientes, and a civil war followed. Álvaro Obregón decisively defeated Villa in 1915, and he split his remaining forces into guerrilla bands. At Namiquipa he rounded up the wives of men who had formed a home guard and allowed his soldiers to rape them, although some historians argue that crimes he did not commit were attributed to him.

On 9 March 1916 nearly 100 of his men attacked Columbus, New Mexico, in which 18 Americans and about 80 Villistas died. President Wilson sent 5,000 soldiers under General Frederick Funston, and John Pershing's force, using aircraft and trucks, pursued Villa fruitlessly until February 1917.

After Carranza's fall in 1920 Villa negotiated an amnesty with the interim president Adolfo de la Huerta and received a landed estate on condition that he retire from politics. On 20 July 1923 he was shot dead in an ambush in Parral, most likely on the orders of Plutarco Elías Calles and President Obregón. His body was stolen from its grave in 1926 and the head removed. In 1976 his remains were reburied in the Monument to the Revolution in Mexico City.

He is generally regarded in Mexico as a hero who stood up to the United States, the subject of corridos, films and novels, while some American media call him a murderer. His biographer Friedrich Katz judged that his time as governor of Chihuahua might in some ways be called the first welfare state in Mexico.
pandara-vanniyan: Kulasegaram Vairamuthu Pandara Vanniyan was a native of the Vanni and is said to have reigned there from 1785. Much about his family is unclear, but reports give him a sister, Nallanachal Vanniyan, and two younger brothers who served as his minister and his commander. He married into the family of Kumarasinghe Maha Vanniya of Nuwara Wewa, and so gained political power in the southern Vanni as well as the north. He is said to have lived at Kumulamunai, in the present Mullaitivu District.

The Vanni served as a buffer zone between the north and south of Sri Lanka. After the Portuguese captured the Jaffna Kingdom in 1621 the region was under their nominal control, and around 1782 the Dutch defeated the Vanniar chieftains.

Pandara Vanniyan is said to have defeated the Dutch officer Lieutenant von Driberg several times. Against the British, the Vanniars carried on a predatory warfare in Mannar and Trincomalee and reached the Jaffna Peninsula, and the British built forts to keep them at bay. In alliance with the Kandy Kingdom he rose to expel the British from his district. On 25 August 1803 he attacked the Government House at Mullaitivu, drove out the garrison under Captain Edward Mudge of the 19th Regiment and seized the fort and its cannons. He then overran the northern districts as far as Elephant Pass.

He turned from conventional warfare to guerrilla tactics, but the British organised a three-pronged attack from Jaffna, Mannar and Trincomalee. Von Driberg, who had stayed on after the British ousted the Dutch, defeated him on 31 October 1803 at Katsilaimadu, capturing a cannon given to him by the Kandyan king Sri Wickrema Rajasinghe. His houses were burned and his people dispersed into the jungle and out of the Vanni.

No longer a ruler, Pandara Vanniyan withdrew to areas near the Kandy Kingdom. Accounts of his end differ: by one he died fighting the British, by another he remained there until September 1810, when British forces ambushed him, and later died of his injuries. Von Driberg set up a granite monument at Katsilaimadu recording the defeat; in 2010 it was found broken. Prime Minister Ranasinghe Premadasa declared him a national hero in 1982, and a statue stands in Vavuniya. Tamil nationalists honour him as an epic hero, and he is the subject of a novel by M. Karunanidhi and of a play by Mullaimani Ve Cuppiramaniyam that won a prize from the Ceylon Art Council in 1964.
pandavas: The name Pandava means descendants of Pandu. According to the Adi Parva of the Mahabharata, Pandu was crowned king of the Kuru kingdom although he was younger than his blind brother Dhritarashtra. Cursed by a sage to die if he touched a wife in desire, he withdrew to the forest with his wives Kunti and Madri. Kunti had received a boon from the sage Durvasa allowing her to have a son by any god, and at Pandu's request she used it and shared her mantra with Madri.

Yudhishthira was fathered by the god Dharmadeva, Bhima by Vayu, Arjuna by Indra and the twins Nakula and Sahadeva by the Ashvins. After Pandu's death Kunti brought the boys to Hastinapura, where they were raised with their cousins the Kauravas, the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra.

Duryodhana, the eldest Kaurava, resented his cousins. When Yudhishthira was named crown prince, Duryodhana and his uncle Shakuni had a palace of flammable lac built at Varnavarta, but Vidura warned the Pandavas and they escaped by a tunnel. Arjuna then won the hand of Draupadi, princess of Panchala, in an archery contest, and all five brothers married her. Dhritarashtra partitioned the kingdom and gave them barren Khandavaprastha, which they built into the city of Indraprastha.

Shakuni then drew Yudhishthira into a game of dice, in which he lost his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi. In a last game the loser was to spend twelve years in exile and a thirteenth in disguise, and the Pandavas lost. They spent that year as servants at the court of King Virata of Matsya, and when they returned the Kauravas refused to give back the kingdom.

The Kurukshetra War lasted eighteen days. All hundred Kauravas and their army were killed, and the Pandavas, aided by Krishna, won at great cost. Yudhishthira was crowned, and the brothers ruled Hastinapura for thirty-six years before setting out with Draupadi for Mount Kailash.

The Harivamsa Purana, of the 8th century CE, tells the Jain version of their story. In the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand villagers perform the Pandav Lila, a ritual re-enactment of episodes from the epic in song, dance and recitation.
pandya-dynasty: The Pandyas, also called the Pandyas of Madurai, were one of the three great kingdoms of Tamilakam, with the Cholas and the Cheras; their rulers were known together as the three crowned rulers, the mu-ventar. The dynasty existed since at least the 5th to 3rd centuries BCE, and its origin and timeline are difficult to establish. Early Pandya chieftains ruled Pandya Nadu, which included the inland city of Madurai and the southern port of Korkai. Greek accounts, the edicts of the Maurya emperor Ashoka and Tamil-Brahmi coins and inscriptions suggest their continuity from the 3rd century BCE.

Tamil legend tells that three brothers, Cheran, Cholan and Pandyan, ruled together at Korkai, and that the two others then left to found their own kingdoms. The Silappatikaram says the Pandya emblem was a fish. Medieval Pandya kings claimed descent from the Lunar Race, and tradition holds that the Sangams, the academies of Tamil poets, were held at Madurai under their patronage.

The early Pandyas faded into obscurity with the rise of the Kalabhra dynasty. Kadungon revived the kingdom in the late 6th century, and from the 6th to the 9th century the Chalukyas of Badami or the Rashtrakutas, the Pallavas of Kanchi and the Pandyas dominated south India, often invading the Chola country, the Chera country, Venadu and Sri Lanka. The Pandyas declined with the rise of the Cholas of Thanjavur in the 9th century and were in constant conflict with them.

They entered a golden age under Maravarman I and Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I in the 13th century. Jatavarman I, about 1251, expanded the kingdom into the Telugu country as far as Nellore, into south Kerala, and conquered northern Sri Lanka. Maravarman Kulasekhara I defeated an alliance of the Hoysalas and the Cholas in 1279 and invaded Sri Lanka, from where the Tooth Relic of the Buddha was carried away. Rule was shared among several royals, one holding primacy.

An internal crisis coincided with the Khalji invasion of south India in 1310-11. Sultanate raids followed, with the loss of south Kerala in 1312, of north Sri Lanka in 1323 and the establishment of the Madurai Sultanate in 1334. Later Pandyas ruled from Tenkasi and Tirunelveli.

Early Pandya rulers are traditionally associated with Jainism and later with Shaivism. Pandya Nadu was home to major temples, among them the Meenakshi Temple in Madurai, which were large employers and landowners and also served as banks, schools and dispensaries. The Pandyas issued silver punch-marked and copper coins bearing the fish, their emblem. The dynasty is considered one of the longest-ruling in the world, in power from roughly 500 BCE to 1618 CE, though its extent varied greatly.
panjikent: Panjakent, also written Penjikent, lies in the Sughd province of Tajikistan on the river Zeravshan. The ruins of the old town are on the outskirts of the modern city. Downstream, on the tugay-vegetated floodplain of the river, lies the Sarazm Important Bird Area. The ancient town stood about 90 km from Samarkand, to which it was a vassal state.

Ancient Panjakent, known as Panchekanth, was a small but flourishing town of the Sogdians in pre-Islamic Central Asia. The Sogdians settled in city states in the Zeravshan valley and the surrounding oases, clustered mostly around Samarkand. These states had strong rivalries, their own traditions and ruling families, and a very decentralised political system. The town grew in the 5th century, when established businessmen and landowners made their livelihoods there. In 722 Arab Muslim forces besieged and took it, and its last ruler, Divashtich, fled into the upper Zeravshan but was captured and sentenced to death.

For around fifty years the town was ruled by new administrators, and towards the end of the 8th century the town on the upper terraces was depopulated and relocated. Records of a Penjikent rulership written in Sogdian were found not far away on Mount Mug. According to Arab geographers, in the 10th century Panjakent had a formal Friday mosque, which distinguished a town from a village; it was the easternmost city of Sogd and became well known for its walnuts.

The ruins have yielded numerous murals, and many are now displayed in the Hermitage Museum and in the National Museum of Antiquities of Tajikistan in Dushanbe. They show details of dress and daily life, and a great variety of influences: Greek decorative styles meet the Iranian narratives of the Shahnameh and the epic cycle of Rostam, scenes of festivities alternate with combats, and local cults mix with Iranian and Hindu deities. One painting shows Shiva with a halo and a sacred thread, clad in a tigerskin and seated on a cushioned seat supported by two bulls, with attendants in Sogdian dress.

The production of paintings began in the 5th century and stopped in 722 with the Arab invasion, when many works were damaged or destroyed. The Russian archaeologist Boris Marshak spent more than fifty years excavating the ruins. He stayed on as director of the excavation after Tajik independence and through the civil war of 1992 to 1997, and worked with the government of Tajikistan to protect the site.
pannonia: Pannonia was a province of the Roman Empire bounded on the north and east by the Danube, on the west by Noricum and upper Italy, and on the south by Dalmatia and upper Moesia. It included western Hungary, western Slovakia, eastern Austria, northern Croatia, north-western Serbia, northern Slovenia and northern Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the Early Iron Age Transdanubia was inhabited by the Pannonians, a collection of Illyrian tribes. Celtic groups, the Scordisci, the Boii and others, later held much of the region, and the Dacian king Burebista overcame several of them between 65 and 50 BCE.

Rome's advance began with the foundation of Aquileia in 181 BCE. In 35 BCE Octavian captured Siscia after a month-long siege and occupied much of the Sava valley. In 15 BCE the future emperor Tiberius defeated the Scordisci, and his operations of 12 to 9 BCE almost certainly brought the whole of Transdanubia under Roman control. Augustus later claimed in his Res Gestae that Tiberius had brought the Pannonian peoples under Roman authority. The Bellum Batonianum, a revolt led by the Breuci under Bato the Breucian and the Daesitiates under Bato the Daesitiate, lasted three years until the last rebel laid down arms in 9 CE. Illyricum was then divided into Dalmatia and Pannonia.

Claudius finished the occupation and began building the frontier, the limes. Under Trajan, between 103 and 107, the province was divided into Pannonia Inferior and Pannonia Superior, the latter with most of the urbanised areas and three legions. Wars with the Marcomanni and Quadi under Marcus Aurelius, from 166, brought heavy destruction and loss of life to Pannonia. Diocletian and his successors divided it into four provinces, Prima, Valeria, Savia and Secunda. In 324 Constantine I annexed the plains to the east up to a new limes, the Devil's Dykes.

Rome lost the province in stages. In 433 Flavius Aetius ceded part of it to the Huns, and after the Hunnic empire collapsed in 454, Emperor Marcian settled large numbers of Ostrogoths there as foederati. Justinian I's Eastern Roman Empire held southern parts in the 6th century, the Avars invaded in the 560s, and Slavs settled over time. In the 790s the Franks invaded and used the name Pannonia for a new frontier province, the March of Pannonia.

Roman Pannonia was fairly productive, with oats and barley its chief crops, and timber an important export until the forests were cleared. Native settlements were organised in cantons, while most large towns were of Roman origin, among them Carnuntum, Vindobona, Aquincum, Savaria, Sirmium and Siscia. Christianity began to spread in the province in the 2nd century. A dialect called Pannonian Latin developed and went extinct around the 6th century. The ancient name survives in the modern term Pannonian plain.
paolo-uccello: The sources for his life are few: Giorgio Vasari's biography, written 75 years after his death, and a few contemporary official documents. Born Paolo di Dono, he was probably born in Pratovecchio, near Arezzo, the hometown of his father Dono di Paolo, a barber-surgeon. His mother, Antonia, came from a high-born Florentine family. His nickname Uccello, "little bird", came from his fondness for painting birds.

From 1412 until 1416 he was apprenticed to the sculptor Lorenzo Ghiberti, creator of the doors of the Florence Baptistery, whose workshop was then the premier centre of Florentine art. It was around this time that his lifelong friendship with Donatello began. He was admitted to the painters' guild, the Compagnia di San Luca, in 1414, and joined the Arte dei Medici e degli Speziali in 1415.

By 1424 Uccello was earning his own living. That year he painted episodes of the Creation and the Fall for the Green Cloister of Santa Maria Novella in Florence, followed by scenes from the life of Noah, which brought him great fame. In 1425 he travelled to Venice to work on the mosaics for the façade of San Marco, all since lost, and he was back in Florence in 1431. In 1443 he painted the figures on the clock of the Duomo and designed stained glass windows for it.

Around the mid-1450s he painted the three panels of the Battle of San Romano for the Palazzo Medici, commemorating the Florentine victory over the Sienese in 1432. Their foreshortened forms, extending in many planes, give a controlled structure to the chaos of battle. From 1465 to 1469 he worked in Urbino with his son Donato for the Confraternity of Corpus Domini, painting the predella of its altarpiece, the Miracle of the Profaned Host.

In his Florentine tax return of August 1469 Uccello declared that he was old and ailing, his wife was ill, and he could no longer work. He made his testament on 11 November 1475 and died on 10 December at the hospital of Florence, aged 78. He was buried in his father's tomb in the church of Santo Spirito.

Vasari wrote that Uccello was obsessed with perspective and would stay up all night in his study trying to grasp the exact vanishing point. He worked in the Late Gothic tradition, emphasising colour and pageantry, and his style was idiosyncratic; he left no school of followers. His perspective influenced painters such as Piero della Francesca, Albrecht Dürer and Leonardo da Vinci.
paolo-veronese: Veronese took his usual name from Verona, where he was born in 1528, the fifth child of a stonecutter named Gabriele and his wife Caterina. He was first known as Paolo Spezapreda, after his father's trade, and later took the surname Caliari because his mother was the illegitimate daughter of a nobleman, Antonio Caliari. By 1541 he was apprenticed to Antonio Badile, later his father-in-law, and in 1544 to Giovanni Francesco Caroto, both leading painters in Verona. Trained in the Mannerism then popular in Parma, he soon developed a preference for a more radiant palette.
In 1551 the Giustiniani family commissioned an altarpiece from him for the church of San Francesco della Vigna in Venice, and in 1552 Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga commissioned one for Mantua Cathedral.

Veronese moved to Venice in 1553 after receiving his first state commission, ceiling frescoes in the Hall of the Council of Ten in the Doge's Palace. His ceilings of 1557 in the Marciana Library won a prize judged by Titian and Jacopo Sansovino.

In the late 1550s he decorated the Villa Barbaro at Maser, a new building by Andrea Palladio, with frescoes that combine portraits of the family, mythological figures and ceilings opening to blue skies. His Wedding at Cana, painted in 1562–1563 for the monastery of San Giorgio Maggiore, was to cover 66 square metres; the contract required premium pigments and as many figures as possible, and it includes portraits of Titian and Tintoretto and a self-portrait. In 1565 he married Elena Badile, the daughter of his first master. He headed a family workshop that included his brother Benedetto and his sons Carlo and Gabriele, which went on after his death in 1588, signing its works Haeredes Pauli.

In 1573 Veronese completed a Last Supper for the refectory of the Basilica of Santi Giovanni e Paolo, replacing a painting by Titian that had been burnt in a fire. At 5.55 by 12.80 metres, it showed a banquet that included German soldiers, dwarves and animals.

On 18 July 1573 the Venetian Inquisition summoned him to explain these figures, which it considered extraneous to the Last Supper. He told the tribunal that painters take the same liberties as poets and madmen. The Inquisition ordered him to repaint the scene; he opposed this remedy but was compelled to retitle the work The Feast in the House of Levi. The interrogation is described as cautionary rather than punitive. His admirers have included Rubens, Watteau, Tiepolo, Delacroix and Renoir, though his work has been felt not to permit expression of the profound.
papacy: According to Catholic tradition, the apostolic see of Rome was founded by Saint Peter and Saint Paul in the first century. The Catholic Church teaches that the bishop of Rome succeeded Saint Peter, to whom, in its reading of Matthew 16, Jesus gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the powers of binding and loosing. Cyprian of Carthage, in his Letter 55 of about 251 CE to Pope Cornelius, recognised the bishop of Rome as Peter's successor.

The word pope comes from the Greek páppas, father. In the early centuries it was applied, especially in the East, to all bishops and senior clergy. It became reserved in the West to the bishop of Rome during the reign of Leo I (440 to 461), though this was made official only in the 11th century.

In ancient times popes helped spread Christianity and intervened in doctrinal disputes. In the Middle Ages they played a role of secular importance in Western Europe, often arbitrating between Christian monarchs, and their influence eventually rivalled that of territorial rulers. From the 8th century until 1870 the pope was sovereign of the Papal States, and since the Lateran Treaty of 1929 he has headed the much smaller Vatican City State. Between 1309 and 1378 the popes lived in Avignon, France, a period often called the Babylonian captivity. The First Vatican Council defined the pope's authority on 18 July 1870, and in 1870 the dogma of papal infallibility was proclaimed for the rare occasions when the pope speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals.

The pope was originally chosen by the senior clergy in and near Rome. In 1059 the electorate was restricted to the cardinals, and in 1179 the votes of all cardinal electors were made equal. The last pope elected when not yet a bishop was Gregory XVI in 1831, and the last not a cardinal was Urban VI in 1378. Popes adopt a new name on accession.

His official seat is the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran, and his residence the Apostolic Palace. Antipopes are claimants not canonically elected; briefly in the 15th century three separate lines of popes claimed authenticity. Eastern Orthodox churches and the Anglican Communion accept apostolic succession and a primacy of honour but reject the pope as Peter's successor in any other sense than other bishops.
papeete: Papeete lies on the island of Tahiti, in the Windward Islands, which are part of the Society Islands. The name Papeʻete means water from a basket. It is an effect of a naming taboo under the reign of Pōmare I, when the Tahitian word for water, vai, was replaced by pape; the older name Vaiʻete is still recognised in some areas, such as the Marquesas. The city has a tropical monsoon climate with high temperatures and humidity throughout the year. Its wet season covers most of the year, and the dry season is short, only August and September.

The town's growth in the late 19th century is recorded in its public works. A water tower at Faʻaiere, with a capacity of 150,000 litres, supplied the town with drinking water; a light railway on an inclined plane 220 metres long overcame a difference in altitude of 37 metres, with a steam-driven winch hauling three narrow-gauge trucks at a time.

In a letter of 18 June 1891 to Governor Theodore Lacascade, Paul Decauville mentioned an order for 15 kilometres of portable rail track, probably for a tramway from Papeʻete to Punaʻauia. In 1902 the post office had to be moved, and instead of being demolished it was lifted from the subsoil and moved whole on a Decauville railway.

After the outbreak of the First World War, German vessels shelled Papeʻete, causing loss of life and significant damage. The city's growth later received a boost when France moved its nuclear weapon test range from Algeria, which had become independent, to the atolls of Moruroa and Fangataufa, about 1,500 kilometres to the east of Tahiti, and built the Faʻaʻā International Airport, opened in 1962. Rioting followed French nuclear tests in 1987 and on 5 September 1995, when a riot lasted two days and damaged the airport.

Papeʻete is the capital of French Polynesia, an overseas collectivity of the French Republic, and the administrative capital of the Windward Islands. It is the main centre of government, commerce and finance of French Polynesia, and a commonly used port of call. Landmarks include the Cathedral of Notre Dame, the Territorial Assembly, the Papeʻete Market and Bougainville Park. The Territorial Assembly stands on the site of the royal residence and palace of Queen Pōmare IV, who ruled from 1827 to 1877.
papiamento: Scholars dispute where Papiamento came from, and its precise history has not been established. Its parent language is West Iberian Romance, but some derive it from Portuguese and the Portuguese-based creoles, others from Spanish. Most linguists now believe it emerged from the Portuguese-based creoles of the West African coasts, since it shares many features with Cape Verdean Creole and Guinea-Bissau Creole. Bart Jacob has argued that it is a relexified offshoot of an early Upper Guinea Portuguese Creole carried to Curaçao from Senegambia in the second half of the 17th century, when the Dutch held the slave-trading island of Gorée. A local-development theory instead proposes a Portuguese-African pidgin formed in the Caribbean, with later Dutch and Spanish influences.

In 1634 the Dutch West India Company took possession of the islands, deporting most of the remaining Arawak and Spanish population and making them a hub of the Dutch slave trade between Africa and the Caribbean. After 1654 the Jewish and Portuguese-speaking population of the islands grew substantially, as Portuguese-speaking Jews and their allies fled Northeast Brazil. The Sephardic community became the main merchants, and everyday trading was conducted in Papiamento. The language itself dates from about 1650.

About 80 per cent of the vocabulary is Iberian in origin and about 20 per cent Dutch, with some words from Native American and African languages. Many Iberian words cannot be assigned to Portuguese or Spanish, such as por fabor and señora. Words of Taíno and Arawak origin, mostly for plants and animals, include maishi, corn, and kunuku, farm; African ones include pinda, peanut, from Kongo mpinda. The grammar is typical of Atlantic creoles: time and aspect markers are used instead of tenses, there is no grammatical gender, and the plural is marked by the suffix -nan on definite nouns.

There are two main dialects, Papiamento on Aruba and Papiamentu on Curaçao and Bonaire. Curaçao and Bonaire adopted the phonetic Römer-Maduro-Jonis spelling in 1976, and Aruba approved a more etymological one in 1977.

Widespread use in official documents is first seen in the early 18th century. The oldest preserved texts are letters, the earliest of 1775. In the 19th century most materials on the islands were written in Papiamento, including Roman Catholic school books and hymnals. The Catecismo Corticu of 1837, the first printed book in the language, was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2009, and the first newspaper, Civilisadó, appeared in 1871. Papiamento became an official language of Aruba in 2003 and of the Netherlands Antilles in 2007. The anthems of Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao are in it.
papua-new-guinea: The country covers 462,840 km2 and includes a large mainland and hundreds of islands in Melanesia, north of Australia. It lies where the north-moving Indo-Australian plate meets the west-moving Pacific plate, which gives it a highly variable geography, active volcanoes and frequent earthquakes. Mountains cover at least 72% of the country, and the highest point is Mount Wilhelm, at 4,509 metres. The Torres Strait, 152 kilometres wide, separates it from Australia's Cape York Peninsula. This terrain helps explain why the population is largely rural and divided into many small communities.

Archaeological evidence indicates that modern humans first reached what became New Guinea around 42,000 to 45,000 years ago. Agriculture was developed independently in the New Guinea highlands around 7000 BCE, making it one of the few areas where people domesticated plants without outside influence. Austronesian-speaking peoples of the Lapita culture had reached the Bismarck Archipelago by about 3,300 years ago. Communities were linked by trade, and bananas and sugarcane probably passed from New Guinea to other regions along these networks, but each community otherwise functioned largely independently.

European names for the island date from the 16th century: Jorge de Menezes called it Ilhas dos Papuas in 1526, and Yñigo Ortiz de Retez named it Nueva Guinea in 1545. In 1884 the eastern half was divided between German New Guinea in the north and British New Guinea in the south. The British territory was ceded to Australia in 1902 and became the Territory of Papua. Australia occupied German New Guinea during the First World War and then ruled it as a League of Nations mandate. The two territories were united in 1949, after fierce fighting there in World War II, and the country became independent in 1975. Europeans brought together communities that had sometimes been hostile or had no relationship at all.

Papua New Guinea is a Commonwealth realm with a governor-general representing the monarch and a unicameral National Parliament of 118 seats, in a Westminster system. Its capital and largest city is Port Moresby. There are 840 known spoken languages, the most of any country, and English and Tok Pisin serve as common languages. Most people live in customary communities, and the constitution protects traditional communities and lifestyles.
papyrus: Papyrus was first manufactured in Egypt as far back as the 3rd millennium BCE, and it is known to have been used at least as early as the First Dynasty. The earliest archaeological evidence was excavated in 2012 and 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, an ancient Egyptian harbour on the Red Sea coast: the Diary of Merer, dated about 2560 to 2550 BCE, at the end of the reign of Khufu, describes the last years of the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The Egyptians also used papyrus reeds for boats, mats, rope, sandals and baskets. The Greek word biblos, from which bibliography and bible derive, referred to the inner part of the plant.

Papyrus was made from the stem of the sedge Cyperus papyrus. The outer rind was removed and the sticky inner pith cut lengthwise into strips about 40 centimetres long. The strips were laid side by side with their edges slightly overlapping, and a second layer was placed across them at right angles. While still moist, the layers were hammered into a single sheet, which was dried under pressure and polished with a rounded object. Sheets were glued together into a roll, a scroll, and texts were normally written first on the side where the fibres ran along the roll.

Pliny the Elder and Isidore of Seville described six grades sold in the Roman market. Papyrus is stable in a dry climate such as Egypt's, but humid conditions let mould destroy it, and in Europe it seems to have lasted only decades. It was cheap and easy to produce, but fragile, and it was not pliable enough to fold without cracking.

Late in its history papyrus began to be gathered into codices, which early Christian writers soon adopted. Parchment, made from animal skins, gradually overtook it in West Asia and Europe. By the beginning of the 4th century CE the most important books were being made on parchment, which was more durable in moist climates and could be written on both sides. As trade networks declined, papyrus lost its cost advantage outside Egypt. The latest certain uses in Europe are a papal decree of 1057 and an Arabic document of 1087. In Egypt it continued in use until the cheaper paper introduced from the Islamic world replaced it.

Papyri give the only surviving copy of Menander, as well as the Egyptian Book of the Dead and the Ebers, Edwin Smith, Rhind and Westcar papyri. The first modern discovery of papyrus rolls was made at Herculaneum in 1752, and the Dutch historian Caspar Reuvens began scholarly study with the Leyden papyrus, published in 1830.
paracel-islands: The archipelago includes about 130 small coral islands and reefs, most of them grouped into the northeastern Amphitrite Group or the western Crescent Group. They are spread over a maritime area of around 15,000 square kilometres, with a land area of only about 7.75 square kilometres. The highest point, an unnamed location on Rocky Island, is 14 m above sea level. The islands lie about 350 km southeast of Hainan Island, equidistant from the coastlines of China and Vietnam. The climate is tropical, with abundant rainfall and annual typhoons, and the surrounding waters are productive fishing grounds.

The Amphitrite Group was named after the French frigate Amphitrite, which observed the islands while carrying a Jesuit mission to Canton in 1698–1700. Woody Island, the largest of the Paracels at 213 hectares, lies at its centre. The islands of the Crescent Group are named after senior figures of the British East India Company, among them James Drummond, Thomas Pattle, John William Roberts and Jonathan Duncan.

The word paracel is of Portuguese origin and probably comes from the Spanish placer, used by navigators for shallow sandy seas or submerged banks. Portuguese maps of the early 16th century marked a group of flooded islands in the area, and from the mid-1500s the group was called Ilhas do Pracel. Chinese works from the Song dynasty onward described large groups of maritime features such as Qianli Changsha and Wanli Shitang, and Xisha, meaning Western Sands, became the standard Chinese name in the 20th century. The Vietnamese name Hoàng Sa, Yellow Sands, appears in documents dating back to 1483.

The People's Republic of China, Vietnam and the Republic of China on Taiwan all claim sovereignty, and each presents its own historical case. Chinese accounts date an interest to the second century BCE; Vietnamese accounts point to the planting of a flag in 1816 and ten inscribed steles installed in 1836. Between 1881 and 1883 the German navy surveyed the islands each year without seeking permission from France or China, and published the results in 1885. China has controlled the whole archipelago since the Battle of the Paracel Islands in January 1974.
parachute: The earliest recorded attempt to slow a fall with fabric is that of Armen Firman, an Andalusian who in 852, at Córdoba, jumped from a tower wearing a large cloak. It was recorded that there was enough air in the folds of the cloak to prevent great injury. The earliest evidence of a purposely designed parachute dates from the Renaissance. The manuscript of the 1470s attributed to Francesco di Giorgio Martini shows a free-hanging man clutching a crossbar frame attached to a conical canopy, with four straps running to a waist belt. The canopy looks too small to give effective resistance, but the basic concept is apparent.

In 1691 Simon de La Loubère reported that at the court of King Narai of Ayutthaya a man would jump from a high place holding two large umbrellas, landing in trees, on rooftops and sometimes in rivers. The French physicist Louis-Sébastien Lenormand read the report a century later. He made the first recorded public jump in 1783 and in 1785 coined the word, joining the Italian para, from parare, to ward off, to the French chute, a fall.

In 1911 Grant Morton made the first parachute jump from an aeroplane, a Wright Model B flown by Phil Parmalee at Venice Beach, California, holding a throw-out parachute in his arms. In the same year Gleb Kotelnikov invented the first knapsack parachute, although Hermann Lattemann and his wife Käthe Paulus had already jumped with bagged parachutes in the last decade of the 19th century. On 4 February 1912 Franz Reichelt died jumping from the Eiffel Tower while testing a wearable parachute.

The first military users were artillery observers on tethered balloons in the First World War. A waist harness pulled the lines and canopy from a bag hung on the balloon as they jumped. The Germans adopted them on a large scale for balloon crews, then the British and the French. In fixed-wing aircraft the lines often tangled in a spinning machine, and no parachutes were issued to the crews of Allied heavier-than-air aircraft.

After the war Major Edward L. Hoffman of the United States Army led an effort to combine the best features of several designs. The resulting Airplane Parachute Type-A had a soft pack worn on the back, a ripcord and a pilot chute that draws out the main canopy. Leslie Irvin tested it by jumping from an aeroplane in 1919, and it went into production. After the Second World War parachuting became a popular sport, and nylon replaced silk.
paraguay: Paraguay lies between latitudes 19° and 28°S in the central region of South America and is divided by the Río Paraguay into two regions. The eastern region has mostly grassy plains and wooded hills, while the western region, known as the Chaco and part of the Gran Chaco, has mostly low, marshy plains. The far eastern forest belt receives an average of 170 centimetres of rain a year, the western Chaco no more than 50 centimetres. Although landlocked, Paraguay reaches the Atlantic Ocean by the Paraná–Paraguay Waterway, a system of navigable channels shared by five countries.

The Guaraní had lived in eastern Paraguay for at least a millennium when the Spanish arrived. The Gran Chaco in the west was inhabited by nomads, of whom the Guaycuru peoples were most prominent, and the Paraguay River roughly divided the agricultural Guaraní from them. The Mbayá were known for their warrior traditions and were not fully pacified until the late 19th century. Juan de Salazar de Espinosa founded Asunción on 15 August 1537, and it became the centre of the Spanish colonial province of Paraguay.

In the eighteenth century Jesuit missions developed reductions to gather Guaraní populations and protect them from virtual slavery by Spanish settlers and Portuguese slave raiders, the bandeirantes. The reducciones flourished in eastern Paraguay for about 150 years, until the Spanish Crown expelled the Jesuits in 1767. Paraguay overthrew the local Spanish administration on 14 May 1811. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, nicknamed El Supremo, ruled from 1814 until his death in 1840 with very little outside contact, intending a utopian society based on Rousseau's Social Contract. The Triple Alliance War of 1864 to 1870 cost the country half its prewar population and around a quarter to a third of its territory. Paraguay then prevailed in the Chaco War with Bolivia of 1932 to 1935.

Asunción is the capital and largest city. Paraguay is a unitary presidential republic of seventeen departments and a capital district. The population was 6,109,944 at the 2022 census, and most people live in the east. Paraguayan culture is a fusion of European and Southern Guaraní traditions: more than 80% of Paraguayans speak both Spanish and Guaraní. The ruins of two eighteenth-century Jesuit missions, La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Paraguay is a founding member of Mercosur, the United Nations and the Organization of American States.
paraguayan-war: Since independence, Brazil and the Spanish-American countries of South America had been troubled by territorial disputes, because the old Tordesillas line of 1494 did not match the actual occupation of the land. Brazil and Argentina struggled for hegemony in the Río de la Plata region. Brazil recognised Paraguay's independence in 1844, when Argentina still regarded it as a breakaway province. Brazil intervened in unstable Uruguay in 1851, 1855 and again in 1864, against Atanasio Aguirre, and this last intervention led to the war. The traditional view holds that Paraguay's president Francisco Solano López used the Uruguayan War as a pretext to gain control of the Platine basin, but the causes are also attributed to border conflicts and to Brazilian and Argentine meddling in Uruguay.

Paraguay began with over 60,000 trained men, 400 cannons and a squadron of steamboats. Paraguay took the initiative by invading the Brazilian province of Mato Grosso on 14 December 1864, followed by Rio Grande do Sul and the Argentine province of Corrientes. By the end of 1865 the Triple Alliance was on the offensive, and its armies invaded Paraguay in April of the following year.

On 10 October 1866 Brazil gave unified command to the Marquess of Caxias, who in the Pikysyry campaign took the army through the swamps of the Gran Chaco to cross behind the fortified Paraguayan line, leading to the fall of Asunción. Defeated in conventional warfare, Paraguay conducted a guerrilla resistance that further destroyed its army and civilians. The Count of Eu led the Campaign of the Hills from 1869, including the battles of Piribebuy and Acosta Ñu, where more than 5,000 Paraguayans died. López was killed by Brazilian forces at Cerro Corá on 1 March 1870.

Casualty figures are hotly disputed. Estimates of the share of its population that Paraguay lost range from 7 percent to 69 percent, and disease, hunger and exhaustion caused most of the deaths. Among the Brazilians, disease killed more than wounds did, and some historians think cholera was a leading cause. Paraguay lost about 140,000 square kilometres of disputed territory to Brazil and Argentina and was occupied until 1876, and its large war debt was forgiven in 1943 by Getúlio Vargas.

The war brought the Brazilian Empire to its peak of influence, but its public debt and the social crisis that followed are regarded as crucial factors in the fall of the Empire and the proclamation of the First Brazilian Republic.
paraiba: Paraíba is a state in the Brazilian Northeast, bordered by Rio Grande do Norte to the north, Ceará to the west, Pernambuco to the south and the Atlantic Ocean to the east. Its coast reaches Ponta do Seixas, the easternmost point of the mainland Americas, and the interior rises to the Borborema Plateau, where Pico do Jabre, at 1,208 metres, is the state's highest peak. Most of its territory has a hot semi-arid climate. It takes its name from the Paraíba river, and its area is about 56,467 square kilometres.

Before Europeans came, the Potiguara, part of the Tupi group, lived between the coast and the Borborema Plateau along the Paraíba do Norte river, and the Kiriri and Ariús lived further west. Colonisation began in 1534, when King John III of Portugal divided Brazil into fifteen captaincies. Most of what is now Paraíba fell under the Captaincy of Itamaracá, which was troubled by French piracy, especially of wood, animal skins and amber. Its sugar made the captaincy one of the most successful regions of Portuguese America.

The Dutch, who had seized Salvador in 1624, first appeared on Paraíban soil on 20 June 1625, in the Bay of Traição. Admiral Boudewijn Hendricksz allied with the Potiguara, but troops from Paraíba, Pernambuco and Rio Grande and from indigenous peoples defeated the Dutch on 1 August, at a cost to the Potiguara of 600 to a thousand dead. From 1670 colonists, led by bandeirantes such as Domingos Jorge Velho, pushed into the interior, with the enslavement and massacre of indigenous peoples. The captaincy was annexed to Pernambuco in 1756 and restored in 1799. Paraíba joined the Pernambuco Revolution of 1817, which sought Brazilian independence and spread through the Northeast, and it became a federal state in November 1889 when the republic was proclaimed.

João Pessoa is the coastal capital, and Campina Grande, in the interior, is among the fifteen largest municipalities of the Northeast. The 2022 census counted 3,974,687 people, and Portuguese is the language of the state. The economy has long drawn on sugarcane, cattle, shoes and leather goods, and tourism. A copper-bearing tourmaline of vivid blue-green colour was found in the Batalha mine in 1987. The Festa Junina, the Saint John festival brought by the Portuguese, is a major celebration.
paramaribo: Paramaribo lies on the banks of the Suriname River, about 15 kilometres inland from the Atlantic Ocean, in the Paramaribo District. The city is named for the Paramaribo people who lived at the mouth of the river, and the name is from the Tupi-Guarani para, large river, and maribo, inhabitants. The name is probably a corruption of the name of a native village, spelled Parmurbo in the earliest Dutch sources. It has a tropical rainforest climate with no true dry season.

The first Dutch settlement at the site was a trading post established in 1613 by Nicolaes Baliestel and Dirck Claeszoon van Sanen. English and French traders also tried to settle in Suriname, including a French post founded in 1644 near the present city. All these early settlements were abandoned before English settlers, sent by the governor of Barbados, Lord Francis Willoughby, arrived in 1650. They founded a town on the site, protected by Fort Willoughby, and in 1662 King Charles II granted Willoughby the settlement and its surrounding lands. Around 1665 the village of Paramaribo was expanded and quickly outranked the earlier settlement of Torarica.

In 1667, during the Second Anglo-Dutch War, a squadron under Abraham Crijnssen conquered Paramaribo, and the Treaty of Breda in 1667 confirmed it as the leading town of the Dutch colony of Suriname. The fort was renamed Fort Zeelandia after the Dutch province that had financed the fleet. The population has always been diverse. Many of the first British settlers were Jews, and the Neveh Shalom Synagogue, one of the oldest synagogues in the Americas, stands in the city. The population grew greatly after 1873, when formerly enslaved people, freed in 1863, were allowed to stop working for their former masters and to leave the sugar plantations.

Fires repeatedly devastated the old town, notably in January 1821, when over 400 buildings were destroyed, and in September 1832, when nearly 50 were lost. The enslaved men Kodjo, Mentor and Present were found guilty of arson and burnt alive. Paramaribo has remained the capital of Suriname through its colonial days and the independence of 1975.

Paramaribo is the capital and largest city of Suriname and holds almost half of the country's population. The Dutch colonial town of the 17th and 18th centuries along the left bank of the river became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002, and its original architecture and street plan have largely remained intact. Landmarks include Fort Zeelandia, the Presidential Palace, the Roman Catholic cathedral of St Peter and St Paul, the Suriname Mosque and the Kwakoe memorial to the abolition of slavery. The city is the business and financial centre of the country.
parana-entre-rios: Paraná stands on the eastern shore of the Paraná River, opposite the city of Santa Fe, capital of the neighbouring Santa Fe Province. Its original name was Bajada, meaning landing. The climate is Pampean, classed as humid subtropical, with an average annual temperature of 18 °C. Winters have mild days and very cold nights, with occasional frosts, while summers are hot and bring most of the rain, about 1,069 millimetres in a year. The city and the whole province lie in an area of high tornado risk, particularly in spring and summer.

In 1730 inhabitants of Santa Fe settled on the other shore of the river and called the place Baxada del Paraná. The first settlers had been forced out of Santa Fe by raiding Payaguá and Muños peoples. They settled in what is now the Square of the first of May, where they built a fort, other defences and a series of huts. Their numbers eventually became stable enough for them to move from defence to offence, and they almost wiped out both peoples. In the middle of the 19th century the city served for some years as the capital of the Argentine Confederation, until 1861.

Paraná is the seat of the provincial government of Entre Ríos and an important river port for the transshipment of cereals, cattle, fish and lumber from the surrounding region. Its industries include the manufacture of cement, furniture and ceramics. The city centre combines colonial churches with buildings in European styles such as the 3 de Febrero Theatre and the Government House, and the Cathedral blends several architectural styles. The Hernandarias Subfluvial Tunnel, inaugurated in 1969, links the city to Santa Fe beneath the river. Its main sports clubs include the basketball team Atlético Echagüe and the football clubs Patronato and Atlético Paraná.
parana-river: The Paraná takes its name from Guarani words meaning river or sea, and eastern South America has an immense number of river names containing para- or parana-. The river forms at the confluence of the Paranaíba and Rio Grande in southern Brazil and runs southwest for about 619 kilometres to the city of Saltos del Guaira in Paraguay. For roughly the next 200 kilometres it forms the boundary between Paraguay and Brazil, up to the confluence with the Iguazu River, and after that it is the border between Paraguay and Argentina.

It turns west for some 820 kilometres and meets the Paraguay River, its largest tributary, then runs south for about 820 kilometres through Argentina and turns east near Rosario. Below the city of Diamante it splits into several arms and forms the Paraná Delta. Its final stretch, under 500 kilometres, ends at the Uruguay River, where the two form the Río de la Plata.

The first European to go up the Paraná was the Venetian explorer Sebastian Cabot, who did so in 1526 while working for Spain. Between 1973 and 1984 the Itaipu Dam was built, creating a massive, shallow reservoir. It flooded the Guaíra Falls, the Sete Quedas, a series of seven cascades once said to rival the Iguazu Falls. A second major hydroelectric project, the Yacyretá Dam, was built jointly by Paraguay and Argentina. The dams blocked ship navigation to cities further upstream, and the rising river flooded the lower parts of Encarnación.

Navigation became a matter of dispute between Paraguay and Argentina. Argentina wished to build a bridge across the river, while Paraguay would facilitate it only if the navigation issue was settled. A bilateral agreement on a bridge was signed in October 1964, and an agreement endorsing free navigation, requiring each nation to treat the other's vessels as its own, was signed in January 1973. Water-level records exist from 1904, because the river is used by oceangoing ships.

The Paraná and its tributaries drain much of south-central South America, including nearly all of Paraguay, much of southern Brazil, northern Argentina and south-eastern Bolivia. The basin contains large cities including São Paulo, Buenos Aires, Rosario, Asunción and Brasília. Much of the river is navigable as part of the Paraná–Paraguay and Tietê–Paraná waterways, linking inland cities in Argentina and Paraguay with the ocean. Fishing is a livelihood along its banks, and the delta is a well-known place for watching birds.
pargali-ibrahim-pasha: Little is known of Ibrahim's early years. He was born at Parga, and his ethnic origin is uncertain: older Ottoman sources call him a Frenk, later ones the son of an Italian fisherman from Genoa, and others have called him Greek, Albanian or Croatian. Evliya Çelebi stated that his family came from Razgrad. He was taken to Manisa through the devşirme system and entered the service of Prince Suleiman, remaining at his side until his death. He took part in the Belgrade campaign of 1521 and the Rhodes campaign of 1522, and rose to be chief of the imperial chamber.

On 27 June 1523 Ibrahim was appointed Grand Vizier in place of Piri Mehmed Pasha, directly from the chief of the imperial chamber, in a manner unprecedented in Ottoman law and tradition. The 17th-century writer Koçi Bey criticised the appointment as a breach of established rule. In May 1524 he married at a wedding lasting two weeks, though the identity of his wife is debated, and he was then sent to Egypt to restore order after the rebellion of Hain Ahmed Pasha.

In 1526 he commanded the campaign against Hungary that ended in victory at Mohács, and in March 1527 he was granted the rank of serasker. The number of tughs symbolising imperial power was raised from four to seven, and he was allowed to carry six.

He took part in the First Siege of Vienna in 1529 and conducted the negotiations for the Treaty of Constantinople of 1533 with Austria. From 1526 Suleiman left foreign policy largely to him, and he received ambassadors, with the help of Alvise Gritti, son of Andrea Gritti, Duke of Venice. In the Irakeyn campaign against the Safavids he captured Tabriz in August 1534. He spoke Turkish, Persian, Greek and Italian, played the violin and patronised poets. In his thirteen years as vizier he commissioned mosques, madrasas, baths and fountains, among them mosques in Constantinople, Mecca, Thessaloniki, Razgrad and Kavala.

Ibrahim had been invited to the palace for iftar, and in the night of 14 and 15 March 1536 four deaf-mute executioners strangled him in his chamber on the sultan's orders. The reason is not certain. Suggested factors include his pursuit of power and wealth, his support for Prince Mustafa, which allegedly led Hürrem Sultan to turn Suleiman against him, his harsh conduct in the Iraq campaign and his extravagance. Ottoman historians held that the empire declined after his death, and the poet Latîfî wrote that people understood his worth only once he was gone. Modern historians regard him as one of the most important Ottoman grand viziers.
paris: Paris lies in northern central France, in a north-bending arc of the river Seine, whose crest includes two islands, the Île Saint-Louis and the larger Île de la Cité, which form the oldest part of the city. The Seine's mouth on the English Channel is about 375 kilometres downstream. The city is relatively flat, with its lowest point 35 metres above sea level, and the highest of its hills, Montmartre, rises to 130 metres. Excluding the outlying parks, it covers an oval of about 87 square kilometres, enclosed by the 35-kilometre ring road, the Boulevard Périphérique, and since an annexation in 1860 it has had 20 arrondissements.

The Parisii, a Gallic tribe, inhabited the Paris area from around the middle of the 3rd century BCE. A major north–south trade route crossed the Seine on the Île de la Cité, which gradually became an important trading centre, and the Parisii traded with river towns as far away as the Iberian Peninsula and minted their own coins.

Julius Caesar conquered the Paris Basin for the Roman Republic in 52 BCE, and the Roman town of Lutetia grew on the Left Bank into a prosperous city with a forum, baths, temples, theatres and an amphitheatre. By the end of the Western Roman Empire it was known as Parisius. According to legend, Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, introduced Christianity in the middle of the 3rd century CE and was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre.

For almost all of its history, except for a few brief periods, Paris was governed directly by representatives of the king, emperor or president of France. In the 17th century the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture was established in 1648, and urbanism laws have been strictly controlled since the early 17th century. Between 1853 and 1870 Napoleon III and his Prefect of the Seine, Baron Haussmann, rebuilt the city centre, creating wide boulevards, standard facades of cream-grey Paris stone and major parks around the centre.

Paris is the capital and largest city of France, with a city population of 2.04 million and a metropolitan population of 13.3 million. The National Assembly granted it municipal autonomy in 1974, and Jacques Chirac became its first elected mayor in March 1977. Its population peaked at 2.9 million in 1921. In the 19th and early 20th centuries artists including Manet, Monet and Renoir worked there, and Impressionism, Cubism and Art Deco all evolved in the city. It hosts UNESCO, whose headquarters have been there since November 1958, and the OECD, and it has hosted the Summer Olympics in 1900, 1924 and 2024.
paris-commune: On 2 September 1870 France was defeated at the Battle of Sedan and Emperor Napoleon III was captured. Republican deputies proclaimed a Republic and formed a Government of National Defence, and the German army had surrounded Paris by 20 September. Paris workers had long demanded that the city have its own elected council, and during the siege demonstrations demanded a Commune.

After Paris faced famine and the armies were defeated, national elections on 8 February 1871 returned about 400 deputies favouring a constitutional monarchy. The National Guard in Paris had not been disarmed and had on paper 260 battalions. On 18 March two brigades climbed Montmartre to seize its 170 cannons, which had been paid for by public subscription, but National Guard members gathered there, and the Guard seized control of the city.

The Commune held its first meeting on 28 March and voted among other things to abolish the death penalty and military conscription. On 2 April it declared the separation of church and state, seized the property of religious congregations and ordered Catholic schools to become secular. The Vendôme Column honouring Napoleon I was pulled down on 16 May.

Adolphe Thiers assembled a new army at Versailles under Patrice de MacMahon, and fighting began on the outskirts of Paris in late March. Both sides shot prisoners, and on 5 April the Commune passed a Decree on Hostages. On 21 May fifty thousand soldiers entered the city through an unguarded section of the wall. Fighting went on street by street through the semaine sanglante, and the last Communards were shot at Père Lachaise cemetery on 27 May.

The army officially recorded 43,522 prisoners, and the Commune had executed the Archbishop of Paris, Georges Darboy, and about one hundred hostages in its final days. The Third Republic tried 15,895 prisoners and found 13,500 guilty. Ninety-five were sentenced to death, 251 to forced labour and 1,169 to deportation, usually to New Caledonia. All surviving prisoners and exiles were pardoned in 1880. One unconfirmed estimate from 1876 put the toll of Communards at 20,000.

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels drew lessons from the Commune, and Engels called it the dictatorship of the proletariat. Anarchists such as Mikhail Bakunin supported it as a rebellion against the state. The wall at Père Lachaise where prisoners were shot is called the Communards' Wall and is the site of annual commemorations.
paris-peace-conference-1919-1920: In 1917 US president Woodrow Wilson commissioned about 150 academics to research the topics likely to arise in peace talks and to develop principles for the negotiations. Their work was summarised in the Fourteen Points, which became the basis of the terms of the German surrender and of the Armistice of 11 November 1918. The conference brought together diplomats from 32 countries and nationalities. Germany, Austria-Hungary, Turkey and Bulgaria were given no voice in the deliberations, and Russia was represented, though not by its actual government.

The conference formally opened on 18 January 1919 at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris, a date chosen because it was the anniversary of the proclamation of William I as German Emperor in 1871. Delegates were assigned to 52 commissions, which held 1,646 sessions on topics ranging from prisoners of war to undersea cables. The five great powers, France, Britain, Italy, Japan and the United States, controlled it, and the Big Four leaders, Georges Clemenceau, David Lloyd George, Wilson and Vittorio Emanuele Orlando, met informally 145 times and agreed all major decisions before they were ratified.

Clemenceau's chief aim was to weaken Germany militarily, strategically and economically. Italy sought the territories promised in the secret Treaty of London. Japan proposed a racial equality clause for the League's Covenant on 13 February and claimed Germany's concessions in Shantung. The Western powers transferred those concessions to Japan, which sparked student protests in China on 4 May, later known as the May Fourth Movement; the Chinese delegation was the only one that did not sign the Treaty of Versailles.

The main result was the Treaty of Versailles with Germany, which had 15 chapters and 440 clauses. Article 231 of the treaty placed responsibility for the war on "the aggression of Germany and her allies", a provision that humiliated German leaders and citizens, and Germany stopped paying reparations after 1931, having delivered only a small portion. German and Ottoman overseas possessions passed as mandates chiefly to Britain and France, and new boundaries were drawn, sometimes after plebiscites.
