Delegations from Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania won recognition of their independence, while Ukraine, Ireland, Korea and Vietnam were effectively ignored.

The senior statesmen stopped working personally on the conference in June 1919, but historian Michael Neiberg notes that the formal peace process did not end until the Treaty of Lausanne of July 1923. The settlement is considered one of the great watersheds of 20th-century geopolitics, and its exclusion of the defeated powers later gave rise to political resentments that lasted decades.
parliament-of-finland: The Parliament of Finland was preceded by the Diet of Finland, which had succeeded the Riksdag of the Estates in 1809 and was tetracameral. The Diet of Porvoo of 1809 met in several buildings in Porvoo, assembled only once and did not reconvene until 1863. When the unicameral Parliament was established by the Parliament Act in 1906, Finland was an autonomous grand duchy under the Russian tsar, who ruled as Grand Duke and not as an absolute monarch. Universal suffrage and eligibility were introduced: women could vote and run for office as equals, as could landless people, with no minority excluded. The first election was held in 1907, and the first Parliament had 19 female representatives, an unprecedented number, which grew to 21 by 1913.

The first years were difficult. Between 1908 and 1916 the power of the Parliament was almost completely neutralised by Tsar Nicholas II and the so-called sabre senate, a bureaucratic government formed by Imperial Russian Army officers during the second period of Russification. The Parliament was dissolved and new elections held almost every year. In the 1916 election the Social Democrats won a majority, the only time one party has held a parliamentary majority, and coalition governments have therefore been the rule. Until the Constitution Act of 1919 the body was known in Swedish as lantdagen, the old term for the Diet.

The Parliament has been dissolved before the end of its term fourteen times; the most recent was on 4 June 1975. It first met in a volunteer fire brigade house at Keskuskatu 7, and in 1911 moved to the Heimola House, designed by Onni Tarjanne. Both buildings were later demolished. The Parliament House now stands in central Helsinki.

The Parliament has 200 members, 199 elected every four years from 13 multi-member districts by the proportional D'Hondt method, plus one member from Åland. It passes legislation, decides the state budget, approves international treaties and supervises the government, which it can bring down. It may override presidential vetoes, and changes to the constitution need approval by two successive parliaments with an election between them. Most members work in parliamentary groups that correspond to political parties.

Its 17 committees include the Grand Committee, which deals with European Union matters, and the Constitutional Law Committee, which oversees constitutional questions because Finland has no constitutional court. The Committee for the Future assesses long-term developments. Each year the Parliament elects a speaker and two deputy speakers on the first day of the session, and members enjoy parliamentary immunity.
parmenides: Parmenides was born in the Greek colony of Elea in southern Italy to a wealthy and aristocratic family. Diogenes Laërtius gives his father's name as Pires. The same writer passes on two divergent accounts of his teacher. One, following Sotion, says he first studied with Xenophanes but did not follow him, and later preferred the Pythagorean Aminias. Another, following Theophrastus, makes him a disciple of Anaximander.

The date of his birth is not known. Apollodorus, as transmitted by Diogenes Laërtius, puts his prime in the years 504 to 500 BCE, which would place his birth about 40 years earlier. Plato's dialogue Parmenides shows him visiting Athens at about the age of 65, when Socrates was a young man, which would suggest a birth around 515 BCE. Most modern classicists regard that visit and meeting as fiction, and some scholars prefer other dates. He is generally thought to have been in his prime around 475 BCE.

Plutarch, Strabo and Diogenes Laërtius, following Speusippus, agree that Parmenides took part in the government of his city, organising it and giving it an admirable code of laws. In 1969 the plinth of a statue of the 1st century CE was excavated at Velia, the later Elea. It names Parmenides, son of Pires, and calls him a physicist, the word then used for philosophers who studied nature. Its third word, ouliadēs, may mean simply a native of Elea or a member of a medical school devoted to Apollo Ulius, which would make him a physician as well as a legislator. Other specialists hold that the plinth shows only his social importance in the city.

The only known work is a poem in dactylic hexameter, later titled On Nature. About 160 verses survive from an original total probably near 800, largely through long excerpts made by Sextus Empiricus and Simplicius of Cilicia. It had three parts: a proem with an allegorical narrative, the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion, of which only small fragments and prose paraphrases remain.

In the Way of Truth, a goddess teaches that what is cannot have come from what is not, since non-Being cannot be thought or spoken of. Being is therefore eternal, indivisible, unchanging and without time, and it cannot move, because that would require space it does not already occupy. The Way of Opinion describes the world of appearances, built on the opposites of light and dark, where the senses lead mortals into false conceptions. He is credited with first defining ontology as a discipline separate from theology.

Parmenides founded the Eleatic school, continued by Zeno of Elea and Melissus of Samos. Zeno devised arguments to defend his views against critics, and Plato counted him among his main influences, alongside Socrates and the Pythagoreans.
parmigianino: Parmigianino, meaning the little one from Parma, was the eighth child of Filippo Mazzola and Donatella Abbati. His father died of the plague two years after his birth, and the children were raised by their uncles Michele and Pier Ilario, who according to Vasari were modestly talented artists. He completed a chapel decoration in San Giovanni Evangelista begun by his uncle and had finished the Bardi Altarpiece by the age of eighteen. In 1521 he was sent to Viadana to escape the wars between the French, Imperial and papal armies. There he painted two tempera panels and met Correggio, who was at work on the fresco decoration of the cupola.

In 1524 he travelled to Rome with five small paintings, among them the Circumcision of Jesus and his Self-portrait in a Convex Mirror, hoping for the patronage of Pope Clement VII. Vasari records that he was hailed there as a Raphael reborn. In January 1526 he agreed to paint the Vision of Saint Jerome for the church of San Salvatore in Lauro, but the Sack of Rome in 1527 drove him and many other artists out of the city. He lived in Bologna for nearly three years and was back in Parma by 1530.

In 1531 he was commissioned to paint two altarpieces for the unfinished church of Santa Maria della Steccata. The work was still unfinished in 1535. The Madonna with the Long Neck, which he began in 1534, was meant for the chapel of the family of Elena Baiardi. Parmigianino was a pioneer of Italian etching and designed chiaroscuro woodcuts that other artists cut. He made his etchings and chiaroscuro prints between 1527 and 1530 in Bologna, and although his output was small, it had a considerable influence on Italian printmaking. He also led a trend towards three-quarter and full-length portraits, previously mostly reserved for royalty.

Around this time he became a devotee of alchemy. Scholars now think his scientific interests may have come from a search for a new medium for his etchings. He did little work in the church, and the confraternity banned him from continuing. He was imprisoned for two months for breach of contract and was replaced by Giulio Romano, who also withdrew.

He died of a fever in Casalmaggiore on 24 August 1540, aged 37, and was buried in the church of the Servite Friars. His cousin Girolamo Bedoli and Bedoli's son Alessandro Mazzola were among those he influenced. His drawings are outstanding, and his portable works are now in major museums in Italy and elsewhere.
parsis: The Parsis are an ethnoreligious community of the Indian subcontinent. According to the Qissa-i Sanjan, a Parsi epic of the 16th century and the only account of their early years, they descend from Zoroastrian Persians who fled persecution after the Arab conquest of Iran. It was composed at least six centuries after their tentative date of arrival and places the first group in Khorasan. The earliest migrants settled among the Hindus of present-day Gujarat after Jadi Rana, the Rajput king of Sanjan, gave them refuge. A Parsi priest answered his fear that the kingdom was full by adding sugar to a vessel of milk, to show that they would blend in and enrich the local culture.

The Parsis are the older of the subcontinent's two Zoroastrian communities. The other, the Irani community, descends from migrants of Qajar Iran. Their mother tongue is Gujarati or Marathi, and the word Parsi means Persian. The migration from the Sasanian lands continued between the 7th and 10th centuries.

The Qissa says little about the centuries after the founding of Sanjan beyond the establishment of the Fire of Victory, an Atash Bahram, at Sanjan and its later move to Navsari. Until the 17th century most Parsis lived in farming communities in Gujarat. After the commercial treaty between the Mughal emperor Jahangir and James I of England, the East India Company gained the right to build factories in Surat, and many Parsis moved to the English settlements to take the new jobs. When the company transferred its headquarters from Surat to Bombay in 1687, the Parsis followed, and they soon held posts of trust in government and public works.

In the 1860s and 1870s the linguist Martin Haug interpreted Zoroastrian scripture in Christian terms, at a time when English and American missionaries were criticising the Parsis for polytheism. The community, which had no theologians of its own, largely accepted his reading.

Who counts as a Parsi is contested. It is generally accepted that a Parsi is descended from the original Persian refugees and has been admitted to the faith through the navjote ceremony, which is held when a child can recite the required prayers, ideally before puberty. The 2011 census of India counted 57,264 Parsis, and the community lives mostly in cities, with its highest density in Greater Mumbai.

Traditionally the dead are taken to a Tower of Silence, because earth, fire and water are sacred and are not to be defiled by the dead. The Parsis became highly influential in trade, industry, culture and philanthropy, and Jamsetji Tata and Dadabhai Naoroji are among their best-known members.
parthenon: The first attempt to build a sanctuary for Athena Parthenos on the site began shortly after the Battle of Marathon. The Older Parthenon was still under construction when the Persians razed the Acropolis in 480 BCE. In the mid-5th century BCE, when the Acropolis had become the seat of the Delian League, Pericles started a building project that produced the Parthenon, the Propylaia, the Erechtheion and the Temple of Athena Nike. The Parthenon was built in thanksgiving for the victory in the Greco-Persian Wars, and like most Greek temples it also served as a treasury. Phidias had general supervision and charge of the sculpture, and the architects Ictinos and Callicrates began work in 447 BCE.

The Parthenon is an octastyle peripteral Doric temple, with eight columns at each end where six was usual and seventeen along the sides, and an Ionic two-chambered cella. Its lines deviate slightly from strict straightness: the stylobate bulges upward at the centre by 10.3 centimetres over 70 metres, and the columns swell and incline inward. The cella housed the gold and ivory statue of Athena Parthenos by Phidias, dedicated in 439 or 438 BCE and now lost. The frieze of the entablature had 92 metopes showing the battles of gods and Giants, of Athenians and Amazons, and of Lapiths and Centaurs. An Ionic frieze around the cella, carved about 443 to 438 BCE, is thought to show the Panathenaic procession.

A fire shortly after the middle of the 3rd century CE destroyed the roof and much of the interior. The building later became a church of the Virgin Mary, and after the Ottoman conquest a mosque with a minaret and mihrab. Cyriacus of Ancona in 1436 was the first person since antiquity to describe it as a temple of Athena. On 26 September 1687, during the Morean War, a Venetian mortar round blew up the gunpowder magazine the Ottomans kept inside, blowing out the central part of the building. From 1800 to 1803 the 7th Earl of Elgin removed many sculptures, now in the British Museum. Greece formally asked for their return in 1983. A conservation effort began in 1975.
parthia: Parthia lay in north-eastern Iran, with part in southern Turkmenistan. The Kopet Dag range bordered it on the north and the Dasht-e Kavir desert on the south; Media lay to the west, Hyrcania to the north-west, Margiana to the north-east and Aria to the east. Under the Arsacids it was united with Hyrcania as one administrative unit. By the Sasanian period the name had shifted towards the central Iranian plateau, and Islamic authors placed it in central and western Iran.

The Parthians spoke Parthian, a north-western Iranian language, and wrote little. They had a lively oral tradition of minstrel-poets, whose word gosan survives in Armenian as gusan. Written Parthian is known mainly from nearly three thousand ostraca found at Nisa. Society was mostly rural, dominated by large landholders with serfs and slaves. Nisa, west of present-day Ashgabat, was one of the earliest Arsacid capitals and was renamed Mithradatkirt under Mithridates I.

Before the Achaemenids the region seems to have been subject to the Medes. It appears as a satrapy in the Behistun inscription of Darius I, about 520 BCE, and Parthia was among the first provinces to accept Cyrus the Great. A revolt against Darius, put down by the governor Hystaspes, occurred around 522–521 BCE. Its governor Phrataphernes commanded a Parthian unit at Gaugamela in 331 BCE and surrendered to Alexander the Great, who reappointed him.

Under the Seleucids, the governor Andragoras declared independence after the death of Antiochus II. The Parni, an eastern Iranian people led by Arsaces and his brother Tiridates, then invaded, seized the rest of Parthia and killed Andragoras. In 209 BCE Antiochus III forced Arsaces II to accept vassal status, and the Arsacids asserted independence again from Phraates I.

From Parthia the Arsacids extended their rule over most of Greater Iran, but their power rested on the Parthian noble families, who from about 105 BCE often opposed the monarch. Wars with Rome, nomad incursions and noble infighting weakened the dynasty, and Ardashir I defeated Artabanus IV in April 224. Parthia was probably the first region he conquered.
parthian-empire: The Arsacid dynasty takes its name from its founder, Arsaces I, a chieftain of the Parni, a nomadic Iranian tribe within the confederation of the Dahae. The Parni most likely spoke an eastern Iranian language. They conquered Parthia, a north-eastern province of Iran then held by Andragoras, who was in revolt against the Seleucid Empire, and afterwards adopted Parthian as the court language. Some scholars argue instead that Arsaces was a native Parthian rather than one of the invading Parni. Mithridates I, who reigned from about 171 to 132 BCE, greatly expanded the realm by taking Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids.

At its height the empire stretched from the northern Euphrates, in what is now central-eastern Turkey, to present-day Afghanistan and western Pakistan. Its seat of government moved from Nisa to Ctesiphon on the Tigris. Rome and Parthia competed to place their own kings in Armenia. The Parthians destroyed the army of Marcus Licinius Crassus at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE, and in 40–39 BCE took the whole Levant except Tyre before Mark Antony led a Roman counterattack. Under Phraates IV, in 20 BCE, the Parthians returned the legionary standards lost at Carrhae, which Augustus presented as a political victory. Later Roman emperors invaded Mesopotamia and took Seleucia and Ctesiphon.

Civil wars between rival claimants proved more dangerous than foreign invasion. In 224 CE Ardashir I, ruler of Istakhr in Persis, revolted and killed the last Arsacid king, Artabanus IV, and founded the Sasanian Empire. The Arsacid line continued through the royal houses of Armenia, Iberia and Caucasian Albania.

Parthian government was more decentralised than the Achaemenid. The ruler was titled King of Kings and accepted many local kings as vassals, among them those of Armenia, Atropatene, Adiabene, Hatra, Elymais and Persis, who minted their own coins. There was no standing army, though troops could be raised quickly, and the king kept a small armed guard. The standard currency was the silver drachma, minted at Hecatompylos, Seleucia and Ecbatana.

The empire was culturally mixed. The Arsacids at first styled themselves philhellenes, friends of the Greeks, and Greek remained an official language while Aramaic served as the common tongue; an Iranian cultural revival followed, and Vologases I was the first to put the Parthian script on his coins. Most Parthians were polytheistic, and Greek and Iranian gods were often identified with each other. Few native sources survive, so much of Parthian history is known from Greek, Roman and Chinese writers.
partition-of-india: In 1905 the Viceroy, Lord Curzon, split the Bengal Presidency into the Muslim-majority province of Eastern Bengal and Assam and the Hindu-majority province of Bengal, which transformed nationalist politics. When World War II began in 1939, Lord Linlithgow declared war on India's behalf without consulting Indian leaders, and the Congress provincial ministries resigned in protest. The Muslim League held Deliverance Day celebrations and supported Britain.

At a press conference on 3 June 1947 Lord Mountbatten announced 14 August 1947 as the date of independence and set out the Mountbatten Plan. The legislative assemblies of Punjab and Bengal would meet by religious group and vote on partition, Sind and Baluchistan would decide for themselves, the North-West Frontier Province and the Sylhet district of Assam would hold referendums, and a boundary commission would be set up. The separate independence of Bengal was ruled out.

The Indian Independence Act 1947 ended the British Raj, and the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan came into legal existence at midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947. Bengal and the Punjab were divided according to district-wide Muslim or non-Muslim majorities, and the army, navy, civil service, railways and treasury were shared. The princely states were released from their obligations to Britain and left their rulers to accede to India or Pakistan or to stay independent; the rulers of Hyderabad and of Jammu and Kashmir, among others, chose independence.

The boundary was revealed only on 17 August, two days after independence. The commission had taken longer than the partition itself. Mountbatten was accused of rushing the process and is alleged to have influenced the Radcliffe Line in India's favour. Murshidabad and Malda, though Muslim-majority, went to India, and Hindu-majority Khulna to Pakistan.

No one had expected population transfers: minorities were supposed to stay where they were, except in Punjab, where a transfer was organised because of communal violence. The new governments were unequipped for a two-way migration of such magnitude, and massive violence occurred on both sides of the border. Total migration across Punjab is estimated at 12 million, about 6.5 million Muslims into West Punjab and 4.7 million Hindus and Sikhs into East Punjab, and some describe the violence there as a retributive genocide. Sindh saw no mass violence.

On 13 January 1948 Mahatma Gandhi began a fast to stop the violence, and by 18 January, when he ended it, religious leaders had pledged harmony; the fast is credited with ending communal violence. Estimates of the dead remain disputed. East Bengal became East Pakistan in 1955 and Bangladesh after the war of 1971. The violence created an atmosphere of hostility and suspicion between India and Pakistan.
partitions-of-poland: By the mid-18th century the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was in disorder. The liberum veto, developed in the reign of Władysław IV, let a single deputy strike down an act, and foreign diplomats bribed nobles to use it. In 1730 Prussia, Austria and Russia agreed in secret to keep the commonwealth's laws unchanged. At the Repnin Sejm of 1767 Catherine II's ambassador forced a constitution on the commonwealth that guaranteed the liberum veto and undid earlier reforms. The resentment this caused led to the War of the Confederation of Bar of 1768 to 1772, in which poorly commanded Polish forces were defeated by the regular Russian army.

The First Partition was agreed in Vienna in February 1772, and the occupation manifesto was issued on 5 August 1772. The commonwealth lost about 30 per cent of its territory and half its population, about four million people. Prussia took most of Royal Prussia, Ermland and the Netze District, Austria received Galicia with the salt mines of Bochnia and Wieliczka, and Russia took lands east of the Dvina and Dnieper including Vitebsk, Polotsk and Mstislavl. The so-called Partition Sejm approved the cession on 18 September 1773 under Russian military threat.

The Constitution of 3 May 1791 enfranchised the bourgeoisie and separated the branches of government. Russia invaded in 1792, and Prussia agreed with Russia to take more land. At the Grodno Sejm, in the presence of Russian forces, deputies accepted the Second Partition, signed on 23 January 1793, which left only one third of the 1772 population in Poland. The Kościuszko Uprising of 1794 failed, and on 24 October 1795 the three powers divided what remained. Stanisław August Poniatowski abdicated at Grodno on 25 November 1795.

The commonwealth was eliminated for 123 years. By the Third Partition Russia held 45 per cent of the commonwealth's population, Austria 32 per cent and Prussia 23 per cent. Napoleon set up the Duchy of Warsaw in 1807, and after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Russia created the Congress Kingdom of Poland. Under Russian rule Poles suffered confiscation of property, deportation and the closure of their universities after the uprising of 1831. In the Austrian sector, Galicia, Poles had representation in parliament and their own universities. Polish poets and politicians went into emigration, and Polish legions fought alongside Napoleon. The Treaty of Versailles and the end of the First World War allowed full independence to be restored in 1918.
party-of-labour-of-albania: In the 1920s Albania was the only Balkan country without a communist party. The first Albanian communists were followers of the clergyman and politician Fan S. Noli, who reached Moscow, formed the National Revolutionary Committee and joined the Comintern. A first Albanian Communist Party was formed in the Soviet Union in August 1928, but no unified organisation existed in Albania until 1941. Following the German attack on the Soviet Union in June 1941, Josip Broz Tito, following Comintern directives, sent two Yugoslav delegates, Miladin Popović and Dušan Mugoša, who helped unite the Albanian communist groups. The party was formed on 8 November 1941 by a delegation from Shkodër, with Enver Hoxha of the Korça branch as its leader.

The party dominated the National Liberation Movement formed in 1942, which drove out the German occupiers on 29 November 1944. From then Albania was a communist state without a period of coalition government. In the elections of 2 December 1945 voters were offered a single list from the Democratic Front, organised by the party, which received 93.7 per cent of the vote. The party was renamed Party of Labour of Albania in 1948, after Joseph Stalin suggested in 1947 that the name should reflect the peasant majority.

Relations with the Soviet Union were close until 1953; in 1961 Hoxha broke with Moscow over Nikita Khrushchev, purged pro-Moscow members such as Liri Belishova and Koço Tashko, and aligned with Mao Zedong's China. Albania left the Warsaw Pact in 1968, and in 1978 Hoxha declared that it would find its own road to socialism.

Hoxha led the party until his death in 1985, and his successor, Ramiz Alia, began gradual reforms. On 11 December 1990 Alia announced that the party had abandoned its monopoly of power. It won the elections of 1991, the first contested ones in decades, and on 13 June 1991 dissolved and refounded itself as the Socialist Party of Albania.

Its ideology was Hoxhaism, an anti-revisionist variant of Marxism–Leninism, and its organisation followed democratic centralism. The 1976 constitution named it the leading political force of state and society. The Party Congress met every five years and elected the Central Committee, which in turn elected a Politburo and a Secretariat. Its daily paper was Zëri i Popullit and its monthly journal Rruga e Partisë.
pashto: Pashto is an Eastern Iranian language of the Indo-European family, sharing features with Eastern Middle Iranian languages such as Bactrian, Khwarezmian and Sogdian. Some linguists derive it from Avestan or a close relative, others place it nearer to Bactrian, and neither view is universally accepted. Loanwords have been traced in Pashto as far back as the third century BCE and include words from Greek and probably Old Persian. After the 7th century most borrowings came from Persian and Hindi-Urdu, with Arabic words arriving mostly through Persian.

In the 16th century Bayazid Pir Roshan introduced 13 new letters to the Pashto form of the Arabic script, which was further modified over the years and now has 45 to 46 letters. The Pata Khazana, a manuscript presented in 1944 by Abdul Hai Habibi as an anthology of Pashto poets reaching back to the 8th century, has been discredited by linguistic analysis and its authenticity is disputed.

Pashto is natively spoken in north-western Pakistan and in southern and eastern Afghanistan, mainly by ethnic Pashtuns, with estimates of 35 million to 55 million speakers. In historical Persian literature it was also called Afghani. It is one of the two official languages of Afghanistan alongside Dari, and the regional language of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and northern Balochistan in Pakistan. Pashto is a subject-object-verb language with split ergativity, two genders, two numbers and four cases, and it uses prepositions, postpositions and circumpositions. Its dialects fall into a soft southern group and a hard northern group, and no single standard form is agreed.

Pashto has a long oral tradition of proverbs, stories and poems. From the 16th century written poetry became popular, and it rose further in the 17th century with Khushal Khan Khattak (1613 to 1689), who used verse to call for Pashtun unity against Mughal rule, and Rahman Baba (1650 to 1715), both regarded as leading poets. Others include Pir Roshan, Nazo Tokhi and Ahmad Shah Durrani, founder of the Durrani Empire.

Persian remained the language of the Afghan royal court and government. King Amanullah Khan began promoting Pashto as a marker of ethnic identity after the Third Anglo-Afghan War of 1919, and a royal decree of 1936 under Zahir Shah gave it official status. In 1964 the constitutional assembly reaffirmed it, when Afghan Persian was renamed Dari. In British India, Bacha Khan founded in 1921 the Anjuman-e Islah al-Afaghina to promote Pashto, and about 80,000 people attended its annual meeting in 1927.
pashupatinath-temple: The Pashupatinath Temple stands on the banks of the sacred Bagmati River in Kathmandu and is dedicated to Pashupati, regarded as a manifestation of Shiva. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979, one of seven monument groups in the designation of the Kathmandu Valley, which describes it as an extensive Hindu temple precinct of temples, ashrams, inscriptions and images raised over the centuries. The complex covers 246 hectares and includes 518 small temples besides the principal pagoda-style temple. Hindu tradition holds that the shrine is the head of Shiva, whose body stretches to the Kashi Vishwanath Temple in India.

The temple is the oldest Hindu temple in Kathmandu and is considered pre-Vedic in origin. According to the Shiva Purana, Shiva hid underground as a bull while the Pandavas searched for him, and reappeared with his head at Pashupatinath, hump at Kedarnath, face at Rudranath, arms at Tungnath and navel at Madhyamaheshwar.

Its existence is recorded as early as 400 CE. According to the chronicle Gopal Raj Vamshavali it was built by the Licchavi king Prachanda Deva, while another chronicle says it was a linga-shaped shrine before Supuspa Deva built a five-storey temple there. A medieval king, Shivadeva, who reigned from 1099 to 1126, rebuilt it, and Ananta Malla added a roof. A Rama temple of the 14th century and the Guhyeshwari Temple, mentioned in an 11th-century manuscript, stand nearby. The present form dates from a renovation in 1692, after termites and earthquakes had damaged the earlier structures.

The main temple is built in Newari pagoda style on a square platform, with two roofs of copper covered in gold, four doors sheathed in silver and a gold pinnacle. Its main image is a stone Mukhalinga, a metre high, with faces in four directions and a silver base bound with a silver serpent. Only four priests may touch it, from the Bhatta group; the Rajbhandaris act as treasurers, caretakers and assistant priests. Maha Shivaratri and Teej are among the festivals held there. Buddhists also hold the site sacred, linking it with mahasiddhas such as Padmasambhava, who in Vajrayana tradition meditated at its cremation ground.
pasok: The Panhellenic Socialist Movement was founded on 3 September 1974, after the collapse of the Greek military dictatorship of 1967–1974. Its founder was Andreas Papandreou, son of the liberal leader and three-time Prime Minister Georgios Papandreou, and its co-founder was the trade unionist Georgios Daskalakis. Its founding mottos were National Independence, Popular Sovereignty, Social Emancipation and Democratic Process. Papandreou rejected the Venizelist heritage of his father and stressed that he was a socialist, not a liberal.

In the November 1974 elections the party won 13.5% of the vote and 15 of 300 seats, third behind New Democracy and the Centre Union – New Forces. In November 1977 it doubled its vote and won 93 seats, becoming the main opposition party.

In October 1981 the party won 48.1% of the vote and 172 seats, forming the first socialist government in Greece since 1924. Papandreou had campaigned for withdrawal from NATO and the European Economic Community, but changed course after pressure from within the party. The party won again in June 1985 with 46% and 161 seats. Scandals and austerity then eroded its standing, and it lost the elections of June 1989 with 40% against 44.3% for New Democracy. Papandreou was prosecuted in the Koskotas scandal and acquitted, and he led the party to victory again in October 1993 with 47%.

In January 1996 Papandreou retired after a long hospitalisation and died six months later. Costas Simitis, candidate of the modernising, pro-European wing, succeeded him and won the elections of September 1996 and April 2000. In 2001 Greece was confirmed for the Eurozone. Simitis resigned as leader on 7 January 2004 and was followed by George Papandreou, son of Andreas. New Democracy won in March 2004, and PASOK returned to power in October 2009 with 43.92% of the vote and 160 seats.

The governments of Andreas Papandreou introduced a welfare state, including a National Health System that brought modern medical procedures to rural areas, and indexed pensions to the minimum wage. In family law they abolished the dowry, legalised civil marriage and established a New Family Code that made wives and husbands equal partners. The left-wing wartime Resistance was formally recognised, and leftist refugees of the Civil War were allowed to return to Greece.

PASOK and New Democracy were the two major parties from the restoration of democracy until 2012, and PASOK dominated the country from 1981 to 2004. The Greek debt crisis then cost it much of its support: it fell from 160 seats in 2009 to 13 in January 2015, a decline that became known as Pasokification, a term for the decline of centre-left parties across Europe.
pasquale-paoli: Pasquale Paoli was born in the hamlet of Stretta in Morosaglia, Corsica, the second son of the physician and patriot Giacinto Paoli, one of three Generals of the People in the revolt against Genoese rule. The Corsicans regarded the Genoese as failing in government, citing the high murder rate from vendetta, raids by Barbary pirates, oppressive taxes and economic depression. After the rebellion of 1729 Genoa called in foreign troops. When the Corsicans surrendered to the French in 1739, Giacinto went into exile in Naples with his fourteen-year-old son, who received a classical education there and in 1741 joined the Corsican regiment of the royal Neapolitan army.

Corsican exiles in Italy were seeking a skilled general. Pasquale opposed a plan to ask the Knights of Malta to take command and proposed a native Corsican government instead, and a popular election called at Caccia made him General-in-Chief. Only the highland clans voted, and the lowlanders chose Mario Matra, who was soon killed in battle. Paoli confined the Genoese to their citadels, and in November 1755 the people ratified his constitution, which proclaimed Corsica sovereign and independent of Genoa and is described as the first written under Enlightenment principles. He founded a university at Corte, the capital, in 1765, and wished Italian to be the official language.

Genoa ceded Corsica to France by the Treaty of Versailles in May 1768, and France began its conquest that September. Paoli fought a guerrilla war from the mountains but was defeated at Ponte Novu in 1769 and took refuge in England. In London he joined the circle of Samuel Johnson, James Boswell recorded his account in An Account of Corsica, and George III gave him a pension.

After the French Revolution, Paoli returned in 1790 under an amnesty and was elected unanimously president of the department of Corsica. He broke with the Revolution over the execution of the king, and in 1793 a consulta at Corte seceded from France and asked for British protection. The Bonapartes, who had denounced him as a traitor, were driven from the island. A British fleet under Admiral Samuel Hood arrived in 1794, and the Anglo-Corsican Kingdom lasted until 1796 under George III as sovereign head of state, though the relationship was never clearly defined. The Crown invited Paoli to resign, and he sailed for England in October 1795. He died in London on 5 February 1807; his bones were brought back to Corsica in 1889.
passau: Passau is known as the Dreiflüssestadt, the City of Three Rivers, because the Danube is joined there by the Inn from the south and the Ilz from the north. The old town lies at the confluence, and its position makes it liable to flooding: the peak levels of floods as far back as 1501 are marked on a wall of the Old City Hall, and flood water reaches the base of that wall on average about once every five years. The city is dominated by the Veste Oberhaus and the Veste Niederhaus, parts of the former fortress of the bishop on the crest between the Danube and the Ilz.

In the 2nd century BCE many of the Boii, pushed north across the Alps by the Romans, founded a capital that the Romans called Boiodurum, now in the Innstadt district of Passau. The Romans also held a castrum called Batavis, named for the Batavi, a Germanic tribe who often served as auxiliaries; it stood in the province of Raetia, while the late Roman castrum of Boiotro lay in Noricum. In the second half of the 5th century St. Severinus established a monastery there, and the site suffered repeated raids by the Alemanni.

The bishops of Passau also exercised secular authority as prince-bishops in the area around the city. By the Treaty of Passau in 1552, Archduke Ferdinand I, representing Emperor Charles V, secured the agreement of the Protestant princes to submit the religious question to a diet, which led to the Peace of Augsburg in 1555. In the Renaissance and early modern period the city was one of the most prolific centres of sword making in Germany after Solingen. Smiths stamped blades with the Passau wolf, which superstitious warriors believed made the bearer invulnerable, and the practice of placing magical charms on swords was for a time called Passau art.

A fire in 1662 destroyed most of the city, which was rebuilt in the Baroque style. Passau was secularised in 1803 and divided between the Electorate of Bavaria and the Electorate of Salzburg; the Salzburg portion became part of Bavaria in 1805.

Passau has about 50,000 inhabitants, some 12,000 of them students at the University of Passau. St Stephen's Cathedral, a work of Italian Baroque built by the architect Carlo Lurago, has an organ with 17,774 pipes that was long held to be the largest church pipe organ in the world. Many Danube river cruises begin in the city.
passion-of-jesus: The Passion, from the Latin patior, to suffer, is described in the four canonical gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. The first three, the Synoptic Gospels, give similar accounts, while John's varies significantly. Scholars do not agree which events belong to the Passion narrative. Some begin it after the arrest and before the resurrection, so that it holds only the trials, crucifixion and death. Others take a broader approach that includes the triumphal entry, the Last Supper, the burial and the resurrection.

Christians interpret passages of the Old Testament as prophecies of the Passion, above all Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12, which describes a sinless man who atones for the sins of his people by voluntary suffering. In the Gospel of Mark Jesus predicts his own Passion and resurrection three times.

A comprehensive account includes his triumphal entry into Jerusalem, the cleansing of the Temple, where he expels livestock merchants and money-changers, his anointing by a woman a few days before Passover, and the Last Supper, where he predicts his betrayal. On the way to Gethsemane he predicts that Peter will deny him three times. The gospels give differing accounts of his trial. Mark describes two proceedings, one before Jewish leaders and one before the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate, and Matthew and John generally follow him. Luke alone adds a third, in which Pilate sends Jesus to Herod Antipas, who mocks him and returns him to Pilate.

All the gospels relate that Pilate released a man named Barabbas instead of Jesus. Matthew, Mark and John have Pilate offer the crowd a choice, whereas Luke has the crowd demand Barabbas's release. Some manuscripts of Matthew call him Jesus Barabbas.

The Passion is commemorated each year in Christianity during Holy Week. Most denominations read a narrative of it, especially on Good Friday, and in the Roman Rite whole congregations take part in reading the Passion Gospel on Palm Sunday and Good Friday. The Stations of the Cross, a series of reflections on Christ carrying the cross, began with Francis of Assisi and spread through the Catholic Church in the medieval period.

Each episode, such as the Flagellation or Entombment, has been shown thousands of times in art, the Crucifixion most of all, and Albrecht Dürer produced three versions of his Passion print cycle. Passion plays are performed in many Catholic countries, notably at Oberammergau in Germany.
passover: According to the Book of Exodus, God commanded Moses to tell the Israelites to slaughter a lamb and mark their doorframes with its blood. God would then bring the tenth plague, the death of all the firstborn in Egypt, but would pass over the marked homes, which gives the festival its name. Modern scholars widely believe that Passover originated separately from the Exodus narrative. They suggest that it formed from the merger of a pastoral protective rite, in which the blood of a sheep was daubed on the lintels and doorposts to keep demonic forces out of the home, and a spring agricultural festival of unleavened bread connected with the barley harvest. Some scholars disagree with the theory of two merged festivals.

The practice is also attested outside the Bible. A 5th-century BCE Aramaic papyrus letter from Elephantine in Egypt refers to the removal of leaven. The work Jubilees, from the Ptolemaic period, and the Herodian-era writers Josephus and Philo mention the slaughter of the lambs on the 14th of Nisan, and Philo says the banquet included hymns and prayers.

Passover begins on the 15th day of the Hebrew month of Nisan, which is considered the first month of the year. Because the Hebrew day begins at sunset, the holiday starts on the evening before. In Israel it lasts seven days, with the first and last days major holidays; outside Israel, Orthodox and Conservative communities keep eight days. It is one of the Three Pilgrimage Festivals.

Jews are forbidden to own or eat leavened foods, called chametz, during the holiday. On the night of the 14th of Nisan households search for any remaining leaven, and on the following morning it is burned.

While the Tabernacle and later the Temple in Jerusalem stood, the focus of the festival was the Passover sacrifice. Every family large enough to eat a young lamb or goat offered one at the Temple on the afternoon of the 14th of Nisan and ate it that night, roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs; no bone could be broken and no meat left until morning.

Families now gather on the first night, or the first two nights outside Israel, for the seder, a ritual meal whose name means order. The story of the Exodus is retold from the Haggadah, four cups of wine are drunk, and the youngest child asks the four questions, beginning with why this night differs from all other nights. Matzah, unleavened bread, and maror, bitter herbs standing for the bitterness of slavery, are eaten. From the second night Jews begin counting the Omer, the fifty days until Shavuot.
pasteurisation: Heating wine for preservation was known in China from 1117 CE. In 1768 the Italian priest and scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani showed that a product could be made sterile by thermal processing, when meat broth that he boiled for an hour and sealed at once did not spoil. In 1795 the French military offered a prize of 12,000 francs for a new method of preserving food, and the Parisian chef Nicolas Appert won it in January 1810 after some fourteen or fifteen years of experiment, by sealing food in glass jars and boiling them.

Louis Pasteur's gentler method came in the summer of 1864 at Arbois. He wanted to cure the frequent acidity of the local aged wines, and found that heating young wine to only about 50 to 60 °C for a short time killed the microbes, so that the wine could be aged without loss of quality.

Pasteurisation is a mild heat treatment, usually below 100 °C, that destroys or deactivates the microorganisms and enzymes that spoil food or carry disease. Most bacterial spores survive, so it is not sterilisation. The conditions depend on how acidic the food is. In acidic foods such as fruit juice and beer the treatment inactivates enzymes and destroys spoilage microbes, while in milk and liquid eggs it is designed to destroy pathogens as well.

For milk, high-temperature short-time pasteurisation uses 71.5 °C for 15 seconds and gives a refrigerated shelf life of about two weeks. Ultra-high-temperature treatment at 135 °C for one to two seconds, with special packaging, extends shelf life to three months without refrigeration.

Pasteurisation was first used to stop wine and beer souring, and it was many years before milk was treated. As cities grew and supply chains lengthened, raw milk, often days old, came to be recognised as a source of disease. Between 1912 and 1937 some 65,000 people in England and Wales alone died of tuberculosis contracted from milk. Franz von Soxhlet suggested pasteurising milk in 1886, and in 1910 Ernst Lederle, as Commissioner of Health, introduced mandatory pasteurisation of milk in New York City. Pasteurisation prevents diseases such as tuberculosis, brucellosis and diphtheria, and milk is now considered a safer food.
pasto: Pasto, officially San Juan de Pasto, lies in the Atriz Valley on the Andes cordillera, at the foot of the Galeras volcano, which rises to 4,276 metres. Most of the city lies between 2,520 and 2,700 metres above sea level, and some settlement on the volcano's flanks exceeds 3,000 metres. Although it is close to the equator, its altitude gives it a mild climate, with average highs of only 15 to 18 degrees and about 800 millimetres of rain a year. The Pan-American Highway links it northwards with Popayán and southwards with Ipiales, 78 kilometres away on the border with Ecuador, and a paved road of 284 kilometres leads west to the Pacific port of Tumaco.

The city takes its name from the Pastos, the Indigenous people who lived in the region when the Spanish arrived, although the Atriz Valley itself was inhabited by the Quillacingas. The conquistador Sebastián de Belalcázar founded Pasto in 1537. In 1539 another conquistador, Lorenzo de Aldana, moved it to its present site and gave it the name San Juan de Pasto. A man of Italian origin, Guido Bucheli, was a major contributor to its economy and expansion.

Pasto has been an administrative, cultural and religious centre of the region since colonial times, and for this reason is known as the theological city of Colombia. During the wars of independence against Spain it was a royalist city. Partly because of that stance and partly because of its geographical position, it remained isolated from the rest of Colombia for a long time after independence.

Pasto is the capital of the department of Nariño and had a population of 392,930 in the census of 2018. The larger companies of the department are based there, working in food, beverages and furniture, and it trades chiefly with Ecuador. The University of Nariño is one of several universities in the city.

The Blacks and Whites' Carnival, held between 2 and 7 January each year, is one of its most important events, with floats portraying legends and traditions. A local craft, Barniz de Pasto, is a pre-Columbian technique in which the natural rubber of the mopa-mopa tree is coloured, stretched over woodwork and cut into designs. Lake Guamuez, or La Cocha, lies 27 kilometres away, with the island of La Corota, a National Forest Sanctuary. Chaza, a traditional ball game played with heavy wood and leather drums on a rectangular court, is practised in Nariño and parts of Ecuador.
patagonia: Patagonia is bounded by the Pacific Ocean on the west and the Atlantic on the east, and to the south by the Strait of Magellan, the Beagle Channel and the Drake Passage. Its western side, the southern section of the Andes, has lakes, fjords, temperate rainforests and glaciers; the high rainfall there and the low sea-surface temperatures feed the largest ice fields in the Southern Hemisphere outside Antarctica.

The east has deserts, tablelands and steppes. About 90 percent of the region lies in Argentina and about 10 percent in Chile. Its northern limit is not precisely defined, but the Colorado and Barrancas rivers are commonly taken as that of Argentine Patagonia. The name comes from patagón, which Magellan used in 1520 for the native peoples whom his expedition thought to be giants, now believed to have been the Tehuelche.

Human habitation dates back thousands of years. The site of Monte Verde in Chile has evidence of human activity around 14,500 years before the present. At the Spanish arrival most peoples were hunter-gatherers, travelling on foot over the eastern plains and by dugout canoes and dalcas in the western channels, while communities in a small part of the north-west practised limited agriculture.

After the failure of Spanish settlement on the Strait of Magellan, the Chiloé Archipelago became a Spanish base protecting western Patagonia, and Valdivia, re-established in 1645, acted as a sentry. In the 18th century the Spanish ordered the depopulation of the Guaitecas Archipelago to deprive privateers and pirates of support.

In the early 19th century many Mapuche migrated to Patagonia and lived as nomads raising cattle or raiding the Argentine countryside; the stolen cattle travelled to Chile along the Camino de los chilenos. Argentina built a trench, the Zanja de Alsina, in the 1870s against the raids. After independence, Chile and Argentina asserted sovereignty and colonized the region in the 19th and early 20th centuries; this expansion, with military campaigns, severely disrupted indigenous societies and led to a sharp population decline. Sheep farming, introduced in the late 19th century, became a principal economic activity, and oil was discovered near Comodoro Rivadavia in 1907.

Patagonia is governed by Argentina and Chile. Argentina's part is divided into the provinces of Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut, Santa Cruz and Tierra del Fuego. In Chile, the Aysén and Magallanes regions lie entirely within it. Its main economic activities are sheep farming, oil and gas in Argentina, and fishing, salmon aquaculture and tourism in Chile. The steppe is one of the last strongholds of the guanaco.
pataliputra: Pataliputra stood where the Ganges, the Gandhaka and the Son rivers met, a position that made it a water fort, or jaldurga, and let it dominate the river trade of the Indo-Gangetic Plain. One traditional etymology derives the name from the pāṭalī tree; another makes it the son of Pāṭali, daughter of a Raja Sudarsan. The city was also called Kusumapura, city of flowers. The Greek ambassador Megasthenes, who lived there under the Maurya Empire and called it Palibothra, described a city in the shape of a parallelogram, surrounded by a ditch and a wall with 570 towers and 64 gates. Strabo adds that the walls were of wood.

The place began as a village, Pataligrama, fortified by the Magadha ruler Ajatashatru; the date given is 490 BCE. Jain and Hindu sources name his son Udayabhadra as the king who moved the capital there from Rajgriha. Archaeological evidence shows urban growth no earlier than the 3rd or 4th century BCE. Under Ashoka it was one of the world's largest cities, with an estimated population of 150,000 to 400,000, and early Buddhist texts record the Third Buddhist council there.

Faxian, visiting about 400, found the people rich and described hospitals where the poor were treated without charge. Xuanzang in 637 found the old city in ruins, with a small walled town of about 1,000 people by the river. Suggested causes of the decline are a shift in the course of the Ganges, a flood on the Son recorded in a later Jain work and placed in the late 500s, and destruction by Hunas in the early 500s. An inscription of the Pala king Dharmapala from the early 800s describes it as a river port and royal camp. Sher Shah Suri later made it his capital under the name Patna.

Much of the ancient city lies buried under modern Patna. Its site was first identified in modern times by Laurence Waddell in 1892, and excavations have been made at Kumhrar, Bulandi Bagh and Agam Kuan. They have found stretches of the wooden palisade over several kilometres, but no stone fortifications. At Kumhrar the remains thin out from the 300s and stop about 600, and a thick layer of ash in the hall of 80 pillars suggests that it was burnt.
pathankot: Pathankot lies in the northernmost part of Punjab, close to the Kangra district of Himachal Pradesh, and is known as the gateway to Himachal. It stands at an average elevation of 332 metres between the Ravi and Chakki rivers, with the Shiwalik foothills to the south and east and the snow-capped Himalayas to the north. The city is the headquarters of Pathankot district.

The Mahabharata and the grammarian Panini mention the region as Audumbara, classed as an ayudhajivi sangha, a warrior community, and many ancient coins of the Audumbara kingdom have been found at sites in Pathankot. Alexander Cunningham of the Archaeological Survey of India held that its fort was originally built in the ancient period.

From the 11th to the 16th century Pathankot was the first capital of Nurpur State, which was earlier known as Dhameri, a corruption of Audumbari. The city takes its name from the Pathania clan of Pahadi Rajputs, chieftains of Nurpur. In Mughal India the name Dhameri was changed to Nurpur during the reign of Shah Jahan. Under the Sikh Empire, Jarnail Jai Singh Kanhaiya of the Kanhaiya Misl invaded Pathankot and annexed it from the Pathania Rajputs, and it was merged with Punjab under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Moran Sarkar, a Muslim dancing girl whom Ranjit Singh married, lived in a fortress at Pathankot from 1811 until her death.

After the First Anglo-Sikh War in 1845 the British annexed the hill regions from the Sikhs, and Pathankot was part of Kangra until it was merged with Gurdaspur district in 1853. At the partition of India the border demarcation committee's initial plan was to place Pathankot, then in Gurdaspur district, in Pakistan and Shakargarh district in India. In the end Shakargarh went to Pakistan, and Gurdaspur district, with Pathankot, went to India.

Pathankot is a major railway junction, where the lines from Amritsar and Delhi meet and all services to Jammu pass. It is also the lower terminus of the narrow-gauge Kangra Valley Railway, built by the British, which runs 128 km to Joginder Nagar and links the mountainous regions of western Himachal Pradesh to the national network. Its economy rests on agriculture, trade and transport, and the area produces wheat, maize and litchi. The most common languages are Punjabi, Pahari and Hindi. Keshopur Chhamb, near the city, is the only major natural wetland in the state.
pathet-lao: The Pathet Lao, Lao for Lao Nation, was officially the Lao People's Liberation Army. It traces its roots to the Second World War and to the Lao Issara, an anti-French, non-communist nationalist movement formed on 12 October 1945. It was renamed the Pathet Lao in 1950, when it was adopted by Lao forces under Souphanouvong, who joined the Viet Minh's revolt against French colonial authorities in the First Indochina War. In August 1950 he joined the Viet Minh at their headquarters north of Hanoi and became head of the Pathet Lao, with a political arm called Neo Lao Issara, the Free Lao Front. The movement was dependent on the Vietnamese communists from its foundation.

In 1953 Pathet Lao fighters accompanied a Viet Minh invasion of Laos from Vietnam and set up a government at Viengxay in Houaphanh province. The Geneva Conference of 1954 required foreign forces to withdraw and allowed the Pathet Lao to establish itself in Laos's two northern provinces, though the Viet Minh and North Vietnamese never fully left the border areas. A coalition government of monarchists and communists was formed in 1957, but in 1959 fighting resumed after two Pathet Lao battalions chosen for integration into the Royal Lao Army were surrounded and fled to North Vietnam.
North Vietnam formed Group 959 in September 1959 to secure the supply route to South Vietnam, later known as the Ho Chi Minh trail, and to train and supply the Pathet Lao.

A neutrality agreement was signed in Geneva on 23 July 1962 and the Pathet Lao joined another coalition government in June 1962, leaving it and resuming the fighting by April 1963. The armed forces took the name Lao People's Liberation Army in October 1965, with estimated strength rising from 25,000 in June 1965 to over 48,000 in 1970, and depended on the People's Army of Vietnam for weapons. China also supplied guns, grenades and bullets and trained over 700 officers. After the Paris Peace Accords the Pathet Lao and the Lao government signed the Vientiane Treaty, a cease-fire, on 21 February 1973. The movement gained control of the whole country in 1975.

The Pathet Lao's supreme headquarters lay in the Viengxay Caves near Xam Neua. Its forces were divided into regular, regional and militia or guerrilla units, with Vietnamese advisers attached, and its units had political commissars down to company level. Training stressed political indoctrination above military skill, and recruits came by appeals to patriotism or by a draft.
patna: Ancient Patna, known as Pataliputra, was the capital of the Magadha Empire under the Haryanka, Nanda, Mauryan, Shunga, Gupta and Pala dynasties. Traditional Buddhist literature has Ajatashatru, the king of Magadha, choose a site on the bank of the Ganges and fortify it so that he could better fight the Licchavis of Vaishali, and says that Gautama Buddha passed through in the last year of his life.

The Chinese Buddhist traveller Faxian, who visited India between 399 and 414 CE, stayed in the city for many months translating Buddhist texts. Pataliputra was home to scholars including Aryabhata, Vātsyāyana and Chanakya. After the Gupta Empire broke up the city passed through uncertain times, and Bakhtiar Khilji's capture of Bihar in the 12th century ended its standing as a political and cultural centre.

Sher Shah Suri revived Patna in the middle of the 16th century, building a fort of which nothing survives and a mosque that does. Akbar reached the city in 1574 to put down the Afghan chief Daud Khan, and Abul Fazl described a flourishing trade in paper, stone and glass and in the rice later known in Europe as Patna rice. In 1704 Aurangzeb agreed to his grandson Prince Muhammad Azim's request to rename it Azimabad. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, was born in Patna on 22 December 1666, and Patna Sahib is one of the most sacred Sikh pilgrimage sites.

In the 17th century Patna became a centre of international trade. The English East India Company set up a factory there in 1620 for calico and silk, and it grew into a trading centre for saltpetre; Portuguese traders had a factory there from at least 1580. In 1763 Nawab Mir Qasim ordered the killing of 45 mostly British employees and 200 sepoys of the Company in the Patna massacre. The Company annexed the city in 1793. In 1912, when the Bengal Presidency was partitioned, Patna became the capital of the province of Bihar and Orissa.

Patna is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of Bihar and the seat of the Patna High Court. It lies mainly on the southern bank of the Ganges, at the meeting of rivers that include the Son, Gandak and Punpun, and covers about 250 square kilometres. The pilgrimage centres of Vaishali, Rajgir, Nalanda, Bodh Gaya and Pawapuri are nearby. It remained the capital of Bihar after independence in 1947, including after Jharkhand became a separate state in 2000.
patriarch-nikon: Nikon was born Nikita Minin in 1605, the son of a Mordvin peasant farmer, in the village of Veldemanovo, about 96 kilometres from Nizhny Novgorod. He became a novice at the Makaryev Monastery at twelve, then returned home, married and served as a parish priest, later in Moscow. After his three children died by 1635 he persuaded his wife to take the veil and became a monk on Anzersky Island in the White Sea, taking the name Nikon. He became abbot of the Kozheozersky Monastery in 1643 and in 1646 impressed Tsar Alexis, who made him archimandrite of the Novospassky Monastery in Moscow.

At Novospassky he joined the Zealots of Piety, a circle around the tsar's confessor Stefan Vonifatiyev that sought a revival of Orthodox piety after the Time of Troubles. In 1649 he became metropolitan of Great Novgorod, where he quelled a riot by leading a religious procession. Elected patriarch on 1 August 1652, he accepted only after the tsar and the boyars knelt before him, and after imposing a vow of obedience in all matters of Church dogma and observance.

Nikon consulted Greek prelates and scholars of Constantinople and Kiev, who convinced him that the Muscovite service-books and many icons differed from Greek models. A synod of 1654 and a council of 1656 approved revising the books and anathematised the dissenters, among them Paul, bishop of Kolomna. He ordered the search for icons influenced by Western baroque and forbade tent-like churches. Later research, such as Meyendorff's, found that the Muscovite books followed an older recension than the Greek ones. The reforms led to the Old Believers. He founded the Valday Iversky, New Jerusalem and Kiy Island monasteries.

Between 1652 and 1658 he was a colleague of the tsar rather than a minister, and ruled as chief while Alexis campaigned in the wars with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. He held that the supreme bishop is higher than the tsar and opposed the Legal Code of 1649, which made the Church subservient to the state. In 1658, estranged from Alexis, he took off his vestments and withdrew to the New Jerusalem Monastery without resigning.

A pan-Orthodox synod presided over by the patriarchs Paisius of Alexandria and Macarius III of Antioch found him guilty of reviling the tsar and the Church, of deposing Bishop Paul contrary to the canons and of beating and torturing dependants. He was reduced to the status of a monk and sent to the Ferapontov monastery, while the same council confirmed his reforms. Allowed to return under a partial pardon in 1681, he died at Tropino on 17 August of that year, on the way to New Jerusalem.
patrice-de-macmahon: The MacMahon family is of Irish origin. After losing much of its land in the Cromwellian confiscations of 1652, a branch supported the deposed James II in 1688 and settled in France, applying for French citizenship in 1749. Patrice de MacMahon was born on 13 June 1808 at the Château de Sully near Autun in Burgundy, the sixteenth and second-youngest son of Baron Maurice-François de Mac Mahon. The family, a military one, had decidedly royalist politics. He entered the military school at Saint-Cyr on 23 October 1825 and joined the army in 1827.

MacMahon served in the French conquest of Algeria from 1830, was commended at the seizure of Algiers and was wounded at the Siege of Constantine in 1837. He became a colonel in December 1845 and a general of brigade in 1848, and in 1852 he organised in Algeria the plebiscite that approved the coup d'état of 1851. In the Crimean War he won a victory at the Battle of Malakoff in September 1855, where he is reputed to have said 'Here I am; here will I stay!' At Magenta in 1859 he advanced his troops without orders at a critical moment, which assured the French victory; Napoleon III made him a Marshal of France and Duke of Magenta.

He was Governor General of Algeria from 1864, a post in which he did not distinguish himself and which drew numerous complaints. In 1870 he led the main French army in the Franco-Prussian War, suffered defeats in Alsace and was seriously wounded at Sedan; with the Emperor he was made prisoner on 1 September. In May 1871 he led the Semaine Sanglante, the week-long campaign that defeated the Paris Commune.

In May 1873 the royalist and conservative majority of the National Assembly elected MacMahon President, with one vote against. Many hoped he would hold office until a Bourbon pretender could restore the monarchy, but he refused to meet the Count of Chambord and accepted a seven-year mandate on 9 November 1873. He remained above parties during the Constitutional Laws of 1875. After the Republican victory of 1876 he reluctantly accepted governments under Jules Dufaure and Jules Simon.

In the crisis of 16 May 1877 he dismissed Simon, had the Senate dissolve the Chamber of Deputies and campaigned across the country, but the elections of 14 October gave the Republicans a majority of 120 seats. He resigned on 30 January 1879, succeeded by Jules Grévy. He died on 17 October 1893 and was buried at the Invalides after a state funeral.
patrice-lumumba: Patrice Lumumba was born Isaïe Tasumbu Tawosa on 2 July 1925 in Onalua, in the Kasaï province of the Belgian Congo, to Julienne Wamato Lomendja and François Tolenga Otetshima, a farmer. He belonged to the Tetela ethnic group. Raised in a Catholic family, he attended a Protestant primary school, a Catholic missionary school and finally the government post office training school, where he passed the one-year course with distinction. He was known as a vocal, precocious young man who pointed out his teachers' errors in front of his classmates, and he spoke Tetela, French, Lingala, Swahili and Tshiluba.

Lumumba helped found the Mouvement National Congolais in 1958 and quickly became its leader. Unlike other Congolese parties, it did not rest on an ethnic base, and its platform of independence, gradual Africanisation of government, state-led economic development and neutrality in foreign affairs drew a large popular following. In December 1958 he represented it at the All-African Peoples' Conference in Accra, hosted by Kwame Nkrumah. Independence was set for 30 June 1960, after elections held in May in which the MNC won a plurality, and Lumumba became the first prime minister.

On 5 July 1960 troops of the Force Publique mutinied against their commander, General Émile Janssens, and the mutiny spread; this opened the Congo Crisis. Katanga and South Kasai declared independence, and Lumumba sent the army to put down the secessions. On 5 September President Joseph Kasa-Vubu announced Lumumba's dismissal, and Lumumba in turn declared the president deposed over the radio. On 14 September Mobutu Sese Seko announced a coup. Lumumba was captured while trying to reach Stanleyville, held at the barracks at Thysville from 3 December, and sent to Katanga in January 1961.

Lumumba was killed on 17 January 1961 by the separatist Katangan authorities of Moïse Tshombe, with two associates, Maurice Mpolo and Joseph Okito. Belgian officers dug up and dissolved the bodies. Katangan radio announced on 13 February that he had been killed by villagers after escaping. His killing caused protests in at least twenty countries. Letters of Belgian ministers show that they wanted his elimination and facilitated his transfer to Katanga. In 2002 Belgium formally apologised for its role, admitting moral responsibility. In 2022 a tooth of his, the only remains, was returned to his family. He is widely seen as a martyr of anti-colonial liberation and the pan-African movement.
patricio-aylwin: Patricio Aylwin Azócar was born on 26 November 1918 in Viña del Mar, the eldest of the five children of Miguel Aylwin and Laura Azócar. He studied at the Law School of the University of Chile and qualified as a lawyer, with the highest distinction, in 1943. He taught administrative law at the University of Chile from 1946 to 1967 and at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile from 1952 to 1960. He married Leonor Oyarzún Ivanovic on 29 September 1948, and they had five children. His paternal line was British: an ancestor, Richard Aylwin, emigrated from England to Chile in 1833.

Aylwin entered politics in 1945 by joining the Falange Nacional, of which he was president in 1950–51. When it became the Christian Democratic Party he served seven terms as its president between 1958 and 1989. He was elected a senator in 1965 and became president of the Senate in 1971. During the government of Salvador Allende he led the democratic opposition within and outside Congress, and he is credited, to some degree, with trying to find a peaceful solution to the political crisis.

After the 1973 coup he led his party twice, and in 1979 he spoke for the group that opposed the plebiscite approving a new constitution. He was among the first to advocate accepting that constitution as a reality in order to ease the return to democracy.

Aylwin was at the centre of the movement that defeated Augusto Pinochet in the plebiscite of 5 October 1988. Afterwards he took part in negotiations that produced 54 constitutional reforms and made a peaceful transition possible.

Aylwin was elected president on 14 December 1989 and governed from 1990 to 1994. The military under Pinochet remained powerful, and the constitution preserved its influence, so that the government could not achieve goals such as restructuring the Constitutional Court. Direct municipal elections were begun, the first in June 1992. A tax reform of 1990 raised revenue and allowed social spending to rise from 9.9 to 11.7 per cent of GDP, a new labour law widened trade union rights, and more than 100,000 homes were built. He was succeeded in 1994 by Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle. Aylwin died on 19 April 2016.
patrick-henry: Patrick Henry was born on 29 May 1736 on the family farm, Studley, in Hanover County, Virginia. His father John Henry was an immigrant from Aberdeenshire, and his mother Sarah Winston Syme was a wealthy widow from a prominent local family. Henry was tutored at home by his father after about the age of ten. Because custom gave the family's land, stock and slaves to his older half-brother John Syme Jr., he had to make his own way. At sixteen he opened a store with his brother William, which failed.

While helping at Hanover Tavern he studied law on his own, and in April 1760 he passed the examination at Williamsburg, although his knowledge of procedure was scant. He soon became prominent through his victory in the Parson's Cause against the Anglican clergy.

Henry won a seat in the Virginia House of Burgesses in May 1765. In 1774 he was a delegate to the First Continental Congress. At the Second Virginia Convention in March 1775 he urged that a militia be raised independent of royal authority, and on 23 March he defended this in the speech for which he is best known. In May he led militia towards Williamsburg after the royal governor, the Earl of Dunmore, had marines seize the colony's gunpowder, and he stopped only when a member of the Governor's Council agreed to pay for it.

In May 1776 the Fifth Virginia Convention passed unanimously a resolution based largely on his, declaring Virginia independent and instructing its delegates in Congress to press for American independence. He served on the committee that drafted the Virginia Declaration of Rights and the state's first constitution, and he was elected the first governor of the new state. He served five one-year terms in all, the last two from 1784.

Henry feared a strong federal government. He declined appointment as a delegate to the 1787 Constitutional Convention, and he actively opposed ratification of the Constitution, both because he feared a powerful central government and because it had as yet no Bill of Rights. He was a slaveholder throughout his adult life and hoped to see slavery end, but he had no plan beyond ending the importation of slaves.

Henry wrote little, and only a handful of his papers and a few of his speeches survive, which has frustrated his biographers. Thomas Jefferson filled the gap with his own, often negative, recollections, and these have adversely affected Henry's historical reputation. He helped found Hampden-Sydney College, and the Red Hill Patrick Henry National Memorial preserves his final home and gravesite.
patrick-pearse: Pearse was born on 10 November 1879 at 27 Great Brunswick Street, Dublin, where his father, James Pearse, a mason and monumental sculptor, ran a stonemasonry business that gave the family a comfortable middle-class life. His mother, Margaret Brady, was from Dublin, and her father's family were native Irish speakers from County Meath. His maternal grandfather had supported the Young Ireland movement and later joined the Irish Republican Brotherhood. The influence of his grand-aunt Margaret, together with his schooling at the CBS Westland Row, gave him an early love of the Irish language and culture.
In 1896 he joined the Gaelic League, and in 1903 he became editor of its newspaper An Claidheamh Soluis. He took a degree in modern languages and was called to the bar in 1901.

Believing that the Irish school system raised young people to be good Englishmen or obedient Irishmen, Pearse founded a bilingual school for boys, St Enda's School, in 1908 and later moved it to The Hermitage in Rathfarnham. In November 1913 he was invited to the inaugural meeting of the Irish Volunteers. In December 1913 he was sworn into the Irish Republican Brotherhood, and in 1914 he became the Volunteers' Director of Military Organisation. By 1915 he sat on the IRB's Supreme Council and its secret Military Council, which planned a rising during the war. On 1 August 1915 he gave the graveside oration for the Fenian Jeremiah O'Donovan Rossa.

He also wrote stories and poems in Irish and English, plays in Irish, and essays on politics, language and education, among them The Murder Machine. He composed republican lyrics for the song Oró Sé do Bheatha 'Bhaile. The critic Louis de Paor considers him the most accomplished poet of the early Gaelic revival.

When the Easter Rising began on Easter Monday, 24 April 1916, Pearse read the Proclamation of the Irish Republic outside the General Post Office. He was chosen as President of the Republic and was the person most responsible for drafting the Proclamation. After six days of fighting he ordered the surrender. He was court-martialled and shot by firing squad, with Thomas Clarke and Thomas MacDonagh the first to be executed, on the morning of 3 May 1916, at the age of 36. His brother Willie was also executed. The British commander in Ireland, Sir John Maxwell, advised against returning the bodies to the families, fearing that the graves would become martyrs' shrines. Pearse came to be seen by many as the embodiment of the rebellion.
patrick-white: Patrick Victor Martindale White was born in Knightsbridge, London, on 28 May 1912, to Australian parents who were on an extended honeymoon. The family returned to Sydney when he was six months old. White developed asthma at the age of four, a condition that had killed his maternal grandfather, and his health was fragile throughout childhood.

From 1932 he studied French and German literature at King's College, Cambridge. After graduating in 1935 he was determined to stay in England and become a writer, supported by an allowance of £400 a year from his father. In London he met the Australian painter Roy de Maistre, who encouraged him to break from naturalistic prose and write from the inside out.

White's first published novel, Happy Valley (1939), won the Gold Medal of the Australian Literature Society. In the Second World War he served as an intelligence officer in the Royal Air Force; in Alexandria in 1941 he met Manoly Lascaris, who became his life companion. They settled in February 1948 on a small farm at Castle Hill, then semi-rural, outside Sydney. Discouraged by the reception of The Aunt's Story, White had a religious experience in late 1951 that gave him a belief in God and the inspiration to resume work on The Tree of Man (1955), which he described as an attempt to suggest every possible aspect of life through the lives of an ordinary man and woman.

That novel and Voss (1957) established his reputation in Britain and the United States, though Australian critics were divided; the poet A. D. Hope called his prose pretentious verbal sludge. Voss won the first Miles Franklin Award, and Riders in the Chariot (1961) won it again. The Eye of the Storm was published in August 1973, and in October White received the Nobel Prize in Literature, cited for an epic and psychological narrative art which had introduced a new continent into literature.

White's fiction concerns individuals, often alienated from society, who try to grasp a higher reality: pioneer settlers, explorers, artists, the simple-minded. He portrayed Australian society as materialistic and conformist, and in 1958 satirised what he called the Great Australian Emptiness. His style drew on the modernism of Joyce, Lawrence and Woolf, shifting between past and present and between the viewpoints of different characters. From the late 1960s he opposed the Vietnam War and supported Aboriginal self-determination, nuclear disarmament and environmental causes. In 1975 he founded the Patrick White Award with the prize money from his Nobel Prize.
pattadakal: Pattadakal, also called Raktapura, stands on the west bank of the Malaprabha River in Bagalkot district, about 23 kilometres from Badami and about 9.7 kilometres from Aihole, both important centres of Chalukya monuments. The river turns northwards a kilometre before it reaches the site, and in Hindu tradition a north-flowing river is called Uttarvahini Ganga. The place was considered holy for this reason. Its name means stone of coronation, and Chalukya kings held coronation ceremonies there, among them Vinayaditya in the 7th century CE. It was also known as Kisuvolal, the valley of red soil, and Ptolemy refers to it as Petirgal.

The early Chalukya rulers of the 5th and 6th centuries were followers of Vishnu who later became followers of Shiva, so the temples are generally dedicated to Shiva. There are ten major temples, nine Hindu and one Jain, with many small shrines. They are built of local sandstone, and some sculpture is of polished black granite. Four temples are in the Chalukya Dravida style of the south, four in the Nagara style of the north, and the Papanatha temple fuses the two.

The oldest of the Hindu temples is the Sangameshwara, built under Vijayaditya Satyashraya and left unfinished at his death. The Virupaksha temple, the largest and most sophisticated, was sponsored by Queen Lokmahadevi after the campaigns of King Vikramaditya II against the Pallavas. Its inscription names the chief architect, Gunda Anivaritacharya, and artists' names are inscribed beneath the panels they worked on.

The nearby Trailokeshwara temple was sponsored by Queen Trailokyamahadevi. The last temple is the Jain Narayana temple, probably of the 9th century and possibly sponsored by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna II. Inscriptions in old Kannada record grants by kings and queens, and one 8th-century column carries both the Siddhamatrika and Kannada scripts.

The friezes show scenes from the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and the Bhagavata Purana. Art historian Cathleen Cummings reads the sculpture as an expression of Hindu kingship and of the tension between the householder's life and that of the renouncing monk.

Pattadakal is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which UNESCO has described as a harmonious blend of architectural forms from northern and southern India. It is protected under Indian law and managed by the Archaeological Survey of India. The Virupaksha temple is still an active place of Hindu worship.
paul-doumer: Joseph Athanase Doumer, commonly known as Paul, was born on 22 March 1857 at Aurillac in the Cantal department into a family of modest means. A former student of the Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, he became a professor of mathematics at Mende in 1877 and taught at Remiremont from 1879 to 1883, leaving on health grounds to become chief editor of a regional newspaper, the Courrier de l'Aisne. In 1878 he married Blanche Richel. They had eight children, four of whom were killed in the First World War.
