He was initiated into Freemasonry in 1879 and became Grand Secretary of the Grand Orient de France in 1892.

Doumer entered politics in 1885 as chef de cabinet to Charles Floquet, president of the Chamber of Deputies, and was elected Radical deputy for the Aisne in 1888. Defeated in 1889, he was returned in 1890 by the arrondissement of Auxerre. As minister of finance in 1895–1896 he tried without success to introduce an income tax.

When he arrived in Indochina the colonies were losing millions of francs a year, and his taxes were meant to put them on a paying basis. Vietnamese, Cambodians and Laotians who could not or would not pay lost their houses and land and often became day labourers. He made Indochina a market for French products and a field for French investment. In 1898 he persuaded the French government to approve the railway to Yunnan, with a view to annexing the south of that province.

Back in France he was elected deputy for Laon, refused to support the ministry of Émile Combes and led a group of dissident Radicals that eventually helped bring it down. He was president of the Chamber from 1902 to 1905, minister of finance again in 1925 and president of the Senate from 1927. On 13 May 1931 he was elected president of the Republic, defeating the better-known Aristide Briand.

On 6 May 1932, at the opening of a book fair at the Hôtel Salomon de Rothschild in Paris, Doumer was shot by Paul Gorguloff, a Russian émigré, while talking to the author Claude Farrère. He died in hospital at 04:37 on 7 May, the second French president to be assassinated and the first to be shot. Gorguloff wrote that the act was a protest on behalf of exiled White Russians and against France's relations with the Soviet Union; he was guillotined four months later. Doumer wrote L'Indo-Chine française (1904) and Le Livre de mes fils (1906).
paul-gauguin: Gauguin was born in Paris on 7 June 1848, the son of Clovis Gauguin, a liberal journalist who had to flee France when his newspaper was suppressed, and Aline Chazal, daughter of the engraver André Chazal and of the author and early socialist activist Flora Tristan. In 1850 the family settled in Peru, where he had a privileged childhood until the age of six. After schooling in France he signed on as a pilot's assistant in the merchant marine and then served two years in the French navy. In 1873 he married the Dane Mette-Sophie Gad, and they had five children.

He worked as a stockbroker and began painting in his spare time, befriending Camille Pissarro, who introduced him to other Impressionist artists. The financial crisis of 1882 damaged his brokerage career and led him to paint full time. He showed 19 paintings and a wood relief at the eighth and last Impressionist exhibition in May 1886.

Under the influence of folk art and Japanese prints, his work moved towards Cloisonnism, with flat areas of colour and heavy black outlines, as in The Yellow Christ of 1889, and later towards Synthetism. In 1887 he travelled with the painter Charles Laval to Panama, where he worked as a labourer on the French canal, and then to Martinique. Vincent van Gogh and his brother Theo, a dealer with the firm Goupil & Cie, admired his Martinique paintings, and Theo bought three of them for 900 francs.

After a successful auction at the Hôtel Drouot in February 1891, Gauguin sailed for Tahiti on 1 April, stating his aim of escaping European civilization and everything artificial and conventional. He returned to France in August 1893 and left for Tahiti again on 28 June 1895.

In the Marquesas Islands he found a society that, as in Tahiti, had lost much of its cultural identity; the population had fallen from some 80,000 in the 18th century to 4,000, largely through Western diseases. In 1903 he campaigned against the island's gendarmes and on 27 March was fined 500 francs and sentenced to three months' imprisonment for libel. Weak, in great pain and using morphine, he died suddenly on 8 May 1903.

Retrospective exhibitions at the Salon d'Automne in Paris in 1903 and 1906 strongly influenced the French avant-garde, above all Pablo Picasso, whose work of 1906 led to Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907. In the 21st century critics have described his Primitivist depictions of Tahiti as colonialist and have pointed to his sexual exploitation of Tahitian girls.
paul-henri-spaak: Paul-Henri Spaak was born on 25 January 1899 in Schaerbeek into a prominent family. His mother, Marie Janson, was a socialist and the first woman to enter the Belgian Senate, and his father, Paul Spaak, was a poet and playwright. In 1914 he tried to join the Belgian army during the German invasion, was captured and spent two years as a prisoner of war in Germany. He then studied law in Brussels and played tennis for Belgium in the 1922 Davis Cup. As a lawyer he defended Communists accused of conspiracy and the Italian anarchist student Fernando de Rosa, who had tried to kill Crown Prince Umberto of Italy.

He joined the Belgian Labour Party in 1920, was elected deputy in 1932 and became Minister of Transport in 1935. From February 1936 he was Foreign Minister, keeping to Belgium's neutrality, and from May 1938 to February 1939 he was prime minister for the first time. After the German invasion of May 1940 he and Hubert Pierlot, with part of the government, reached London in October 1940. In exile he promoted a customs union with the Netherlands and Luxembourg, which became Benelux. After the war he was prime minister from 13 to 31 March 1946, the shortest government in Belgian history, and again from March 1947 to August 1949, when women received the vote.

He chaired the first session of the United Nations General Assembly and was the first President of the Council of Europe's Consultative Assembly, resigning in December 1951 after it rejected a proposal for a European political authority. In 1955 the Messina Conference made him chairman of the committee whose Spaak Report led to the Treaties of Rome, signed on 25 March 1957.

From 1957 to 1961 Spaak was Secretary General of NATO, succeeding Lord Ismay, and clashed repeatedly with Charles de Gaulle. He was Belgium's foreign minister for eighteen years between 1939 and 1966. He retired from politics in 1966, published his memoirs, Combats inachevés, in 1969 and died at Braine-l'Alleud on 31 July 1972. Nicknamed Mr. Europe, he is counted among the founding fathers of the European Union, and a building of the European Parliament in Brussels bears his name.
paul-i-of-russia: Paul was the son of Peter III and Catherine II, who was born Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst. Catherine hinted in one edition of her memoirs that her lover Sergei Saltykov was Paul's father, but later recanted and named Peter III. Empress Elizabeth took the infant almost at once, and he had limited contact with his mother. He was put in the charge of the governor Nikita Ivanovich Panin. He became crown prince in 1762, when his father took the throne, but within months Catherine deposed Peter III and Paul remained heir apparent. Mother and son kept a distant relationship. Paul criticised her expansionist wars in a dissertation on military reform, Reflections, which added to her suspicion of a conspiracy around him.

Catherine suffered a stroke on 17 November 1796 and died without regaining consciousness. Paul's first act as emperor was to look for her testament and, if possible, destroy it, since he feared it would exclude him in favour of his son Alexander. He then promulgated the Pauline Laws, establishing strict male primogeniture in the House of Romanov, rules that lasted to the end of the dynasty. He also imposed the first limits on serfdom with the Manifesto of three-day corvée. He reversed many of his mother's policies, freed Alexander Radishchev, Nikolay Novikov and Tadeusz Kościuszko, and sought to curtail the privileges of the nobility.

His army reforms, including Prussian uniforms impractical for active duty, were deeply unpopular. In foreign policy he recalled the troops Catherine had sent towards Persia. In 1799 he joined the Second Coalition against Revolutionary France with Britain and Austria, but withdrew after setbacks, and later led the Second League of Armed Neutrality against Britain. After the death of King Erekle of Kartli-Kakheti, civil war broke out over the succession, and one claimant appealed to Russia; Paul signed a decree incorporating the kingdom into the Russian Empire. He was also Grand Master of the Russian Knights Hospitaller from 1799 to 1801.

Paul's attempts to impose a code of chivalry on the nobility alienated many advisers. A conspiracy organised by Peter Ludwig von der Pahlen, Nikita Petrovich Panin and José de Ribas was delayed by de Ribas's death in December 1800. On the night of 23 March 1801 (11 March in the old style) dismissed officers entered his bedroom in the newly completed Saint Michael's Castle, tried to force him to sign an abdication, and strangled and trampled him to death after Nikolay Zubov struck him with a sword. His son Alexander I succeeded him. There is some evidence that Paul was venerated as a saint by Russian Orthodox people, though no Orthodox Church canonised him.
paul-kruger: Stephanus Johannes Paulus Kruger was born on 10 October 1825 at Bulhoek, a farm in the Steynsburg area of the Cape Colony, the third child of the farmer Casper Jan Hendrik Kruger. As a child he took part in the Great Trek. He had almost no education apart from the Bible, which he took literally and knew in large part by heart. He became a burgher at sixteen, settled near Rustenburg and married Maria du Plessis in 1842. As field cornet he took part in the Battle of Dimawe against the Tswana chief Sechele I in 1852, when the Boer commando wrecked David Livingstone's mission at Kolobeng.

A protégé of the Voortrekker leader Andries Pretorius, Kruger witnessed the signing of the Sand River Convention in 1852. In 1863 he was elected Commandant-General, a post he held for a decade. He became vice president in March 1877, shortly before Britain annexed the republic as the Transvaal, and led two deputations to London against the annexation. He was the leading figure in the movement to restore independence, which ended in the Boers' victory in the First Boer War of 1880 to 1881, and he served in an executive triumvirate until he was elected president in 1883.

In 1884 Kruger led a third deputation to London, which secured the London Convention, under which Britain recognised the South African Republic as fully independent. After gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, the uitlanders, mostly British, provided almost all tax revenue but had no vote. This question dominated his presidency, which was renewed in 1888, 1893 and 1898, and led to the Jameson Raid of 1895 to 1896 and the Second Boer War.

He took no part in the fighting, directing the war from Pretoria by telegram. He left South Africa on 11 September 1900, was carried from Mozambique to Marseille on the Dutch warship Gelderland and refused to return after the British victory. He died in Switzerland in 1904, and his body was returned for a state funeral in Pretoria. Admirers see him as a tragic folk hero; critics call him a stubborn defender of an unjust cause and an oppressor of black Africans.
paul-robeson: Robeson was born in Princeton, New Jersey, in 1898, to Reverend William Drew Robeson and Maria Louisa Bustill. His mother belonged to the Bustills, a prominent Quaker family of mixed ancestry. His father was of Igbo origin and had been born into slavery; he escaped from a plantation in his teens and in 1881 became minister of Princeton's Witherspoon Street Presbyterian Church.

In late 1915 Robeson became the third African-American student ever enrolled at Rutgers, and the only one at the time. When he tried out for the football team, teammates played so roughly that his nose was broken and his shoulder dislocated, until the coach, Foster Sanford, announced that he had made the team. He was elected class valedictorian. He studied at New York University School of Law, moved to Columbia Law School in February 1920 and married Eslanda Goode in August 1921. He soon gave up law because of racism.

In December 1924 Robeson won the lead role in Eugene O'Neill's All God's Chillun Got Wings. In 1928 he played Joe in the London production of Show Boat, and the composer Jerome Kern said he had formed the melody of "Ol' Man River" after hearing the organ-like tones of Robeson's speaking voice. In 1933 he starred as Brutus in the film The Emperor Jones, the first film to feature an African American in a starring role.

Robeson saw the struggle against fascism in the Spanish Civil War as a turning point that made him a political activist. He changed the last verse of "Ol' Man River", replacing a fatalistic verse with one of defiance, and in Wales recorded a message that became his epitaph: "The artist must take sides." On 12 June 1956 he appeared before the House Un-American Activities Committee, where he invoked the Fifth Amendment. After his passport was returned in June 1958, he toured Europe, appeared in Othello at Stratford-upon-Avon in April 1959, and in October 1958 became the first black performer to sing at St Paul's Cathedral in London.

Robeson returned to the United States in December 1963 and lived mainly in seclusion. In 1965 he was hospitalised with double pneumonia and a kidney blockage. He died in Philadelphia on 23 January 1976, aged 77, after complications of a stroke, and was buried in Ferncliff Cemetery in Hartsdale, New York.

He was one of the most influential participants in the Harlem Renaissance and brought Negro spirituals into the American mainstream. He was among the first artists to refuse to perform to segregated audiences. The NAACP awarded him its Spingarn Medal in 1945.
paul-the-deacon: Paul was born Winfrid, son of Warnefrid, about 720 in the Duchy of Friuli; Paulus was his monastic name. An ancestor named Leupichis had come to Italy in 568 in the train of Alboin, King of the Lombards, and received lands at or near Cividale del Friuli. During an invasion by the Avars his five sons were carried off to Pannonia, but one of them returned and restored the family's fortunes. Paul's father Warnefrid was his grandson.

Because his family was possibly noble, Paul received an exceptionally good education, probably at the court of the Lombard king Ratchis in Pavia, where a teacher named Flavian taught him the rudiments of Greek. He was probably secretary to Ratchis's successor, Desiderius.

After Desiderius's daughter Adelperga married Arichis II, duke of Benevento, Paul wrote at her request a continuation of Eutropius's Summary of Roman History. He lived at the court of Benevento for at least several years before 774, when Charlemagne captured Pavia. He eventually entered a monastery on Lake Como, and before 782 the great Benedictine house of Monte Cassino, where he made the acquaintance of Charlemagne.

Around 776 his brother Arichis was carried off to Francia as a prisoner after a revolt in Friuli, and Paul wrote to Charlemagne on his behalf, after which Arichis was freed. Paul became an important contributor to the Carolingian Renaissance. In 787 he returned to Monte Cassino, where he died on 13 April, probably in 799.

His chief work is the Historia Langobardorum, an incomplete history in six books written after 787 and no later than 795 or 796. It covers the Lombards from their origins in the north and their migration to Italy in 568 to the death of King Liutprand in 744, and is written from a Lombard point of view. It is especially valuable for the relations between the Franks and the Lombards. Among his sources were the Origo gentis Langobardorum and the Liber pontificalis, and he drew heavily on Bede, Gregory of Tours and Isidore of Seville.

His Historia Romana continues Eutropius down to 553, with extracts from the Scriptures and ecclesiastical historians added because Adelperga complained that Eutropius said nothing of church affairs. At the request of Angilram, Bishop of Metz, he wrote a history of the bishops of Metz to 766, the first work of its kind north of the Alps. He also compiled a collection of homilies for Charlemagne, much used in the Frankish churches.
paul-von-hindenburg: Hindenburg was born on 2 October 1847 in Posen, then in the Kingdom of Prussia, into a family of minor Prussian nobility. He enlisted in the Third Regiment of Foot Guards after his cadet education. In the Austro-Prussian War of 1866 he was knocked unconscious at Königgrätz when a bullet pierced his helmet, but wrapped his head in a towel and resumed command of his detachment.

He served in the Franco-Prussian War as a battalion adjutant and attended the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles on 18 January 1871. He entered the Kriegsakademie in Berlin in 1873, joined the General Staff, rose to lieutenant general in 1900 and retired in 1911.

Living in retirement in Hannover when the First World War began, he was selected on 22 August 1914 to command the German Eighth Army in East Prussia, with Erich Ludendorff as his chief of staff, after the previous commander Maximilian von Prittwitz had panicked. He became a field marshal on 1 November 1914. In February 1915 an attack encircled an entire Russian corps and captured more than 100,000 men in the Second Battle of the Masurian Lakes.

In 1916 he replaced Erich von Falkenhayn as Chief of the Great General Staff. He and Ludendorff used the Kaiser's extensive delegation of authority to the Supreme Army Command to establish a de facto military dictatorship. In 1917 they pressed Chancellor Bethmann Hollweg to accept unrestricted submarine warfare. After the armistice Hindenburg stepped down and retired again in 1919.

After Friedrich Ebert's death on 28 February 1925, the parties of the right chose Hindenburg as their candidate, and he won the second round with the support of the Bavarian People's Party and because the Communists refused to withdraw their candidate. He took office on 12 May 1925.

In March 1930, on the advice of Kurt von Schleicher, he appointed Heinrich Brüning chancellor of a presidential government, which the historian Eberhard Jäckel judged within the letter of the constitution but against its spirit. At 84 he was persuaded to run again in 1932, supported by parties that saw him as the only hope of defeating Hitler.

Opposed to Hitler, he nevertheless reluctantly agreed in January 1933 to appoint him chancellor in a coalition cabinet. After the Reichstag fire of February 1933 he approved the Reichstag Fire Decree, which suspended civil liberties, and he signed the Enabling Act of 1933. He died on 2 August 1934, after which Hitler combined the presidency with the chancellery.
pausanias-geographer: Nothing is known of Pausanias apart from what historians can piece together from his own writing. He was probably born about 110 into a Greek family and was probably a native of Lydia in Asia Minor. From about 150 until his death around 180 he travelled throughout the mainland of Greece, writing about monuments, sacred spaces and significant geographical sites along the way.

He grew up and lived under the rule of the Roman Empire but valued his Greek identity, history and culture. He wished to describe the glories of a Greek past that was still relevant in his lifetime, even though the country was beholden to Rome. His journey through the land of his ancestors was an attempt to establish a place in the world for this new Roman Greece, connecting the myths and stories of ancient culture to those of his own time.

In writing the Description of Greece, called Helládos Periḗgēsis in Greek, Pausanias sought to put together a lasting written account of all things Greek, panta ta hellenika. He wrote from his own observation. Unlike a modern travel guide, he tends to elaborate on a site with a discussion of an ancient ritual or a myth connected with it. He also makes natural history digressions, on the signs that herald an earthquake, the phenomena of the tides, the ice-bound seas of the north, and the fact that at the summer solstice the noonday sun casts no shadow at Syene (Aswan).

His style is straightforward and direct, and his descriptions of works of art are plain and unadorned. Some translators note that his use of prepositions and tenses can be hard to render in English; he sometimes uses a past tense where the present might be expected, which they interpret as an effort to place himself in the same time as his audience. He never doubts the existence of the gods and heroes, but he criticises some myths and legends as differing from earlier traditions that he relates. He is frank about his limits, and where he quotes second-hand information he says so.

Until twentieth-century archaeologists concluded that he was a reliable guide to the sites being excavated, classicists largely dismissed his writings as purely literary. Following Ulrich von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, they tended to regard him as a purveyor of second-hand accounts who had not visited most of the places he described. Modern archaeological research has revealed the accuracy of much of his information, and his writing about Tartessos is aiding present research into its existence, location and culture.
pavlo-skoropadsky: Pavlo Petrovych Skoropadsky was born on 15 May 1873 in Wiesbaden into a noble family that traced its origin to the Zaporozhian Cossacks; one ancestor, Ivan Skoropadsky, was Hetman of the Zaporozhian Host from 1708 to 1722. He spent his first five years in Germany, learned German first, then grew up at Trostianets under his grandfather, who kept Cossack and Ukrainian traditions. Educated at the Page Corps in Saint Petersburg, he became an officer in 1893, fought in the Russo-Japanese War, became aide-de-camp to Nicholas II in 1912 and a lieutenant general in 1916.

In July 1917 Lavr Kornilov ordered him to Ukrainise his 34th Army Corps, which he did reluctantly, and it became the 1st Ukrainian Corps. In October 1917 he was named honorary Otaman at the first Congress of the Free Cossacks. His family had thought of itself as Little Russian, and he preferred the Russian language, which set him apart from many Ukrainian political leaders.

In April 1918 German troops, present in Ukraine under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, carried out a coup against the socialist Ukrainian People's Republic and made Skoropadsky Hetman of Ukraine. He formed a cabinet of mainly Russian speakers, Tsarists and Slavophiles and committed Ukraine to federation with a restored Russian Empire. Some Ukrainian nationalists denounced him as a German collaborator supported by wealthy landowners, and others thought him too pro-Russian. Grain requisitioned violently by German and Austrian troops fuelled rural opposition. His government nevertheless gained credit in certain circles for effective administration, diplomatic ties with many countries, a peace treaty with Soviet Russia and many schools and universities, among them the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine.

After Germany signed an armistice on 11 November 1918, his military and international support was in doubt. An uprising led by Symon Petliura nominally restored the Ukrainian People's Republic under the Directoria, a provisional government of five directors chaired by Volodymyr Vynnychenko, and Skoropadsky signed an abdication document on 14 December 1918.

Skoropadsky went into exile in Germany in 1919, settled in Berlin's Wannsee district and led the Hetmanite movement, refusing in later years all offers to collaborate with the Nazis. In the last weeks of the war in Europe he fled the Soviet advance with the retreating German army and died at Metten Abbey on 26 April 1945 after being wounded in the bombing of Plattling. His movement, which influenced a Ukrainian monarchist programme modelled on the Cossack state, continued into the early 1980s.
paxos: Paxos is the smallest of the seven main Ionian Islands, with an area of 25.3 square kilometres. It lies about 15 kilometres from the southern tip of Corfu and at about the same distance from the mainland town of Parga. With the nearby island of Antipaxos and adjoining islets it is also called Paxi or Paxoi. The island is about 10 kilometres long and up to 3 kilometres wide, stretching north-west to south-east. Much of its hilly landscape is covered in olive groves, running from the harbour community of Lakka in the north through Magazia to Gaios, the main town. The west coast has steep white chalky cliffs with several blue caves.

In Greek mythology Poseidon created the island by striking Corfu with his trident, so that he and his wife Amphitrite could have peace and quiet. According to tradition the Phoenicians were the first settlers, and the name is believed to come from a Phoenician word meaning trapezoidal.

The island has been inhabited since prehistoric times. In 229 BCE, during the First Illyrian War, the Battle of Paxos was fought between Greek and Illyrian fleets, as the historian Polybius records in The Histories. The Romans ruled the island in the 2nd century BCE, and later it fell prey to pirates in the Byzantine era and the Middle Ages, and to crusaders. The Venetians gained control at the end of the 14th century.

During the Napoleonic Wars the Ionian Islands were occupied by the French and by a Russo-Turkish alliance. Paxos surrendered on 13 February 1814 to the Royal Navy frigate HMS Apollo and 160 troops from the 2nd Greek Light Infantry and the 35th Regiment of the Royal Corsican Rangers. The United Kingdom established the United States of the Ionian Islands in 1815, and in 1864, after the coronation of George I of Greece, Paxos and the other Ionian Islands were ceded to Greece.

Olive oil production, soap manufacture and fishing were supplanted by tourism as the main industry in the mid-1960s, which brought a construction boom that greatly altered the coast around Gaios. The municipality has 2,466 inhabitants. Ferries link Gaios with Igoumenitsa on the mainland and with Corfu. The island belongs to the Cultural Village of Europe network and hosts the annual Paxos Festival of young performers, founded by John Gough.
paysandu: The city stands on the banks of the Uruguay River, which forms the border with Argentina. It lies 378 kilometres northwest of Montevideo, at the junction of Route 3 and Route 90. A short distance to the north the General Artigas Bridge links Uruguay with Entre Ríos Province in Argentina, south of Colón.

Paysandú has a humid subtropical climate, with warm to hot summers and cool winters in which frosts and fog occur. Rainfall is spread evenly through the year, though winters are slightly drier, and averages 1,181 mm.

Paysandú was founded in October 1756 and had acquired the status of villa, or town, before the independence of Uruguay. On 8 June 1863 it was raised to the status of ciudad, or city, by Law No. 780. General Leandro Gomez led Uruguayan forces against Brazilian forces that invaded in 1864–1865, and a battle took place on 2 December 1864. The city is known as La Heroica, the Heroic City, for its resistance during the siege.

From the late nineteenth century Paysandú received a significant influx of Italian immigrants, who settled in both urban and rural areas. Many were at first engaged in river transport, trade and agriculture. By the early twentieth century the city had become one of the principal centres of Italian settlement in Uruguay, second only to Montevideo, and various associations and institutions were established to serve the community. By 1992 about 65 per cent of the population of the department was estimated to be of Italian descent. Settlers also came from Switzerland, Poland, Germany, Russia, Ukraine and Belgium.

Paysandú is the capital and most populous city of Paysandú Department, with a population of 81,550 in 2023. Its industries include the Norteña brewery, Azucarlito (sugar), Paylana (woollen fabrics) and Paycuero (leather), and it is the centre of the plantation forest industry in Uruguay, with many companies planting and harvesting eucalyptus. The Uruguay River has recreational beaches, and the city has a centre of the University of the Republic.
peace-of-augsburg: Charles V had issued the Augsburg Interim in 1548, a ruling on the two religious creeds in the empire that he hoped a general council of the Catholic Church would resolve. Its 26 articles largely reflected Catholic practice, though they allowed the clergy to marry and the laity to receive both bread and wine. The Protestant territories resisted and proclaimed their own Interim at Leipzig the following year. In 1552 the Protestant elector Maurice of Saxony and his allies overthrew the Interim by revolt, and the Peace of Passau that summer gave the Lutherans religious freedom, but only until the next imperial Diet, which was called for early 1555.

The treaty was signed at Augsburg on 25 September 1555 and negotiated on the emperor's behalf by his brother Ferdinand. It rested on three principles. The first, cuius regio, eius religio (whose realm, his religion), let a prince choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his domain. Subjects who would not conform had a period in which to emigrate and sell their estates, a new idea in the 16th century, though serfs were in effect excluded from the right.

The second, the reservatum ecclesiasticum, held that if the prelate of an ecclesiastical state changed his religion, its inhabitants did not have to follow; he was expected to resign. The third, the Declaratio Ferdinandei, exempted knights and some cities where the reformed religion had been practised since the mid-1520s. Ferdinand inserted it at the last minute on his own authority, and it was kept secret for almost two decades. Article 17 excluded all who belonged to neither confession, so that Zwinglians and Anabaptists were left without legal recognition, and Calvinism was not recognised either.

The settlement ended the first wave of organised military action between Protestants and Catholics, but it left problems unresolved. The ecclesiastical reservation was tested in the Cologne War of 1583 to 1588, after the prince-archbishop Gebhard Truchsess von Waldburg converted to Protestantism. The Catholic revocation of the Declaratio Ferdinandei in the Edict of Restitution of 1629 helped fuel the Thirty Years' War, and the Peace of Westphalia later forbade rulers to convert their subjects by force and gave serfs the right to emigrate. The Peace has been described as the first step on the road toward a European system of sovereign states. Charles V, meanwhile, abdicated and divided the Habsburg lands between his brother Ferdinand and his son Philip II.
peace-of-pressburg-1805: The treaty followed the French victory over the Russians and Austrians at the Battle of Austerlitz on 2 December 1805. A truce was agreed on 4 December and negotiations began. Johann I Joseph, Prince of Liechtenstein, and the Hungarian Count Ignác Gyulay signed for the Austrian Empire, and Charles Maurice de Talleyrand for France, on 26 December 1805 at Pressburg, today Bratislava. The Holy Roman Emperor Francis II and Napoleon Bonaparte were the principals.

Beyond clauses of peace and amity, the treaty took Austria out of the Third Coalition and required substantial concessions. It repeated the French gains of the earlier treaties of Campo Formio and Lunéville. Recent Austrian acquisitions in Italy and southern Germany were ceded to France and Bavaria. Venetia, Istria and Dalmatia were incorporated into the Kingdom of Italy, of which Napoleon had become king earlier that year, and the Principality of Lucca and Piombino was recognised as independent of the Holy Empire.

Austrian holdings in Swabia passed to the King of Württemberg and the Elector of Baden, while Bavaria received Tyrol and Vorarlberg and the former Free Imperial City of Augsburg. Austrian claims on those German states were renounced without exception. As a minor compensation Austria annexed the Electorate of Salzburg, under Habsburg rule since 1803, and its elector, the emperor's brother, received the Duchy of Würzburg, created from lands of the former prince-bishopric. The treaty also provided for an indemnity of 40 million francs to France.

Francis II recognised the kingly titles assumed by the Electors of Bavaria and Württemberg, which foreshadowed the end of the Holy Roman Empire. Within months, after Napoleon had created the Confederation of the Rhine, Francis II renounced his title as Holy Roman Emperor. Remaining territorial questions, including the establishment of the new border along the Isonzo river, were settled by the Treaty of Fontainebleau on 10 October 1807.
peace-of-riga: The First World War removed state borders across Europe, and the Treaty of Versailles re-established Poland's independence after a century and a half of partition. The Russian Civil War gave Poland, under Józef Piłsudski, a chance to regain parts of the former Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. In 1920 Piłsudski's offensive into Ukraine, meant to establish an independent Ukraine allied to Poland, was met by a Soviet counter-offensive into central Poland, which the Soviets saw as a land bridge to Western Europe. The war culminated in the Battle of Warsaw, won by the Poles, and further setbacks persuaded Soviet Russia to negotiate.

Talks began in Minsk on 17 August 1920 and moved to Riga, where they resumed on 21 September. The chief negotiators were Jan Dąbski for Poland and Adolph Joffe for the Soviet side, and an armistice signed on 12 October took effect on 18 October. Soviet delegates offered substantial territorial concessions, but the Polish delegation, dominated by the National Democrats, preferred a border further west to keep non-Polish minorities below one third of the population. A parliamentary delegation rejected an offer that would have left Minsk on the Polish side.

The treaty has 26 articles. Poland recognised Soviet Ukraine and Belarus and withdrew recognition of the Ukrainian People's Republic, its only ally in the war, which meant giving up Piłsudski's federal programme. The border lay about 250 kilometres east of the Curzon Line and brought large numbers of Ukrainians and Belarusians into the Second Polish Republic. Russia and Soviet Ukraine abandoned claims to lands west of the line. Poland was to receive 30 million gold rubles and railway materials worth 29 million gold rubles, and Russia was to return works of art taken from Polish lands after 1772. Both sides renounced war compensation, and article 7 guaranteed minorities the use of their language and religion.

The Allied Powers, who had backed the Curzon Line, were at first reluctant to recognise a treaty made without them. France, the United Kingdom, Italy and Japan recognised it in March 1923, and the United States in April. In Poland it was criticised from the start; Piłsudski, who took part only as an observer, called it an act of cowardice, and on 15 May 1921 he apologised to Ukrainian soldiers at the internment camp at Kalisz. The treaty contributed to the failure of his plan for a Polish-led federation of Eastern Europe. It lasted until the Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, and a 1945 agreement redefined the borders.
peace-of-westphalia: Europe had been battered by the Thirty Years' War and by the overlapping Eighty Years' War, begun about 1568, in which the Dutch Republic struggled for independence from Spain. The Thirty Years' War, centred on the Holy Roman Empire, killed between 4.5 and 8 million people. The Peace of Prague of 1635 ended most of its religious aspects. Negotiations between France and the Emperor began in Cologne in 1636 but were blocked by Cardinal Richelieu, who insisted on including all his allies. In December 1641 Sweden, France and the Empire agreed a preliminary peace at Hamburg.

The main talks were held in the neighbouring Westphalian cities of Münster and Osnabrück, both kept neutral and demilitarised. The Empire and France negotiated in Catholic Münster, and the Empire and Sweden in Osnabrück, which was held by Protestant forces. A total of 109 delegations took part, but they never met in plenary session; they arrived between 1643 and 1646 and left between 1647 and 1649. The papal nuncio Fabio Chigi and the Venetian envoy Alvise Contarini acted as mediators. Portugal did not take part, because Spain threatened to withdraw.

Two treaties were signed in October 1648: the Treaty of Münster, between the Emperor and France with their allies, and the Treaty of Osnabrück, between the Emperor and Sweden with theirs. The Dutch Republic and Spain signed their own treaty on 30 January 1648.

The settlement recognised Catholicism, Lutheranism and Calvinism, Calvinism receiving legal recognition for the first time. It replaced the principle by which subjects followed their ruler's religion: rulers could no longer dictate the religion of their subjects, and 1 January 1624 was fixed as the normal year for deciding a state's official religion. France kept the bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun and received the cities of the Décapole in Alsace, except Strasbourg, and Pignerol. Sweden received an indemnity of five million thalers, Western Pomerania, Wismar and the Prince-Bishoprics of Bremen and Verden, which gave it a seat in the Imperial Diet. France and Sweden became guarantors of the imperial constitution.

Pope Innocent X condemned the settlement in the brief Zelo Domus Dei as null, void and unjust. Some terms were ambiguous: The Swedish-Brandenburg border in Pomerania was settled only in 1653. Many scholars of international relations see the Peace as the origin of Westphalian sovereignty, but some historians argue that this view emerged in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Older accounts say the Emperor was stripped of power, but modern research holds that he kept significant influence, for example in the Imperial Diet.
peanut: The genus Arachis is native to South America, east of the Andes, around Peru, Bolivia, Argentina and Brazil. The cultivated peanut, Arachis hypogaea, arose from a hybrid between two wild species, thought to be Arachis duranensis and Arachis ipaensis. The first hybrid would have been sterile, but spontaneous chromosome doubling restored its fertility. Genetic analysis suggests the hybridisation happened only once, giving rise to a wild form found in a few places in north-western Argentina, and by artificial selection to the cultivated plant.

Domestication made the plant bushier and more compact, with a different pod structure and larger seeds. Cultivation spread from its centre of origin and formed further centres of diversity in Peru, Ecuador, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. The oldest known remains of pods, about 7,600 years old, were found in Peru, where dry conditions preserve organic material; cultivation almost certainly began earlier in the moister centre of origin.

The peanut is a legume grown mainly for its seeds, which are held in pods that develop underground, a trait called geocarpy and unusual among legumes. After fertilisation a short stalk grows into the soil, and the fruit ripens there. Botanically the pods are not nuts. Like other legumes, peanuts harbour nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules, which improve soil fertility and make them valuable in crop rotation.

The seeds yield oil and are eaten roasted, boiled or ground into peanut butter and sauces. Peanut sauces are used in Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, and in the Indian subcontinent peanuts are made into chikki, a sweet brittle. The plant tops are used for silage and the oilcake left after pressing is fed to livestock. Between 1.4 and 2 per cent of people in Europe and the United States experience allergic reactions to peanuts, which can be fatal.

Many pre-Columbian cultures, such as the Moche, depicted peanuts in their art, and cultivation was well established in Mesoamerica before the Spanish arrived. The conquistadors found the plant, called tlālcacahuatl in Nahuatl, on sale in the marketplace of Tenochtitlan. European traders later spread it across the tropics and subtropics. In West Africa it substantially replaced the Bambara groundnut, another legume whose pods ripen underground.

In the United States peanuts were introduced in the colonial period and grown as a garden crop; from 1870 they served as animal feed until human consumption grew in the 1930s. George Washington Carver promoted the peanut in the American South, where repeated cotton planting had depleted the soil. Marcellus Gilmore Edson of Montreal patented a process for making peanut butter in 1884, and it became well known after the Beech-Nut company sold it at the St. Louis World's Fair in 1904.
pearl-river: The Pearl River, in Chinese Zhujiang, is an extensive river system in southern China. The name is also used for the watersheds of its tributaries in Guangdong, the Xi, Bei and Dong rivers, which all flow into the South China Sea through the Pearl River Delta. Measured from the furthest reaches of the Xi River, the system of the Pearl, Xi, Xun, Qian, Hongshui and Nanpan rivers is 2,400 kilometres long. It is China's third-longest river system after the Yangtze and the Yellow River, and its second largest by volume after the Yangtze.

The Pearl River Basin covers 453,700 square kilometres. It drains most of Guangdong and Guangxi, which together are known as Liangguang, as well as parts of Yunnan, Guizhou, Hunan and Jiangxi, and the northernmost parts of Cao Bằng and Lạng Sơn provinces in Vietnam. The name Pearl River is also given to one branch within the delta, the widest distributary but a short one, which is first so called just north of Guangzhou. The name comes from the pearl-coloured shells lying in the riverbed where it flows through Guangzhou.

Its mouth forms a large bay in the south-east of the delta, the Pearl River Estuary, where the Bocca Tigris separates Shiziyang in the north from Lingdingyang in the south, and Jiuzhouyang at the southern tip is surrounded by the Wanshan Archipelago. The bay separates Macau and Zhuhai from Hong Kong and Shenzhen, and the Bocca Tigris is regularly dredged to keep it open to ocean vessels. Cities on the river system include Liuzhou, Guilin, Nanning, Wuzhou, Zhaoqing, Foshan, Dongguan and Zhongshan, as well as Guangzhou, Hong Kong, Macau, Shenzhen and Zhuhai.
peasants-revolt: The Black Death reached England in 1348 and killed an estimated half of the population. Labour became scarce, labourers could charge more for their work, wages rose sharply and the profits of landowners were eroded. Some people were still unfree serfs who owed work on their lords' land, though serfdom was relatively rare in the south-east. The war with France that Edward III began in 1337 put the English armies under heavy financial pressure by the 1370s, and Edward's grandson Richard II came to the throne in 1377 aged ten. London was also unsettled, with riots in 1377 over John of Gaunt and resentment of Flemish weavers and of the expanding royal courts.

The trigger was the arrival of the royal official John Bampton in Essex on 30 May 1381 to investigate unpaid poll taxes. At Brentwood he met representatives of nearby villages, and when he tried to arrest Thomas Baker of Fobbing, violence broke out and three of his clerks were killed. The revolt spread quickly across the south-east. People from many walks of rural society, including artisans and village officials, burned court records and opened prisons. They wanted lower taxes, an end to serfdom and the removal of the king's senior officials. Inspired by the sermons of the cleric John Ball and led by Wat Tyler, Kentish rebels advanced on London.

King Richard, then aged 14, withdrew to the Tower of London, since most royal forces were abroad or in the north. On 13 June the rebels crossed London Bridge and entered the city, where they attacked prisons, destroyed the Savoy Palace and burned law books in the Temple. The next day Richard met them at Mile End and agreed to most demands, including the abolition of serfdom, while rebels entered the Tower and killed Simon Sudbury, the Lord Chancellor, and Robert Hales, the Lord High Treasurer. Wat Tyler died on 15 June. Elsewhere, John Wrawe raised Suffolk, and Henry Despenser, Bishop of Norwich, defeated the rebel leader Geoffrey Litster at North Walsham in June.

On 30 June the king ordered serfs to return to their former service, and on 2 July the charters signed under pressure were formally revoked. Parliament met in November and blamed the revolt on greedy royal officials, kept the labour laws and asked for changes in the royal council. General pardons followed, with exceptions such as the men of Bury St Edmunds. The name Peasants' Revolt was not used by chroniclers, who were hostile to the rebels; many rebels were not peasants but artisans and village officials, and no sympathetic contemporary account survives. The revolt deterred later Parliaments from raising more taxes for the war in France.
pec: The city lies in the Rugova region on the eastern section of the Accursed Mountains, beside the Lumbardh of Peja, a tributary of the White Drin. The Serbian name Peć comes from the South Slavic word for cave, pećina, after nearby caves, while the Albanian name is Peja. In Ottoman times it was İpek, and other names include the Latin Pescium and the Greek Episkion, meaning Episcopal City. The medieval city was possibly built on the ruins of Siparant(um), a Roman municipium, and settlements in the region date back to the Paleolithic period.

After Slavic settlement in the 6th century the Byzantine Empire and the First Bulgarian Empire fought for control of the area until it fell under Serbian rule. Between 1180 and 1190 the Serbian Grand Prince Stefan Nemanja annexed Peja and its district of Hvosno from the Byzantine Empire. After the monastery of Žiča was burned by the Cumans in the 1290s, the seat of the Serbian archbishop moved to the Patriarchal Monastery of Peć. Under Emperor Stefan Dušan the city became a major religious centre, the seat of the Serbian Orthodox Church from 1346 until the Serbian Patriarchate of Peć was abolished in 1766.

The town passed to Ottoman rule after its capture in 1455 and became the centre of the Sanjak of İpek, whose first sanjakbey was the Albanian Mahmud Pasha Dukagjini. The Ottoman tax register of 1582 lists 158 households, only 15 of them Christian. In 1688 Peja became the seat of the Pashalik of Peja under Mahmut Pasha of Begolli, whose family governed the region until the pashalik was disbanded between 1821 and 1831. The League of Peja, led by Haxhi Zeka, was founded in 1899 to defend the rights of Ottoman Albanians and ended its operations after an armed clash with Ottoman forces in 1900.

Montenegro took the city on 28 October 1912 during the First Balkan War. Austria-Hungary held it from 8 January 1916, and Serbian forces retook it on 13 October 1918, after which it became part of Yugoslavia. It was part of Zeta Banovina from 1931 to 1941. In the Kosovo War the city suffered heavy damage and mass killings, and more than 80 percent of its houses were damaged or destroyed.

The Patriarchal Monastery of Peć is a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of the Medieval Monuments in Kosovo. The city also keeps Ottoman buildings, among them the Bajrakli Mosque, the hamam and the bazaar, and the 18th-century home of Tahir Beg, which houses the Ethnographic Museum. The municipality had 82,745 inhabitants in the census of 2024. The Rugova Gorge, entered through the north-west of the city, became a national park in 2013.
pechenegs: The Pechenegs were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who spoke the Pecheneg language, which died out centuries ago and is poorly documented. Medieval authors knew them by many names, among them Patzinakoi in Byzantine Greek and Bajanak in Arabic and Persian texts. Mahmud Kashgari described them in the 11th century as a branch of the Oghuz Turks. Omeljan Pritsak places their homeland between the Aral Sea and the middle Syr Darya.

After the Turkic Khaganate collapsed in 744, the Oghuz, allied with the Karluks and Kimaks, defeated them near the Aral Sea before 850 and most Pechenegs migrated towards the Volga. The Khazars and Oghuz then attacked them again, and they moved west, expelling the Hungarians from lands along the Kuban and the upper Donets.

By the 9th and 10th centuries the Pechenegs controlled much of the steppes of south-eastern Europe and the Crimean Peninsula. Byzantium allied with them against other steppe peoples, and Tsar Simeon I of Bulgaria employed them against the Magyars, whom they drove west of the Dnieper by 892. For more than two centuries they raided the lands of Rus', sometimes in full wars, as in 920, but Rus' and Pecheneg forces also allied at times, as in the Byzantine campaign of 943.

In 968 they besieged Kiev. Some joined Prince Sviatoslav I on his Byzantine campaign of 970 to 971, but they ambushed and killed him in 972, and according to the Primary Chronicle their khan Kurya made a chalice of his skull.

Vladimir I of Kiev defeated them and founded Pereyaslav on the site, and Yaroslav I the Wise defeated them in 1036, after which Cumans and Torks replaced them in the Pontic steppe. At the Battle of Levounion in 1091 a combined Byzantine and Cuman army under Alexios I Komnenos destroyed them as an independent force, and Byzantium defeated them again at Beroia in 1122.

Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos lists eight Pecheneg tribal groupings, four on each side of the Dnieper, divided into 40 sub-tribes, probably clans, each under a great prince. Three of the eight, the Erdim, Čur and Yula, formed the Kangars and were thought more valiant and noble than the rest. After 1091 Alexios I settled defeated Pechenegs in the district of Moglena in a unit of their own. South of the Danube they lost their identity and became assimilated, mostly with Romanians and Bulgarians, and around 150 villages of Pechenegs settled in the Hungarian kingdom.
pecs: Pécs lies in the Carpathian Basin in the centre of Baranya, close to the border with Croatia. The Mecsek hills border it to the north and a rolling plain to the south, and the city has a significant mining past. The oldest archaeological finds in the area are about 6,000 years old, and before the Romans arrived it was inhabited by Celts.

The Roman name Sopianae possibly comes from the plural of a Celtic word, sop, meaning marsh. The Hungarian name Pécs most likely derives from a Proto-Slavic or Illyrian word meaning five, echoing the medieval Latin names Quinque Basilicae and Quinque Ecclesiae, which refer to five churches.

The Romans founded Sopianae at the beginning of the 2nd century, in an area peopled by Celts and Pannoni tribes, as one of several wine-producing colonies in the province of Pannonia. When Pannonia was divided into four administrative divisions, Sopianae became the capital of the division named Valeria. Charlemagne arrived in 791, when the Avars ruled the area, and annexed it to the Holy Roman Empire. A document written in Salzburg in 871 gives the first mention of the medieval city, as Quinque Basilicae.

Although the county's seat was the nearby castle of Baranyavár, Pécs became an important religious centre. Stephen I founded the Roman Catholic Diocese of Pécs in 1009, and Louis I the Great founded the first university in Hungary there in 1367. After the Battle of Mohács in 1526 the armies of Suleiman occupied the city, and its centuries of Ottoman rule left the largest number of Turkish Ottoman buildings in Central Europe.

The first census, ordered by Joseph II in 1787, counted 8,853 residents. In 1777 Queen Maria Theresa had raised Pécs to the rank of free royal town, at a cost to the city of 83,315 forints. Industry grew in the second half of the 19th century, with iron and paper factories, coal mining and, after 1867, railways to Barcs and, from 1882, to Budapest.

Pécs is the administrative and economic centre of Baranya County and the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Pécs. The Early Christian Necropolis of Pécs, Roman tombs and mausoleums from around the 4th century, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2000. The city also keeps the Gazi Kasim Mosque, consecrated as a church after the Ottoman retreat, a cathedral of the 11th century and a Bishop's Palace of the 12th. It is known for the Zsolnay porcelain that decorates many of its buildings, and the University of Pécs, the oldest in Hungary, remains based there.
pedanius-dioscorides: Dioscorides was a native of Anazarbus in Cilicia, in Asia Minor. He probably studied medicine nearby at the school in Tarsus, which had a pharmacological emphasis, and he dedicated his medical books to Laecanius Arius, a medical practitioner there. He wrote that he had lived a soldier's life, but his work refers almost solely to plants found in the Greek-speaking eastern Mediterranean, which suggests that he accompanied military campaigns or travelled as a civilian, though less widely than is sometimes supposed. The name Pedanius is Roman, and may indicate that an aristocrat of that name sponsored him to become a Roman citizen.

Between 50 and 70 CE Dioscorides wrote De materia medica, in Greek Peri hules iatrikes, a work in five volumes that became the precursor of all modern pharmacopoeias. It presents about 600 plants, and it also records the Dacian, Thracian, Roman, ancient Egyptian and North African names of some plants, names that would otherwise have been lost. Its descriptions are sometimes obscurely phrased, and some of its botanical identifications remain guesses. It is the chief historical source for the medicines used by the Greeks, Romans and other peoples of antiquity.

Unlike many classical authors, Dioscorides was not rediscovered in the Renaissance, because his book never left circulation; in Western materia medica it eclipsed the Hippocratic corpus into the early modern period. In the medieval period it circulated in Greek, Latin and Arabic, and manuscripts were often supplemented with commentary and additions from Arabic and Indian sources. The commentary of Ibn al-Baitar has helped scholars identify many of the plants.

The best-known illustrated copy is the Vienna Dioscurides, made in Constantinople in 512 or 513. Densely illustrated Arabic copies survive from the 12th and 13th centuries, and Greek manuscripts survive in the monasteries of Mount Athos. John Goodyer translated the work into English in 1655, and it was published by Oxford University Press in 1934. It formed the core of the European pharmacopoeia through the 19th century, and Linnaeus named the plant genus Dioscorea, which includes the yam, after him.
pedro-alvares-cabral: Pedro Álvares de Gouveia was born in 1467 or 1468, the former year being the more likely, at Belmonte in central Portugal. He was a son of Fernão Álvares Cabral and Isabel Gouveia, one of five boys and six girls. Little is certain about his life before 1500. He began to use his father's surname only later, supposedly after his elder brother's death in 1503.

On 15 February 1500 Cabral was appointed capitão-mor of a fleet bound for India, following Vasco da Gama's newly opened route around Africa. The aim was to return with spices and to open trade, bypassing the monopoly of Arab, Turkish and Italian merchants. The fleet of 13 ships left Lisbon on 9 March 1500. On 23 March a nau commanded by Vasco de Ataíde, with 150 men, disappeared without trace. The fleet then sailed far to the west, and on 22 April 1500 anchored near what Cabral named Monte Pascoal, on the eastern coast of present-day Brazil.

Cabral at first took the land for a large island, but after following its coast he became convinced it was a continent. It lay within the Portuguese sphere under the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494, and he claimed it for the Crown, sending a ship to inform King Manuel I. Around 5 May the fleet turned east. A storm in the South Atlantic on 23 or 24 May cost four ships, among them one commanded by Bartolomeu Dias, and 380 men.

At Calicut, reached on 13 September, Cabral negotiated with the Zamorin and obtained permission to set up a factory. On 16 or 17 December the factory was attacked by some 300 Arabs and Indians, or by several thousand according to other accounts, and more than 50 Portuguese were killed. Cabral looted and burned the Arab fleet and bombarded the city. He then allied with the ruler of Cochin, loaded spices, and set out for Portugal on 16 January 1501.

Manuel I chose Cabral to command a fleet to avenge the losses at Calicut, but he was relieved for reasons that remain uncertain, possibly because he opposed giving Vicente Sodré independent command of part of it. Vasco da Gama led the fleet that left in March 1502. Cabral left the court for good, and few records of his later life survive. His voyage was little remembered for over 300 years, until Emperor Pedro II of Brazil sponsored research on it from the 1840s.
pedro-calderon-de-la-barca: Calderón was born in Madrid on 17 January 1600 into the minor nobility. His father, Diego Calderón, a mountain hidalgo, held the post of secretary of the Council and Chief Accounting Office of the Treasury and served the Habsburg kings Philip II and Philip III. His mother, Ana González de Henao, had family roots in the Spanish Netherlands.

She died in 1610, when Pedro was ten. He was educated at the Jesuit Colegio Imperial in Madrid with a view to taking orders, but studied law at Salamanca instead. He also served as a soldier and became a knight of the Order of Santiago before he turned to the priesthood.

His theatrical debut was a history play about King Edward III of England, first performed on 29 June 1623 at the Royal Alcázar of Madrid, during the surprise visit of Charles, Prince of Wales, who had come to negotiate a marriage alliance with the Spanish Habsburgs. Born while Lope de Vega was still defining the unwritten rules of Golden Age theatre, Calderón initiated what has been called the second cycle of that theatre. Lope pioneered its forms and genres, and Calderón polished and perfected them. He wrote 120 comedias, 80 autos sacramentales and 20 short comedic pieces called entremeses.

Because his plays were usually produced at the court of the King of Spain, he had access to the most modern scenography and worked with Cosme Lotti on complex stage effects, notably in the autos sacramentales. These one-act allegorical plays, performed in the open air during the feast of Corpus Christi after the procession of the Host, usually treat the miracle of Transubstantiation.

Calderón took special care with dramatic structure, using fewer scenes than Lope and fewer metres, and often revisited and reworked his plays long after they were first staged. He made regular use of metafictional devices, having characters joke about the clichés they are expected to follow.

His cape-and-sword comedies have intricate plots worked out with great precision, and his honour tragedies confront reason with emotion, intellect with instinct and love with vengeance, themes shaped by his Jesuit education and his admiration for Thomas Aquinas and Francisco Suárez. His masterpiece, La vida es sueño, asks whether each person's fate is already written or whether free will can alter the future.

His reputation fell in the 18th century, and in 1765 a law forbade performance of the autos on Corpus Christi as sacrilegious and in bad taste. August Wilhelm Schlegel's translations then revived him as a banner figure of German Romanticism. His plays were also translated and performed in English in his lifetime: Samuel Pepys saw free translations from Calderón in London in 1667, and Percy Bysshe Shelley later translated a large part of El mágico prodigioso.
pedro-de-alvarado: Pedro de Alvarado was born in 1485 in Badajoz, Extremadura, the son of Gómez de Alvarado and Leonor de Contreras. Little is known of his youth, and tales of his exploits in Spain that became popular legends are of doubtful truth. He and his brothers crossed the Atlantic before 1511, and he soon befriended Hernán Cortés in Santo Domingo. He took part in the conquest of Cuba, became a prosperous hacienda owner and in 1518 captained a ship in Juan de Grijalva's expedition along the coasts of Yucatán. In 1519 he joined Cortés's expedition to Mexico. The Aztecs called him Tōnatiuh, because of his blond hair and his temper.

Cortés sent Alvarado to invade Guatemala with 180 cavalry, 300 infantry, four cannons and thousands of allied Mexican warriors. The Kaqchikel lords received the Spanish at Iximche on 14 April 1524 and supplied soldiers against the K'iche' and the Tz'utujil. On 27 July 1524 Alvarado declared Iximche the first capital of Guatemala.

He soon demanded 1,000 gold leaves from the Kaqchikel kings, and the Kaqchikel fled their city on 28 August 1524. War followed, and the kings did not surrender until 9 May 1530. On the Pacific plain Alvarado defeated the Pipil near Izcuintepeque and burned the town, and in 1529 he was accused of excessive brutality there. In Cuzcatlan the Pipil defeated him and wounded him in the left thigh, and his brother Gonzalo de Alvarado completed the conquest by 1528.

In December 1527 the king named him governor of Guatemala and adelantado. Historians judge that greed drove him to excessive cruelty, and his Spanish contemporaries denounced his brutality. He resisted the Crown's efforts to set up orderly taxation in Guatemala.

In 1541 Alvarado had assembled 13 ships and about 550 soldiers for an expedition to China and the Spice Islands. Cristóbal de Oñate then asked for help against the Mixtón revolt in Nueva Galicia, and Alvarado went to relieve him at Nochistlán. A horse that had been spooked crushed him, and he died a few days later, on 4 July 1541. Decades later his daughter Leonor de Alvarado Xicoténcatl had his remains moved to the cathedral at Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala, now Antigua Guatemala. After his death his widow Beatriz de la Cueva was elected governor of Guatemala, the only woman to govern a major division of the Americas in Spanish colonial times.
pedro-de-valdivia: Pedro de Valdivia is believed to have been born in Villanueva de la Serena in Extremadura, to an impoverished hidalgo family. In 1520 he joined the royalist army of Charles I in the Revolt of the Comuneros, then fought in Flanders in 1521 and in Italy between 1522 and 1527, including the Battle of Pavia. He was involved in the sack of Rome in May 1527. He sailed to South America in 1535, spent a year in present-day Venezuela and went to Peru in 1537, where he sided with Francisco Pizarro against Diego de Almagro at the Battle of Las Salinas in 1538. As a reward he received an encomienda with a silver mine at Potosí, which made him rich.

Valdivia asked Pizarro for permission to conquer the lands south of Peru and was appointed lieutenant governor. He sold his lands and mine to finance the expedition, and in December 1539 signed a partnership with Pedro Sánchez de la Hoz. The expedition left Cuzco in January 1540 with 150 Spaniards, about 1,000 Peruvian auxiliaries and a few African slaves, together with Inés de Suárez, and crossed the Atacama Desert. He founded Santiago de la Nueva Extremadura on 12 February 1541, at the foot of the Huelén hill. After Pizarro was murdered in 1541, the town council made him governor, and he removed Chile from Peruvian control, acknowledging only royal authority.

On 11 September 1541 people led by Michimalonco attacked Santiago while Valdivia was away; Inés de Suárez led the defence, and the city was destroyed. He rebuilt it, and La Serena was founded under his orders. In 1546 he reached the Biobío River, and returned to Peru in 1547 to join the royal army against Gonzalo Pizarro. Tried in Lima on charges of tyranny and public immorality, he was confirmed as governor in 1549. He founded Concepción on 5 October 1550, and La Imperial, Valdivia, Angol and Villarrica in 1551 and 1552. His twelve letters to Charles I survive.

In December 1553 Mapuche forces under Lautaro, who had been Valdivia's page, destroyed the fort at Tucapel. Valdivia rode there and was routed at the Battle of Tucapel, since the Mapuche had learned to counter cavalry with pikes. He was captured and killed. Contemporary chroniclers gave different accounts; Diego de Rosales, who spoke with several Mapuche, described a ritual killing in front of a crowd.
His career and death are chronicled in Alonso de Ercilla's epic poem La Araucana. Valdivia never permanently subdued the Mapuche, whose resistance in the Arauco War continued after his death.
pedro-i-of-brazil: Pedro was born on 12 October 1798 at the Queluz Royal Palace near Lisbon, the fourth child of John VI of Portugal and Carlota Joaquina, of the House of Braganza. In late November 1807, when he was nine, the royal family fled a French army sent by Napoleon and reached Rio de Janeiro in March 1808. He preferred physical pursuits to the classroom: he trained horses, worked wood and became an able composer under Marcos Portugal, later writing Brazil's Independence Anthem.

The Liberal Revolution of 1820 forced John VI back to Portugal in April 1821, leaving Pedro to rule Brazil as regent. On 5 June 1821 Portuguese troops under Jorge Avilez mutinied, and Pedro rode out alone to negotiate, warning that it was the last time he would yield under pressure.

The Portuguese government threatened to revoke the autonomy Brazil had enjoyed since 1808, and Pedro chose the Brazilian side, declaring independence on 7 September 1822. He was acclaimed emperor on his 24th birthday, 12 October, and crowned on 1 December. He had to force several provinces to submit, and the last Portuguese holdouts surrendered in early 1824. He then crushed the Confederation of the Equator, a failed secession in the northeast.

A rebellion in the southern province of Cisplatina in 1825, backed by the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, led to the Cisplatine War, and Brazil lost the province in 1828. In March 1826 Pedro briefly became King of Portugal as Pedro IV before abdicating in favour of his daughter Maria II, whose throne his brother Miguel usurped in 1828. His affair with Domitila de Castro damaged his reputation, and from 1826 to 1831 he struggled with parliament over whether ministers were chosen by the monarch or the legislature.

On 7 April 1831 Pedro abdicated in favour of his son Pedro II and sailed for Europe. He took the title Duke of Braganza and in July 1832 invaded Portugal at the head of an army, in a conflict that became a struggle between liberals and absolutists across the Iberian Peninsula. He died of tuberculosis on 24 September 1834, a few months after the liberals had triumphed.

He is known in Brazil as the Liberator. The liberal leader Evaristo da Veiga, one of his harshest critics, wrote after his death that Brazil and Portugal owed him much of their freedom and their representative government.
pedro-ii-of-brazil: Pedro was born on 2 December 1825 in the Palace of São Cristóvão in Rio de Janeiro, the seventh child of Emperor Pedro I and Empress Maria Leopoldina, a daughter of Francis II, the last Holy Roman Emperor. His father's abdication and departure for Europe in 1831 left the five-year-old prince as emperor and began a regency marked by political instability. Pedro I chose José Bonifácio de Andrada as guardian, and the governess Mariana de Verna, whom the boy called Dadama, was a surrogate mother to him.

Ending the regency brought stability, though a group of courtiers led by Aureliano Coutinho gained influence over the shy young emperor. Between 1848 and 1852 he faced three crises. Illegal slave imports, banned in 1826 under a treaty with the United Kingdom, continued, and a British act of 1845 allowed British warships to seize Brazilian ships involved in the trade. The Praieira revolt in Pernambuco began on 6 November 1848 and was put down by March 1849. The Eusébio de Queirós Law of 4 September 1850 gave the government wide powers against the slave trade, and by 1852 Britain accepted that it had been suppressed.

In the 1850s Pedro advanced a program of conciliação, to reduce partisanship, and melhoramentos, material developments, as railways, the telegraph and steamship lines linked the country. He was also a patron of learning and in March 1840 became the first Brazilian photographer. The Paraguayan War, which began in 1864 when Paraguay invaded Mato Grosso, lasted five years, and he devoted his energy to raising troops and warships, warning in 1866 that the war must end as honour demanded, whatever the cost.

He travelled to Europe in 1871 and to the United States in 1876, where the press called him the Yankee Emperor. In 1887 poor health took him to Europe, and in Milan on 22 May 1888 he learned that slavery had been abolished in Brazil.

In 1889 Pedro was overthrown in a coup led mainly by military elites who favoured a republic. Unwilling to provoke civil conflict, he accepted exile. His wife, Teresa Cristina, died three weeks after they reached Europe, and he lived modestly at Cannes and then in Paris. He never supported a restoration. He died of pneumonia on 5 December 1891. Historians have attributed the fall of the monarchy chiefly to his own indifference to its fate, and later historians have ranked him highly among Brazilian rulers.
pehr-evind-svinhufvud: Pehr Evind Svinhufvud af Qvalstad was born in Sääksmäki into a Finland-Swedish noble family that had been ennobled in Sweden in 1574 and introduced to the Finnish House of Nobility in 1818. His father, a sea captain, drowned off Greece in 1863. After his grandfather's death in 1866 he moved to Helsinki with his mother and sister, studied at the Imperial Alexander University and took a Master of Laws degree in 1886. He worked as a lawyer and judge and sat in the Estate of Nobles in the Diet of Finland.

When Imperial Russia began its Russification policy in 1899, Svinhufvud became a central figure in the legal resistance. In 1902 the Turku Court of Appeal began proceedings against Governor-General Bobrikov, who answered by dismissing sixteen of its officials, Svinhufvud among them. He was elected to the new Parliament in 1906 and was its Speaker from 1907 to 1912; his opening speeches on legality led the Tsar to dissolve Parliament in 1909 and 1910. In November 1914 he was exiled to Tomsk in Siberia after refusing the orders of a Russian procurator, and he returned after the February Revolution.

He became Chairman of the Senate on 27 November 1917. With Carl Enckell and Gustaf Idman he went to Saint Petersburg, where the Soviet government agreed to recognise Finnish independence at the end of December. During the Finnish Civil War he led the White government while Mannerheim commanded its armies, and he pardoned 36,000 Red prisoners in the autumn of 1918. Named Regent in May 1918, he travelled to Berlin to ask Wilhelm II to allow Prince Oskar to become king; the monarchy was for him a means of securing German support. After Germany's defeat he stepped down in favour of Mannerheim.

After the war he withdrew from public life and took up the Civil Guard and competitive shooting. Prime minister from 1930 on the insistence of the Lapua Movement, he won the presidential election of 1931 by 151 votes to 149 against Ståhlberg. In February 1932 he ended the Mäntsälä Rebellion with a radio speech calling on the rebels to surrender. He left most foreign policy to his foreign ministers, and in 1937 the Social Democrats and the Agrarian party voted against him.

Svinhufvud died at Luumäki in 1944. He is praised for his commitment to legality under Russian rule and for his firm handling of the Mäntsälä Rebellion, and criticised for one-sided political activity and for relying wholly on Germany in 1918. Known to many as Ukko-Pekka, or Old Man Pekka, he was widely popular. A statue by the sculptor Wäinö Aaltonen was erected outside the Parliament House in 1961.
peisistratus: Peisistratus came from the deme of Philaidae near Brauron in eastern Attica, and his father was Hippocrates. He first became known as an Athenian general who captured the port of Nisaea in Megara in about 565 BCE, which broke a trade blockage that had contributed to food shortages in Athens. After Solon left Athens the city remained divided, and Aristotle reports three factions based on geography and economics: the Plains, led by Lycurgus, the Coast, led by Megacles, and the men of the Highlands, who backed Peisistratus. They included the poor, recent immigrants who feared losing citizenship, and lenders who were denied the ability to collect their debts.

His first period of power began in 561 BCE and lasted about five years, until the Plains and the Coast joined forces to expel him. Megacles then invited him back on condition that he marry Megacles's daughter. According to Herodotus, a tall woman named Phye was dressed as Athena and driven in a chariot to announce that the goddess was bringing him back to her acropolis. The alliance broke down because Peisistratus would not have children by his new wife, and he went into a second exile of about ten years.

He settled near Mount Pangaeus, where nearby gold and silver mines paid for mercenaries. With the help of allies including the Thebans and Lygdamis of Naxos, he returned and held power from 546 BCE until his death, the longest of his three periods.

In this last period he built on Solon's economic work. He revived olive production and lent money to peasants for land and tools, funded by a tax on agricultural production that Aristotle puts at ten percent. He sent judges round the countryside to try cases on the spot. He had the Iliad and Odyssey copied in a permanent version and increased the visibility of the Panathenaic festival, which added recitations of Homeric poems and athletic competitions. Abroad he made allies in the Aegean, and installed Miltiades the Elder in the Thracian Chersonese.

His eldest son Hippias succeeded him. In 514 BCE Harmodius and Aristogeiton plotted against the brothers, but only Hipparchus was killed. Hippias then ruled more harshly, and the Alcmaeonids helped bring about his removal when the Spartans liberated Athens in 510 BCE. Hippias and the other Pisistratids were exiled and given safe passage to Sigeion. Peisistratus's unification of Attica and his economic and cultural improvements are seen as having laid groundwork for the later pre-eminence of Athens.
peking-university: After China's defeat in the Sino-Japanese War, intellectuals including Kang Youwei, Liang Qichao and Yan Fu called for reform of the education system. On 11 June 1898 the Guangxu Emperor authorised the Imperial University of Peking, called in Chinese Jingshi Daxuetang, as part of the Hundred Days' Reform. It was formally established on 3 July 1898, when the emperor approved the charter written by Liang. William Alexander Parsons Martin was its first president. Most of the reforms were abolished when the Empress Dowager Cixi seized power on 21 September, but the university survived with reduced scope. It opened on 31 December with 160 students instead of the 500 planned, teaching mathematics, astronomy, physics, botany and zoology.

After the Xinhai Revolution the Imperial University was renamed the Government University of Peking in 1912 and the National University of Peking in 1919. Cai Yuanpei was appointed president on 26 December 1917. Inspired by the German model of academic freedom, he introduced faculty governance and democratic management. The university became the country's largest institution of higher learning, with 14 departments and more than 2,000 students. He recruited figures of the New Culture Movement, among them Hu Shih, Li Dazhao, Chen Duxiu and Lu Xun, while conservatives such as Gu Hongming also taught there.

On 1 May 1919 students learned that the Treaty of Versailles would allow Japan to take over Germany's rights in Shandong province. On 4 May students from thirteen universities marched to Tiananmen, demanding that the Beiyang government refuse to sign and that three officials who they believed cooperated with Japan be dismissed. Strikes and boycotts of Japanese goods spread to China's major cities, and the government released arrested students, dismissed the three officials and did not sign the treaty. During the Second World War, from 1938 to 1946, its staff joined those of Tsinghua and Nankai universities in the National Southwestern Associated University at Kunming.

In 1952, after the founding of the People's Republic, the university merged with Yenching University in a nationwide restructuring of universities, and in April 2000 Beijing Medical University was merged into it. It now has eight faculties and six affiliated hospitals, and a Shenzhen Graduate School opened in 2001. The main campus in Haidian stands on the former site of Qing dynasty imperial gardens and keeps traditional Chinese landscaping, including pagodas and Weiming Lake. The American architect Talbot Hamlin designed some of the buildings put up between 1919 and 1922. Tu Youyou, an alumna, was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2015.
pelagius-of-asturias: Pelagius was born around 685, but the details of his early life are largely unknown. He was traditionally depicted with Visigothic origin, though recent scholarship increasingly supports the idea that he was a nobleman of Hispano-Roman descent, linked to the local Asturian elite. He is believed to be the son of Favila. The Chronica Albeldense, written three centuries after his death, says Favila was a dux of Gallaecia killed by the Visigothic king Wittiza, while the Chronicle of Alfonso III calls Pelagius a grandson of Chindasuinth and says his father was blinded in Córdoba at Wittiza's instigation. Both agree that Wittiza exiled him from Toledo.

A later tradition tells of Munuza, the Berber governor of Iegione, who was attracted to Pelagius's sister and sent word to Tariq ibn Ziyad, who ordered Pelagius captured and sent to Córdoba. If Munuza's seat was Gijón, the Arabs had already established their rule in Asturias, and Pelagius may not have led a local resistance.

At some point Pelagius is said to have rebelled, for reasons that are unknown; such rebellions by local authorities were a common theme in Visigothic Spain. A Muslim army under the command of Alkama and the Christian bishop of Seville, Oppa, was sent against him. In a battle near Covadonga Alkama was killed and Oppa captured. Moorish chronicles describe Pelagius and his small force as thirty wild donkeys. Dates for the battle vary between sources.

Pelagius was elected princeps of the Asturians by the local magnates in the Visigothic manner and made his capital at Cangas de Onís. His kingdom, at first centred on the eastern Asturias, soon grew. He married his daughter Ermesinda to the future king Alfonso I, son of his eastern neighbour, Duke Peter of Cantabria.

Pelagius reigned for eighteen or nineteen years until his death in 737 and was succeeded by his son Fafila. He was buried in the church of Santa Eulalia de Abamia, near Cangas de Onís. King Alfonso X of Castile later moved his remains, with those of his wife Gaudiosa and his sister, to the Holy Cave of Covadonga.

He is credited with initiating the Reconquista, the Christian reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula, and with establishing the Asturian monarchy. The chief sources for his life are two Latin chronicles written in the late ninth century in the kingdom he founded, the Chronica Albeldensia of about 881 and the Chronicle of Alfonso III.
peloponnese: The Peloponnese is a peninsula at the southern tip of mainland Greece, covering 21,549.6 square kilometres.
