His father spent most of his reign trying to maintain Macedonian hegemony over Greece and, later, against an expanding Roman Republic. After defeat in the Second Macedonian War Philip had to accept Roman power in Greece, and he later helped Rome in the war against Nabis in 195 BCE and the Aetolian War of 191–189 BCE. Perseus is recorded as having commanded Macedonian troops in both the Second Macedonian War and the Aetolian War.

Because he was a concubine's son, he feared the throne might pass to his legitimate younger brother Demetrius, who had been sent to Rome as a hostage and led a pro-Roman faction at court. In 180 BCE Perseus forged a letter, supposedly from the Roman general Titus Quinctius Flamininus, suggesting that Demetrius was planning to overthrow Philip, and it persuaded Philip to execute Demetrius.

Philip died the next year, and Perseus succeeded him on 22 June 179 BCE. In 178 BCE he married Laodice V, daughter of Seleucus IV of Syria. In 172 BCE Eumenes II of Pergamon, fearing Macedonian expansion, accused Perseus before the Roman Senate of threatening the stability of the Greek world, and soon Rome and Perseus went to war in the Third Macedonian War of 171–168 BCE. Perseus had some initial success, but the war ended with his decisive defeat by the Roman general Lucius Aemilius Paullus at the Battle of Pydna and his surrender. The Antigonid kingdom was dissolved and replaced with four republics.

Perseus was led captive in the triumph of Paullus in 167 BCE and imprisoned in Rome with his half-brother Philippus and his son Alexander. According to Plutarch, the Romans decided after two years to kill him by keeping him from sleeping until he died of exhaustion in 166 BCE, while Livy writes that he was shown clemency and kept in good conditions at Alba Fucens for the rest of his life.

His son Alexander, still a child at Pydna, was held at Alba Fucens, became a skilled metalworker, learned Latin and worked as a public notary. In 149 BCE Andriscus, claiming to be a son of Perseus, announced he would retake Macedonia, but the Romans defeated him in 148 BCE. In 146 BCE the four republics were dissolved and Macedon became a Roman province.
persian-gulf: The Persian Gulf, sometimes called the Arabian Gulf, is a mediterranean sea in West Asia of some 251,000 square kilometres. It is 989 kilometres long and about 56 kilometres wide at its narrowest, in the Strait of Hormuz, which joins it to the Gulf of Oman. The water is shallow, averaging 50 metres in depth. At its north-western end the Shatt al-Arab delta carries the waters of the Euphrates and the Tigris. Eight states have coasts on it: Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

During most of the Last Glacial Period much of the Gulf was dry land, a floodplain where several rivers met. The modern sea formed as sea levels rose between about 12,000 and 6,000 years ago. Seagoing vessels from the mid-sixth millennium BCE have been found at H3 in Kuwait, when the Gulf belonged to a trade network linking Ubaid settlements in Mesopotamia with communities along its coast. At the end of the fourth millennium BCE the Dilmun civilization dominated its southern part. Between 625 BCE and 226 CE a succession of Persian empires held the northern side, and the Achaemenid navy kept bases on the Shatt al-Arab and in Bahrain, Oman and Yemen.

In 1521 a Portuguese force under Antonio Correia invaded Bahrain for its pearl industry, after Afonso de Albuquerque had captured the kingdom of Hormuz. On 29 April 1602 Shah Abbas of the Safavid Empire expelled the Portuguese from Bahrain, and in 1622, with British naval support, he took the island of Hormuz; trade moved to Bandar Abbas. Piracy was prevalent until the nineteenth century, and the British mounted the Persian Gulf campaign of 1819, which led to the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 with the sheikhs of the Pirate Coast. From 1763 until 1971 Britain held varying degrees of political control over several Gulf states.

The name Persian Gulf is the historical and internationally established one, though Arab governments use Arabian Gulf or the Gulf. The Gulf and its coastlands hold very large reserves of petroleum and natural gas, and Qatar and Iran share the largest gas field across the median line.
persian-language: Modern Persian is a continuation of Middle Persian, an official language of the Sasanian Empire (224–651 CE), which was itself a continuation of Old Persian, used in the Achaemenid Empire (550–330 BCE). It originated in the region of Fars in southwestern Iran. Old Persian is attested in cuneiform inscriptions from the 6th to the 4th century BCE, the oldest being the Behistun Inscription from the time of King Darius I (reigned 522–486 BCE). Middle Persian is attested in Pahlavi and Manichaean scripts, and New Persian literature was first recorded in the ninth century, after the Muslim conquest of Persia. Gernot Windfuhr treats New Persian as an evolution of both earlier stages, but states that none of the known Middle Persian dialects is its direct predecessor.

Persian belongs to the Western Iranian group of the Iranian languages. It has three standard varieties: Iranian Persian, Dari in Afghanistan and Tajiki in Tajikistan, all based on classic Persian literature and mutually intelligible to a relatively high degree. Iranian Persian and Dari are written in the Persian alphabet, a modified form of the Arabic alphabet; after the Arab conquest it took about 200 years before Persians adopted the Arabic script in place of Pahlavi. Tajiki is written in a Cyrillic alphabet.

Modern Persian has no grammatical gender and its usual word order is subject–object–verb. Its core vocabulary is of Middle Persian origin, but it also contains a considerable number of Arabic loanwords. John R. Perry estimates that about 20 percent of everyday vocabulary, and around 25 percent of that of classical and modern literature, is of Arabic origin.

Persian was the first language to break the monopoly of Arabic on writing in the Muslim world, and Persian poetry became a tradition in many eastern courts. It served as a language of bureaucracy even for non-native speakers, among them the Ottomans in Anatolia, the Delhi Sultanates and Mughals in the Indian subcontinent, and the Pashtuns in Afghanistan. It influenced Turkic, Armenian, Georgian, Greek and Indo-Aryan languages, as well as other Iranian ones. Works written in it include the Shahnameh by Ferdowsi, the works of Rumi, the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, the Divân of Hafez and the Gulistan and Bustan by Saadi Shirazi. Approximately 130 million people speak it worldwide.
persius: According to the Life preserved in the manuscripts, Persius was born into an equestrian family of good stock on both sides at Volterra, a small Etruscan city. He lost his father when he was six, and his stepfather died a few years later. At twelve he came to Rome, where he was taught by Remmius Palaemon and the rhetor Verginius Flavus. Over the next four years he made friends with the Stoic Lucius Annaeus Cornutus, the lyric poet Caesius Bassus and the poet Lucan. He also became close to Thrasea Paetus, with whom he shared many journeys over ten years, and met Seneca, whose genius did not impress him.

As a boy Persius wrote a tragedy on an episode of Roman history and another work, probably on travel. Reading the satires of Lucilius made him want to write in that manner, and he began a book of satires, but he wrote seldom and slowly, and an early death prevented him from finishing it. After his death Cornutus suppressed everything but the satires, altered them slightly and handed them to Bassus for editing. They were an immediate success and became very popular in the Middle Ages. They are written in hexameters, apart from a short prologue in scazons, and run to fewer than seven hundred lines.

The first satire censures the literary tastes of the day as a reflection of moral decadence. The others deal with what may justly be asked of the gods, the importance of having a definite aim in life, the need for self-knowledge among public men, the Stoic doctrine of liberty, introduced with generous allusions to Cornutus, and the proper use of money. Persius describes the seamy side of life, especially the link between excess of consumption and moral failure, and shows little of Horace's easy acceptance of human weakness.

Persius died young, leaving his considerable fortune to his mother and sister. He was said to have a gentle disposition and to have lived a life of devotion to his mother Fulvia Sisennia, his sister and his aunt. His style is obscure, and its straining of expression and excess of detail compare poorly with the clear prose of Seneca's letters, yet some judge that in earnestness and moral purpose he reaches the highest note of Roman satire. Montaigne mentions him several times. Isaac Casaubon, Otto Jahn and John Conington produced important editions.
personal-computer: Early experimental machines could be operated by a single attendant: ENIAC, operational in 1946, could be run by one highly trained person. Computers for laboratory, instrumentation or engineering work, such as the Bendix G15 and LGP-30 of 1956, were operated interactively, but they were far too expensive to be owned by an individual. The personal computer depended on advances in semiconductor technology: the silicon integrated circuit chip, developed by Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor in 1959, the MOS transistor, developed by Mohamed Atalla and Dawon Kahng at Bell Labs, and the first single-chip microprocessor, the Intel 4004 of 1971, developed by Federico Faggin.

A personal computer is designed to be operated directly by an end user, rather than by a computer expert, administrator or technician, and it does not rely on time-sharing by many people at once. In 1968 the SRI researcher Douglas Engelbart gave a preview of features that later became staples, among them e-mail, hypertext, word processing, video conferencing and the mouse, though the demonstration needed technical staff and a costly mainframe.

By the mid-1970s some microprocessor-based machines were sold in kit form, mainly to hobbyists, programmed with toggle switches and displaying results on front panel lamps. The Micral N, built from 1972 around the Intel 8008, was the earliest commercial, non-kit microcomputer based on a microprocessor, and a few hundred were sold.

Early personal computers were very expensive, but falling production costs and the commercial availability of microprocessors from the mid-1970s made them affordable to small businesses and individuals. In the early 1980s home computers were developed for household use and typically used a television as the display. The Sinclair ZX Spectrum, introduced in 1982, sold 8 million units and the Commodore 64 17 million.

The IBM Personal Computer was released in 1981, and IBM PC compatibles soon followed, so that the term PC came to refer to them. By 1984 mass-market systems with graphical user interfaces were available. In 1991 the World Wide Web was made available for public use, and powerful personal computers together with the Internet became the foundation for a significant part of modern life.
perth: Perth lies mostly on the sandy, relatively flat Swan Coastal Plain, between the Darling Scarp and the Indian Ocean. The Swan River, also known as Derbarl Yerrigan, runs through it; the Dutch captain Willem de Vlamingh named it for the black swans he found there when exploring in 1697. The central business district and the port of Fremantle both stand on the river. Summers are hot, sunny and dry and winters mild and wet, a hot-summer Mediterranean climate. The nearest city of more than 100,000 people is Adelaide, over 2,100 km away, which makes Perth one of the most isolated major cities in the world.

People have lived in the Perth area for at least 48,000 years. Noongar country covers the south-west corner of Western Australia, and the wetlands of the Swan Coastal Plain hold spiritual importance and were a source of food. The Whadjuk Noongar are the traditional owners of the land, and the Noongar name for the place is Boorloo. In 1619 the Dutch explorer Frederick de Houtman sighted the coast near present-day Perth, which he and Jacob Dedel called Dedelsland.

Perth was founded as the administrative centre of the Swan River Colony in 1829, the first comprehensive European settlement in the west of the continent, after New South Wales had set up a convict-supported outpost at King George's Sound in 1826 in response to rumours of French annexation. Stirling's proclamation of the colony was read at Fremantle on 18 June 1829. The name honours Sir George Murray, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies, who sat in the House of Commons for Perthshire. The colony was officially designated Western Australia in 1832.

In 1850, at the request of farmers and businesspeople short of labour, Western Australia accepted convicts, and over eighteen years 9,721 arrived on 43 ships, outnumbering the roughly 7,300 free settlers. Queen Victoria announced Perth's designation as a city in 1856, but it remained a tranquil town. After a referendum in 1900 Western Australia joined the Federation of Australia in 1901, the last colony to agree, and only after concessions that included a transcontinental railway from Port Augusta to Kalgoorlie. From 1927 to 1954 Indigenous people were prohibited from entering large parts of Perth.

Perth is the capital and largest city of Western Australia and the fourth most populous city in Australia, a position it has held since 1984. Mining booms in the late 20th century made it the headquarters of significant mining operations in the state. Kings Park and Botanic Garden is one of the world's largest inner-city parks, and Fremantle Prison is a World Heritage Site.
perth-amboy: Perth Amboy lies in northeastern Middlesex County, New Jersey, within the New York metropolitan area, and borders the Arthur Kill. The Lenape called the point on which it stands Ompoge, meaning level ground or standing upright. The name Amboy descends from that word, and the colonists later joined it to the name of their settlement. Perth Amboy and South Amboy, across the Raritan River, are together called the Amboys, and the city is linked to Staten Island by the Outerbridge Crossing.

Scottish colonists settled the place around 1683, recruited to occupy the share of the East Jersey colony owned by Robert Barclay, a Quaker who later became the province's absentee governor. They called it New Perth in honour of James Drummond, 4th Earl of Perth, one of the twelve associates of the company of Scottish proprietors. In 1686 it was designated capital of East Jersey, while Burlington was capital of West Jersey; after the two were united as a royal colony in 1702, the two cities alternated as capital of the province. A royal charter followed on 4 August 1718, and the New Jersey Legislature confirmed the city's status on 21 December 1784.

By the middle of the 19th century immigration and industry had transformed the city. Factories such as A. Hall and Sons Terra Cotta, Guggenheim and Sons and the Copper Works Smelting Company employed many residents, and the city became the tidewater terminal of the Lehigh Valley Railroad and a coal shipping point. Immigrants from Denmark, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Italy, Russia and Austria dominated the factory jobs and formed close ethnic neighbourhoods such as Budapest, Dublin and Chickentown. The Perth Amboy Public Library, one of the first Carnegie libraries in the state, opened in 1903.

The waterfront keeps the Perth Amboy Ferry Slip, once an important crossing on the route south from New York City and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, as well as the Proprietary House, the former governor's mansion, which now holds a museum. St. Peter's Episcopal Church and the Raritan Yacht Club, one of the oldest yacht clubs in the United States, also stand there. The 2020 census counted 55,436 people, and most residents are Hispanic, with Puerto Rican and Dominican communities among them.
perth-scotland: Perth stands on the banks of the River Tay, on a natural mound raised slightly above the flood plain. The area has been occupied since the arrival of Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, and nearby standing stones and circles date from about 4000 BCE. Close to the city is Scone Abbey, which formerly housed the Stone of Scone, on which the kings of Scots were traditionally crowned. The name comes from a Pictish word for a wood or copse, related to the Welsh perth, meaning hedge or thicket. In the later medieval period its inhabitants called it St John's Toun, after the church of St John the Baptist.

The frequent residence of the royal court gave Perth the reputation of a capital of Scotland. King William the Lion granted royal burgh status in the early 12th century. The city became one of the richest burghs in the country, trading with France, the Low Countries and the Baltic and importing Spanish silk and French wine. It grew from a plan of two parallel streets, High Street and South Street, linked by vennels. In 1437 King James I was assassinated in Perth by followers of Walter Stewart, Earl of Atholl, at Blackfriars church.

In 1559 a sermon by John Knox in St John's Kirk was followed by the sacking of the Greyfriars and Blackfriars houses, two of the city's four monastic institutions. Jacobite supporters occupied the city in 1689, 1715 and 1745. Perth Academy was founded in 1760, and linen, leather, bleach and whisky became major industries. The first railway station opened in 1848. In 1829 Sir George Murray, born in Perth, asked that the new Swan River Colony in Western Australia be named Perth.

Perth is the administrative centre of Perth and Kinross and the historic county town of Perthshire. It has been known as the Fair City since Sir Walter Scott published The Fair Maid of Perth in 1828. St John's Kirk, much altered, keeps a 15th-century brass candelabrum imported from the Low Countries, a rare survival in Scotland. Its arms, recorded on a seal of 1378, show a paschal lamb holding a saltire, and the North Inch and South Inch were given to the city in 1377 by King Robert III.
peru: Peru covers 1,285,216 km2 on the Pacific coast of South America, the third-largest country on the continent. The Andes run parallel to the ocean and define three traditional regions: the costa, a narrow and largely arid coastal plain; the sierra, the highlands, which include the Altiplano and the highest peak, Huascarán at 6,768 metres; and the selva, the Amazon rainforest, which covers almost 60 percent of the country.

The Amazon basin covers 75% of Peruvian territory, and Lake Titicaca, shared with Bolivia, is the largest lake in South America. The name may derive from Birú, a local ruler near the Bay of San Miguel in Panama, and the Capitulation of Toledo of 1529 gave it legal status as the name of the province that was the Inca Empire.

The earliest evidence of people in Peruvian territory, about 12,500 BCE, comes from Huaca Prieta. The Caral-Supe civilization flourished on the coast, and the Chavín culture, from 1500 to 300 BCE, was probably more a religious than a political phenomenon. Later coastal cultures included the Paracas, Nazca, Moche and Chimu. The Chimu flourished from about 1140 to 1450 as a loose confederation of walled cities with its capital at Chan Chan, and in the highlands the Tiahuanaco and Wari cultures developed large urban settlements between 500 and 1000 CE.

The Spanish Empire conquered the region in the 16th century, and Charles V established a viceroyalty, the Kingdom of Peru, with its capital at Lima. According to the historian Noble David Cook, the Amerindian population fell from nearly 5–9 million in the 1520s to around 600,000 in 1620, mainly from infectious disease. The National University of San Marcos was founded in Lima in 1551. Peru proclaimed independence in 1821 and completed it in 1824, with the battle of Ayacucho. Guano exploitation brought relative stability until the War of the Pacific, 1879–1884.

Peru is a unitary semi-presidential republic under its 1993 constitution, with a president elected for five years without immediate re-election. The population was 33,396,698 in estimates to 2022, about 80 percent of them urban, and the Lima metropolitan area has over 9.8 million people. Spanish is the main language, but many Peruvians speak Quechuan languages, Aymara or other Indigenous languages.
perugino: Pietro Vannucci was born in Città della Pieve, Umbria, the son of Cristoforo Maria Vannucci. His nickname marks him as from Perugia, the chief city of Umbria. Scholars dispute the standing of his family: some hold that he worked his way out of poverty, others that the family was among the wealthiest in the town. He most likely began studying painting in local workshops in Perugia, such as those of Bartolomeo Caporali or Fiorenzo di Lorenzo.

According to Vasari he was apprenticed in the Florentine workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio alongside Leonardo da Vinci, Domenico Ghirlandaio and Filippino Lippi, and Piero della Francesca is thought to have taught him perspective. In 1472 he was enrolled as a master in the Confraternity of St Luke. He was one of the earliest central Italian painters to work in oil.

Around 1480 Pope Sixtus IV called him to Rome to paint fresco panels on the walls of the Sistine Chapel. These included the Baptism of Christ and the Delivery of the Keys; Pinturicchio went with him and became his partner. The frescoes on the altar wall were later destroyed to make room for Michelangelo's Last Judgement. Between 1486 and 1499 he worked mainly between Florence and Perugia, keeping a studio in each. In 1496 the bankers' guild of Perugia asked him to decorate the audience hall of the Collegio del Cambio, with planets and zodiac signs on the vault and sacred scenes on the walls; he placed his own portrait bust on the central pilaster.

He became one of the priors of Perugia in 1501. Michelangelo is said to have called him a bungler in art, and Perugino brought an unsuccessful action for defamation. His Annunziata Altarpiece in Florence, painted in 1504 to 1507, was accused of lack of innovation, and he lost his students. Pope Julius II summoned him to paint a ceiling in the Vatican, but soon preferred Raphael, who had been trained by Perugino, and from 1512 Perugino retired to Perugia.

His last frescoes were painted in 1521 and 1522 in churches and monasteries around Umbria. He died of the plague in 1523 at Fontignano and, like other victims, was hastily buried in an unconsecrated field, the spot now unknown. He left considerable property and three sons. Vasari states that he had very little religion and doubted the immortality of the soul. His likely pupils included Raphael, whose early work shows his influence most, and Perugino's Marriage of the Virgin, now in Caen, served as the model for Raphael's Sposalizio of 1504. Perugia dedicated a monument to him in 1923.
pervez-musharraf: Pervez Musharraf was born on 11 August 1943 in Delhi, British India, to an Urdu-speaking family of Sayyids. His father, Syed Musharrafuddin, worked in the foreign office of the British Indian government and became an accounting director, and his mother, Zarin, took a degree in English literature at Delhi University. In 1961, aged 18, he entered the Pakistan Military Academy at Kakul.

Musharraf first saw battle with an artillery regiment during the Second Kashmir War of 1965 and received the Imtiazi Sanad medal for gallantry. In 1987 he commanded a new brigade of the Special Services Group near the Siachen Glacier. Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif promoted him to four-star general and Chief of the Army Staff in October 1998. From March to May 1999 he ordered the secret infiltration of forces into the Kargil district, and a fierce Indian offensive nearly led to a full-scale war. Sharif withdrew support in July under international pressure, which antagonised the army, and Sharif's attempt to dismiss Musharraf was followed by the coup of October 1999.

Musharraf governed as Chief Executive, appointed himself president on 20 June 2001, and in August 2002 issued the Legal Framework Order, which made many amendments to the Constitution. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 he allied Pakistan with the United States against the Taliban. His government liberalised the media and presided over rapid economic growth, while his rule also saw curbs on the judiciary and a growing insurgency in the North-West Frontier Province.

His dismissal of Chief Justice Iftikhar Chaudhry in March 2007 and the state of emergency of November cost him support, and he announced his resignation on 18 August 2008. He founded the All Pakistan Muslim League in 2010. On 17 December 2019 a special court sentenced him in absentia to death for suspending the constitution in November 2007. He died on 5 February 2023, aged 79, of amyloidosis, and was buried with military honours in Karachi. Judgements of his rule are sharply divided between those who credit him with economic stabilisation and those who point to the erosion of democratic institutions.
pescennius-niger: Gaius Pescennius Niger was born around 135 into an old Italian equestrian family and was the first of it to become a Roman senator. According to the Historia Augusta his parents were Annius Fuscus and Lampridia. Little is known of his early career; he may have held an administrative post in Egypt and served in a campaign in Dacia early in the reign of Commodus. He was elected suffect consul in the late 180s, and Commodus made him imperial legate of Syria in 191.

News of the murder of Pertinax and the auctioning of the imperial title to Didius Julianus reached him in Syria. Niger was well regarded in Rome, and a popular demonstration there called on him to come and claim the throne. Julianus is alleged to have sent a centurion east to assassinate him at Antioch. The eastern legions proclaimed Niger emperor by the end of April 193, and he took the additional name Justus, the Just. Septimius Severus had claimed the title on 14 April and later propaganda made Niger the first rebel, but Niger's envoys to Rome were intercepted by Severus, who entered the city in early June 193.

Niger won the support of the governors of the Asiatic provinces, among them Asellius Aemilianus, who occupied Byzantium for him, and took control of Egypt. His resources were weaker, however: six legions against the sixteen Danubian legions of Severus. His force defeated part of Severus' army under Lucius Fabius Cilo at Perinthus, but in the autumn of 193 Severus' general Tiberius Claudius Candidus defeated Aemilianus at Cyzicus, and Niger had to abandon Byzantium for Nicaea, where he was beaten again in December. He held the passes of the Taurus Mountains for some months while support fell away: Laodicea and Tyre changed sides, and Egypt and the legate of Arabia declared for Severus by February 194.

In May 194 Niger met Severus' general Publius Cornelius Anullinus at Issus and was decisively defeated after a long struggle. He was captured while trying to flee from Antioch to Parthia and beheaded, and his head was taken to Byzantium, which refused to surrender, and later to Rome, where it was displayed. Severus stormed and destroyed Byzantium and then rebuilt it. The Historia Augusta says he put Niger's wife and children to death, but the work is unreliable, and one scholar judges it more likely that they were allowed to live in retirement. His name means black Pescennius, a nickname that contemporaries linked to his dark-skinned neck.
peshawar: Peshawar lies in the broad Peshawar Valley, which mountain ranges surround on three sides, with the fourth side opening to the Punjab plains. The city stands on the level floor of the valley, known as the Gandhara Plains. Its economic importance has long rested on its position at the entrance to the Khyber Pass, the ancient route by which most trade between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent passed. Its name derives from the reconstructed Sanskrit Puruṣapura, meaning City of Men; the Chinese monks Faxian in the 5th century and Xuanzang in the 7th recorded it under Chinese equivalents of that name.

Its recorded history reaches back to at least the 6th century BCE. The city likely first existed as a small village in the 5th century BCE, near the Gandharan capital of Puṣkalāvatī, close to present-day Charsadda. In the winter of 327–326 BCE Alexander the Great subdued Gandhara, and the valley afterwards came under Seleucus I Nicator. Puruṣapura served as capital of the Kushan Empire under Kanishka the Great in the 2nd century CE. The Ghaznavids conquered it from the Hindu Shahis in 1001, after Sabuktigin first fought the Hindu Shahis under their king Anandpal in 986–87.

Emperor Babur captured Peshawar in July 1526, called it Begram and rebuilt its fort. It remained an important centre on the trade routes between India and Central Asia under Mughal rule; over one thousand camel-loads of merchandise were destroyed by an accidental fire at the Bala Hissar fort in 1586. Sher Shah Suri began building the Grand Trunk Road in the 16th century. Nader Shah's Afsharid Empire held it from 1738, and the Durrani Empire later made it a winter capital. The East India Company annexed it in 1849. In 1901 it became capital of the North-West Frontier Province.

Peshawar has been part of Pakistan since 1947 and is the capital and largest city of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Until the mid-1950s it was enclosed within a city wall with sixteen gates. The University of Peshawar was established there in 1950. Hindko was long its common language, but Pashto has since become the main one, and Pashtuns now form most of the population, while the Peshoris, its original urban population, remain in the old Walled City. The city has a hot semi-arid climate and a population of about 1.9 million.
pest-hungary: Pest lies on the eastern bank of the Danube and makes up about two thirds of the area of Budapest. It is flatter and much more heavily urbanised than Buda across the river. According to Ptolemy the settlement was called Pession in antiquity, and its official Roman name was Contra-Aquincum, after the Roman town of Aquincum on the opposite bank, in what became Óbuda. The name Pest may instead come from a Slavic word meaning furnace or oven, probably referring to a local cave where fire burned. The spelling Pesth was used in English as late as the early 20th century.

Pest began as a Celtic settlement and then became a fortified Roman camp, Contra-Aquincum, facing the military border camp at Aquincum. Remains of the Roman camp can still be seen at Március 15. tér. In the Middle Ages Pest was an independent city, separate from Buda, which became an important economic centre between the 11th and 13th centuries. Its first written mention dates from 1148.

The Mongol invasion of Hungary destroyed Pest in 1241, but it was rebuilt soon afterwards. In the 15th century Pest was mostly Hungarian, while Buda had a German-majority population. In 1838 the Danube flooded the city, with parts under as much as eight feet of water, and the flood destroyed or badly damaged three quarters of its buildings. The first permanent bridge between Pest and Buda, the Széchenyi Chain Bridge, was built in 1849, and in 1873 the two cities were unified with Óbuda as Budapest.

Many of the best-known sites of Budapest lie in Pest: the Inner City, the Parliament, the Opera, the Great Market Hall, Heroes' Square and Andrássy Avenue. In colloquial Hungarian the name Pest is sometimes used for the whole of Budapest. Pest was the birthplace of the writer and statesman László Teleki, the painter Henrik Weber, Theodor Herzl, founder of the political Zionist movement, and the illusionist Harry Houdini.
petar-ii-petrovic-njegos: He was born Radivoje Petrović in the mountain village of Njeguši, near Cetinje, to a family of the Petrović clan, and became the spiritual and political leader of Montenegro after the death of his uncle Petar I. In 1833 he travelled to Saint Petersburg, where he was consecrated despite being under the canonical age of thirty, and Emperor Nicholas I granted him 36,000 rubles. Russia also pressed for a Governing Senate in 1832 to regulate the powers of the vladika.

His taxation policies were unpopular with the tribes and caused several revolts. To strengthen the Petrović name he arranged the canonization of Petar I in October 1834. He enlarged the Perjanici and the Gvardija, built roads, artesian wells and two gunpowder factories at Rijeka Crnojevića, and introduced the Obilić Medal for Valour. A defeat at Podgorica in 1832 and the Ottoman invasion of 1843 under Osman Pasha showed how hard it was to resist the Ottoman Empire.

Njegoš began writing poetry at seventeen, drawing on Serb folklore, lyric poetry and biblical stories. His works include The Voice of a Stone-Cutter (1833), The Ray of the Microcosm (1845), The Mountain Wreath (1847) and The False Tsar Stephen the Little (1851), which are all epic poems. The Mountain Wreath was seen after his death as the Montenegrin national epic and, for Serbs, evoked the Kosovo epics. Gavrilo Princip knew it by heart.

He met the language reformer Vuk Stefanović Karadžić in Vienna, and his travels brought him into contact with ideas of South Slav unity. In 1848 he corresponded with Prince Aleksandar of Serbia and Ilija Garašanin; they agreed that, in a unified Serbian state, Aleksandar would be hereditary secular leader and Njegoš Patriarch of a unified Serbian Orthodox Church.

By 1849 Njegoš had tuberculosis. He travelled to Italy in 1850 and again in January 1851, visiting Venice, Milan, Genoa, Rome and Pompeii, and died in October 1851. He was first buried at the Cetinje Monastery, and in 1855 his remains were moved to the chapel on Mount Lovćen that he had designed and had built in 1845. In 1916 the Austro-Hungarian occupiers had them returned to Cetinje; the chapel was reconstructed and he was reburied there in September 1925.
pete-seeger: Peter Seeger was born on 3 May 1919 in Manhattan. His father, Charles Louis Seeger Jr., a composer and musicologist, established the first musicology curriculum in the United States at the University of California, Berkeley, and helped found the discipline of ethnomusicology. His mother, Constance de Clyver Seeger, was a concert violinist who later taught at the Juilliard School.

His parents did not press him to play an instrument, and he took up the ukulele on his own. In the summer of 1935 he heard the five-string banjo for the first time at a folk festival near Asheville, North Carolina. In 1936 he joined the Young Communist League, and in 1942 he joined the Communist Party USA, which he left in 1949.

In 1941 Seeger co-founded the Almanac Singers with Millard Lampell and Lee Hays, a topical group that was meant to act as a singing newspaper for industrial unionisation and other progressive causes. He later co-founded the Weavers, and in 1943 he recorded the album Songs of the Lincoln Battalion in support of the republican side in the Spanish Civil War. In 1948 he wrote How to Play the Five-String Banjo, which sold over 100,000 copies in its 1962 edition, and he devised the long-neck Seeger banjo.

During the blacklist years of the late 1950s and early 1960s he earned money teaching music in schools and summer camps and touring colleges, and he recorded as many as five albums a year for Folkways Records. His songs against war, including Where Have All the Flowers Gone?, written with Joe Hickerson, and Turn! Turn! Turn!, adapted from Ecclesiastes, won wide currency. In 1963 he helped organise a Carnegie Hall concert for the Highlander Folk School, and he sang We Shall Overcome on the walk from Selma to Montgomery. In 1966 he and his wife Toshi founded the Hudson River Sloop Clearwater, which works to protect the Hudson River.

Seeger died on 27 January 2014. He said that it was he who changed the words of We Shall Overcome from the traditional we will overcome to the more singable we shall. He coined the phrase Woody's children for the new generation of politically committed folk singers, and the Byrds had a number one hit with Turn! Turn! Turn! in 1965. His championing of the five-string banjo helped make it known across the United States as an American folk instrument, where it had once been largely limited to Appalachia.
peter-behrens: Peter Behrens studied painting in his native Hamburg, in Düsseldorf and in Karlsruhe from 1886 to 1889. In 1890 he married Lilly Kramer and moved to Munich, where he worked at first as a painter, illustrator and bookbinder in an artisanal manner. He moved in bohemian circles interested in the reform of lifestyles, and the Munich Secession, in which young artists called for art that reflected modern German life, formed part of his background. In 1899 Grand Duke Ernst Ludwig of Hesse invited him to the recently founded Darmstadt Artists' Colony.

At Darmstadt he designed everything in his Jugendstil house of 1901, from furniture to towels and pottery, and the project is regarded as the turning point of his life, since it showed him a talented architect in his first building. In 1903 he became director of the Kunstgewerbeschule in Düsseldorf, where he reformed the teaching of design. In 1907 he was one of the founders of the German Werkbund, which aimed to raise the level of taste in Germany by improving everyday objects and products.

In 1907 the electrical firm AEG retained him as artistic consultant. He designed its logotype, products and publicity, which is why he is considered the first industrial designer, and a series of factories in Berlin, above all the Turbine Factory of 1909. His growing office trained assistants who became leading modernists: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, Le Corbusier, Adolf Meyer, Jean Kramer and Walter Gropius. He also designed the German Embassy in St Petersburg in 1912 and the administration building for Continental AG in Hannover, built in 1912 to 1914.

After the First World War he turned to Brick Expressionism in the Technical Administration Building of Hoechst AG outside Frankfurt, built between 1920 and 1924. From 1922 to 1936 he headed the architecture school at the Academy of Fine Arts Vienna. His house New Ways in Northampton, designed in 1926 for Wenman Joseph Bassett-Lowke, is often regarded as probably the first modernist house in Britain, and he later worked in the style of New Objectivity, as in the tobacco factory at Linz, completed in 1935.

In 1936 Behrens left Vienna to teach at the Prussian Academy of Arts in Berlin, reportedly with Hitler's approval, and took part in plans for the rebuilding of Berlin, receiving the commission for the new AEG headquarters on Albert Speer's planned axis. He died at the Hotel Bristol in Berlin on 27 February 1940, where he had sought refuge from his country estate. He also designed three typefaces for the Klingspor Type Foundry.
peter-ii-of-yugoslavia: Peter was born on 6 September 1923 in Belgrade, the eldest son of Alexander I of Yugoslavia and Maria of Romania. His godparents included King George V of the United Kingdom, for whom the Duke of York stood proxy. He was tutored at the Royal Palace and then attended Sandroyd School in Surrey. On 9 October 1934, at the age of eleven, he succeeded to the throne after his father was assassinated in Marseille during a state visit to France, and a regency was set up under his father's cousin Prince Paul.

Paul held that he must hand the kingdom to Peter unaltered when he turned eighteen, and he resisted attempts to revise the 1931 constitution. On 20 August 1939 he did allow an agreement between the prime minister Dragiša Cvetković and Vladko Maček of the Croatian Peasant Party, which created a Banovina of Croatia with substantial autonomy. It was very unpopular with the Serbs.

Prince Paul declared on 25 March 1941 that Yugoslavia would join the Tripartite Pact. Two days later General Dušan Simović led a pro-British coup in the name of the seventeen-year-old Peter, who climbed down a drain-pipe to greet the rebels. Simović saluted him as king, and the crowds in Belgrade cheered him. Germany attacked on 6 April 1941; the Luftwaffe bombed Belgrade, killing between 3,000 and 4,000 people, and the government surrendered on 17 April. Italy, Bulgaria, Hungary and Germany annexed parts of the country, and the rest was governed by two German-controlled puppet governments.

Peter reached London in June 1941, where a government-in-exile was set up. His engagement to Princess Alexandra of Greece and Denmark, announced in July 1943, caused controversy at home, since Serbian tradition held that a leader must not marry during a national emergency. He dismissed the prime minister Slobodan Jovanović, who opposed the announcement. The couple married in March 1944.

In November 1944 the prime minister Šubašić agreed with Stalin that Peter would not return until a plebiscite was held, and that a three-man regency council would govern meanwhile; Peter objected that he was twenty-one and needed no regent. The Constituent Assembly, elected on 11 November 1945 amid reported fraud and intimidation, deposed him on 29 November 1945 and proclaimed a republic. Peter settled in the United States and lived much of his exile in the Chicago area.

He suffered from depression and alcoholism, and developed cirrhosis of the liver. He died in Denver on 3 November 1970 after a failed liver transplant and was buried at the Saint Sava Monastery Church in Libertyville, Illinois. His remains were returned to Belgrade on 22 January 2013 and buried at Oplenac on 26 May 2013.
peter-iii-of-aragon: Peter was the eldest son of James I of Aragon and his second wife Violant of Hungary. On 13 June 1262 he married Constance II of Sicily, daughter and heiress of Manfred of Sicily, and he gained military experience in his father's wars against the Moors. When James died in 1276 the Crown's lands were divided: Peter received the Kingdom of Aragon, the Kingdom of Valencia and the Principality of Catalonia, while his younger brother became James II of Majorca. Peter and Constance were crowned at Zaragoza in November 1276.

Peter's early years as king brought revolt in Catalonia, led by the viscount of Cardona and backed by several counts, who resented his severity under his father and his failure to summon the General Court of Catalonia. In 1280 he besieged the rebels at Balaguer for a month and defeated them. Abroad, he prepared a fleet of 140 ships with 15,000 men to invade Tunisia. After the Sicilian Vespers, the uprising against Charles I of Anjou on 30 March 1282, a Sicilian embassy asked him to take the throne, which he claimed through Constance. He landed at Trapani on 30 August 1282 and was proclaimed king in Palermo on 4 September. Pope Martin IV excommunicated him.

His admiral Roger of Lauria defeated the French at the Battle of Malta and in the Gulf of Naples in 1284, where Charles of Salerno was taken prisoner. Peter and Charles agreed to settle their quarrel by a duel at Bordeaux, which never took place. At home he faced the Union of Aragon and was forced to grant the Privilegio General, and he took Albarracín from the noble Juan Núñez de Lara. In 1284 Pope Martin IV granted Aragon to Charles of Valois and sanctioned a crusade, and a large French army entered Roussillon, took Girona in 1285, but then lost its fleet to Roger of Lauria at Les Formigues on 4 September and was struck by dysentery. Philip III of France died in October.

Peter died at Vilafranca del Penedès in November 1285, one month after Philip III, and was buried at the Monastery of Santes Creus. In his will of 2 November 1285 he told his successor to return Sicily to the pope and release Angevin prisoners, but his successors ignored it: Alfonso III inherited Aragon, James II received Sicily and Frederick later succeeded James there. The kingdom was to remain a tenaciously pursued inheritance of the Aragonese royal house for five centuries. Peter was a patron of troubadours and wrote two sirventesos himself, and Dante placed him in Purgatory singing in accord with his former rival Charles I of Anjou.
peter-iii-of-russia: Peter was born on 21 February 1728 at Kiel in the duchy of Holstein-Gottorp, the son of Duke Charles Frederick and Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna, a daughter of Peter the Great. His mother died a few weeks after his birth and his father in 1739, and he became Duke of Holstein-Gottorp at eleven. His maternal aunt Elizabeth, Empress of Russia, proclaimed him her heir presumptive in 1742. He converted to Orthodoxy that November, which disqualified him from the Swedish throne. Elizabeth arranged his marriage to Sophia of Anhalt-Zerbst, who took the name Catherine, on 21 August 1745. Their son was the future Paul I.

Peter became emperor on 5 January 1762 and in 186 days of government passed 220 new laws. He exempted nobles from compulsory service in peacetime, forbade landowners from murdering peasants on pain of lifelong exile, ended the persecution of the Old Believers and abolished the Secret Chancellery. He issued a manifesto on secularising church lands, which Catherine later began to carry out, and founded Russia's first state bank.

He withdrew Russia from the Seven Years' War, signed a peace with Prussia on 5 May 1762 and gave up Russian conquests in Prussia. He also planned a war against Denmark-Norway to recover parts of Schleswig for Holstein. Many in the army and at court feared further concessions to Prussia, and in spring 1762 Catherine, with Grigory Orlov and others, began plotting against him.

On 28 June 1762 [O.S.] Catherine marched to the Winter Palace and was proclaimed ruler. Peter tried to reach Kronstadt by boat but was turned back, and he was arrested and forced to abdicate. He was taken to Ropsha, where he died. The official cause was a severe attack of colic and an apoplectic stroke, while others say he was assassinated.

Catherine's memoirs describe him as an idiot, a view repeated in older histories, while the historian Elena Palmer portrays him as an open-minded reformer. Several pretenders claimed to be Peter, the best known being Yemelyan Pugachev, who led a rebellion in 1774. In December 1796 Paul I had his remains reburied in the Peter and Paul Cathedral.
peter-kropotkin: Pyotr Alexeyevich Kropotkin was born in Moscow on 9 December 1842, the youngest of four children. His father, Alexey, was a royal officer who owned serfs in three provinces. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was three, and he and his brother Alexander were raised mostly by their German nurse. In 1862 he chose to serve with the Amur Cossacks in east Siberia, a post that allowed him to travel and become financially independent of his father. There the exiled poet Mikhail Mikhailov introduced him to anarchism by recommending an essay by Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.

In 1872 Kropotkin travelled to Switzerland, where he met the Jura Federation of followers of Mikhail Bakunin and was converted to anarchism. In 1879 he started the fortnightly Le Révolté in Geneva, which published his articulation of anarchist communism, the idea of distributing the product of work by need. In France he was imprisoned for almost four years. He then lived in England until 1917 and co-founded the monthly Freedom in London in late 1886.

In The Conquest of Bread (1892) he proposed an economy of voluntary cooperation in which everyone could take what they needed from the social product. In Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902) he answered the social thinkers who stressed competition by arguing that cooperation made for the success of species. He returned to Russia in June 1917 and refused the Provisional Government's offer of a cabinet seat. He argued with Lenin against the Bolsheviks' hostage policy and centralisation.

Kropotkin died of pneumonia on 8 February 1921. His family refused an offer of a state funeral, and the Bolsheviks permitted a restrained official memorial in Moscow, the last major anarchist demonstration of the period in Russia, since the movement and his writings were suppressed later that year. He had little influence on the Russian Revolution, but his books and pamphlets were the most widely read of anarchist literature and influenced revolutionaries such as Nestor Makhno and Emiliano Zapata.
peter-paul-rubens: Rubens was born on 28 June 1577 to Jan Rubens and Maria Pypelincks, whose family came from Antwerp. His father, a lawyer, converted to Calvinism, and in 1568 the family fled to Cologne, fearing persecution under the Duke of Alba. After Jan Rubens died in 1587 the family moved to Antwerp, where Peter Paul studied Latin and classical literature. In 1590 he had to start working, and after serving as a page to a countess he began an apprenticeship with the landscape painter Tobias Verhaecht in 1592.

In 1600 Rubens travelled to Italy, where in Venice he saw paintings by Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto. He entered the service of Duke Vincenzo I Gonzaga of Mantua, painting portraits of the ducal family and copying works in his collection, and in 1601 went on to Rome, where he studied classical sculpture and the art of Michelangelo, Raphael and Leonardo. He returned to Antwerp in 1608, and in September 1609 was appointed court painter by Archduke Albert and the Infanta Isabella Clara Eugenia, with permission to keep his studio in Antwerp. He married Isabella Brant on 3 October 1609, and from 1610 he lived and worked in a villa he designed, now the Rubenshuis Museum. His pupils and collaborators included Anthony van Dyck.

In 1621 Marie de' Medici commissioned him to paint two cycles for the Luxembourg Palace in Paris, and the one on her own life was installed in 1625. After the Twelve Years' Truce ended in 1621 the Spanish Habsburg rulers entrusted him with diplomatic missions, and between 1627 and 1630 he travelled between the courts of Spain and England to seek peace between the Spanish Netherlands and the Dutch Republic. Philip IV of Spain raised him to the nobility in 1624, Cambridge gave him an honorary degree in 1629, and Charles I of England knighted him in 1630. His output was large: Michael Jaffé's catalogue lists 1,403 works, not counting the many copies made in his workshop.

In 1630 Rubens, whose first wife Isabella had died four years earlier, married the 16-year-old Helena Fourment, who became the model for the full-figured women of many of his paintings of the 1630s. In 1635 he bought the Steen, an estate outside Antwerp, and painted landscapes there. He died on 30 May 1640 of heart failure resulting from chronic gout and was buried in Saint James' Church in Antwerp, where a family chapel was completed in 1650 with an altarpiece he painted himself. He is considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, and the terms Rubensian and Rubenesque are derived from his name.
peter-stuyvesant: Peter Stuyvesant was born around 1610, probably at Peperga in Friesland, the son of Balthasar Stuyvesant, a Reformed Calvinist minister, and Margaretha Hardenstein. He went at 20 to the University of Franeker, where he studied languages and philosophy, but was expelled after seducing his landlord's daughter. His father sent him to Amsterdam, where he joined the Dutch West India Company.

In 1630 the company made him a commercial agent on Fernando de Noronha, and in 1638 he was moved to Curaçao, where he became acting governor of the colony, and also of Aruba and Bonaire, until 1644. That April he led an attack on Saint Martin, where he was wounded in the leg, which was amputated; he later wore a wooden peg studded with silver nails.

In 1645 the company chose him to replace Willem Kieft as director-general of New Netherland, and after a delay for confirmation he arrived at New Amsterdam by May 1647. The colony was in terrible condition, with only 250 to 300 men able to bear arms. Telling its people that he would govern them as a father his children, he appointed an advisory council, the Nine Men, in September 1647. His administration issued building codes and built a protective wall on Wall Street, the canal that became Broad Street, and Broadway. He created a system of fire wardens and a volunteer fire watch, the first volunteer fire department in America.

His most notable success came against New Sweden, which he invaded and annexed in 1655. The Treaty of Hartford of 1650 was a victory for the English, as he gave up claims to the Connecticut Valley. He was strongly committed to the Dutch Reformed Church. He refused Lutherans a church, tried to bar Jewish refugees, and ordered the public torture of the Quaker preacher Robert Hodgson in 1657; company directors reversed some of these measures.

In 1664 Charles II ceded New Netherland to his brother, the Duke of York, and four English ships with 450 men under Richard Nicolls seized the colony. The settlers refused to fight, forcing Stuyvesant to surrender. The Articles of Capitulation were signed on 6 September 1664 and the city was renamed New York; they secured civil rights and freedom of religion. He spent his last years on his farm, the Great Bouwerie, which gave its name to the Bowery, and died in August 1672. The historian Eleanor Bruchey called him a difficult man thrust into a difficult position, whose religious intolerance worsened relations with colonists. His name is now attached to places in Manhattan and beyond, including Stuyvesant Square and Bedford-Stuyvesant.
peter-the-great: Peter was born on 9 June 1672 and grew up at the Izmaylovo Estate. When his father, Tsar Alexei, died in 1676 the throne passed to Peter's half-brother Feodor III. When Feodor died in 1682 without children, the Miloslavsky and Naryshkin families, the families of Alexei's first and second wives, disputed the succession. Ivan V was next in line but was weak-minded and blind, and the Boyar Duma, the council of nobles, chose the ten-year-old Peter, with his mother Natalya Naryshkina as regent. A hole was cut in the back of the throne so that she could whisper to the two boys, who ruled jointly until Ivan's death in 1696.

In March 1697 Peter travelled to Western Europe on an 18-month journey with a large delegation, the Grand Embassy, hoping to find allies against the Ottoman Empire; he failed to enlarge the anti-Ottoman alliance. In 1699 he moved the new year from 1 September to 1 January and had years counted from the birth of Christ. In 1700 he refused to allow a new patriarch to be elected, and the church later came under a Holy Synod controlled by a procurator.

He declared war on Sweden in the Great Northern War. The Russian army was defeated at Narva in 1700, but the Swedish king Charles XII then turned against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which gave Peter time to reorganise his army. Russia captured Nöteborg, renamed Shlisselburg, and founded Saint Petersburg on the Neva, and in 1712 Peter moved the capital there from Moscow. After his victory Russia annexed much of the eastern Baltic coast and became an empire. He created a Governing Senate in 1711 and a Table of Ranks in 1722, and brutally suppressed rebellions by the Streltsy, the Bashkirs, Astrakhan and the Bulavin Rebellion.

Peter's health was never robust. He began to suffer from problems of the bladder in the winter of 1723 and died early on 8 February 1725 at the age of 52; an autopsy found his bladder infected with gangrene. He is buried in the Saints Peter and Paul Cathedral. A story that he caught his fatal illness rescuing drowning soldiers rests on a single source and is viewed with scepticism by some historians. For Old Believers he was the Antichrist, because of the calendar changes and the poll tax, and mid-19th-century Slavophiles deplored the westernisation of Russia. The so-called Will of Peter the Great was a forgery made in Paris on Napoleon's order in 1812.
peter-tordenskjold: Peter Jansen Wessel was the tenth child of the Trondheim alderman Jan Wessel. An unruly boy, he stowed away on a ship to Copenhagen in 1704 and tried without success to become a naval cadet. The king's chaplain, Peder Jespersen, sent him on a voyage to the West Indies and at last found him a cadetship. After voyages to the East Indies he was made second lieutenant on 7 July 1711. The Norwegian admiral Waldemar Løvendal gave him the four-gun sloop Ormen and in June 1712 the 18-gun Løvendals Galej, against the advice of the Danish admiralty, which thought him unreliable.

He took part in the destruction of Swedish transports at Rügen on 29 September 1712. On 26 and 27 July 1714, off Lindesnes, he fought the 28-gun Swedish privateer Olbing Galley until both ships were badly damaged, then sent to thank her crew and to ask for more ammunition so as to go on. King Frederick IV had him court-martialled for disclosing his lack of ammunition and for risking his ship against a stronger one; he was acquitted on 15 December and made captain on 28 December.

At Kolberg on 24 April 1715 he captured the Swedish Rear-Admiral Hans Wachtmeister and the frigate Hvita Örn, which became his flagship. At Dynekilen on 8 July 1716, with two frigates and five smaller ships, he took or destroyed around 30 Swedish vessels. A failure against the Gothenburg squadron in 1717 brought a second court-martial in 1718, which was quashed after Ulrik Christian Gyldenløve intervened. He became rear-admiral in December 1718 and vice-admiral after partly destroying and partly capturing the Gothenburg squadron on 26 September 1719.

On 12 November 1720, aged 30, he was killed by the sword of the Livonian colonel Jakob Axel Staël von Holstein in a duel at Gleidingen near Hildesheim. The quarrel arose at a dinner where Tordenskiold spoke of a friend cheated at gambling. As duelling was against Danish law, his body was brought to Holmen Church without much ceremony. He is named in the Danish anthem Kong Christian stod ved højen mast of 1778 and the Norwegian anthem Ja, vi elsker dette landet of 1864. A story that at Marstrand his men moved from post to post to seem more numerous gave Danish and Norwegian the phrase Tordenskjold's soldiers.
peterborough: Peterborough lies 74 miles (119 km) north of London on the River Nene, on the western edge of the Fens. The land is flat and in places below sea level; Holme Fen, just south of the city, is said to be the lowest point on land in Britain. The city has been called the Gateway to the Fens. Settlement began here because the Nene creates permanently drained land at this point. The Oxford Clay, dug in brick pits, has yielded fossils of Jurassic marine reptiles and, in 1898, a sauropod skeleton later named Cetiosauriscus.

The Flag Fen site east of the city centre shows Iron Age settlement and what is thought to be religious activity. The Romans founded a fortified garrison town at Durobrivae, now Water Newton, around the middle of the 1st century CE, and a large fort at Longthorpe, perhaps as early as 44 to 48 CE, built for about 3,000 soldiers. The area produced Nene Valley Ware, traded as far as Cornwall and the Antonine Wall.

The original town was the monastery of Medeshamstede, founded in 655. From the late tenth century the name became Burgh, possibly after Abbot Kenulf built a defensive wall around the abbey, which was dedicated to Saint Peter; this became Peterborough. The present cathedral was rebuilt between 1118 and 1238. When the abbey church became a cathedral in 1541 the last abbot became the first bishop and the town was deemed a city. Catherine of Aragon and Mary, Queen of Scots were buried there, though Mary's remains were later moved to Westminster Abbey by her son James I.

The Great Northern Railway's line from London to York, opened in 1850, turned a market town into an industrial centre known for brickworks and engineering. The Great Fire of Peterborough destroyed much of the old centre on 22 August 1956, and the city was designated a new town in the 1960s.

The 2021 census counted 192,178 people in the urban area, and the city is a unitary authority within Cambridgeshire. Peterborough Cathedral, one of the most intact large Norman buildings in England, is known for its early English Gothic west front with three great arches. The Nene Viaduct of 1847, by Sir William and Joseph Cubitt, is the oldest surviving cast-iron railway bridge in the country.
petra: Petra lies in a basin surrounded by mountains on the eastern flank of the Arabah valley, which runs from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Flash floods visit the area, but excavations show that the Nabataeans controlled them with dams, cisterns and water conduits, which stored water through long droughts and created an artificial oasis. Enclosed by rocks and watered by a perennial stream, the city had the advantages of a fortress and controlled the commercial routes to Gaza, to Bosra and Damascus, to the Red Sea, and across the desert to the Persian Gulf.

By 7000 BCE some of the earliest recorded farmers had settled at Beidha, just north of Petra. In the Iron Age the area was held by the Edomites. The Nabataeans, a northern Arabian people who had roamed the desert with their herds, settled there in the fourth century BCE, and their name for the city appears to have been Raqēmō. Petra flourished in the first century CE, when its population peaked at an estimated 20,000 and Al-Khazneh, possibly the mausoleum of the king Aretas IV, was built.

In 106 the Romans annexed the Nabataean realm as the province of Arabia Petraea. The native dynasty ended, but the city continued to flourish under Roman rule. Its importance declined as sea-based trade routes grew, and an earthquake in 363 destroyed many buildings and crippled the water system. Petra became the capital of the Byzantine province of Palaestina III, and papyri found in the Byzantine Church show that it still thrived in the sixth century. The site was lost to the outside world until the Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt reached it in 1812.

Petra is a World Heritage Site, called the Rose City for its sandstone. Visitors enter through the Siq, a narrow gorge ending at Al-Khazneh, the Treasury. Other monuments include the Royal Tombs, among them the Urn Tomb, which was made into a church in 446, and the High Place of Sacrifice on Jebel Madbah. The Monastery, Ad Deir, the largest monument, dates from the first century BCE and is thought to have been dedicated to the deified king Obodas I.
petrarch: Petrarch was born on 20 July 1304, the son of Ser Petracco and his wife Eletta Canigiani. His birth name was Francesco di Petracco, which he Latinized to Franciscus Petrarcha. His family followed Pope Clement V to Avignon, where the papacy had moved in 1309. His father, a notary, insisted that he and his brother Gherardo study law, at Montpellier from 1316 to 1320 and at Bologna from 1320 to 1326. Petrarch preferred Latin literature and thought the seven years wasted. His father once threw his books into a fire.

After their parents died, Petrarch and his brother returned to Avignon in 1326, where he held clerical offices that left time for writing. His Latin epic Africa, about the Roman general Scipio Africanus, made him a European celebrity. On 8 April 1341 he was crowned on the Capitoline Hill in Rome by the senators Giordano Orsini and Orso dell'Anguillara, the second poet laureate since classical antiquity. He travelled widely and served as an ambassador.

He collected crumbling Latin manuscripts, and in 1345 he found in the Chapter Library of Verona Cathedral a collection of Cicero's letters not known to have survived, the Epistulae ad Atticum. About 1368 he moved with his daughter Francesca and her family to Arquà in the Euganean Hills near Padua, where he spent his remaining years in religious contemplation. The da Carrara lords of Padua seized his library, and its manuscripts are now scattered across Europe.

Petrarch is best known for the Rerum vulgarium fragmenta, or Canzoniere, a collection of 366 poems, 317 of them sonnets. The poems centre on Laura, whom he said he first saw in the church of Sainte-Claire d'Avignon on 6 April 1327. She may have been Laura de Noves, though he always denied that she was an invented figure. The Petrarchan sonnet still bears his name, and in the 16th century Pietro Bembo made his verse a model for the Italian language.

Most of his writing was in Latin, including the Secretum, an imagined dialogue with a figure inspired by Augustine of Hippo, and a large body of letters. He valued the study of ancient history and literature as the study of human thought and action, and is often called the father of humanism. He is credited with creating the idea of a historical "Dark Ages", a notion most modern scholars find inaccurate and misleading.
petrobras: Petrobras was created in 1953 under President Getúlio Vargas with the slogan The Oil is Ours, and was given a legal monopoly in Brazil. Brazil then produced only 2,700 barrels of oil a day. The REDUC refinery near Rio de Janeiro began operating in 1961, and the Cenpes research centre opened in Rio in 1963. In 1961 the company's geologist Walter K. Link published a memorandum implying that exploring offshore was more promising than onshore. In 1963 Petrobras found the Recôncavo Baiano and Carmópolis oil fields, and in 1968 it set up the subsidiary Petroquisa for petrochemicals.

The oil crisis of 1973 halted the company's growth and ended the Brazilian miracle, a period of annual growth above 10%; Petrobras came close to bankruptcy. A discovery in the Campos Basin in 1974 restored its finances, and in 1975 the government temporarily allowed foreign operators into Brazil. Production reached 1 million barrels a day in 1997 and passed 2 million barrels of oil equivalent a day in 2003.

Law 9.478 of 1997 ended the monopoly and created the National Petroleum Agency, and in 1999 the agency signed agreements with other companies. In 2000 Petrobras set a world record for deep-water exploration at 1,877 metres. In 2006 the P-50 platform in the Campos Basin made Brazil self-sufficient in oil. In 2007 and 2008 discoveries in the Santos Basin, among them the Tupi field, about 300 km off the coast of Rio de Janeiro, opened the pre-salt reserves. In 2010 the company completed a share offering of US$70 billion to develop the new fields.

The company is headquartered in Rio de Janeiro and operates in refining, exploration and production, distribution, gas and power, biofuels and international business. Brazil's government directly holds 54% of its voting common shares. Its shares are traded on B3 in Brazil and on the New York and Madrid stock exchanges. Brazil accounted for 92% of its production in 2014, and the company has also held assets in Bolivia, Colombia, Argentina and elsewhere.

Operation Car Wash, a federal police investigation begun in Curitiba, expanded from a money-laundering inquiry to allegations that Petrobras executives took bribes for awarding inflated contracts to construction firms. Petrobras agreed in 2018 to pay settlements to US and Brazilian authorities and shareholders.
petronas: Oil exploration in the region began before Malaysia existed. Royal Dutch Shell started in Miri, Sarawak, after Charles Brooke signed the first Oil Mining Lease in 1909, and the first well was drilled there in 1910. Shell was still the only oil company in the area in 1963, when the Federation of Malaya united with Sarawak and Sabah to become Malaysia, and it brought the country's first offshore oilfield into production in 1968.

Several factors in the early 1970s led the government to found a state-owned company. The oil price rose from US$1.50 a barrel in 1972 to US$12.00 after war in the Middle East and an oil embargo by OPEC. Other countries had adopted production sharing agreements in place of concessions. The government also believed that foreign companies did not inform it properly of discoveries in their concessions, and the New Economic Policy of the early 1970s encouraged Malaysians, and bumiputeras in particular, to take control of modern industries.

Production-sharing contracts between Petronas and foreign oil companies were signed in 1976. Of the oil produced, 20 per cent went to the companies to recover costs and 10 per cent was paid as royalty, shared equally between the federal and state governments. The remaining 70 per cent, the profit oil, was divided 70:30 between Petronas and the companies, and Petronas did not take over the companies' equity.

Early in the 21st century the company expanded abroad. In March 2000 it finalised an oil production deal in Chad, and in July 2000 it found oil in the Samarang-Asam Paya contract area in Sabah. In 2001 it began construction on the Chad-Cameroon Integrated Oil Development and Pipeline Project. It also sponsored the Sauber Formula One team from 1995 to 2009, and then the Mercedes team.

Petronas is a legal entity incorporated under the Malaysian Companies Act 1965, and the federal government is its sole shareholder. Its logo, designed in 1974 by Dato' Johan Ariff, combines an oil drop with the letter P, in emerald green for the sea from which oil and gas are drawn. It is vertically integrated, with exploration, refining, distribution, power generation and trading. Petronas Carigali is its principal exploration and production subsidiary, and the Malaysia Petroleum Management division has overseen the country's upstream assets since the company was established. It also runs a research university, Universiti Teknologi Petronas, built in 1997 at Seri Iskandar in Perak.
petronas-twin-towers: Planning of the Petronas Towers began on 1 January 1992 and included rigorous tests and simulations of wind and structural loads. César Pelli chose a distinctive postmodern style intended to create a 21st-century icon for Kuala Lumpur. Seven years of construction followed on the site of the former Selangor Turf Club, starting on 1 March 1993 with excavation, which meant moving 500 truckloads of earth every night to dig 30 metres down. The superstructure began on 1 April 1994.

Test boreholes showed that the site sat on the edge of a cliff, with decayed limestone under one half and soft rock under the other, so the whole site was moved 61 metres to rest on the soft rock. Because the bedrock lay so deep, the towers stand on very deep foundations of 104 concrete piles, 60 to 114 metres long. Each tower's concrete raft, 4.6 metres thick, was poured continuously over 54 hours.

The structural system is a tube in tube design, invented by the Bangladeshi-American architect Fazlur Rahman Khan. The towers are built largely of reinforced concrete, with a steel and glass facade whose motifs resemble Islamic art, and their cross section is based on the Rub el Hizb, with circular sectors added to provide office space. Because importing steel was costly, the builders used super high-strength concrete, which is familiar to Asian contractors and twice as effective as steel in reducing sway, though it makes the building twice as heavy on its foundation.

The government required completion within six years, so two consortia worked at once. A Japanese group led by the Hazama Corporation built Tower 1 and a South Korean group led by Samsung C&T built Tower 2. A batch of concrete once failed a strength test and halted construction, at a cost of US$700,000 a day, and one floor was demolished. A double-decker skybridge joins the towers on the 41st and 42nd floors, 170 metres above the ground, and also lets people move between the towers in high winds.

The towers stand at 451.9 metres and were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004, when Taipei 101 surpassed them. They remain the tallest twin skyscrapers, ahead of the original World Trade Center towers in New York. Below them are the Suria KLCC shopping centre, the Petronas Philharmonic Hall, home of the Malaysian Philharmonic Orchestra, and the 6.9-hectare KLCC Park. The towers are a major landmark of Kuala Lumpur.
petrozavodsk: Petrozavodsk stretches for some 27 kilometres along the western shore of Lake Onega. Its name means Peter's factory, combining the name of Peter the Great with the Russian zavod, factory. Archaeological finds show a settlement on the site as long as seven thousand years ago, and during the Middle Ages several lakeside villages marked it. A map by the Flemish cartographer Abraham Ortelius at the end of the 16th century places a settlement called Onegaborg there, and Finnish forces later used a translation of that name, Äänislinna, during their occupation in the Continuation War.

On 11 September 1703 Prince Menshikov founded the settlement of Petrovskaya Sloboda at the behest of Peter the Great, who needed a new iron foundry to make cannon and anchors for the Baltic Fleet during the Great Northern War. The foundry was first called Shuysky zavod and later Petrovsky zavod, after the reigning monarch. By 1717 the settlement was the largest in Karelia, with about 3,500 inhabitants, a timber fort, a covered market and miniature palaces of the Tsar and Menshikov. After Peter's death it was depopulated, and the factory closed in 1734.

Catherine the Great revived the industry in 1773 with a new iron foundry, named Alexandrovsky after Alexander Nevsky, to supply cannon for the Russo-Turkish Wars; Charles Gascoigne supervised its expansion in 1787–96. In her municipal reform of 1777 the settlement became a town named Petrozavodsk, and a Neoclassical centre was built around the Round Square.

In 1784 it replaced Olonets as the administrative centre of the region, and Olonets Governorate, abolished by Emperor Paul, was revived in 1801 with Petrozavodsk as its centre. From 14 October 1941, during the Finnish occupation of 1941–1944, Finnish authorities opened concentration camps, eleven by the time the city was recaptured. A commemorative site was created in 1992 for several hundred people shot during the Great Terror.

Petrozavodsk is the capital and largest city of the Republic of Karelia. It is distinguished among towns of northern Russia by its Neoclassical heritage, including the Round Square of 1775 and the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, consecrated in 1832. Its institutions include the National Museum of the Republic of Karelia, founded in 1871, and Petrozavodsk State University. The suburb of Martsialnye Vody, founded by Peter the Great in 1714, is the oldest spa in Russia, and boats from the harbour reach Kizhi, a World Heritage Site with an outdoor museum of ancient wooden architecture.
peugeot: The Peugeot family of Valentigney, near Montbéliard in Franche-Comté, began manufacturing in 1810 with a steel foundry, which soon made saws and other hand tools. Around 1840 to 1842 it added coffee grinders. In the 1850s it introduced waist corsets made with light steel blades, in 1874 pepper grinders, and about 1880 bicycles. On 20 November 1858 Émile Peugeot applied for the lion trademark, and in 1882 Armand Peugeot introduced the penny-farthing called Le Grand Bi, with a range of other bicycles.

Armand Peugeot became interested in the automobile early, after meeting Gottlieb Daimler and others. The first Peugeot car, a three-wheeled steam car designed by Léon Serpollet, appeared in 1889, and only four were made, since steam power was heavy and slow to warm up. In 1890, after meeting Daimler and Émile Levassor, Peugeot abandoned steam for a four-wheeled car with a petrol engine built by Panhard under Daimler licence. One was sold to the young Alberto Santos-Dumont, who exported it to Brazil. Automobiles Peugeot was created in 1896. The company had a long record in racing, including victories at the Indianapolis 500 in 1913, 1916 and 1919.

During the Second World War Peugeot made armoured vehicles for the German war effort, while its management was generally sympathetic to the French Resistance. Workers sabotaged production, and Rudolphe and Jean-Pierre Peugeot lent one hundred thousand francs to the Special Operations Executive agent Harry Rée. After a bombing raid in July 1943 that left 110 dead, management agreed with Rée to continue sabotage at the Sochaux plant to avoid further bombing. Car production restarted in 1946 with the 202, and the 203 of 1947 remained in production until 1960. The 403 of 1955 sold a million copies, and the 404 of 1960 won the East African Safari Rally four times.

In 1974 Peugeot bought 30% of Citroën and took it over completely in 1975, forming the PSA Peugeot Citroën group. The Peugeot 205, launched in 1983, is largely credited with turning the company's fortunes around, and the 206 became the best-selling Peugeot model of all time, with 8,358,217 cars sold by 2012.

Peugeot's Sochaux plant is still a large manufacturing site and houses the Peugeot Museum. Peugeot cars have won six European Car of the Year awards, the first for the 504 in 1969 and the second for the 405 in 1988.
pforzheim: Pforzheim lies at the northern rim of the eastern Black Forest and the edge of the hilly Kraichgau, in an open valley where the rivers Enz, Nagold and Würm meet. Because of this it is called the three-valleys town and the Gateway to the Black Forest. It stands about halfway between Stuttgart and Karlsruhe, on the border of Baden and Württemberg, on the Baden side. Romans settled the site earlier than the present centres of Stuttgart and Karlsruhe, and built a ford just past the confluence of the three rivers for their military highway.

Its position later made Pforzheim a centre of the timber-rafting trade, which carried logs from the Black Forest down the Enz, Nagold and Würm, the Neckar and the Rhine, to markets that included the Netherlands, where the timber was used in shipbuilding and for the foundations of Amsterdam. Guilds of tailors, bakers, weavers, wine-growers, skippers and timber raftsmen were founded between 1410 and 1512. In 1501 Margrave Christoph I of Baden-Baden issued an ordinance on the rafting profession. Margrave Karl II installed the Protestant Reformation in the Margraviate of Baden in 1556, when Pforzheim was its capital, and the town stayed Protestant for centuries.

In 1618 Pforzheim had an estimated 2,500 to 3,000 inhabitants and was the largest town in Baden. In 1645, near the end of the Thirty Years' War, Bavarian troops burned the old town. In 1718 an institution for orphans, the sick and the poor opened in the former Dominican convent by the Enz; some fifty years later it became the starting point of the town's jewellery and watchmaking industries. In 1836 Ferdinand Öchsle invented a device for measuring the sugar content of grape juice, still used in winemaking. Watchmaking revived from 1900 and thrived in the 1920s.

Pforzheim is a city of more than 135,000 inhabitants in Baden-Württemberg, known as the Goldstadt for its jewellery and watchmaking. On the evening of 23 February 1945 the Royal Air Force carried out the largest of its air raids on the city, one of the most devastating area bombardments of the Second World War. About 17,600 people, nearly a third of the population, were killed, and about 83 per cent of the buildings were destroyed. The Allies believed that precision instruments were made there and that the town was a transport centre.

After French occupation it was administered by the United States from 1945 to 1948, and was rebuilt over the following twenty years. The rubble was heaped on the Wallberg hill, where a monument stands.
phalanx: The first use of the word comes from Homer, who in the Iliad uses it of hoplites fighting in an organised battle line, to set formation combat apart from the individual duels common in his poems. Ancient Greek writers used it more broadly for any massed infantry formation.
