Historians have not agreed on how the Greek formation relates to earlier ones, since the shield wall and spear hedge were widely known.

Traditionally the hoplite phalanx has been dated to the 8th century BCE in Sparta, but this is under revision. It was perhaps devised in the 7th century BCE, after the city of Argos introduced the aspis, the shield that made the formation possible. The Chigi vase, dated to 650 BCE, shows hoplites with aspis, spear and javelins.

In the hoplite phalanx of c. 800–350 BCE the men lined up in close order, locked their shields together and projected the spears of the first few ranks over the front rank of shields. Each hoplite carried his shield on his left arm, which protected the man to his left, so the man at the extreme right was only half protected and the whole line tended to drift to the right. Each hoplite supplied his own equipment; his main weapon was a spear, the dory, about 2.4 metres long.

The Macedonian phalanx and those of the Hellenistic successor states developed from it. The phalangites carried the sarissa, a pike at least 14 feet long and more probably 18, which was wielded with both hands. Hoplite phalanxes were usually eight ranks deep or more, Macedonian ones usually sixteen, and sometimes thirty-two.

Battles between phalanxes took place on open, flat plains, where it was easier to keep formation, and usually ended when one side fled. The most widely accepted reading of the sources is the othismos, a pushing match in which the rear ranks kept pressure on the front; no Greek art shows it, and the theory remains unresolved. At Marathon in 490 BCE the Athenians thinned their phalanx to lengthen their front, and at Leuctra the Theban general Epaminondas deepened his left flank to fifty ranks.

The formation was weakest against lighter, more flexible troops, as at Lechaeum, where an Athenian force led by Iphicrates routed a Spartan mora. A Macedonian phalanx was very vulnerable on its flanks and rear and could lose cohesion on broken ground, as at Cynoscephalae and Pydna, where Roman legionary centuries engaged the phalangites hand to hand. After Alexander the Great the phalanx slowly declined, and as Rome conquered most of the Hellenistic successor states the armies that used it ceased to exist.
pharaoh: The word pharaoh derives from the Egyptian pr ꜥꜣ, meaning great house, which named the royal palace and was long used only in phrases referring to the court. Under the New Kingdom it became a form of address for the king himself. The earliest confirmed use for a ruler is a letter to Akhenaten (reigned c. 1353–1336 BCE), and an inscription referring to Thutmose III (c. 1479–1425 BCE) may be earlier. The first dated attachment of the title to a king's name is in year 17 of Siamun, in the tenth century BCE.

Scholars nevertheless use the word for every ruler of Egypt from the First Dynasty (c. 3150 BCE) to 30 BCE. Early kings bore up to three titles, the Horus name, the Sedge and Bee name and the Two Ladies name; the Golden Horus name, the nomen and the prenomen were added later, and by the Middle Kingdom the formal titulary had five names.

The king was the intermediary between the gods and the people. He owned all the land of Egypt, enacted laws, collected taxes and commanded the army, and he officiated at religious ceremonies and chose the sites of new temples. Officials acted only in his name, by delegated power. From the Pyramid Texts his task was summed up in a maxim, bring Maat and repel Isfet, that is, promote order and repel chaos.

Regalia expressed the office. The red crown, the Deshret, stood for Lower Egypt and the white crown, the Hedjet, for Upper Egypt; the double crown, the Pschent, is first documented in the middle of the First Dynasty. The rearing cobra, the uraeus, appears from the reign of Den. No ancient Egyptian crown has ever been found, not even in the tomb of Tutankhamun.

Egyptians often regarded the pharaoh as divine. In the Early Dynastic Period he was the incarnation of Horus; by the time of Djedefre in the 26th century BCE he was held to have no human father, his mother having been impregnated by the sun god Ra. Under the New Kingdom he was thought to possess the living royal ka of Amun-Re, received at his coronation. Temple texts called Darius the Great (522–486 BCE) a divine being, and such descriptions continued for Alexander the Great and the Ptolemaic rulers.

Herodotus reports that Egyptian priests rejected the divinity of the king, and rabbinic literature later depicted Pharaoh as a man who falsely proclaimed himself a god. Through the Hebrew Bible and the Qur'an, which spells the title firʿawn, it became the usual name for the kings of ancient Egypt.
pharisees: The name Pharisee comes from the Greek Pharisaios, from an Aramaic word meaning set apart. It may refer to their separation from Gentiles and sources of ritual impurity, or from irreligious Jews. The Pharisees emerged largely from the scribes and sages and were active from the middle of the 2nd century BCE until the destruction of the Temple in 70 CE. Josephus first mentions them in connection with Jonathan Apphus, successor of Judas Maccabaeus.

The Pharisees held that all Jews had to observe the purity laws, which applied to the Temple service, outside the Temple. They also stood out for their adherence to the laws and traditions of the Jewish people in the face of assimilation. Josephus considered them the most expert and accurate expositors of Jewish law, and estimated that there were about 6,000 of them before the fall of the Second Temple.

Under the priestly Hasmonean dynasty the Pharisees did not support the wars of expansion or the forced conversion of the Idumeans. The rift widened when a Pharisee named Eleazar insulted the ruler John Hyrcanus at his table. Hyrcanus's son Alexander Jannaeus sided openly with the Sadducees, and the resulting riot and brief civil war ended in a bloody repression of the Pharisees. His widow, Salome Alexandra, was favourably inclined towards them, and under her reign their influence grew greatly, especially in the Sanhedrin, which they came to dominate.

After the Jewish–Roman wars the Zealots were crushed, the last dying at Masada in 73 CE, and the Sadducees, whose teachings were tied to the Temple, disappeared with its destruction. Of the major sects of the Second Temple period, only the Pharisees remained.

Josephus says the Pharisees held that people have free will but that God also foresees human destiny. The sources differ on their view of the afterlife: according to the New Testament they believed in the resurrection of the dead, while Josephus says they held the soul to be immortal. They applied Jewish law to everyday life, in a form of Judaism that did not depend on the Temple and in which leaders were determined by scholarly achievement rather than birth. The standard view is that they accepted an Oral Torah alongside the written Scripture, though Anthony J. Saldarini argued that there is no direct evidence for this.

Their view of law as a way for ordinary people to engage with the sacred in daily life let them answer the questions raised by the loss of the Temple, and their responses formed Rabbinic Judaism. The Pharisees appear in the New Testament in conflict with Jesus, but Nicodemus and Gamaliel were Pharisees, and Paul the Apostle declared himself one.
pharnavaz-i-of-iberia: Pharnavaz I was a king of Kartli, the ancient Georgian kingdom known as Iberia in classical antiquity. The Georgian Chronicles credit him with founding the kingship of Kartli and the Pharnavazid dynasty, while other chronicles, such as The Conversion of Kartli, make him the second Georgian monarch. Most scholars, going by medieval evidence, place his rule in the 3rd century BCE. He is not directly attested in non-Georgian sources, and his story is full of imagery from folk tradition. According to the c. 800 chronicle The Life of Kings, he traced his descent from Kartlos, the mythical ancestor of the Georgians. His name is based on the Persian word farnah, the divine radiance that ancient Iranians believed marked a legitimate ruler.

In the royal annals Pharnavaz lost his family at the age of three, when Azon, installed by Alexander the Great, usurped his inheritance. After a dream and the discovery of a hidden treasure in a cave while hunting, he raised an army with the help of Kuji of Colchis and defeated and killed Azon, becoming king at 27. He is said to have acknowledged the suzerainty of the Seleucids, and to have patterned his administration on the Persian kingdom. The annals credit him with dividing Iberia among regional governors called eristavis, under a commander-in-chief, the spaspet. Strabo gives the Iberian army as 70–80,000. Modern scholars treat the reform as most likely a back-projection of the medieval pattern onto the distant past.

He is also said to have raised the idol Armazi on a mountain ledge, built a fortress of the same name, fortified Mtskheta, and rebuilt the cities destroyed by Alexander. He allied with North Caucasian peoples, marrying a Durdzuk woman and marrying his sister to a Sarmatian chief. The annals say he created the Georgian script and made Georgian the official language. They give him a reign of 65 years and say that he was buried in front of Armazi and worshipped.

His son Sauromaces I succeeded him. According to the annals, Pharnavaz's grave is undisclosed, and one of the last kings said to have visited it was Mirian III. The Bagrationi dynasty claimed descent from him, and Georgian kings presented themselves as heirs of the kingdom he founded. Some modern scholars have identified him with the Pharasmanes whom Arrian describes visiting Alexander the Great, though others suggest the Greek copyists confused two names.
phidias: Phidias was the son of Charmides of Athens, and the ancients believed that his masters were Hegias and Ageladas. Little is known of his life apart from his works. No original work can be attributed to him with certainty, and what survives is numerous Roman copies of varying fidelity. His earliest works were dedications commemorating the Greek victory at Marathon. His first commission was a group of national heroes with Miltiades as the central figure, and at Delphi he made a great bronze group that included the gods Apollo and Athena, several Attic heroes and Miltiades the Younger.

On the Acropolis of Athens Phidias made the Athena Promachos, a colossal bronze statue of Athena that was visible far out at sea. According to Pausanias he also made the bronze Athena Lemnia for the Athenians living on Lemnos, which Pausanias called the best of all his works to see. In the Hippias Major Plato says that he seldom, if ever, worked in marble, and in antiquity he was known for bronze and for chryselephantine statues, made of gold and ivory.

Plutarch writes that he superintended the great works Pericles ordered on the Acropolis. Inscriptions show that the marble blocks for the pediments of the Parthenon reached Athens only in 433 to 434 BCE, so most of its sculptural decoration may have come from his workshop, with pupils such as Alcamenes and Agoracritus. The ancients thought two works outshone all the others: the Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon and the Statue of Zeus in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia, of about 432 BCE. The Zeus sat on a throne decorated with sculpture, with a body of ivory and a robe of gold, and small copies on coins of Elis give a notion of its pose.

Plutarch says that his friendship with Pericles led the enemies of Pericles to attack him through Phidias. Phidias was accused of keeping some of the gold meant for the Athena Parthenos, and is said to have proved his innocence by weighing the gold robe. He was then accused of impiously portraying himself and Pericles on the statue's shield, which was apparently true. Plutarch records that he was imprisoned and died in jail, while Philochorus says the Eleans put him to death after he finished the Zeus. The historical value of these accounts is debatable.

Excavations at Olympia between 1954 and 1958 uncovered his workshop where Pausanias said it stood, with tools, terracotta moulds and pottery, and a cup inscribed as belonging to Phidias, though its authenticity is disputed. The finds allowed archaeologists to reconstruct how the statue was made. Since about 1910 the Greek letter phi has been used as the symbol of the golden ratio, after Phidias.
philadelphia: Philadelphia lies on the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line, which separates the Atlantic Plain from the Piedmont. The Delaware and Schuylkill rivers are its principal natural bodies of water. The city encompasses about 142.7 square miles, 6 per cent of it water, and its highest point, in Chestnut Hill, is about 446 feet above sea level. The city has been coterminous with its county since 1854.

Before Europeans arrived in the early 17th century, the Lenape, also known as the Delaware Indians, lived in the village of Shackamaxon, in present-day Philadelphia. Most Lenape were pushed out of the region during the 18th century as the Thirteen Colonies expanded, a loss made worse by intertribal conflicts, newly introduced diseases, mainly smallpox, and conflicts with Europeans. In the 1860s the federal government sent most of those remaining in the eastern United States to the Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma.

William Penn, an English Quaker and advocate of religious freedom, founded Philadelphia in 1682, and it became the capital of the colonial Province of Pennsylvania. It hosted the First Continental Congress in 1774 and the Second Continental Congress, which formed the Continental Army, elected George Washington as its commander and adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776. The British Army occupied the city for nine months, from September 1777 to June 1778. The Constitution of the United States was ratified at the Philadelphia Convention. The city served as the national capital on several occasions until 1800, when the new capital at Washington, D.C. was completed.

Philadelphia is the most populous city in Pennsylvania and the sixth most populous in the United States, with about 1.6 million people in the 2020 census. Independence National Historical Park, which holds Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the city has 67 National Historic Landmarks. It claims many firsts in the United States, among them the first library (1731), hospital (1751), medical school (1765) and zoo (1874).
philip-ii-of-france: Philip was born at Gonesse on 21 August 1165, the only son of King Louis VII and his third wife, Adela of Champagne. Because he was a first son born late in his father's life, he was nicknamed Dieudonné, God-given. When Louis VII's health declined, the 14-year-old Philip was crowned and anointed at Reims on 1 November 1179 by Archbishop William of the White Hands. On 28 April 1180 he married Isabella of Hainault, daughter of Count Baldwin V of Hainaut, who brought the County of Artois as her dowry.

From 1190 Philip styled himself King of France (rex Francie), where his predecessors had been kings of the Franks. The chronicler Rigord gave him the epithet Augustus for enlarging the crown lands. The royal demesne grew with the County of Amiens in 1185, Clermont-en-Beauvaisis in 1218 and Alençon in 1219. After a quarrel with Count Philip I of Flanders over the Vermandois, the Treaty of Boves in July 1185 gave the king Amiénois and Artois. He also built a French navy and, late in his reign, could muster some 3,000 knights.

He joined the Third Crusade with Richard I of England, leaving Vézelay on 4 July 1190 and reaching Acre on 20 April 1191; ill with dysentery when the city surrendered on 12 July, he lost zeal, and relations with Richard were strained. Back in France he worked to recover the Vexin. In May 1200 the Treaty of Le Goulet with King John settled Normandy's boundaries, but John's management of Aquitaine led to revolt, which Philip encouraged. In 1214 Philip defeated a coalition of his rivals, including John and the Emperor Otto IV, at the Battle of Bouvines, ending the Angevin Empire.

Philip expelled the Jews from the royal demesne in 1182 and confiscated their goods; ninety-nine were burned alive at Brie-Comte-Robert. In 1198 he allowed them to return. His marriage to Ingeborg of Denmark in 1193 led to his repudiating her the same day and a long dispute with the papacy; he later married Agnes of Merania.

Philip did not take part in the Albigensian Crusade proclaimed by Pope Innocent III in 1208, though he let his nobles join it; its fruits in southern France fell to his son Louis VIII and grandson Louis IX. In Paris he had the main streets paved, built the market of Les Halles, continued Notre-Dame de Paris, built the first Louvre as a fortress, raised a great wall around the city and gave a charter to the University of Paris in 1200. He died on 14 July 1223.
philip-ii-of-macedon: Philip was the youngest son of King Amyntas III and Eurydice of Lynkestis, born in 383 or 382 BCE. After the assassination of his brother Alexander II he was sent as a hostage to Illyria, and was later held at Thebes, then the leading city of Greece, from about 368 to 365 BCE, where he received a military and diplomatic education from Epaminondas. He returned to Macedon in 364 BCE. When his brother Perdiccas III died in battle against the Illyrians in 359 BCE, Philip was appointed regent for the infant Amyntas IV but took the kingdom for himself. He faced Paeonians and Thracians who had invaded the east and an Athenian force landed with a pretender.

Philip drove back the Paeonians and Thracians, defeated 3,000 Athenian hoplites and strengthened his army. Its cavalry grew from 600 to 4,000 men by 334 BCE, soldiers could be promoted and rewarded, and he created the Macedonian phalanx. He defeated the Illyrians in the Erigon Valley, besieged Amphipolis in 357 BCE and kept it, with Pydna, after promising them to Athens. He founded Philippi at Crenides, whose mines gave him much of his gold. At the siege of Methone he lost his right eye. He took Olynthus in 348 BCE and razed it.

As a leader of the Thessalian League, Philip entered the Third Sacred War and won at the Battle of Crocus Field. He made peace with Athens in 346 BCE. His sieges of Perinthus and Byzantium failed, but at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE he defeated Athens and Thebes and was recognised as military leader of the League of Corinth, a Greek confederation against Persia. In 336 BCE he sent Parmenion and 10,000 men into Asia Minor to prepare an invasion to free the Greeks of the western coast.

Philip was assassinated in October 336 BCE at Aigai, while entering the theatre during celebrations of the marriage of his daughter Cleopatra to Alexander I of Epirus. One of his bodyguards, Pausanias of Orestis, stabbed him. The motives are disputed. Aristotle says only that Pausanias had been offended by Attalus. Later writers link the killing with Alexander and Olympias, but some modern historians find these accounts improbable. Alexander succeeded him.

Philip had seven wives. In 1977 Manolis Andronikos excavated the Great Tumulus at Aigai near Vergina, and Tomb II is now generally held to be Philip's, partly because a skull shows damage to the right eye. He founded cities including Philippi and Philippopolis, today Plovdiv. Some Greeks honoured him with cult, such as an altar to Zeus Philippeios at Eresos and the Philippeion at Olympia.
philip-ii-of-spain: Philip was born in Valladolid on 21 May 1527, the son of Emperor Charles V and Isabella of Portugal, and belonged to the House of Habsburg. He was raised in the Castilian court and tutored by humanists, among them Juan Martínez Siliceo, the future archbishop of Toledo. He had a good command of Latin, Spanish and Portuguese but never equalled his father as a polyglot. Although an archduke of Austria, he felt himself culturally Spanish and was seen as a foreigner in the Holy Roman Empire, which ultimately impeded his succession to the imperial throne.

Philip was invested with the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily in 1554 and married Queen Mary I of England at Winchester Cathedral on 25 July 1554, becoming jure uxoris king of England and Ireland until her death in 1558. He considered himself the chief defender of Catholic Europe against the Ottoman Empire and the Protestant Reformation. His realms were a personal union of separate kingdoms, each guarding its own rights, so his authority was often overruled by local assemblies. Charles V had left him a debt of about 36 million ducats, and Philip defaulted on his loans several times, the first in 1557.

In the Netherlands, discontent over taxation and the persecution of Protestants led to the Iconoclast Fury of 1566 and open warfare in 1568. The Duke of Alba had Lamoral, Count of Egmont and Philip de Montmorency, Count of Horn executed in Brussels in 1568, and civilians were massacred at Mechelen, Naarden, Zutphen and Haarlem.

The conflicts lasted for the rest of his life. In 1584 he signed the Treaty of Joinville, funding the French Catholic League. In 1588 he sent an armada to invade England and overthrow Elizabeth I; it was repulsed in a skirmish and wrecked by storms on its return, and further armadas in 1596 and 1597 also failed.

Philip died on 13 September 1598 at El Escorial, aged 71, after a prolonged illness, likely cancer. His bed was placed so that he could watch the liturgy at the church's main altar, and despite severe pain he kept reviewing state papers to the end.

The Spanish conquest of the Philippines, named in his honour, was completed in his reign, and he finished building El Escorial in 1584. Historical opinion of him was heavily shaped by enemy propaganda, which he refused to answer, and his negative foreign reputation developed into the Spanish Black Legend. The historian Helmut Koenigsberger wrote that no personality in modern history had been as enigmatic and controversial.
philip-iii-of-france: Philip was born in Poissy on 1 May 1245, the second son of King Louis IX and Margaret of Provence. He became heir to the throne when his older brother Louis died in 1260. In 1262 he was married to Isabella of Aragon, in line with the Treaty of Corbeil, and his father knighted him on 5 June 1267. Louis IX also wrote the Enseignements for him, which presented justice as the first duty of a king.

Philip accompanied his father on the Eighth Crusade to Tunis in 1270. An epidemic of dysentery struck the army after it took Carthage, killing Philip's brother John Tristan on 3 August and Louis IX on 25 August. Philip, aged 25 and himself ill, was proclaimed king in Tunis. His uncle Charles I of Naples negotiated a treaty with the Hafsid caliph of Tunis on 5 November 1270. Philip's wife Isabella died after a fall from her horse while pregnant. He was crowned at Reims on 15 August 1271.

Philip kept most of his father's domestic policies, including the ordinances against seigneurial warfare, which he reinforced in October 1274. On 21 August 1271 his uncle Alphonse, Count of Poitiers and Toulouse, died childless, and Philip united his lands with the royal domain. In 1272 he campaigned against Roger-Bernard III, Count of Foix, who had invaded the County of Toulouse; the count surrendered and was imprisoned for a year, then freed. The Treaty of Orléans of 1275 gave France influence in Navarre by arranging a marriage between one of his sons and the heiress Joan, and French governors were sent there. A revolt in 1276 was put down by Robert II, Count of Artois.

After the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 Pope Martin IV granted Aragon to Philip's son Charles, and Philip launched the Aragonese Crusade, at the urging of his wife Marie of Brabant and of Charles of Naples. He took Girona on 7 September 1285, but dysentery struck the camp. The retreating French were defeated at the Col de Panissars on 1 October, and Philip died at Perpignan on 5 October 1285. His son Philip IV succeeded him. His reign added Toulouse, Auvergne, Guînes and Alençon to the royal domain, though the failed war nearly bankrupted the monarchy.
philip-iii-of-spain: Philip was born in Madrid on 14 April 1578, the son of King Philip II of Spain and his fourth wife, Anna of Austria, who was his niece and cousin. After the death of his half-brother Don Carlos, Prince of Asturias, Philip II made closer arrangements for his other sons, appointing Juan de Zúñiga as Philip's governor and García de Loaysa as his tutor. The education followed guidelines set by Father Juan de Mariana, stressing moderation and personal discipline. Philip married his cousin Margaret of Austria, sister of the future Emperor Ferdinand II, on 18 April 1599, a year after becoming king.

Philip withdrew from his subjects to an unprecedented degree and left government to his favourite, the Duke of Lerma, who had been made a royal counsellor within hours of the accession and managed most audiences. Spanish representatives overseas, called proconsuls, increasingly followed independent policies. From 1612, and certainly by 1617, the Lerma administration was crumbling, as his enrichment in office became a scandal and his own son, the Duke of Uceda, grew alarmed at his spending. Philip remained close to Lerma and supported him in becoming a cardinal in March 1618.

Spain suffered serious economic problems. From 1599 to 1600 and for several years afterwards, bubonic plague killed over 10% of the population. In 1609 Philip decreed the expulsion of the Moriscos, descendants of Muslims who had converted to Christianity, of whom there were almost 200,000 in the south alone. The decree was timed to coincide with a truce in the Eighty Years' War.

Philip inherited the Dutch revolt and the Anglo–Spanish War. After the failure of the Spanish invasion of Ireland at the Battle of Kinsale he accepted that further attacks on England were unlikely to succeed. After the financial crisis of 1607 Spain could no longer pursue the war in the Netherlands, and with the accession of James I of England the war ended through the Treaty of London. The resulting period of peace, called the Pax Hispanica, lasted until Spain entered the Thirty Years' War in the final years of the reign.

In 1619 Philip travelled to Portugal, where he was received with enthusiasm, although nobles complained that they received no favours. He died in Madrid on 31 March 1621 and was succeeded by his son Philip IV, who swiftly removed the last remnants of the Sandoval regime from court. Known in Spain as Philip the Pious, he has generally left a poor legacy with historians, who have described him as an undistinguished man, though he ruled the Spanish Empire at its height.
philip-iv-of-france: Philip was born in 1268 at the fortress of Fontainebleau, the son of the future Philip III and his first wife, Isabella of Aragon. His grandfather Louis IX died on crusade in 1270, and his mother died in January 1271 after falling from a horse. In May 1276 his elder brother Louis died, and the eight-year-old Philip became heir apparent. Rumour held that Louis had been poisoned at the instigation of his stepmother, Marie of Brabant, whose own first son was born that month. His schooling was entrusted to Guillaume d'Ercuis, his father's almoner. Through his marriage to Joan I of Navarre he was also King of Navarre and Count of Champagne.

Philip was crowned at Reims on 6 January 1286, aged seventeen. He relied on a professional bureaucracy of legalists, such as Guillaume de Nogaret and Enguerrand de Marigny, and left unpopular policies to them. His reign saw the emergence or consolidation of the King's Council, the Parlement and the Court of Auditors. His opponent Bernard Saisset, bishop of Pamiers, said of him that he was neither man nor beast but a statue.

A feud between English and French sailors in 1293 led Philip to summon Edward I, as Duke of Aquitaine, to his court. Edward agreed to give up Gascony temporarily, but war followed from 1294. In Flanders, Count Guy of Dampierre renounced his fealty and the Franco-Flemish War began in 1297; Flemish town militias defeated the French at the Battle of the Golden Spurs on 11 July 1302, but Philip prevailed at Mons-en-Pévèle in 1304, and by the treaty of Athis-sur-Orge in 1305 Flanders lost Lille, Douai and Orchies. The wars drove him to debase the coinage, which brought unrest and rioting in Paris in December 1306.

Philip expelled the Jews from France on 22 July 1306 and confiscated their property. Deeply in debt to the Knights Templar, he had hundreds of them arrested in France on Friday 13 October 1307; they were tortured into admitting heresy, and many were burned at the stake. In March 1314 he had the last Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, burned. His taxation of the clergy led to a violent quarrel with Pope Boniface VIII, whose residence at Anagni was attacked by French forces in September 1303; this eventually led to the Avignon Papacy of 1309 to 1376.

In 1314 his daughters-in-law Margaret and Blanche of Burgundy were accused of adultery in the Tour de Nesle affair. Philip had a stroke while hunting and died at Fontainebleau on 29 November 1314; he is buried at Saint-Denis. His three sons reigned in turn as Louis X, Philip V and Charles IV, and their deaths without surviving sons began a succession crisis that led to the Hundred Years' War.
philip-iv-of-spain: Philip was born in the Royal Palace of Valladolid on 8 April 1605, the eldest son of Philip III and Margaret of Austria. In 1615, aged ten, he was married to the thirteen-year-old Elisabeth of France. Olivares, later his key minister, had been introduced to the prince by his uncle Baltasar de Zúñiga, who led a coalition against the Sandoval family that had dominated Philip III's court. Philip's diffidence was counteracted by Olivares' drive, and when he came to the throne in 1621, aged sixteen, he ordered that all papers needing his signature go first to the count-duke, who remained chief minister for twenty years.

Philip reigned through most of the Thirty Years' War. Zúñiga and Olivares persuaded him to commit Spain to an aggressive policy in alliance with the Holy Roman Empire, and hostilities with the Dutch were renewed in 1621. Spain was a loose collection of kingdoms and provinces with different taxes and privileges, and Olivares set up juntas, small committees that bypassed the slow royal councils but excluded many grandees and caused resentment. Philip doubled and then tripled the naval budget.

Elisabeth conspired with nobles to remove Olivares from court in 1643. Their only surviving son, Balthasar Charles, died in 1646, aged sixteen, and Philip was deeply shocked. In 1649 he married his fourteen-year-old niece Maria Anna to strengthen the tie with Austria. In 1640 the Iberian Union collapsed and John IV took the Portuguese throne. By Philip's death the empire covered about 12.2 million square kilometres, though in other respects Spain was in decline, a process to which his failure to achieve domestic and military reform contributed.

Philip collected art with astonishing enthusiasm and owned over 4,000 paintings at his death. He summoned Diego Velázquez to Madrid in 1624 and kept him for the rest of his career; the two shared an interest in horses, dogs and art. He also favoured the dramatists Lope de Vega and Pedro Calderón de la Barca. He died on 17 September 1665, hoping that his four-year-old son Charles II would be more fortunate than himself.

He left the regency to his wife Mariana, advised by a junta that excluded his illegitimate son John Joseph, which produced a power struggle between them until John Joseph's death in 1679. Known as the Planet King, Philip has been held responsible for Spain's decline, which was mainly due to causes largely beyond the control of any one ruler.
philip-melanchthon: Philipp Schwartzerdt was born on 16 February 1497 at Bretten, where his father, Georg Schwarzerdt, was armorer to Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine. His mother was Barbara Reuter. In 1507 he was sent to the Latin school at Pforzheim, where he was introduced to the Latin and Greek poets and to Aristotle. His great-uncle Johann Reuchlin, a Renaissance humanist, suggested that he follow a humanist custom and change his surname, literally black earth, to its Greek equivalent, Melanchthon. In 1508, when he was eleven, his father and grandfather died within eleven days of each other.

On Reuchlin's recommendation Melanchthon accepted a call from Martin Luther to the University of Wittenberg and became professor of Greek there in 1518, aged 21. He attended the Leipzig disputation of 1519 and replied to attacks by Johann Eck on the authority of Scripture. He married Katharina Krapp, the mayor's daughter, on 25 November 1520. His Loci communes of 1521 discussed the leading thoughts of Paul's Letter to the Romans and set out a doctrine in which faith in God counted for more than good deeds. He also worked with Luther on the translation of the Bible.

The Augsburg Confession, presented at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, was based on Luther's Marburg and Schwabach articles but was mainly Melanchthon's work. He represented Luther at the Diet, since Luther was barred from attending, and Luther did not hide his dissatisfaction with its irenic tone. From 1531 he took part in discussions of the Lord's Supper with Martin Bucer. In 1547 he rejected the Augsburg Interim but made controversial concessions in the negotiations over the Leipzig Interim, which he later regretted. After Luther's death many saw him as the theological leader of the German Reformation, though the Gnesio-Lutherans led by Matthias Flacius accused him of heresy and apostasy.

Melanchthon's manuals were quickly taken up in schools and kept their place for more than a century. Through his Latin and Greek grammars and his work in educational institutions he became the founder of the learned schools of Evangelical Germany. Between 1536 and 1539 he was involved in the refoundation of Wittenberg, the reorganisation of Tübingen and the foundation of the University of Leipzig.

A severe cold caught on a journey to Leipzig in March 1560, followed by fever, led to Melanchthon's death on 19 April 1560. He was buried beside Luther in the Schloßkirche in Wittenberg. He is remembered as the man who systematised Luther's ideas, defended them in public and made them the basis of a religious education.
philip-of-swabia: Philip was born in or near Pavia in the Kingdom of Italy, the tenth child and eighth son of Frederick Barbarossa and his second wife Beatrice I, Countess of Burgundy. He was the fifth and youngest of the sons who survived. The origins of the Hohenstaufen, a name historians have given the dynasty since the 15th century, are unclear. Its prestige rested on descent from the Salian dynasty through Agnes, a daughter of Emperor Henry IV and the grandmother of Barbarossa. Conrad III was elected King of Germany in 1138 against fierce resistance from the House of Welf, and Barbarossa succeeded him in 1152.

Philip enjoyed his brother Henry VI's confidence to a great degree and appears to have been named guardian of Henry's underage son Frederick. In September 1197 he set out to fetch the boy from Apulia for coronation at Aachen. At Montefiascone he heard of Henry's sudden death in Messina on 28 September and returned at once to Germany. On 21 January 1198 he issued a charter for the citizens of Speyer in the name of King Frederick, but events overtook him. Reservations about a child as king led to two elections in 1198, which chose Philip and Otto of Brunswick, and so to the German throne dispute.

Kingship in this empire was exercised without a capital, and Philip had to travel the kingdom to give his rule authority. Of 28 known court days, only twelve took place within the Hohenstaufen sphere of influence. Philip increasingly asserted his kingship against Otto in the lands north of the Alps.

On 21 June 1208 Philip attended the wedding of his niece Countess Beatrice II of Burgundy to Duke Otto of Merania at Bamberg. In the afternoon, after retiring to his private apartments, he was murdered by Count Otto VIII of Wittelsbach. No chronicler witnessed it, and the sources disagree on its course. Most saw a withdrawn marriage promise as the motive: Philip had betrothed his daughter Kunigunde to Otto in 1203, then in November 1207 engaged her to Wenceslaus, son of King Ottokar I of Bohemia.

Otto IV was acknowledged at an Imperial Diet in Frankfurt in November 1208 and crowned emperor by Pope Innocent III the next year. The murderer was found in March 1209 in a granary near Regensburg and beheaded. The chronicler Burchard of Ursperg, loyal to the Hohenstaufen, called Philip meek, mild and kind.
philip-the-arab: Philip was born at what is now Shahba, about 90 km south-east of Damascus, in an Arab district of the Roman province of Arabia Petraea; the city was later renamed Philippopolis. Most historians accept that he was ethnically Arab. His father was a local citizen, Julius Marinus. His brother, Gaius Julius Priscus, was a member of the Praetorian Guard under Gordian III, and he married Marcia Otacilia Severa, with whom he had a son, Philip II, born in 237 or 238.

In 243, during Gordian's campaign against Shapur I of Persia, the praetorian prefect Timesitheus died under unclear circumstances. At Priscus's suggestion Philip took the post, intending that the brothers would control the young emperor. Gordian died in February 244 after a military defeat, in circumstances that are debated.

Philip assumed the purple and made peace with Shapur, paying 500,000 denarii and issuing coins that proclaimed peace made with the Persians. He sent Gordian's ashes to Rome for deification and left Priscus as rector Orientis. Confirmed augustus in the late summer of 244, he named his son caesar and his wife augusta. He courted the Senate, built extensively in his home town, raised it to civic status as Philippopolis, and founded the Actia-Dusaria Games at Bostra.

Building, the tribute to Persia and the donative to the army left him short of money. He raised taxes and stopped paying subsidies to the tribes north of the Danube. In 245 the Carpi crossed the Danube into Moesia, and by the summer of 246 he claimed victory over them. In April 248 he led the celebrations of Rome's thousandth birthday, with coins, games and theatrical shows. He also made his son co-augustus.

From late 248 the Pannonian and Moesian legions proclaimed Pacatianus emperor, the Goths besieged Marcianopolis, the Carpi renewed their attacks and Marcus Jotapianus rose in the east against Priscus's rule and heavy taxation. Philip offered to resign, but the Senate backed him, most vocally the senator Decius, whom he sent with a special command to the Danube. Decius put down the revolt but was proclaimed emperor by the Danubian armies in the spring of 249 and marched on Rome. Philip had by then debased the coinage. His army met Decius near Verona, and Philip was killed in September 249, in the fighting or by his own soldiers. His eleven-year-old son may have been killed with him, and Priscus disappeared.

Eusebius reports a tradition that Philip was a Christian, and Jerome called him the first Christian emperor. Historians generally find this dubious, since non-Christian writers do not mention it and his coinage kept to the Roman state religion.
philip-the-bold: Philip was born at Pontoise on 17 January 1342, the fourth and youngest son of John of Valois and Bonne of Luxembourg; his father became king of France in 1350. He became known as the Bold at the age of 14, when he fought beside his father at the Battle of Poitiers in 1356 and was captured with him by the English. They remained in custody until the terms of their ransom were set in the Treaty of Brétigny of 1360. In 1363 he received the Duchy of Burgundy as an apanage from his father, a reward for his courage at Poitiers.

On 19 June 1369 Philip married Margaret, the 19-year-old daughter of Count Louis II of Flanders. From 1379 to 1382 he helped his father-in-law put down revolts in Flanders, notably in Ghent under Philip van Artevelde, which ended in 1385 with the Peace of Tournai. As count of Flanders by marriage he kept in mind the economic interests of the Flemish cities, which lived by weaving and spinning. Philip also made significant use of gunpowder artillery in his campaigns.

He arranged his children's marriages with a diplomatic design that his successors followed. The double marriage at Cambrai in 1385 of his son John the Fearless and his daughter Margaret to a daughter and son of Albert, Count of Hainault and Holland, prepared the later union of Hainault and Holland with Burgundy and Flanders. He founded the Chartreuse de Champmol near Dijon, a Carthusian monastery built between 1383 and 1388 to house his dynasty's tombs, and in 1395 he outlawed the Gamay grape in favour of Pinot Noir.

When Charles V died in 1380 his successor Charles VI was 11, and a council of four uncles governed France, Philip in the dominant role. He put down a tax revolt, the Harelle, in 1382. On 1 July 1392, when the king went mad on the road to Brittany, Philip took command and was the principal ruler of France until 1402. His seizure of power set off a feud with the king's brother Louis I, Duke of Orléans, that their families continued after both were dead.

Philip died at Halle in Hainaut on 27 April 1404. His territories passed to his eldest son John the Fearless, who also inherited his political position. His tomb, with pleurants and a recumbent effigy by Jean de Marville, Claus Sluter and Claus de Werve, is an outstanding work of Burgundian sculpture and is now in the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Dijon. His successors ruled Flanders until 1482, a period called the Burgundian Netherlands.
philip-the-good: Philip was born on 31 July 1396 in Dijon, the first son of John, Count of Nevers, later John the Fearless, and Margaret of Bavaria. He belonged to a cadet line of the House of Valois. On 28 January 1405, aged eight, he was created Count of Charolais, and in June 1409 he married Michelle of France, daughter of Charles VI. When King Henry V of England invaded France in 1415, his father declared neutrality and forbade him to join the French forces.

In 1419 John the Fearless was assassinated at Montereau during a meeting with the Dauphin Charles, and Philip became Duke of Burgundy. He accused the Dauphin of planning the murder and within days negotiated with the English. In 1420 he allied himself with Henry V under the Treaty of Troyes, and in 1423 his sister Anne married John, Duke of Bedford, regent for Henry VI of England.

On 23 May 1430 Philip's troops under the Count of Ligny captured Joan of Arc at Compiègne and later sold her to the English, who staged a heresy trial before her burning in 1431. In 1435 he signed the Treaty of Arras, which revoked the Treaty of Troyes and recognised Charles VII as King of France. Charles VII and his successors came to see the Burgundian state as an impediment to royal authority and tried to undermine it.

His territories grew by several means. He bought Namur in 1429, took Hainault, Holland, Friesland and Zeeland in 1432 with the defeat of Jacqueline, Countess of Hainault, inherited Brabant and Limburg in 1430, and bought Luxembourg in 1443. In 1456 he saw his illegitimate son David elected Bishop of Utrecht and his nephew Louis de Bourbon Prince-Bishop of Liège. In 1463 he created an Estates-General for the Netherlands on the French model.

Philip crushed two rebellions in Liège, in 1465 and 1467, and died a few weeks after the second in Bruges, on 15 June 1467. He had no fixed capital and moved his court between Brussels, Bruges and Lille. In 1430 he founded the Order of the Golden Fleece, based on the Knights of the Round Table and the myth of Jason. He added about six hundred manuscripts to the ducal library, and his chapel, with composers such as Gilles Binchois and Guillaume Dufay, was the musical centre of Europe.

He married three times; the only one of his three legitimate sons to reach adulthood was Charles, later known as the Bold. He had 24 documented mistresses and fathered at least 18 illegitimate children. Justus Lipsius called him Conditor Belgii, the founder of the Low Countries.
philip-the-handsome: Philip was born in Bruges in 1478, the son of Maximilian I of Austria and Mary of Burgundy. King Louis XI of France spread the rumour that the child was a girl, and at the baptism his step-grandmother Margaret of York showed the boy naked to the crowd to end the doubt. Mary died after a horse accident in March 1482, when he was four. In December 1482 the Treaty of Arras with Louis XI secured his rule over much of the Low Countries but left the Duchy of Burgundy in French hands.

In 1493 the Treaty of Senlis extended his rule to Artois, Burgundy and Charolais, and Maximilian, burdened as new ruler of the Holy Roman Empire, transferred power to the fifteen-year-old Philip. The Burgundian lands welcomed a native-born ruler who spoke their language and was peace-loving. At his inauguration in 1494 he abolished the Great Privilege and restored centralising policies of his great-grandfather and grandfather while abandoning their expansionism.

On 20 October 1496 Philip married Joanna, daughter of Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, at Lier. His sister Margaret married Joanna's brother John, Prince of Asturias. John died in 1497 and their sister Isabella in 1498, and after the death in 1500 of Isabella's infant son Miguel, Joanna became heir to the Castilian and Aragonese crowns. When Isabella of Castile died in 1504 she left Castile to Joanna. The nobles forced Ferdinand to withdraw from the regency, and Philip was recognised as king.

In January 1506 a storm drove Philip and Joanna ashore in Dorset, and Henry VII kept them as guests for six weeks until Philip signed a treaty known as the Malus Intercursus. They landed at Corunna on 28 April 1506. In meetings in June, mediated by Cardinal Cisneros, Ferdinand accepted that Philip and Joanna should take over Castile. Philip was an important patron of Hieronymus Bosch, whom he commissioned in 1504 to paint a large triptych of the Last Judgement, and his chapel included Pierre de La Rue.

Philip died suddenly at Burgos on 25 September 1506, apparently of typhoid fever, though poisoning was widely spoken of and Joanna believed it. He is entombed in the Royal Chapel of Granada. Maximilian appointed Margaret of Austria governor of the Netherlands, and the States General accepted her in April 1507. His son Charles eventually united the Habsburg, Burgundian, Castilian and Aragonese inheritances.

The Belgian historian Jean-Marie Cauchies writes that Philip died too young to show himself a great man and remained above all the heir of the dukes of Burgundy, personifying a prince of peace and concord. Contemporaries remarked on his good looks, which gave him his epithet, and the Venetian ambassador Vincenzo Querini called him physically beautiful.
philip-v-of-macedon: Philip was the son of Demetrius II of Macedon. He was nine years old when his father died in 229 BCE, and his great-uncle Antigonus III Doson administered the kingdom as regent and then as king until his own death in 221 BCE, when Philip was seventeen. As a young man he was attractive and charismatic, compared to Alexander the Great, and according to Polybius he became a universal favourite of the Greeks because of his benevolent conduct towards them. He had a close relationship with Aratus of Sicyon, who held a prominent position at his court until 213 BCE.

In 221 BCE Philip took over the leadership of the Hellenic League, which Antigonus Doson had assembled at Corinth, and led it in the Social War of 220 to 217 BCE against Aetolia, Sparta and Elis. After the sack of Thermum, the Aetolian political and religious capital, the war ended at the conference of Naupactus in 217 BCE. In 215 BCE he signed a treaty with Hannibal Barca. In the First Macedonian War, Rome's alliance with the Aetolian League in 211 BCE weakened his position, but he concluded the Peace of Phoenice in 205 BCE.

Philip then agreed with the Seleucid king Antiochus III to take Egyptian-held territory in Asia Minor, besieging Samos and capturing Miletus. Pergamum and Rhodes were alarmed and appealed to the Romans. While Philip besieged Abydos in the autumn of 200 BCE, a Roman ambassador, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, urged him not to attack Greek states, but in vain. In the Second Macedonian War he was defeated by Titus Quinctius Flamininus at the Battle of the Aous in 198 BCE and at the Battle of Cynoscephalae in June 197 BCE. In 196 BCE he gave up his claim to all Greek cities on the mainland and in Asia Minor, including Corinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, the so-called fetters of Greece.

After the peace Philip cooperated with Rome, supporting it against Nabis of Sparta in 195 BCE and against Antiochus III. The Romans let him keep Demetrias and other territory he had conquered. He turned to rebuilding Macedonia, imposing taxes, exploiting royal property, reopening mines and minting a new currency.

Rome stayed suspicious, and accusations from neighbouring states led to constant interference. His younger son Demetrius, encouraged by Rome to think of the succession, quarrelled with his elder brother Perseus, and Philip reluctantly had Demetrius executed for treason in 180 BCE. He died at Amphipolis towards the end of 179 BCE and was succeeded by Perseus, the last king of Macedon.
philip-v-of-spain: Philip was born on 19 December 1683 at the Palace of Versailles, the second son of Louis, Grand Dauphin, and Maria Anna Victoria of Bavaria. He was created Duke of Anjou at birth. With his elder brother Louis, Duke of Burgundy, ahead of him in the French succession, he was not expected to rule. He was tutored by François Fénelon, Archbishop of Cambrai.

When King Charles II, the last Habsburg to rule Spain, died childless in 1700, his will named Philip as heir, with Philip's younger brother and then Archduke Charles of Austria next in line. Austria argued that Philip's grandmother had renounced the Spanish throne in her marriage contract, while France replied that her dowry had never been paid. After a Royal Council in France, Philip accepted the crown, forfeiting his own and his heirs' claim to the French throne.

His accession brought on the War of the Spanish Succession, in which France and Spain faced the Grand Alliance of England, the Dutch Republic and Austria. Castile supported Philip, while much of Aragon rallied to Archduke Charles. About 400,000 people were killed over the course of the fighting. From 1707 the Nueva Planta decrees centralised rule on the Castilian model and abolished the charters of the kingdoms within Spain, notably the Crown of Aragon; Navarre and the Basque region, which had backed Philip, kept their self-government.

The Treaty of Utrecht recognised Philip as king but required him to cede Menorca and Gibraltar to Great Britain, and the Spanish Netherlands, Naples, Milan and Sardinia to the Austrian Habsburgs, and Sicily and parts of Milan to Savoy. His attempt to overturn these terms in Italy led to the War of the Quadruple Alliance (1718–1720), which ended when he sued for peace. In January 1724 he abdicated for his son Louis I, who died of smallpox in August; Philip returned to the throne in September. Later Spanish forces took Naples and Sicily from Austria and Oran from the Ottomans.

Philip suffered from depression, and his second wife, Elisabeth Farnese, held much control over government; from August 1737 the singer Farinelli eased his illness by singing to him nightly. He died of a stroke on 9 July 1746 and was succeeded by his son Ferdinand VI. His reign of over forty-five years is the longest in Spanish monarchical history. Historians have generally judged him harshly; John Lynch holds that he advanced government only marginally. The economy improved, however, and the state became more centralised, with reforms that culminated under Charles III. He also ended Seville's monopoly of colonial trade.
philip-vi-of-france: Little is recorded of Philip's childhood, since he was of minor royal birth. His father, Charles, Count of Valois, was the younger brother of King Philip IV and strove all his life to gain the throne without success. When Charles died in 1325, he left his eldest son Philip heir to the counties of Anjou, Maine and Valois.

When Charles IV died in 1328 without a son, the closest male relative was Edward III of England, the son of his sister Isabella. The assemblies of French barons and prelates and the University of Paris held that men who derived their right through their mother were excluded under Salic law. Philip, the eldest grandson of Philip III through the male line, became regent and, after Charles's widow gave birth to a daughter on 1 April 1328, was proclaimed king. He was crowned at Reims on 29 May 1328. Edward paid homage for Aquitaine at Amiens on 6 June 1329.

Relations worsened over Aquitaine and over Philip's refuge for David II of Scotland. On 24 May 1337 Philip declared Aquitaine forfeit, after Edward sheltered Robert III of Artois, and so began the Hundred Years' War. The French fleet was destroyed at the Battle of Sluys in June 1340. In 1346 Edward sailed for Normandy, and at the Battle of Crécy the French army was annihilated and Philip barely escaped capture. Calais capitulated in August 1347.

After Crécy the Estates refused to raise money for the king. In 1348 the Black Death struck France, killing one third of the population, including Queen Joan. Philip's second marriage, to his son's betrothed Blanche of Navarre, alienated his son and many nobles. His last major achievement was the acquisition of the Dauphiné and of Montpellier in 1349; the treaty of Romans was concluded with Humbert II, Dauphin of Viennois. He died on 22 August 1350 at Coulombes Abbey and was succeeded by his son John II, leaving France divided and unsettled.
philipp-scheidemann: Philipp Scheidemann was born in Kassel on 26 July 1865, the son of an upholsterer. After his father died in 1879 the family fell into poverty, and he trained as a typesetter and letterpress printer. In 1883 he joined the Social Democratic Party, then banned under Bismarck's Anti-Socialist Laws, and later worked as a newspaper editor in Giessen, Nuremberg, Offenbach and Kassel. From 1909 he wrote dialect stories under the pseudonym Henner Piffendeckel.

Scheidemann entered the Reichstag in 1903. After August Bebel's death in 1913 he took over the chairmanship of the party's parliamentary group with Hugo Haase, and in 1912 he became the first Social Democrat elected a vice president of the Reichstag, though he could not take office until 1918 because he refused the customary visit to the emperor. During the First World War he took a middle line, supporting war credits but opposing a victorious peace and advocating a negotiated peace without annexations, which militarist circles called high treason. From October 1917 he was chairman of the Majority Social Democratic Party alongside Friedrich Ebert.

In November 1918 he concluded that a successful fight against the extreme left was possible only if Wilhelm II abdicated, and on 6 November he said the party must put itself at the head of the movement or anarchy would follow. From the balcony of the Reichstag he proclaimed the German Republic. In February 1919 the National Assembly meeting in Weimar elected Ebert president, and Ebert asked Scheidemann to form a government. He served as Reich minister president from 13 February to 20 June 1919 and resigned because the cabinet could not agree on accepting the Treaty of Versailles.

He remained in the Reichstag until 1933 and was mayor of Kassel from 1920 to 1925. On 4 June 1922 two men sprayed prussic acid at his face during a walk; strong winds saved him, and the attackers were caught and sentenced to long prison terms. The extreme right and left both made his name a term of abuse for supporters of the Republic. His Memoirs of a Social Democrat appeared in 1928.

After the Nazis came to power Scheidemann went into exile in February or March 1933, first to Salzburg, then through Czechoslovakia, Switzerland, France and the United States to Denmark in 1935. He was deprived of his German citizenship on the first expatriation list of 25 August 1933, and his diaries were confiscated and are considered lost. He died in Copenhagen on 29 November 1939, and in 1953 his ashes were moved to Kassel. His critical writings from exile were published only in 2002.
philippa-of-hainaut: Philippa was the second of five daughters, and one of eight children, born to Count William I of Hainaut and Joan of Valois, a granddaughter of King Philip III of France. Her birth in Valenciennes is dated 1310, though she may have been born as late as 1315. She grew up in the Low Countries when the region was becoming a major trading centre, and was well versed in finance and diplomacy.

In the summer of 1326 Isabella of France, queen of England, came to the court of Hainaut to seek aid to depose her husband Edward II. Her son Edward accompanied her, and a betrothal was arranged in exchange for assistance. The couple were second cousins, so a papal dispensation was needed and was sent by Pope John XXII in September 1327. Philippa married Edward by proxy in October 1327, and the marriage took place at York Minster on 24 January 1328.

Unlike many earlier queens, Philippa did not alienate the English by keeping a foreign retinue. Her coronation was postponed for two years because Queen Mother Isabella did not wish to give up her own status, and she was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 18 February 1330. She gave birth to her first son, Edward, that June. In October 1330 the king took power by arresting the regents, Isabella and Roger Mortimer, 1st Earl of March, and Mortimer was executed for treason.

As the Hundred Years' War drained the treasury, Philippa advised Edward III to take an interest in commercial expansion. She established the textile industry in Norwich by encouraging Flemish weavers to settle there and promoted coal mining in Tynedale. In 1346, while her husband was abroad, she served as regent; when the Scots invaded she gathered the English army and rallied the soldiers before the Battle of Neville's Cross, where King David II of Scotland was taken prisoner. In 1347 she is remembered for persuading the king to spare the Burghers of Calais. She was also a patron of the chronicler Jean Froissart.

Philippa died on 15 August 1369 at Windsor Castle of an illness similar to oedema, and after a state funeral on 9 January 1370 was buried at Westminster Abbey, with an alabaster effigy by Jean de Liège. Edward III was buried beside her eight years later. They had thirteen children, five sons of whom lived into adulthood, and three children died of the Black Death in 1348. The Queen's College, Oxford, was founded by her chaplain Robert de Eglesfield in her honour.
philippe-petain: Philippe Pétain was born on 24 April 1856 at Cauchy-à-la-Tour in the Pas-de-Calais, the only son of a peasant family. He entered the Saint-Cyr Military Academy in 1876 and served in various garrisons with the chasseurs, the elite light infantry, until 1899, after which he alternated between staff and regimental posts. By the outbreak of the First World War he held the rank of colonel.

Pétain led his brigade at the Battle of Guise in August 1914 and was promoted rapidly, commanding the Second Army from July 1915. At the Battle of Verdun in 1916 he rotated divisions out after two weeks on the front line and organised truck transport along the Voie Sacrée, which helped to bring the German offensive to a halt in July. After the failure of General Nivelle's offensive in April 1917 provoked mutinies in nearly half the French infantry divisions on the Western Front, Pétain became Commander-in-Chief. He restored morale by talking to the men, promising no more suicidal attacks and granting rest and leave, and held 3,400 courts martial; 554 mutineers were sentenced to death, but over 90 per cent had their sentences commuted.

He received his baton as Marshal of France on 8 December 1918. In the interwar years he was Inspector-General of the Army, commanded French forces in Morocco against the Rif tribes in 1925, was elected to the Académie française in 1931 and served as Minister of War in 1934. He became ambassador to Nationalist Spain in 1939 and joined Paul Reynaud's government as Deputy Prime Minister on 18 May 1940.

On 16 June 1940, as the Fall of France neared, Reynaud resigned and President Albert Lebrun appointed Pétain in his place. His government sought an armistice with Germany. On 10 July the Congress of the French Parliament voted 569 to 80, with 18 abstentions, to give the cabinet power to draw up a new constitution, ending the Third Republic; nearly all French historians and every postwar French government regard the vote as illegal. The next day Pétain took near-absolute powers as head of the French State at Vichy. He met Hitler at Montoire on 24 October 1940, and neither he nor his deputies Laval, Flandin and Darlan resisted German requests for indirect aid. In August 1944 the Germans moved him to Sigmaringen.

After the war Pétain was tried for treason from 23 July to 15 August 1945 and sentenced to death; the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment because of his age and service in the First World War. He died on 23 July 1951 at Port-Joinville on the Île d'Yeu, aged 95. Charles de Gaulle said his life was successively banal, then glorious, then deplorable, but never mediocre.
philippine-american-war: Andrés Bonifacio founded the Katipunan on 7 July 1892 to win independence from Spanish rule by armed revolt, and the revolution began in August 1896 when the Spanish discovered it. Emilio Aguinaldo, mayor of Cavite El Viejo, gained control of the revolution and was elected president of a revolutionary government on 22 March 1897; his government had Bonifacio executed for treason on 10 May 1897. By an agreement of 14 December 1897 the Spanish colonial government was to pay Aguinaldo 800,000 pesos if he went into exile.

Filipino nationalists proclaimed independence in June 1898 and the First Philippine Republic was established in January 1899 under a constitution drafted by the Malolos Congress, with Aguinaldo as president. After the Spanish–American War the United States annexed the Philippines under the Treaty of Paris of December 1898, and on 21 December 1898 President William McKinley proclaimed a policy of benevolent assimilation. The United States recognised neither the declaration of independence nor the republic, and tensions escalated.

Fighting began on 4 February 1899 in the Battle of Manila. The Philippine government issued a proclamation on 2 June 1899 urging the people to continue the war. Filipino forces of between 80,000 and 100,000, most armed only with bolo knives, bows and spears, first fought conventionally against better armed American troops, and on 13 November 1899 Aguinaldo decreed that guerrilla warfare would be the strategy. The Philippine army staged ambushes and raids, such as those at Paye, Catubig and Mabitac, and at first it seemed that a stalemate was possible; McKinley considered withdrawal.

On 20 December 1900 General Arthur MacArthur placed the islands under martial law, and Filipino leaders who kept working for independence were deported to Guam. The Americans carried out reprisals and scorched earth campaigns and forcibly relocated many civilians to concentration camps, where thousands died. Aguinaldo was captured on 23 March 1901, and the United States declared the war over on 4 July 1902.

The war caused up to 250,000 Filipino civilian deaths, mostly from famine and disease, including at least 150,000 in a cholera epidemic towards its end. Some groups kept fighting: the Pulahan movement disbanded in 1907, and the Moro Rebellion in the south ended with the Battle of Bud Bagsak on 15 June 1913. Anti-imperialists in the United States Senate argued that the war contradicted the principles of the Declaration of Independence. The Philippine Organic Act of 1902 created the Philippine Assembly, and the Jones Act of 1916 gave the first official commitment to eventual independence. The Commonwealth was created in 1934, and the United States granted independence in 1946 through the Treaty of Manila.
philippine-revolution: Spain had ruled the archipelago for 333 years. The colony was governed from Mexico from 1565 and paid for by the galleon trade between Manila and Acapulco, which ended in 1815; after Mexico became independent in 1821 the Philippines was governed directly from Madrid. Manila was opened to world trade by a royal decree of 1834, and revolutionary ideas from the French Revolution entered through books and fed the rise of an enlightened principalía class. Abuses by the Spanish government, army and clergy, exposed by the ilustrados, helped create a sense of common cause.

The Propaganda Movement of Filipinos in Madrid published the newspaper La Solidaridad from 1889 to 1895 and pressed for reforms, but the colonial government did not carry out those the Spanish legislature passed. José Rizal founded La Liga Filipina in Manila, was arrested within days and was deported to Dapitan. Andrés Bonifacio and others founded the Katipunan on 7 July 1892; influenced by Freemasonry, it advocated independence through armed revolt, and most of its members came from the lower and middle classes.

Spanish authorities learned of the Katipunan in August 1896, and the revolution began prematurely. Bonifacio's attempt to besiege Manila failed, but rebels in Cavite, led by Mariano Álvarez and the cousins Baldomero and Emilio Aguinaldo, won early victories. A rivalry grew between Bonifacio's Magdiwang faction and Aguinaldo's Magdalo. At the Tejeros elections of 1897 Aguinaldo was elected president, Bonifacio refused to recognise the result, and in May 1897 Bonifacio and his brother Procopio were executed after a trial for treason. Later that year Aguinaldo's government signed the Pact of Biak-na-Bato with Spain, and revolutionary officers went into exile in Hong Kong.

After the United States declared war on Spain in April 1898, Commodore George Dewey's squadron defeated the Spanish fleet at the Battle of Manila Bay on 1 May. Aguinaldo returned on 19 May, and by June the rebels held nearly all the countryside while the cities stayed under Spanish control. On 12 June 1898 he issued the declaration of independence at Kawit.

Neither Spain nor the United States recognised the declaration, and the Treaty of Paris, which ended the war and Spanish rule, was signed without Filipino representatives. The Malolos Congress, whose delegates were all from the ilustrado class, approved a constitution on 21 January 1899. Fighting between Filipino and American forces broke out on 4 February 1899, beginning the Philippine-American War. The Philippines became fully independent on 4 July 1946, fifty years after the revolution began.
philippines: The Philippines consists of about 7,641 islands with a total area of about 300,000 km2, stretching 1,850 kilometres from north to south. They fall into three divisions, Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao, and the 11 largest islands make up about 95 percent of the land. The highest mountain is Mount Apo on Mindanao, at 2,954 metres.

The islands lie on the western fringes of the Pacific Ring of Fire, with 23 active volcanoes and about five recorded earthquakes a day, most too weak to be felt. On an expedition of the 16th century Ruy López de Villalobos named Leyte and Samar Felipinas after the Prince of Asturias, later Philip II of Castile, and the name Las Islas Filipinas was later used for the Spanish possessions. The title Republic of the Philippines appeared in the 1935 constitution.

Evidence of early hominins dates to as early as 709,000 years ago, and bones from Callao Cave may represent an unknown species, Homo luzonensis, who lived 50,000 to 67,000 years ago. The first Austronesians reached the islands from Taiwan around 2200 BCE and settled the Batanes Islands and northern Luzon. The earliest known surviving written record is the Laguna Copperplate Inscription of 900 CE, in Old Malay. By the 14th century large coastal settlements had become trading centres, trade with China had begun under the late Tang dynasty and widened under the Song, and Islam was established in the Sulu Archipelago by the 15th century.

Ferdinand Magellan's arrival marked the beginning of Spanish colonization. Catholicism became the dominant religion, and Manila became the western hub of trans-Pacific trade. The Philippine Revolution began in 1896 and became entwined with the Spanish–American War of 1898, after which Spain ceded the territory to the United States and revolutionaries declared the First Philippine Republic. The ensuing Philippine–American War left the United States in control until the Japanese invasion in the Second World War, and the Philippines became independent in 1946.

Ferdinand Marcos ruled under martial law from 1972 to 1981, and the People Power Revolution overthrew him in 1986. The Philippines is a constitutional republic with a presidential system, in which the president serves a six-year term, and its population was 112,729,484 in July 2024. The largest ethnic group in the 2020 census was the Tagalog, at 26.0 percent, and indigenous peoples comprise 110 ethnolinguistic groups. Spanish and American rule left lasting marks, among them the dominance of Catholicism, the use of English and Spanish surnames resulting from an 1849 edict.
philips: Philips & Co. was founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by Gerard Philips and his father Frederik Philips to make incandescent electric lamps. Gerard's younger brother Anton Philips joined in 1895 and helped expand the commercial side. The business became N.V. Philips' Gloeilampenfabrieken on 11 September 1912, and in 1914 it opened a physics laboratory, later called the NatLab, whose research fed its later work in lighting, radio and medical X-ray equipment. Queen Wilhelmina gave it the Dutch Royal designation in 1916, though Koninklijke entered its legal name only in 1998. In 1924 it joined Osram and other lamp makers in the Phoebus cartel. The Philips Sports Association, which includes the football club PSV Eindhoven, was founded in 1913 for its employees.

In March 1927 experimental shortwave transmissions from the Philips laboratories, using the PCJJ transmitter, were received in the Dutch East Indies, and Eddie Startz began presenting the Happy Station through it in 1928. In 1939 the company introduced the Philishave rotary shaver, invented by its engineer Alexandre Horowitz. Its laboratory also helped revive the Stirling engine, first as a possible power source for portable radios; by the late 1940s it had built a generator set known as the MP1002CA, or Bungalow set.

After the German invasion of the Netherlands in May 1940, several senior executives left the country, while Frits Philips, son of Anton Philips, stayed in Eindhoven. On 6 December 1942 the Royal Air Force carried out Operation Oyster, a low-level raid on Philips sites that produced components for the German war economy. It severely damaged the works and caused substantial civilian casualties in surrounding parts of Eindhoven.

After the war Philips grew into a major maker of televisions, audio equipment and other consumer electronics. In August 1963 it introduced its first Compact Cassette recorder at the Funkausstellung in Berlin, and in the early 1970s the N1500 videocassette recorder, described by the Science Museum Group as the first practical domestic video recorder. In 1984 it and ASM International founded ASM Lithography, later ASML, and in 1987 it joined in founding TSMC. After heavy losses it announced in 1990, under Jan Timmer, plans to cut about 10,000 jobs. In the 2010s it moved towards health technology, transferring most of its television business to TP Vision in 2012 and separating its lighting business in 2016, later renamed Signify.

Philips introduced the compact cassette format, which became a widely adopted standard for tape recording, and later worked with Sony to develop the compact disc standard. It also held a controlling interest in PolyGram, sold to Seagram in 1998. Its headquarters moved from Eindhoven to Amsterdam from 1998, after a decision in October 1997.
philistines: The Philistines lived along the southern coast of Canaan during the Iron Age, in a confederation of city-states called Philistia. Their identity seems to have begun with the arrival in Canaan of a migrant group from the Aegean, thought to have settled around 1175 BCE amid the Late Bronze Age collapse and to have mixed with the indigenous Canaanite societies. Egyptian sources name one of the Sea Peoples as the Peleset, and Ramesses III is said to have settled some of them in southern Canaan after his victory at the Battle of the Delta, around 1175 BCE. Excavation has not confirmed such a settlement.

The Hebrew Bible says the Philistines came from Caphtor, possibly Crete. Most scholars agree on an Aegean origin, because the figurines, pottery and fire-stands of the Philistine strata resemble Aegean ones. A minority holds that the similarities result from later contact. A study of skeletons at Ashkelon in 2019 found that most of their ancestry came from the local Levantine population, with a Southern-European-related share that suggests an influx in the 12th century BCE.

Philistia was a pentapolis of five city-states, Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron and Gath, from Wadi Gaza in the south to the Yarqon River in the north. The Philistines are known chiefly from the Hebrew Bible, which tells of their wars with the Israelites. In it they dominate the Israelites in the time of Samson, capture the Ark of the Covenant at Aphek and keep it for several months, forbid Israelite blacksmiths so that weapons had to be sharpened by the Philistines, and kill King Saul and his sons at Mount Gilboa. The same books tell that David defeated Goliath near the Valley of Elah.

The Philistines came under the rule of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and were vassals of the Assyrians, the Egyptians and then the Babylonians. In 604 BCE Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon defeated them, and the sources suggest that his armies destroyed Ashkelon and Ekron after a revolt and exiled much of the population. By the late 5th century BCE the Philistines no longer appear as a distinct group, though how far they were assimilated is debated.

Excavated Philistine cities show careful town planning with industrial zones. Ekron alone had about 200 olive oil installations, and breweries, wineries and shops selling beer and wine are attested, while complex objects of gold, bronze and iron show skilled metalworking. The Philistines worshipped deities already known in Canaan, among them Baal, Astarte, Asherah and Dagon. Their language is poorly attested. Most Philistine names are Semitic, but Goliath, Achish and Phicol seem non-Semitic, and some scholars suggest that the Philistines first spoke an Indo-European language.
philo-of-alexandria: Philo's dates of birth and death are unknown. He called himself old when he joined the delegation to the emperor Gaius Caligula, and a reference to an event under Claudius suggests that he died between 45 and 50 CE. His family was noble and wealthy. Either his father or his paternal grandfather was granted Roman citizenship by Julius Caesar, and Jerome wrote that he came from a priestly family. His brother Alexander Lysimachus was the tax administrator of customs in Alexandria, a friend of the emperor Claudius and, it was said, the richest man in the city.

Philo was educated in the Hellenistic culture of Alexandria, in the traditions of Judaism and in Greek philosophy. Plato was his largest philosophical influence, above all the Timaeus and the Phaedrus, and he also drew on the Stoics, Homer, Euripides and Demosthenes. He read the Jewish scriptures chiefly in the Greek Septuagint, and how much Hebrew he knew is debated.

He lived in an era of ethnic tension in Alexandria. Some Greeks condemned the Jews for a supposed alliance with Rome, while Rome sought to suppress Jewish identity in Judaea. According to Josephus, the Alexandrian Jewish community chose Philo as their chief representative before Caligula after civil disorder between Jews and Greeks. Josephus says that he and the community refused to treat the emperor as a god or to build statues, altars and temples for him. This is the only event of his life that can be dated with certainty. Philo also recounts that he visited the Second Temple in Jerusalem at least once.

Philo wrote in Greek on philosophy, politics and religion. He used allegory to harmonise the Hebrew Bible, mainly the Torah, with Greek philosophy, following the practice of both Jewish exegesis and Stoicism, though he also often favoured a literal reading. He held the Bible to be the source of all truth and Moses its true medium of revelation. His God is transcendent, without physical features or human emotions, unchangeable and beyond time and space. His Logos has a special relation to humans, as an interpreter of God's designs and a pattern for the shaping of the mind.

About fifty of his works survive and twenty to twenty-five are lost. Most are commentaries on the Torah, among them the Quaestiones on Genesis and Exodus, which survive in Armenian, an Allegorical Commentary on Genesis and an Exposition of the Law. Others include On the Life of Moses and the historical works Ad Flaccum and De legatione ad Gaium.

Early Church Fathers such as Clement of Alexandria and Origen used his work to connect the Bible with philosophy, and Eusebius, Jerome and Ambrose cited him extensively. Rabbinic Judaism gave him little attention.
phitsanulok: Phitsanulok lies in the geographic centre of its province, on the fertile plains along the Nan River, which flows south to join the Chao Phraya. It grew from an older settlement called Song Khwae, meaning two rivers, because it stood between the Nan and the Khwae Noi, which now drains into the Nan ten kilometres to the north. The name Phitsanulok comes from Sanskrit Vishnu and loka, world, and may loosely be translated as Vishnu's heaven.

The area is one of the oldest in Thailand. A moated Dvaravati settlement, Muang Yommarat, lay eight kilometres north-west of the present centre. The Northern Chronicles credit King Thammaracha I of Sukhothai with founding Song Khwae, building Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat and casting the Buddha images Phra Buddha Chinnarat and Phra Buddha Chinnasri. Song Khwae became the royal seat of the Sukhothai Kingdom in 1378. After the last king of Sukhothai died there in 1438, Prince Ramesuan of Ayutthaya ruled it, and in 1448, when he was crowned King Trailokanat, it was incorporated into Ayutthaya.

During the war between Ayutthaya and Lanna, Trailokanat moved his residence to Song Khwae, renamed it Phitsanulok and expanded it to the west bank of the Nan. In the sixteenth century it was the seat of the heir to the Ayutthaya throne. Its ruler submitted to Burma's King Bayinnaung in 1563, and in 1584 Prince Naresuan ordered the evacuation of the cities of the Sukhothai region before a Burmese invasion; Phitsanulok was abandoned until 1593.

After Ayutthaya fell in 1767 a monk, Chao Phra Fang, ruled the town as a local lord until King Taksin of Thonburi took it in 1768.
