In East Asia, the merchant Chang Pogo, angered that Silla subjects fell victim to coastal pirates in the unstable late Tang period, petitioned King Heungdeok for a garrison. In 828 the Cheonghae Garrison was founded at Wando island with an army of 10,000, and Chang became the arbiter of Yellow Sea commerce. The Sindhi Bawarij, active between 251 and 865, looted two treasure ships from Ceylon, which became the casus belli for the Umayyad conquest of Sindh.

The classic era of Caribbean piracy lasted from about 1650 to the mid-1720s, as France, England and the United Provinces built colonial empires and seaborne trade grew. Pirate crews divided plunder under a hierarchy in which the quartermaster could veto the captain, and the loot was more often food, water, weapons and ship's gear than buried treasure. Caught pirates were usually hanged, in England often at Execution Dock on the Thames.

The two-volume A General History of the Pyrates, published in London in 1724, gave the public its picture of the Golden Age of Piracy and inspired later fiction, notably Treasure Island in 1883 and Peter Pan in 1911.
piraeus: Piraeus is a rocky outcropping on the Attic coast, on the east shore of the Saronic Gulf, about eight kilometres south-west of the centre of Athens. In prehistoric times it was an island, joined to the mainland only by a low stretch of land that was flooded by sea water for most of the year. Whenever it dried, it served as a salt field, and its ancient name, the Halipedon, means salt field. Over time the ground silted up and the land passage could be crossed safely at all times. The peninsula has three natural harbours: Cantharus, the main port, and the smaller Zea and Munichia, which are still in use as Pasalimani and Mikrolimano.

The site has been inhabited since at least the 26th century BCE. Piraeus was founded as the port of Athens in the early 5th century BCE. A first harbour concentrated the import and transit trade of Athens and the navy's base in one place. In the Golden Age of Athens the Long Walls fortified the route from the city to the port, and the naval base held 372 trireme shipsheds. From the 3rd century BCE the port declined.

The Ottoman Empire took Piraeus in 1456, when it was called Aslan Liman, Lion Harbour,. Francesco Morosini looted that statue in 1687, during his expedition against Athens in the Morean War, and carried it to the Venetian Arsenal, where it still stands. Under Ottoman rule, and especially before the Greek War of Independence, the place was mostly deserted, apart from the monastery of Saint Spyridon, founded in 1590, and a customs house. When Athens became the capital of the new Greek state in 1832, the port began to grow again as a commercial and industrial centre, with migrants arriving mainly from the Aegean islands. The municipality was established in 1835, when Piraeus had about 300 inhabitants.

Piraeus is a port city within the urban area of Athens, in the Attica region of Greece, and has the country's largest harbour. The central harbour is a hub for commercial and passenger shipping, serving ferry routes to Crete, the Cyclades, the Dodecanese and much of the Aegean, while the smaller harbours serve pleasure craft and fishing boats. Parts of the Themistoclean Walls, the Eëtioneia mole at the harbour entrance, the ancient theatre at Zea and shipshed remains survive, and the Archaeological Museum of Piraeus displays finds from the ancient city.
piri-reis: The only surviving sources for his early life are his own maps, in which he names himself Muhiddin Piri, son of Hacı Mehmed. He was likely born between 1465 and 1470 in Gelibolu (Gallipoli), a major Ottoman naval base. His uncle Kemal Reis was a notable corsair, a state-sanctioned pirate, and under him Piri earned the rank of reis, equivalent to a captain. With the approval of Sultan Bayezid II he sailed west with Kemal Reis and other Ottoman corsairs to aid the Emirate of Granada against the Catholic Monarchs, and as a young man helped bombard the forces besieging Málaga in 1487.

Kemal Reis and Piri Reis were recruited into the Ottoman Navy by Bayezid II. Around the turn of the century Piri Reis fought in the Ottoman–Venetian wars, and at the Battle of Zonchio in 1499 he piloted one of 270 Ottoman ships that broke through a Venetian fleet of 150 to enter the Gulf of Corinth. In 1501, in a naval battle near Valencia, he and his uncle captured a Spaniard who said he had sailed with Columbus and probably carried one of the explorer's charts of the Americas.

Decades later, as grand admiral of the Ottoman fleet in the Indian Ocean, he left Suez on 29 October 1547 with sixty ships to recover Aden, which had been ceded to a local Arab chief seeking Portuguese protection. The citadel fell to him on 26 February 1548, and in January 1549 his fleet captured the sailors of Portuguese ships and burned the vessels. He led successful campaigns in the Red Sea but was beheaded after his retreat from the siege of Hormuz.

All his surviving maps are portolan charts, designed for navigation by dead reckoning. Three works survive in some form: fragments of the world maps of 1513 and 1528 in the Topkapı Palace Museum, and copies of the Kitab-ı Bahriye, since his original manuscripts are lost. The 1513 map is drawn on gazelle skin, and about a third of it survives. Its notes credit part of the Americas to a lost map by Columbus, which an inscription says came from the Spaniard captured near Valencia. He gave the map as a gift to Selim I after the conquest of Egypt in 1517.

The Kitab-ı Bahriye, or Book of the Sea, is the most detailed portolan atlas of the Mediterranean, with 130 chapters in its first version and 210 in the second, which was presented to Suleiman in 1526. His 1528 world map reflects newer discoveries in the Americas. His maps received little appreciation in his lifetime. After the 1929 rediscovery of the 1513 map at the Topkapı Palace, fringe theories claimed it showed an ice-free Antarctica, but studies show no significant similarity with Antarctica's coast.
pirna: Pirna lies in the upper Elbe valley near the Sandstone Mountains, southeast of Dresden, where the Wesenitz flows in from the north and the Gottleuba from the south. It is called the gate to the Saxon Switzerland. Flint tools from the late Paleolithic are the earliest evidence of settlement, and people of the Linear Pottery culture farmed grain and cattle on the loess soil in the Neolithic. About 600 CE the Sorbs succeeded the Germanic tribes of the Elbe valley. The name derives from the Sorbian na pernem, on the hard stone, and is also related to the Slavic deity Perun.

The castle, first mentioned in 1269, probably already existed in the 11th century, and the town was founded by Henry III, Margrave of Meissen, during the second eastern German colonisation. Its streets form a chessboard pattern. It is first mentioned in a document of 1233. In 1293 King Wenceslaus II of Bohemia acquired town and castle from the Bishop of Meissen, and Pirna belonged to Bohemia until 1405. Anton Lauterbach, a friend of Martin Luther, became pastor and superintendent when the Reformation was introduced into Saxony in 1539. In 1544 Maurice, Elector of Saxony, made the castle a fortress, which withstood a siege by Elector John Frederick in the Schmalkaldic War.

On 23 April 1639 Swedish troops under Johan Banér invaded, and in the five-month siege of the fortress the town was greatly devastated; about 600 people were killed in what is called the Misery of Pirna. On 29 August 1756 the small Saxon army fled before the invading Prussians to the levels between Königstein Fortress and Sonnenstein Castle and capitulated there on 16 October. In 1811 the physician Ernst Gottlob Pienitz opened a very large mental hospital at Sonnenstein, but when French troops occupied it on 14 September 1813 they forced the evacuation of 275 patients. Napoleon lived for a time at the Marienhaus on the market that September, and the hospital reopened only in February 1814.

Steamships began on the upper Elbe in 1837 and the railway to Dresden opened in 1848. Pirna became an industrial town from 1862, with mechanical engineering, glass, cellulose and rayon. From early 1940 to the summer of 1942 part of the asylum at Sonnenstein served as a killing centre for the Nazi euthanasia programme, where about 15,000 people were killed; it was closed in 1942 after pressure from the local population, and a permanent exhibition opened in 2000. The town has over 37,000 inhabitants and is the capital of the district Sächsische Schweiz-Osterzgebirge, and its old town has been largely renovated since the 1990s.
pirot: Pirot is the administrative centre of the Pirot District in south-eastern Serbia. The river Nišava divides it into two districts, Tijabara and Pazar. The mountains of Stara Planina, Vlaška Planina, Belava and Suva Planina rise nearby, and four lakes, including Zavoj Lake, lie within its territory. The municipality covers 1,235 square kilometres and more than seventy settlements.

In Roman times the area belonged to Moesia and then to Upper Moesia, and at the end of the 4th century the basin of the Nišava formed the province of Dacia Mediterranea. A military settlement called Turres, Latin for towers, is mentioned in the first half of the 3rd century, set to control and defend the main road, where travellers could rest and change horses. According to Procopius of Caesarea, Justinian I ordered the rebuilding of thirty fortresses between Niš and Sofia, including the towers of Pirot. The Byzantine town of Quimedava, with an early Christian basilica and public baths, stood here until Slavs settled in large numbers.

In the Middle Ages the region belonged to the First Bulgarian State from the beginning of the 9th century and later to the restored Bulgarian state; the Church of St. Petka in Staničenje was built in 1331 and 1332. It was part of Prince Lazar's state when the Ottomans captured it in 1386. Its name derives from the Greek pirgos, tower. Under Ottoman rule it was in the Sanjak of Niš, and Austrian troops took it in 1737; when the Ottomans returned in 1739 the town was burnt and its churches destroyed. By 1836 carpet making was the main occupation.

The Serbian army entered Pirot on 16 December 1877. The Treaty of San Stefano gave the region to Bulgaria, but the Treaty of Berlin in 1878 ceded Pirot and Vranje to Serbia, and part of the Bulgarian population left. Bulgarian forces occupied it briefly in 1885 and again from 1915.

Pirot received city status in February 2016. The 2022 census counted 34,942 people in the urban area and 49,601 in the municipality. It is known for the Pirot carpet, or ćilim, and for opanak footwear and cheese. Pirot Fortress dates to the 14th century, and Stara Planina has a national park.
pisa: Pisa is a city and comune in Tuscany, Central Italy, straddling the Arno just before it empties into the Ligurian Sea, and the capital of the Province of Pisa. Most believe that the name comes from Etruscan and means mouth, since the city lies at the mouth of the Arno. Excavations in the 1980s and 1990s found numerous remains, including the fifth-century BCE tomb of an Etruscan prince, proving the city's Etruscan origin and its role as a maritime city trading with other Mediterranean civilisations.

In the last years of the Western Roman Empire Pisa did not decline as much as other Italian cities, probably because its river system made it easy to defend. It became the main port of the Upper Tyrrhenian Sea and the main trading centre between Tuscany and Corsica, Sardinia and the southern coasts of France and Spain, and its power as a maritime nation reached its apex in the 11th century.

In 1113 Pisa and Pope Paschal II organised, with the count of Barcelona and others, a war to free the Balearic Islands from the Moors. The king and queen of Mallorca were brought to Tuscany in chains, and although the Almoravides soon reconquered the island, the booty financed the cathedral and gave Pisa pre-eminence in the western Mediterranean.

Resentment of Genoa grew again after Frederick II confirmed his supremacy over the Tyrrhenian coast in 1220, and Pisa's strong Ghibelline position set it against the pope, who tried to deprive it of its dominions in northern Sardinia. The decline is said to have begun on 6 August 1284, when the larger Pisan fleet under Albertino Morosini was defeated by the Genoese under Benedetto Zaccaria and Oberto Doria at the Battle of Meloria.

In 1290 the Genoese destroyed the Porto Pisano and covered the land with salt. The loss of thousands of sailors could not easily be made up, and the Arno began to change course, keeping galleys from the port. The end came in 1324, when Sardinia was entirely lost to the Aragonese.

Pisa is best known for the Leaning Tower, the cathedral's bell tower, one of the buildings of the Piazza del Duomo, also called the Piazza dei Miracoli, with the cathedral, baptistery and Campo Santo. The city has more than twenty other historic churches. The University of Pisa has a history going back to the 12th century, and the Scuola Normale Superiore was founded by Napoleon in 1810.
pittacus: Pittacus was a native of Mytilene and the son of Hyrradius. He became a Mytilenaean general. He spoke the Aeolic dialect of Lesbos, and in Plato's Protagoras Prodicus of Ceos calls it barbarian, saying that Pittacus, being from Lesbos and raised with that dialect, did not know how to distinguish words correctly.

Pittacus and his army were victorious in a battle against the Athenians and their commander Phrynon. When the Athenians were about to attack Sigeion, he challenged their general to single combat, on the understanding that the result would decide the war and spare much bloodshed. The challenge was accepted, and he killed his opponent with a broad sword. Polyaenus, in his Stratagems, wrote instead that Pittacus had hidden a net under his shield, caught Phrynon in it, dragged him down and killed him, and that this gave rise to the use of nets in duels between gladiators.

In consequence the Mytilenaeans held Pittacus in high honour and presented the supreme power into his hands. He governed the city for ten years, during which he made laws in poetry. After ten years he resigned his position, and the city and its constitution were brought into good order. He is said to have lived for more than seventy years and to have died in 568 BCE.

Pittacus instituted a law that crimes committed in drunkenness should be punished twofold. It was directed chiefly against the aristocrats, who were more often guilty of drunk and violent behaviour, and was greatly appreciated by the common people. The Suda claims that he wrote a prose work about laws and an elegiac poem of 600 lines, but no trace of either has survived.

Many sayings are attributed to him, among them "Whatever you do, do it well", "Know thine opportunity" and "Do not say beforehand what you are going to do; for if you fail, you will be laughed at". According to legend, when his son was killed and the murderer was brought before him, he dismissed the man, saying that pardon is better than repentance; Heraclitus gives the saying as "Pardon is better than punishment". Another saying, that it is a hard thing to be a good man, is discussed at length in Plato's Protagoras.
piura: Piura lies in northwestern Peru, north of the Sechura Desert along the Piura River, about 981 kilometres from Lima and near the border with Ecuador. It is the capital of the Piura Region and Piura Province, and its population was 484,475 in 2017. The origin of the name is uncertain. One proposal derives it from a Quechua word meaning a supply deposit or granary, while other scholars connect it with the Sechura-Catacao languages and a suffix linked to water. The name first appears in 1535 for the river valley, not for a settlement.

The territory was inhabited by native groups called tallanes and yungas, and later the Muchik culture took control and merged into the Vicús culture. The Chimor, Moche and Wari Empire occupied the area around the city, and Tupac Inca Yupanqui of the Inca Empire ruled it for at least forty years before the Spanish arrived. Francisco Pizarro founded San Miguel de la Nueva Castilla at the Tallán settlement of Tangarará in July or August 1532, the third Spanish city in South America and the first in Peru. Two years later the inhabitants moved to a second settlement near the Monte de los Padres estate, where chroniclers report 23 encomenderos and where they stayed more than forty years.

Around 1578 most inhabitants moved to the port of Paita, discouraged by the harsh climate. Thomas Cavendish, an English pirate, raided and ruined the city between January and May 1587, seizing a large amount of loot, and the inhabitants then moved to their fourth and final site at the head of the Catacaos Valley, beside the pre-Columbian Tacalá Dam. In the viceroyalty Piura was an obligatory stop on the route from Spain to Lima, since each viceroy landed at Paita and travelled through Piura overland.

Piura declared its independence from Spain on 4 January 1821, a few months before Peru did on 28 July 1821. The Department of Piura was created in 1861 with Piura as its capital. In the 1860s the cultivation of Pima cotton, brought from Arizona by Emilio Hilbck, spurred industry and drew many immigrants. The naval hero Miguel Grau Seminario was born in Piura on 27 July 1834, though since 2011 the Peruvian state has given Paita as his official birthplace. Piura is known as the city of eternal heat because it is hot all year round, and it is the commercial and administrative centre of its department.
piye: Piye ruled from Napata, deep in Nubia, and was devoted to the god Amun, as many Nubian kings were. He restored the neglected Great Temple of Amun at Jebel Barkal, first built under Thutmose III, employing sculptors and stonemasons from Egypt. He took the throne names Usimare and Sneferre. As ruler of Nubia and Upper Egypt, he took advantage of the quarrels among Egypt's rulers to extend Nubian power beyond Thebes.

In response, Tefnakht of Sais formed a coalition of the local kings of the Delta and persuaded Piye's nominal ally Nimlot of Hermopolis to change sides. Tefnakht's army marched south and besieged Herakleopolis, whose king Peftjauawybast and the local Nubian commanders appealed to Piye. In his twentieth regnal year he assembled an army and visited Thebes in time for the Opet Festival. His campaign is told in the Victory stela at Gebel Barkal, and he treated it as a holy war, ordering his soldiers to cleanse themselves ritually before battle.

He won at Herakleopolis and took Memphis. Hermopolis fell after a siege of five months, and the kings of the Delta, including Iuput II of Leontopolis, Osorkon IV of Tanis and Nimlot, submitted. Tefnakht withdrew to an island in the Delta and conceded defeat in a letter but refused to pay homage in person. Piye then sailed south to Thebes and went home to Nubia, never to return to Egypt.

Piye's authority reached north only as far as the western oases and Herakleopolis, where Peftjauawybast ruled as a Nubian vassal. The Delta kings, above all Tefnakht, stayed largely free of his oversight. His successor Shebitku later put this right by attacking Sais and defeating Tefnakht's successor Bakenranef in his second regnal year.

Piye was the son of Kashta and Pebatjma and had three or four wives, among them Abar, mother of his later successor Taharqa. His daughter Shepenwepet II was installed at Thebes as God's Wife of Amun. He was buried at el-Kurru near Jebel Barkal, in a chamber cut into the bedrock beneath a pyramid and reached by a stairway of 19 steps. His four favourite horses were buried at the edge of the cemetery, and later members of the dynasty were also buried there.
plaek-phibunsongkhram: Plaek was born on 14 July 1897 in Nonthaburi to a family of durian farmers; his paternal grandfather was a Chinese immigrant from Guangdong, a descent he later concealed. He entered the Royal Military Academy and on graduating in 1914 was commissioned a second lieutenant in the artillery. After the First World War he studied artillery tactics in France. In 1928 King Prajadhipok gave him the noble title Luang, and he became known as Luang Phibunsongkhram.

On 16 December 1938 Phibun replaced Phraya Phahon as prime minister and army commander. An admirer of Italian fascism, he adopted a salute modelled on the Roman one and built a leadership cult with the propaganda minister Luang Wichitwathakan. His Thai Cultural Revolution urged citizens to salute the flag, use the standard Thai language and adopt Western dress, and his government pursued policies against the economic power of the Teochew Chinese. From October 1940 to May 1941 Thailand fought Vichy France over Indochina, and an armistice mediated by the Japanese gave it the disputed territories.

Japanese forces invaded on 8 December 1941, and after one day of resistance Phibun ordered a ceasefire. He signed an alliance with Japan on 21 December and declared war on Britain and the United States on 25 January 1942. The Free Thai Movement grew in opposition, and in 1944 the National Assembly ousted him. He was tried for war crimes after the war but acquitted.

He returned on 8 April 1948, after a military coup in November 1947. His second term aligned Thailand with the United States: he sent 4,000 troops to the Korean War and helped establish SEATO in 1954. He survived the Palace Rebellion of 1949 and the Manhattan Rebellion of 1951, when navy officers seized him aboard a dredge.

After a disputed election in February 1957, Phibun was overthrown on 16 September 1957 by Field Marshal Sarit Thanarat, once his loyal subordinate. He fled to Cambodia, then settled in Japan, and died of heart failure in Tokyo on 11 June 1964.

His reputation remains contested. Royalist histories portray him as an opportunist, and pro-democracy writers as a power-hungry military dictator. Historians such as E. Bruce Reynolds see fascist inspiration in his nationalism, while revisionists such as Nigel Brailey credit him with reforming Thai culture, expanding education and preserving Thailand's independence.
plato: Plato was born in the late fifth century BCE into an aristocratic and influential Athenian family. Through his mother, Perictione, he was a descendant of Solon, the statesman credited with laying the foundations of Athenian democracy. Diogenes Laertius asserted that Plato was a nickname alluding to his robust figure and that his birth name was Aristocles, but modern scholarship widely regards this as false. His brothers Glaucon and Adeimantus appear in the Republic. During his childhood Athens was at war with Sparta in the Peloponnesian War, and both brothers distinguished themselves at the battle of Megara in 409 BCE.

Like all male citizens of Athens, Plato received a traditional education in gymnastics and music. Ancient writers report a tradition that in his youth he wrote poems and tragedies, but burnt them when he met Socrates and turned to philosophy. He soon became a member of Socrates' inner circle. Socrates examined the ideas of his interlocutors by a series of questions, the Socratic method, and turned philosophy from natural philosophy to questions of ethics and politics.

Plato wrote dialogues in which Socrates is usually the primary speaker. Plato never presents himself as a participant. The dialogues discuss religion, human nature, love, perception and reality, and body and soul. His best known contribution is the theory of Forms, first introduced in the Phaedo. It holds that there is an apparent world of material objects grasped by the senses, which constantly changes, and an unchanging and unseen world of Forms, grasped by reason. He also argued for the immortality of the soul, and in the Republic the soul has three parts.

Thirty-five dialogues and thirteen letters have traditionally been ascribed to Plato, though modern scholarship doubts the authenticity of at least some of them. No one knows the exact order in which the dialogues were written. During the Islamic Golden Age, Neoplatonism was revived, and Al-Farabi, inspired by the Republic, proposed an ideal city governed by philosopher-kings. Byzantine scholars reintroduced Plato's texts to Western Europe in the early Renaissance, and about 250 Byzantine manuscripts survive. The edition published by Henricus Stephanus in Geneva in 1578 established the standard Stephanus pagination still in use.
platonic-academy: The site of the Academy lay about 1.5 kilometres north of the Dipylon gates of Athens, near Colonus. Before it was a school it held a sacred grove of olive trees dedicated to Athena, and the hero Akademos was linked to the place. The Spartans would not ravage the grove when they invaded Attica. Plato's school probably grew from informal gatherings at around the time he acquired inherited property at the age of thirty, with Theaetetus of Sunium, Archytas of Tarentum, Leodamas of Thasos and Neoclides among those present. Modern scholars generally place its foundation in the mid-380s BCE, probably after 387.

In Plato's time the group did not charge fees and was exclusive rather than open to the public. There was probably no clear distinction between teachers and students and no formal curriculum, though senior and junior members were distinguished. Two women are known to have studied there, Axiothea of Phlius and Lasthenia of Mantinea. The school seems to have had no particular doctrine: Plato and others posed problems for the rest to solve.

Lectures were given, notably Plato's lecture On the Good, but dialectic was probably more common. Mathematics was almost certainly studied, and Simplicius reports that Plato asked members to find uniform and ordered motions that would account for the irregular movements of the planets. Malcolm Schofield argues that it is hard to know how far the Academy was interested in practical politics.

Diogenes Laërtius divided its history into the Old, Middle and New Academies. Plato's successors as head, or scholarch, were Speusippus, Xenocrates, Polemo and Crates. Under Arcesilaus, who became scholarch around 266 BCE, the school emphasised scepticism, and under Carneades from 155 BCE it still denied that absolute truth could be known. Philo of Larissa left Athens when the First Mithridatic War began in 88 BCE. In 86 BCE Lucius Cornelius Sulla besieged Athens and laid waste the Academy's groves, and the damage seems to have made reopening impossible. His student Antiochus of Ascalon taught elsewhere, in a gymnasium called Ptolemy.

Platonism continued to be taught in Athens in the Roman era. Around 410 CE leading Neoplatonists set up a revived Academy, a private foundation in a large house which Proclus inherited from Plutarch of Athens and Syrianus. It reached its height under Proclus, who died in 485, and its last head was Damascius. The emperor Justinian I closed the school in 529.
plauen: Plauen lies on the upper reaches of the White Elster, a tributary of the Saale, in the Central Vogtlandian Hill Country. It is the largest city of the Saxon Vogtland and the south-westernmost of a string of cities that runs through Zwickau, Chemnitz and Freiberg to Dresden. It is near the borders with Bavaria and the Czech Republic. The Vogtlandian dialect spoken there is a variety of East Franconian with Saxon influences, and the names of the city and of many of its districts are of Slavic origin.

Polabian Slavs founded Plauen in the 12th century as Plawe. It passed to the Kingdom of Bohemia in 1327 and was captured in 1384 by Lippold von Bredow, Archbishop of Magdeburg. In 1466 it passed to Albertine Saxony and in 1569 to the Electorate of Saxony. It became part of the Kingdom of Saxony in 1806, during the Napoleonic Wars, and of the German Empire in 1871.

In the late 19th century the town became a centre of textile manufacture, specialising in chemical lace, called Plauen lace. Around 1910 it was an industrial boomtown, with 121,000 inhabitants at the census and 128,000 in 1912, a peak from which the population has shrunk dramatically since the Second World War. Plauen's Jewish community dated from the early 14th century and numbered several hundred between the wars. Its synagogue, built in 1930 in the Bauhaus style, was demolished in 1938 during Kristallnacht, and most of the Jewish population left or were killed in the Holocaust.

In the 1930s Plauen hosted the first chapter of the Nazi Party outside Bavaria. During the war the Nazis ran a prison there and three subcamps of the Flossenbürg concentration camp, where five hundred women, mostly Polish, and fifty men were held as forced labour. American troops occupied the city on 16 April 1945 and left it to the Red Army on 1 July. As part of the Soviet occupation zone and then of the German Democratic Republic, it held a large Red Army garrison. The first mass demonstration against the communist regime began there on 7 October 1989, the start of a series across the country that led to the reunification of Germany in 1990.

Plauen has a population of around 65,000 and is the seat of the Vogtland District. It and the surrounding Vogtland are known as the historic centre of the German embroidery and lace industry, and the products of the region are protected under the label Plauener Spitze. Its sights include the Old City Hall, the Johanniskirche, the Embroidery Machine Museum, the Fabrik der Fäden museum of textiles and lace, and the Elster Viaduct, the second-largest brick bridge in the world after the Göltzsch Viaduct.
plautus: Little is known of Plautus's early life. He is believed to have been born around 254 BCE in Sarsina, a small town in what is now Emilia-Romagna, in the ancient region of Umbria. According to Morris Marples, he worked in his early years as a stage-carpenter or scene-shifter, which may be the source of his love of the theatre.

His talent as an actor was eventually discovered, and he took the name Maccius, from Maccus, a clownish stock character of Atellan farce, and Plautus, meaning trampled flat, usually understood as flat-footed. Tradition holds that he made enough money to go into the nautical business, which collapsed, and that he then worked as a manual labourer and studied Greek drama, particularly the New Comedy of Menander, in his spare time.

His plays were released between about 205 and 184 BCE, while Roman theatre was still in its infancy and the Roman Republic was expanding in power and influence. He wrote palliata comoedia, the genre devised by Livius Andronicus. His name alone became a hallmark of theatrical success. Some of his plays carry traces of their time: a passage in the Miles Gloriosus beginning hostis tibi adesse, the foe is near at hand, is thought by A.

F. West to comment on the Second Punic War, which lasted from 218 to 201 BCE. Plautus was sometimes accused of teaching the public to mock the gods, since characters compare mortals to gods; in the Miles Gloriosus the braggart Pyrgopolynices claims to have been born one day later than Jupiter.

Plautus adapted Greek New Comedy, which differs greatly from the plays of Aristophanes in being devoid of serious political, social or intellectual content and in focusing on the home and family. Like Menander, he gave weight to the relation of father and son, but Plautus shows a betrayal between them that Menander does not.

His characters, such as slaves, concubines, soldiers and old men, came from Greek stock, but he modified them, and he often practised contaminatio, mixing elements of two or more source plays. His Bacchides, for example, has three tricks where its supposed Greek model, Menander's Dis Exapaton, has two. Of about 270 proper names in the surviving plays, about 250 are Greek, which suggests that his audience understood some Greek. Scholars dispute his originality: some see creativity, others a copyist of Greek models.

His plays are the earliest Latin literary works to survive in their entirety, and he influenced Shakespeare and Molière, whose The Miser is partly modelled on the Aulularia. The oldest manuscript is the Ambrosian palimpsest, thought to date to the 5th century and not discovered until 1815; its parchment was cleaned and a copy of the books of Kings and Chronicles written over it.
pliny-the-elder: Pliny was the son of an equestrian, Gaius Plinius Celer, and his wife Marcella, names known only from a fragmentary inscription found at Verona. He was born at Como, which he regarded as part of old Gallia Transpadana, and his father took him to Rome to be educated. His dates rest on the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 and a statement by his nephew that he died in his 56th year. He had a sister, Plinia, who was the mother of Pliny the Younger, whose letters describe his uncle's work and study regimen in detail. Pliny the Elder bequeathed his notes to his nephew and adopted him in his will.

In 46 CE, at about 23, Pliny entered the army as a junior officer, as young men of equestrian rank did. He served under Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo in Germania Inferior and took part in the conquest of the Chauci in 47 and the building of a canal between the Maas and the Rhine. He later served in Germania Superior under Publius Pomponius Secundus, and probably joined the campaign against the Chatti in 50.

Under Nero he held no high office, lived mainly in Rome, pleaded cases and wrote on safer subjects such as rhetoric and grammar, and a biography of Pomponius Secundus. After Vespasian became emperor in 69, Pliny was kept in a succession of procuratorships. Scholars propose two to four of them, including Gallia Narbonensis in 70, Africa from 70 to 72, Hispania Tarraconensis from 72 to 74 and Gallia Belgica from 74 to 76. He kept good relations with Vespasian and, according to his nephew, went to the emperor before dawn each day.

Pliny produced seven works in 102 volumes, of which only the Natural History survives. Among the lost works was the twenty-volume Bella Germaniae, used by Plutarch, Tacitus and Suetonius, and a thirty-one-volume history continuing that of Aufidius Bassus, which he held back for publication after his death. The Natural History, in 37 books, drew on personal experience, his earlier works and extracts from other writers. One servant read aloud and another wrote down what he dictated, and the collection reached about 160 volumes. Larcius Licinius offered 400,000 sesterces for them, unsuccessfully.

The work is dedicated to Titus. It became a model for later encyclopedias in its breadth, its practice of citing original authors and its index of contents, and some historians call it the first encyclopedia. Pliny died in the eruption of 79, with the book lacking a final revision. According to the younger Pliny, he sailed from Misenum across the Gulf of Naples to rescue friends at Stabiae, and was overcome by toxic gases there.
pliny-the-younger: Pliny was born in Novum Comum (Como, in northern Italy) around 61 CE, the son of Lucius Caecilius Cilo and Plinia Marcella, a sister of Pliny the Elder. His father died while he was still young, and his guardian and teacher was Lucius Verginius Rufus, known for quelling a revolt against Nero in 68. In Rome he studied rhetoric under Quintilian and Nicetes Sacerdos of Smyrna, and grew closer to his uncle.

When Pliny was 17 or 18, his uncle died trying to rescue victims of the eruption of Vesuvius in 79. The elder Pliny's will left his estate to his nephew and adopted him, and the younger man took the name Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus. He married three times; his third wife, Calpurnia, was 14 at the time and 26 years younger than he was.

Pliny was an equestrian by birth, and his career began at the age of 18 along the usual equestrian route. Unlike most equestrians he entered the senatorial order, by election as quaestor in his late twenties. He crossed most of the principal fields of imperial administration, and his career is among the best documented of the period. He survived the reigns of several emperors, including Domitian, who was much detested, and rose in rank throughout.

He was active in the centumviral court, which dealt with inheritance cases, and was a well-known prosecutor and defender in the trials of provincial governors: Baebius Massa of Baetica, Marius Priscus of Africa, Gaius Caecilius Classicus of Baetica, and Gaius Julius Bassus and Varenus Rufus, both governors of Bithynia and Pontus, the province he later governed himself. He is thought to have died suddenly in Bithynia-Pontus around 113, since no event in his letters falls later.

Pliny wrote his first work, a tragedy in Greek, at 14, and later many poems, most of them lost. His only surviving oration is the Panegyricus Traiani, delivered in the Senate in 100, a eulogy of Trajan that contrasts him with Domitian. His largest surviving work is the 247 letters of the Epistulae, in ten books. The first nine are addressed to friends and associates; the tenth, his official correspondence with Trajan, was probably published after his death.

Two letters to the historian Tacitus, written about 25 years after the event, describe the eruption of Vesuvius and the death of his uncle; volcanologists call eruptions of that type Plinian. Another, written about 112, asks Trajan how to treat Christians brought before him on anonymous accusations, and with the emperor's reply it is the earliest surviving Roman document to mention them. A letter of 105 describes his argument for a three-way vote in a Senate trial.
pliska: Pliska lies on the Ludogorie plateau of the Danubian Plain in Shumen Province, 20 km north-east of the provincial capital, Shumen. In 680 the Bulgars under Asparuh crossed the Danube into lands inhabited largely by Slavic farmers. After defeating a Byzantine expedition led by Emperor Constantine IV, Asparuh forced the nearby Slavic tribes to pay tribute, and in 681 the empire signed a treaty recognising the Bulgar state, the first time Byzantium officially acknowledged another state in the Balkans. A Bulgarian chronicle says that Pliska was founded by Asparuh as the capital, though this is archaeologically unsubstantiated.

Pliska was the capital of the First Bulgarian Empire until 893. By the early 9th century it had a defensive wall and a vast outer earthwork with stone revetment, 21 kilometres long, enclosing 2,300 hectares. The Bulgars and Byzantium were almost constantly at war. In 811 the Byzantine emperor Nikephoros I burned the royal residence, which was largely of wood, and Khan Krum soon drove the invaders out. Omurtag rebuilt the city in stone, with a palace in the late Roman manner.

When Boris I converted to Christianity in 864, Pliska's religious buildings were adapted for Christian use, and a monastery attached to the Great Basilica housed disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius. In 886 Boris founded the Pliska Literary School. His son Vladimir tried to restore paganism and the basilica was heavily damaged, and when Boris overthrew him he moved the capital to Preslav in 893. Pliska then declined, and it was destroyed between 969 and 972 during the war of the Rus' and the Byzantines over Bulgaria, and never rebuilt.

The ruins lie 3 km north of the modern village of Pliska and form a National Archaeological Reserve. They include two palaces, the strong stone fortifications and the Great Basilica, which served as a royal church and a national patriarchal cathedral. Excavation has shown that the Outer Town held modest cottages with open ground for livestock, and that the Inner Town had a palace, a basilica and aristocratic buildings behind stone walls. The dating is disputed: some scholars have argued that Pliska was only a seasonal residence, or that its Great Basilica is later than long supposed.
ploiesti: Ploiești, formerly spelled Ploești, is the county seat of Prahova County. It lies in the historical region of Muntenia on the Wallachian Plain, about 56 km north of Bucharest and at an average altitude of 150 m. The city stands on the Dâmbu River, with the Prahova and Teleajen rivers close by. Its position on trade routes linking Transylvania with the Danube basin shaped its growth, and under the soil lies the Mio-Pliocene zone, long exploited for oil, gas and coal, whose Pliocene sands are the main regional reservoirs.

Ploiești is first mentioned in 1503 as a modest village. In 1597 Michael the Brave, Prince of Wallachia, designated it a market town, and it flourished through the 17th and 18th centuries as a centre of commerce and handicrafts. In 1810, under Ottoman administration, it had an estimated 2,024 residents. A road to Brașov opened in 1864 and the railway arrived in 1882. The Mehedințeanu brothers established the world's first large-scale oil refinery in the city, fully operational between 1856 and 1857, which drew foreign capital and rapid growth and earned the city the nickname Capital of Black Gold. In 1870 it was the centre of the Republic of Ploiești, a local revolt by liberal politicians that failed within a day.

In 1916, before the invasion, a British operation under Colonel John Norton-Griffiths sabotaged the oil fields and equipment. In the Second World War the city was the primary source of petroleum for Germany.

The Soviet Air Forces began bombing it in June 1941; the United States Army Air Forces carried out a small raid in June 1942 and the large low-level Operation Tidal Wave on 1 August 1943, which caused severe damage and heavy Allied losses but slowed production only temporarily. Bombing by the USAAF 15th Air Force and the Royal Air Force between April and August 1944 crippled the refineries, and the Red Army entered the city on 24 August 1944. After the war the communist government nationalised the oil industry.

The 2021 census counted 180,540 people, down from a peak of 252,715 in 1992. Oil refining remains its core industry, with refineries linked by pipelines to Bucharest, Constanța and Giurgiu, and it is a junction of roads and railways to Transylvania and Moldavia. Its landmarks include the Palace of Culture, the Oil Museum, the Ploiești Art Museum and the Hagi Prodan Museum, which dates to 1785. The Oil & Gas University of Ploiești moved there in 1967.
plotinus: Plotinus's pupil and biographer Porphyry records in his Life of Plotinus that he died at sixty-six at the end of the second year of the emperor Claudius II, and so calculates that he was born in the thirteenth year of Septimius Severus, about 204.

Eunapius reported that he was born in Lyco, which could mean Asyut in Upper Egypt or a Lycopolis in the Delta. This has led to speculation that his family was Hellenized Egyptian, Greek or Roman. The scholar A. H. Armstrong writes that all that can be said with reasonable certainty is that Greek was his normal language and that he had a Greek education.

Plotinus took up philosophy at twenty-eight, around 232, and travelled to Alexandria. He was dissatisfied with every teacher until an acquaintance suggested he hear the self-taught Platonist Ammonius Saccas. After the lecture he declared, this is the man I was looking for, and he remained with Ammonius for eleven years. Around the age of thirty-eight he decided to investigate the teachings of Persian and Indian philosophers and joined the army of the emperor Gordian III on its march against Persia in 242–243. The campaign failed, and Plotinus reached safety in Antioch only with great difficulty.

In Rome he gained the respect of the emperor Gallienus and his wife Salonina. He once tried to persuade Gallienus to rebuild an abandoned settlement in Campania as a City of Philosophers, whose inhabitants would live under the constitution of Plato's Laws; the subsidy was never granted, for reasons Porphyry did not know.

From about 253 until a few months before his death Plotinus wrote the essays that became the Enneads, a title meaning a group of nine. They were notes and essays he used in lectures and debates. His eyesight was poor, his handwriting atrocious and his spelling careless, so Porphyry polished and edited them into their modern form. Plotinus described three fundamental principles: the One, the Intellect and the Soul. The One is totally transcendent, without division or multiplicity, beyond being and non-being, and he identified it with the Good and with Beauty. All things flow from it by emanation without diminishing it.

He held that true happiness does not depend on worldly fortune. He died in seclusion on an estate in Campania left to him by his friend Zethos, and Eustochius reported his last words: Try to raise the divine in yourselves to the divine in the all. His thought influenced pagan, Jewish, Christian and Islamic thinkers, among them Augustine, the Fatimid teacher Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani and the Renaissance philosopher Marsilio Ficino.
plough: A plough, or plow in the US, is a farm tool for loosening or turning soil before sowing or planting. It may have a wooden, iron or steel frame with a blade attached to cut and loosen the soil, and the trenches it cuts are called furrows. Its main purpose is to turn over the uppermost soil, bringing fresh nutrients to the surface while burying weeds and crop remains. The earliest ploughs had no wheels, and the Romans called such a plough an aratrum. A Sumerian disputation poem of the 3rd millennium BCE personifies the plough in a debate with the hoe.

When agriculture began, soil was turned with digging sticks and hoes. The domestication of oxen in Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Civilisation, perhaps as early as the 6th millennium BCE, gave the draught power to develop the true ard, or scratch plough. A ploughed field of about 2800 BCE has been found at Kalibangan in India.

The heavy iron mould-board plough was invented in China under the Han Empire in the 1st and 2nd centuries and spread from there to the Netherlands. The first mould-board ploughs turned the soil in one direction only, so fields were worked in long strips, and their traditional size, a furlong by a chain, an area of one acre, is the origin of the acre.

The basic mould-board plough was unsuitable for the heavier soils of northern Europe. Wheels allowed heavier ploughs with a larger metal-faced mould board, and these led to greater food production, coinciding with a marked increase in the world's population in the second millennium CE. They needed up to eight oxen, so fields became long and narrow. Four to eight oxen were more than a typical peasant household could muster, so ploughing became a communal effort and contributed to the rise of the manorial system in northern Europe.

By 1837 John Deere, an Illinois blacksmith, was making polished cast steel ploughs for sticky soils. Riding ploughs with multiple mould boards soon followed, and steam engines and then tractors replaced animals as power.
plovdiv: Evidence of habitation in the area goes back to the 6th millennium BCE, when the first Neolithic settlements appeared, and the cultural layers in the city are twelve metres thick. A Thracian settlement named Pulpudeva was later conquered and ruled by Persians, Macedonians, Celts, Romans, Byzantines, Goths, Huns, Bulgarians and Ottoman Turks. Philip II of Macedon settled Thracians and 2,000 Macedonians there in 342 BCE and founded it as Philippopolis. The Roman Republic took it in 168 BCE, and it became the capital of the province of Thracia, at the centre of the road network of inland Thrace. Marcus Aurelius built a new wall around the city.

The Goths under Cniva sacked Philippopolis in 250, and the Huns did so in 441 or 442; the walls were rebuilt each time, and Justinian renewed them again. The city fell to the Bulgars of the First Bulgarian Empire in 863, in the reign of Boris I. Basil II used it as a strategic fortress in the wars against Bulgaria, and the Pechenegs occupied it briefly around 1090. Geoffrey of Villehardouin ranked it the third largest city of the Byzantine Empire after Constantinople and Thessalonica. Kaloyan of Bulgaria destroyed it in 1206, and in 1219 it became the capital of the Crusader Duchy of Philippopolis.

The Ottoman Turks under Lala Shahin Pasha took the city in 1364, though other accounts place its fall after the Battle of Maritsa in 1371. Over about five hundred years it was a sanjak centre at various times, one of the major economic centres of the Balkans beside Constantinople, Edirne, Thessaloniki and Sofia, and its richer citizens built the houses that still stand in the architectural reserve of Old Plovdiv.

The Treaty of San Stefano of 3 March 1878 chose Plovdiv as capital of a restored Bulgaria, but the Congress of Berlin separated the autonomous region of Eastern Rumelia from Bulgaria, and Plovdiv became its capital under a constitution made by the Ottoman Empire. In 1885 Eastern Rumelia joined Bulgaria. A railway linked the city with Constantinople in 1874 and with Sofia in 1888, and in 1892 it hosted the First Bulgarian Fair.

Plovdiv is the second largest city in Bulgaria, on the Maritsa river 144 km southeast of Sofia, spread over seven syenite hills that give it the name City of the Seven Hills. It had a population of 329,489 in 2024. It was the European Capital of Culture in 2019, and the city has more than 200 archaeological sites.
plutarch: Plutarch was born to a prominent family in the small town of Chaeronea, in the Greek region of Boeotia, about 30 kilometres east of Delphi. His family was long established there. His father was named Autobulus and his grandfather Lamprias, and his brothers Timon and Lamprias appear often in his essays and dialogues. He studied mathematics and philosophy in Athens under Ammonius from 66 to 67 CE. At some point he received Roman citizenship, sponsored by Lucius Mestrius Florus, an associate of the emperor Vespasian, and took the name Lucius Mestrius Plutarchus.

Plutarch lived most of his life at Chaeronea, where he served as a magistrate and held the office of archon,. He visited Rome about 70 CE with Florus, who served as a source for his Life of Otho, and he was on familiar terms with Roman nobles including Quintus Sosius Senecio. About 95 CE he became one of the two priests of the temple of Apollo at Delphi, a site that had declined considerably since the classical period. He was also epimeletes of the Amphictyonic League for at least five terms, from 107 to 127, organising the Pythian Games. Plutarch and his wife Timoxena had at least four sons and one daughter. The year of his death is not known.

His best-known work, the Parallel Lives, arranges biographies of illustrious Greeks and Romans in pairs to illuminate their shared virtues and vices. The surviving Lives contain 23 pairs and four single lives, though several others are lost and many survivors are truncated. Plutarch states in his Life of Alexander that he is writing lives and not histories, because a small thing such as a phrase or a jest often reveals character better than battles. His Life of Pyrrhus is the main account of Roman history from 293 to 264 BCE, for which the texts of Dionysius and Livy are lost.

The Moralia is a collection of seventy-eight essays and speeches. It includes a dialogue on the face seen in the orb of the Moon, which served as a source for Galileo, On the Worship of Isis and Osiris, a crucial source on ancient Egyptian religion, and philosophical treatises such as On the Decline of the Oracles. Some works printed with it, including the Lives of the Ten Orators, were falsely attributed to him and are credited to an unknown author called Pseudo-Plutarch.
plutarco-elias-calles: Calles was born Francisco Plutarco Elías Campuzano on 25 September 1877 in Sonora, one of two natural children of a bureaucrat father. He took the surname Calles from the uncle who raised him after his mother's death. The uncle was an atheist and instilled in him a commitment to secular education and disdain for the Roman Catholic Church.

In the Mexican Revolution he supported Francisco I. Madero and then joined the Constitutionalists of Venustiano Carranza, reaching the rank of general by 1915. That year his forces repelled the rival faction under Pancho Villa at the Battle of Agua Prieta, and he became governor of Sonora. In 1920 he joined Adolfo de la Huerta and Álvaro Obregón in the Plan of Agua Prieta, which overthrew Carranza, and served under Obregón as Secretary of the Interior.

Calles took office in 1924 in the first peaceful transfer of presidential power since 1884, backed by the labour confederation CROM and the Laborist Party. His government extended pensions to civil servants, created a cabinet-level ministry of public health, added two thousand rural schools to the thousand his predecessor had founded, and began a national road network, including the Mexican section of the Pan-American Highway, paid for by a gasoline tax. Its finance minister, Alberto J. Pani, advised founding the Banco de México. He also tried to professionalise the army under Joaquín Amaro.

He rejected the Bucareli Agreements of 1923 and began drafting an oil law that would strictly apply Article 27 of the constitution, which made everything under the soil the property of the state, in conflict with foreign oil companies. He also enforced the constitution's secular laws, which banned foreign priests, nationalised church property and let local governments limit the number of priests. Opposition to these anticlerical measures sparked the Cristero War.

Obregón won the 1928 election but was murdered before taking office by José de León Toral, a Catholic militant. Calles was ineligible to return to the presidency, and to avoid a vacuum he created the National Revolutionary Party in 1929, predecessor of the Institutional Revolutionary Party. From 1929 to 1934 he was Mexico's de facto leader, the period called the Maximato. After he backed Lázaro Cárdenas for president, the two quarrelled over labour unions and strikes, and Cárdenas exiled him. President Manuel Ávila Camacho allowed him to return in 1941. He died in Mexico City on 19 October 1945.

Supporters praise his reforms in health, infrastructure and education and his efforts to prevent instability after Obregón's murder, while detractors criticise the escalation of the Cristero War and his crackdowns on unions. His main legacy, in one account, was the pacification of Mexico through the creation of the party.
plymouth-montserrat: Plymouth lies on the lower south-western slope of the Soufrière Hills volcano, on the island of Montserrat in the Leeward Island chain of the Lesser Antilles. The town was laid out in the Georgian era on old lava deposits, close to a volcano that had been inactive for centuries. For centuries it was the only port of entry to the island, and it held almost all of Montserrat's shops and services as well as its seat of government.

After the first European colony on Montserrat was founded in 1632, St. Anthony's Church was established in Plymouth in 1636. It had to be rebuilt several times after earthquakes and hurricanes. On 17 September 1989 Hurricane Hugo destroyed a 55-metre stone jetty in the harbour and left many buildings, including the island's only hospital, unusable.

The volcano began erupting on 18 July 1995, and ash fell across the south of the island. Residents of Plymouth were evacuated in August 1995 and again on 1 December 1995, and for the third and final time on 3 April 1996. The island was divided into risk zones, with entry to the town sometimes banned. On 25 June 1997 an eruption produced pyroclastic surges that killed 19 people. Between 4 and 8 August 1997 further large eruptions destroyed about 80 per cent of the town and buried it under about 1.4 metres of ash, burning many buildings. The Royal Navy helped take the population to safety.

The southern half of the island was declared an exclusion zone. Plymouth, which had about 4,000 inhabitants, remains the de jure capital, while the government works from Brades in the north. The airport was buried in ash and a new one opened in 2005 near Brades. Between 1995 and 2000 two thirds of the island's population fled, many to the United Kingdom, leaving fewer than 1,200 residents in 1997. The volcanic deposits are hard, similar in density to concrete, so clearing the town was judged too costly.
plzen: Plzeň lies about 78 kilometres west of Prague, at the confluence of four rivers, the Mže, Úhlava, Úslava and Radbuza, which together form the Berounka. The first written mention of Plzeň Castle is from 976. King Wenceslaus II founded the city of New Plzeň nearby in 1295, and it quickly became an important place on the trade routes from Bohemia to Nuremberg and Regensburg. In the fourteenth century it had about 3,000 inhabitants, making it the third largest city in Bohemia after Prague and Kutná Hora.

The first written mention of beer brewing is from 1307. During the Hussite Wars Plzeň was the centre of Catholic resistance; Prokop the Great besieged it three times without success. In 1476 the city printed Statuta by Arnošt of Pardubice, the oldest book printed in Bohemia. In the Thirty Years' War Mansfeld took it in 1618, and Imperial troops did not recapture it until 1621.

From the second half of the nineteenth century the city industrialised rapidly. Emil Škoda founded the Škoda Works in 1869, which became the most important engineering company in the country and a crucial supplier of arms to the Austro-Hungarian Army. The Bavarian brewer Josef Groll produced the first batch of modern Pilsner beer on 5 October 1842, using soft local water, Saaz hops and Bavarian-style lagering. In April 1945 Allied bombing raids caused heavy damage, and on 6 May 1945 the 16th Armored Division of General George Patton's Third Army liberated the city.

Plzeň is the capital of the Plzeň Region, and its historic centre has been an urban monument reservation since 1989. The Cathedral of St Bartholomew, built in the Gothic style in the late thirteenth century, has the highest tower in the Czech Republic at 102.6 metres. Beneath the centre runs a labyrinth of tunnels and cellars with a length of 20 kilometres, partly open to visitors. The city was a European Capital of Culture in 2015, and the Pilsner Urquell Brewery is the largest brewery in the Czech Republic.
pocahontas: Pocahontas was born Amonute and was also known as Matoaka; Pocahontas was a childhood nickname that the colonist William Strachey translated as little wanton. Her birth year is unknown, with historians estimating about 1596. Her father was Powhatan, the Mamanatowick of the Powhatan Confederacy, an alliance of about thirty polities in the Tidewater region of Virginia. Her mother's name and origin are unknown. Although popular culture often calls her a princess, she was not in line to succeed her father, since Powhatan's brothers, sisters and his sisters' children stood in line to succeed him.

John Smith arrived in Virginia with 100 other settlers in April 1607. Pocahontas befriended the colonists and played games with the boys at the settlement, and early accounts say she brought food that saved many from starving. Smith's well-known story of her saving him from execution appears only in his 1616 letter to Queen Anne and his 1624 Generall Historie, and scholars dispute it: Karen Ordahl Kupperman sees embroidery, while Frederic W. Gleach suggests Smith misunderstood a ritual of adoption.

In March 1613, during the First Anglo-Powhatan War, Captain Samuel Argall learned that she was visiting the Patawomeck village of Passapatanzy. With the help of the weroance Iopassus he lured her onto his ship, the Treasurer, and held her for ransom. At Henricus the minister Alexander Whitaker taught her Christianity and she took the name Rebecca. She married the tobacco planter John Rolfe on 5 April 1614, and their son Thomas was born in January 1615. Their marriage began eight years of peace between the colonists and the Powhatan, known as the Peace of Pocahontas.

The London Company brought the Rolfes to England, where they arrived at Plymouth on 12 June 1616, to promote investment in Virginia. She was presented to English society as a princess, attended Ben Jonson's masque The Vision of Delight at Whitehall on 5 January 1617, and met Smith, who had been thought dead in Virginia. In March 1617 the Rolfes boarded a ship to return, but she fell gravely ill at Gravesend and died of unknown causes at about 21. She was buried on 21 March 1617 at St George's Church, whose later destruction by fire in 1727 left the grave's exact location unknown.

Many of the stories told of her have been romanticised, and contemporary sources support her friendship with Smith but not a romance, which first appears in 1803. Her descendants run through Thomas Rolfe and his daughter Jane. In 1907 she was the first Native American honoured on a United States stamp.
podgorica: Podgorica lies in central Montenegro, at the confluence of the Ribnica and Morača rivers, where the southern foothills of the Dinaric Alps meet the northernmost part of the Zeta Plain. The name means under the hill. The city is only 15 kilometres north of Lake Skadar and stands at the crossroads of several historically important routes, in fertile lowlands with a favourable climate.

The oldest physical remains in the area are from the late Stone Age. In the Iron Age the area between the Zeta and Bjelopavlići valleys was populated by two Illyrian tribes, the Labeates and the Docleatae, and the nearby town of Doclea had 8,000 to 10,000 inhabitants. The area later passed through many hands, among them the Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire, the Serbian Empire and the Republic of Venice.

The Ottoman Empire captured Podgorica in 1474, and in 1479 built a large fortress there. The existing settlement, with its highly developed merchant connections, became the main Ottoman defensive and attacking bastion in the region. After the Congress of Berlin in 1878 the town was annexed to the Principality of Montenegro, ending four centuries of Ottoman rule. Roads were built to all neighbouring towns in 1902, and tobacco became its first significant commercial product.

In World War II Podgorica was bombed over 80 times, first by the Luftwaffe on 6 April 1941; an attack by the USAAF on 5 May 1944 killed about 400 civilians. It was liberated on 19 December 1944, and 1,691 people had been killed there in the course of the war. Josip Broz Tito promised on 12 July 1946 that the destroyed city would be rebuilt. It was renamed Titograd in 1946 and designated capital of the Socialist Republic of Montenegro, and rapid growth turned a small town into the country's primate city. Its original name was restored after a referendum on 2 April 1992.

Podgorica is the capital and largest city of Montenegro, capital of the independent state since 2006. It is a hub of the country's rail and road network and the centre of its education, science and healthcare. Cetinje, capital for much of Montenegrin history, preserves much of the national cultural heritage. Monuments in and around Podgorica include the Clock tower, the ruins of the Ribnica fortress and remnants of the ancient city of Doclea.
podolia: Podolia lies in west-central and south-western Ukraine and north-eastern Moldova, in the northern part of Transnistria. It covers about 40,000 square kilometres of the East European Plain and is bordered on the south by the Dniester and crossed by the Southern Bug. Its elongated plateau, the Podolian Upland, rises to 144 m. Chernozem, black earth, predominates, making it very fertile farmland. The name derives from Proto-Slavic words meaning by or along and valley or lowland. The traditional capital is Kamianets-Podilskyi, and other chief settlements include Vinnytsia, Khmelnytskyi, Mohyliv-Podilskyi and Bar.

The region has had human inhabitants since the beginning of the Neolithic. Herodotus mentions it as the seat of the Graeco-Scythian Alazones, and the Romans left Trajan's Wall. In the 13th century the Mongols plundered the lowlands, then called Ponizie. Algirdas, Grand Duke of Lithuania, freed them after his victory over the Golden Horde at the Battle of Blue Waters in 1362 and annexed them to Lithuania as Podolia. In 1366 western Podolia with Kamieniec Podolski passed under Polish sovereignty, and after the death of Vytautas in 1430 it was incorporated into the Podolian Voivodeship of the Kingdom of Poland. The Union of Lublin of 1569 reunited western and eastern Podolia within the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.

Podolia was the target of frequent Tatar slave raids. From 1672 it was part of the Ottoman Empire as Podolia Eyalet, a province centred on Kamaniçe and divided into four sanjaks, and it returned to Poland in 1699 with the Treaty of Karlowitz. The Partitions of Poland of 1772 and 1793 gave the western and eastern parts to the Austrian and Russian empires. From 1793 to 1917 part of the region formed the Podolia Governorate of Russia, whose population in 1906 was estimated at 3,543,700, chiefly Ukrainians, with Polish and Jewish minorities.

After the First World War western Podolia came under Polish control, while the Soviet Union kept eastern Podolia. In 1939 the western area became part of Soviet Ukraine. From July 1941 German Einsatzgruppen carried out mass shootings of the Jewish inhabitants. In 1945, when Poland's eastern border was realigned along the Curzon line, the whole of Podolia remained in the Ukrainian and Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republics.

Podolia is known for its folk icon painting, whose long home iconostases on canvas of the late 19th and early 20th centuries are dominated by red, green and yellow; collections are held by the Vinnytsya Art Museum and the Museum of Ukrainian Home Icons in Radomysl Castle. The region is also the birthplace of the Baal Shem Tov, the founder of Hasidic Judaism.
poel: Poel forms the natural northern and eastern boundary of the Bay of Wismar on the German coast, and its northern shore lies on the south side of the Bay of Mecklenburg. It is close to Lübeck, Wismar and Schwerin and belongs to the Hamburg Metropolitan Region. The island is a municipality in the district of Nordwestmecklenburg, made up of the main places Kirchdorf and Oertzenhof and a number of smaller villages. It covers 36.02 square kilometres. The name derives from pole, the Common Slavic word for flat land or field. The Eleventh Edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica (1910 to 1911) cites Wismar Bay as the finest harbour on the Baltic.

The first inhabitants in historic times were Slavs of the Obotrite tribe. In the early 13th century the Slavic ruler Heinrich Borwin I brought German settlers from Dithmarschen and Holstein, who began building the island's church around 1210. Its Romanesque tower is 47 metres high and visible from almost every point on the island, and the nave was enlarged in the Gothic style around 1300. The church has been Lutheran since about 1535.

In 1614 Duke Adolf Friedrich I of Mecklenburg began a fortress near the church, completed in 1618. During the Thirty Years' War the duke had to yield it to imperial troops in 1628, and Swedish troops took it in 1635. After the Treaty of Westphalia in 1648 two-thirds of Poel, with Wismar and Neukloster, were granted to the King of Sweden, while the western third stayed with the Holy Spirit Hospital of Lübeck. The Swedes invested in making Wismar a military centre and neglected the castle, which was in ruins by 1740. In 1803 the Swedish portion was leased for 99 years to the Duke of Mecklenburg. Since 1927 a causeway has connected the island to the mainland.

Most of the island is farmland, and it is also a popular recreational area with fine beaches and sheltered harbours. Timmendorf harbour has a pilot's station and facilities for yachts and fishermen, and Kirchdorf has a yachting harbour and a boatyard. The earthen embankments and most of the moats of the 17th-century fortress can still be seen. The island has 2,873 inhabitants.
poggio-bracciolini: Poggio was born at Terranuova, near Arezzo in Tuscany, a village renamed Terranuova Bracciolini in 1862 in his honour. His father took him to Florence, where he studied Latin under Giovanni Malpaghino of Ravenna, a friend and protégé of Petrarch. His skill as a copyist brought him to the notice of Coluccio Salutati and Niccolò de' Niccoli, who befriended him. He studied notarial law and at twenty-one entered the Florentine notaries' guild. In 1403, on the recommendation of Salutati and Leonardo Bruni, he became secretary to Cardinal Landolfo Maramaldo, and soon joined the Chancery of Apostolic Briefs in the Roman Curia.

Over a career of about fifty years Poggio served seven popes, from Boniface IX to Nicholas V, rising from scriptor to abbreviator, scriptor apostolicus and, under Martin V, apostolic secretary. He remained a layman and considered himself a Florentine working for the papacy. After Martin V's election he spent five years in England, from 1418 until 1423, at the invitation of Cardinal Henry Beaufort, the least productive years of his career. In December 1435 he left his long-term mistress, with whom he had fourteen children, and married the teenage Selvaggia dei Buondelmonti; they had five sons and a daughter.

During the Council of Constance, from 1414, he explored the libraries of Swiss and Swabian abbeys, and his great finds date to 1415-1417. At St Gall he found Cicero's Pro Sexto Roscio, Quintilian, Statius' Silvae and Vitruvius's De architectura; at Cluny and Langres, more orations of Cicero. In January 1417 he found, in a German monastery probably Fulda, the only manuscript of Lucretius's De rerum natura then known, which he sent to Niccoli, whose copy became the model for more than fifty others. He bribed a monk to take a Livy and an Ammianus from the library of Hersfeld Abbey.

Poggio wrote only in Latin, in dialogues such as De avaritia, On Nobility, which defends nobility based on virtue rather than birth, and On the Vicissitudes of Fortune. His Liber Facetiarum, humorous and indecent tales that satirise the clergy, remained popular for centuries. His Historia Florentina continued Bruni's history to 1455. In 1452 he feuded with Lorenzo Valla over the Elegantiae, but they later reconciled. Poggio was a prolific scribe in Humanist minuscule, though later research showed that he did not invent it.

In April 1453 Cosimo de' Medici chose him as Chancellor of the Florentine Republic, in succession to Carlo Marsuppini. He died on 30 October 1459, before finishing his history, and was buried in Santa Croce, where a statue by Donatello stood.
pointe-a-pitre: Pointe-à-Pitre stands on the southwest of Grande-Terre, facing the Caribbean Sea, near the Rivière Salée, the Salt River that separates Grande-Terre from Basse-Terre. It lies on a limestone plateau, which was a factor in the city's construction, and its bay, the Petit Cul-de-Sac Marin, offers a sheltered port. The name means headland of Pitre. It is popularly derived from a Dutch sailor or fisherman called Pieter who may have settled on a promontory in the 17th century, but linguists now question this and suggest the Spanish word pitera, a rope made from agave.

French colonial authorities had long thought of founding a city where Guadeloupe's two main districts meet, but attempts around 1713 to 1730 failed because the swampy ground was unhealthy. During the British occupation of Guadeloupe from 1759 to 1763 a settlement appeared on a hill overlooking the swamps. After Guadeloupe returned to France in 1763 the city was officially founded in 1764 by royal edict under the governor Gabriel de Clieu, and the swamps were drained in the following years, which allowed urban development.

Growth was relatively rapid, partly thanks to the corsairs. A great fire entirely destroyed the city in 1780, and an earthquake destroyed it again in 1843. Its history is marked by many disasters: fires in 1850, 1871 and 1931, earthquakes in 1851 and 1897, hurricanes in 1865 and 1928, and several cholera epidemics. After the 1928 hurricane the architect Ali Tur built much of the city's civil and religious heritage between 1930 and 1935, including the palais de justice, the hospice hospital, the fish hall, several schools and the fire station. Its location and large sheltered port nevertheless made it Guadeloupe's largest city and economic capital.

Pointe-à-Pitre is the second most populous commune of Guadeloupe after Les Abymes, and an economic capital though not the administrative capital, which is Basse-Terre. The commune itself is small, but it is the centre of an urban area of eleven communes holding about 65 percent of the island's population. The main seaport, Port de Jarry, lies across the bay in Baie-Mahault. The former cathedral of St Peter and Paul recalls that the town was the seat of a Roman Catholic diocese, united with Basse-Terre in 1951. Its monuments include the Place de la Victoire, the Schœlcher and Saint-John-Perse museums and the Mémorial ACTe.
pointe-noire: Pointe-Noire stands on a headland between Pointe-Noire Bay and the Atlantic Ocean, near the border with Angola. Before European contact the site was a region around the fishing village of Ndji-Ndji, under the Kingdom of Loango, about 20 kilometres south of its capital Buali. The name, meaning Black Point, comes from Portuguese navigators who in 1484 saw an outcrop of black rocks on the headland.

France acquired the land of the Loango kingdom on 12 March 1883 through a treaty negotiated between Lieutenant Cordier and the king, Manimacosso-Chicusso, and Pointe-Noire was founded that year. French Equatorial Africa was created in 1910, and French companies were allowed to exploit the Middle Congo. In 1923 Pointe-Noire was chosen as the terminus of the Congo-Ocean Railway, which was to link Brazzaville, where river navigation ended, to the coast. The site had to allow a deep-sea port, and it was preferred to Libreville, first proposed. The railway was completed in 1934.

Drinking water reached the city in 1927, when it had about 3,000 inhabitants. A first hospital was built in 1936, and a bank opened a branch that year. The harbour received its first ship in 1942. In 1950 the city had 20,000 inhabitants and became capital of the Middle Congo. After incidents during the 1958 elections, leaders of the Democratic Union for the Defence of African Interests moved the capital to Brazzaville, since Pointe-Noire was under the influence of the opposition.

Pointe-Noire was the most modern city in the country when Congo became independent in 1960. Oil discovered around 1980, exploited largely by the French company Elf Aquitaine, brought rapid growth: the population doubled by 1982 and reached 360,000 in 1994. The civil wars of 1997 and 1999 sent refugees from inland provinces, and the population passed one million. It is the second largest city of the Republic of the Congo, with its main port and fishing industry, and the terminus of the Congo-Ocean Railway.
poitiers: Poitiers stands on a vast promontory between the valleys of the Boivre and the Clain, on the Seuil du Poitou, a shallow gap that connects the Aquitaine Basin in the south to the Paris Basin in the north. The old town occupies a plateau rising about 40 metres above the streams around it, a strong tactical position that mattered especially before and throughout the Middle Ages.

The Celtic tribe of the Pictones founded the town and gave it its name; before Roman influence it was the oppidum of Lemonum, and after the conquest it was called Pictavium. The Romans built at least three aqueducts and an amphitheatre larger than the one at Nîmes. Hilary of Poitiers, the first bishop, held the see from 350 to 367 and evangelised the town; he was exiled by Constantius II and returned at risk of death. The Visigoths later made it one of their principal residences, until Clovis I defeated Alaric II at Vouillé, not far away, in 507, and the town came under Frankish rule.

In the Early Middle Ages Poitiers benefited from its defensible position far from the centre of Frankish power. It was the seat of a diocese from the 4th century and the capital of the county of Poitou. Charles Martel's troops fought an Umayyad army led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi near the city on 10 October 732, a battle also called the Battle of Tours. Eleanor of Aquitaine often lived there, embellished and fortified it, and in 1199 gave it communal rights; in 1152 she married the future Henry II of England in the cathedral.

On 19 September 1356 the English defeated a larger French royal army near the town in the Battle of Poitiers and captured King John II of France. From 1418, under Charles VII, the royal parliament sat in exile at Poitiers until 1436, and in 1429 the town was the site of the formal inquest into Joan of Arc. The university was founded in 1431. In 1569 it withstood a siege by Gaspard de Coligny during the Wars of Religion.

Poitiers is the capital of the Vienne department in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and has a population of 89,427. It is a university town, and Descartes, Rabelais and Joachim du Bellay are among those associated with it. Its preserved buildings include the 4th-century baptistery of Saint-Jean, the 12th-century Church of Notre-Dame-la-Grande and the cathedral, completed at the end of the 12th century.
pol-pot: Pol Pot was born Saloth Sâr in the village of Prek Sbauv, outside Kampong Thom, the son of a prosperous farmer. He was educated at some of Cambodia's most elite schools, boarding from 1942 at a new junior middle school in Kampong Cham, where fellow pupils such as Hu Nim and Khieu Samphan later served in his government. He arrived in Paris on 1 October 1949 on a scholarship to study radio electronics, and joined the French Communist Party in 1951. He returned to Cambodia in 1953 and worked with the Khmer Việt Minh, then taught in Phnom Penh while remaining a central figure in the Marxist-Leninist movement.

In 1959 the movement was formalised as the Kampuchean Labour Party, later renamed the Communist Party of Kampuchea. To avoid repression by Norodom Sihanouk's government, Pol Pot moved to a jungle camp in 1962, and in February 1963 he was elected party secretary. The war against Sihanouk was launched in January 1968. After Lon Nol deposed Sihanouk in March 1970, Sihanouk allied with the Khmer Rouge, and his support greatly helped recruitment. In May 1973 Pol Pot ordered the collectivisation of villages in Khmer Rouge territory. Phnom Penh fell on 17 April 1975, and he secretly entered the abandoned city three days later.

In January 1976 a new constitution renamed the country Democratic Kampuchea. The Khmer Rouge emptied the cities and moved the urban population to collective farms and labour camps, where mass executions, torture, malnutrition and disease were rampant. Money, religion and private property were abolished, and more than 1.3 million people were executed and buried in mass graves. After repeated border clashes and massacres of Vietnamese villagers, Vietnam launched a full-scale invasion on 25 December 1978, and by January 1979 the Khmer Rouge were toppled.

The Khmer Rouge retreated to the jungles near the Thai border and kept fighting until the Vietnamese withdrew in 1989. In June 1997 Pol Pot ordered the killing of Son Sen, which prompted the commander Ta Mok to turn against him. Pol Pot was placed under house arrest and died shortly afterward in 1998. Some Cambodians still leave offerings at his grave in Anlong Veng, while many call the period samai a-Pot, the era of the contemptible Pot.
poland: Poland covers an administrative area of 312,722 square kilometres, the ninth-largest country in Europe.
