When Clement II died in October 1047, Benedict seized the Lateran Palace in November and again became pope, until German troops drove him away in July 1048. Damasus II was then elected and universally recognised. Benedict refused to appear on charges of simony in 1049 and was excommunicated. His later fate is obscure; Leo IX may have lifted the ban. He was buried at the Abbey of Grottaferrata about 1056, and its abbot, Saint Bartholomew of Grottaferrata, said he had been penitent. He remains the only person to have been pope more than once and the only one accused of selling the papacy.
pope-benedict-viii: Benedict VIII was born around 980 as Theophylact, a son of Count Gregory I of Tusculum. His family had already produced three popes: John XI, who reigned from 931 to 935, John XII, from 955 to 964, and Benedict VII, from 973 to 974. He became pope on 18 May 1012. Unusually for a medieval pope, he held strong authority both in Rome and abroad.

An antipope, Gregory VI, forced him to flee Rome, and King Henry II of Germany restored him and was crowned emperor by him on 14 February 1014. The two stayed on good terms throughout his pontificate. When Saracens renewed their attacks on southern Italy, made a settlement in Sardinia and sacked Pisa, the pope allied himself with the Normans, who were beginning to settle in Italy, and brought about the defeat of the Saracens in Sardinia. He also subjugated the Crescentii.

In 1020 he travelled to Germany to confer with Henry about the renewed Byzantine threat in the south of Italy. He reached Bamberg at Eastertide, consecrated its new cathedral and obtained a charter from Henry confirming the donations of Charlemagne and Otto the Great. In 1022 he received Archbishop Æthelnoth of Canterbury, who had come to Rome for the pallium. That year he held a synod at Pavia with the emperor to restrain simony and the incontinence of the clergy.

He backed the reform sponsored by Cluny Abbey, was a friend of its abbot Odilo, and encouraged the Truce of God. Horace Mann judged him one of the few popes of the Middle Ages who was at once powerful at home and great abroad. He died on 9 April 1024 and his brother succeeded him as John XIX.
pope-boniface-viii: Benedetto Caetani was born in Anagni, about 50 kilometres southeast of Rome, a younger son of Roffredo Caetani, a member of a baronial family of the Papal States. His mother, Emilia Patrasso di Guarcino, was a niece of Pope Alexander IV, which kept him not far from the seat of ecclesiastical power and patronage. In 1252 he followed his uncle Pietro Caetani, the new Bishop of Todi, to Todi and began legal studies there.

Pope Celestine V abdicated on 13 December 1294 at Naples, where he had set up his court and lived like a monk. Accounts differ on whether Benedetto pressured Celestine to abdicate or merely showed that Church law allowed it. Benedetto was elected in his place and took the name Boniface VIII.

In 1298 Boniface ordered published the Liber Sextus, a sixth book of canon law that collected papal decisions, some 88 of them his own, with a set of legal principles known as the Regulae Juris. In 1297 he removed Cardinal Jacopo Colonna and his nephew Pietro from the College of Cardinals and excommunicated them. The Colonna declared that his election had been illegal because of Celestine's abdication, and the dispute became open warfare. By the end of 1298 his army had captured Palestrina and razed it, and a new Città Papale later replaced it.

He proclaimed 1300 a jubilee year, and the first of many held in Rome was a success, with an estimate by Giovanni Villani of some 200,000 pilgrims. In his bull Clericis laicos of February 1296 he forbade lay taxation of the clergy without papal approval, which began his conflict with Philip IV of France. In his bull Unam sanctam of 1302 he stated that every human creature must be subject to the Roman pontiff for salvation.

In September 1303 Philip IV's troops attacked the pope's residence at Anagni on 7 September and captured him. Boniface was held for three days and died about a month afterwards, on 11 October 1303. Philip later pressured Pope Clement V into staging a posthumous trial of Boniface for heresy, but no verdict was delivered.

His claims of temporal as well as spiritual power led to bitter quarrels with Albert I of Germany, Philip IV and Dante Alighieri, who wrote his treatise Monarchia to dispute Boniface's claims, and who expected him in the Divine Comedy to arrive among the simoniacs in the eighth circle of Hell. The Liber Sextus remains important to canon lawyers.
pope-callixtus-ii: Guy of Burgundy was born in Besançon, the son of Count William I of Burgundy. At the age of eight he became a member of the cathedral chapter of St. John of Besançon. His brothers Rainald, Stephen and Hugh all died on crusade. Guy first appears in contemporary records when he became archbishop of Vienne in 1088. He held strong pro-papal views on the Investiture Controversy and was appointed papal legate to France by Pope Paschal II.

In 1111 Paschal, under pressure from Emperor Henry V, issued the Privilegium, yielding much of the papal prerogative that Gregory VII had claimed. The concessions met violent opposition, above all in France, where Guy led it. After attending the Lateran Synod of 1112 he convened an assembly of French and Burgundian bishops at Vienne, which denounced lay investiture as heretical and excommunicated Henry V; Paschal confirmed its decrees on 20 October 1112.

After Gelasius II died at Cluny on 29 January 1119, Guy was elected there on 2 February by nine cardinals and crowned at Vienne on 9 February as Calixtus II. At first he seemed willing to negotiate with Henry V, but at a meeting planned near Reims Henry arrived with an army of over thirty thousand men, and Calixtus stayed at Reims, where on 30 October 1119 the emperor and his antipope were excommunicated. Returning to Italy, Calixtus gained the upper hand over the antipope Gregory VIII, who fled to Sutri and was taken prisoner with Norman help.

In 1120 he issued the bull Sicut Judaeis, forbidding Christians on pain of excommunication to force Jews to convert, harm them, take their property, disturb their festivals or interfere with their cemeteries; later popes reaffirmed it. Negotiations with Henry began at Würzburg in October 1121, and the Concordat of Worms was concluded on 23 September 1122. The emperor gave up investiture with ring and crosier and granted free election to sees, while bishops received investiture with the sceptre, with elections held in the emperor's presence in Germany.
To confirm the settlement Calixtus convened the First Lateran Council on 18 March 1123. It also passed decrees against simony, concubinage among clergy and violators of the Truce of God.

In his last years Calixtus worked to restore papal control over the Roman Campagna and rebuilt the church of Santa Maria in Cosmedin. He died on 13 December 1124. The Codex Calixtinus, a twelfth-century collection of tales, liturgy and a guide to the pilgrimage to Santiago, takes its name from a letter attributed to him.
pope-callixtus-iii: Borgia was born in 1378 at La Torreta in the Kingdom of Valencia, then part of the Crown of Aragon, the eldest child of Juan Domingo de Borja y Doncel and Francina Llançol. His sister Isabel became the mother of Pope Alexander VI. He studied grammar, logic and the arts in Valencia and in 1392 went to the University of Lleida, where he obtained a doctorate in both canon law and civil law and began his career as a professor of law. Around 1411 he attended a sermon by Vincent Ferrer, whom he later canonised on 3 June 1455.

Borgia was chosen in 1416 as delegate of the Diocese of Lerida to the Council of Constance, but King Alfonso V of Aragon opposed the council and he did not take part. From 1424 he served the Aragonese king, who wished to see him a cardinal; Pope Martin V refused. During the Great Western Schism he supported Antipope Benedict XIII and was the driving force behind Antipope Clement VIII's submission to Martin V in 1429. Martin V then made him Bishop of Valencia. He acted as a diplomat for the kings of Aragon, tutored Alfonso's illegitimate son Ferrante, and was made a cardinal by Pope Eugene IV on 2 May 1444 after reconciling the pope and Alfonso.

He was elected pope at an advanced age as a compromise candidate in the conclave of 8 April 1455. Less than two years after the fall of Constantinople in 1453, he was chiefly concerned with organising Europe against the Ottoman Empire. A building programme in Rome was cancelled and its money turned to a crusade, and nuncios and preachers were sent across Europe, though the princes were slow to respond because of national rivalries. John Hunyadi defeated the Turks at Belgrade on 22 July 1456. On 29 June 1456 the pope had ordered church bells rung at noon to call the faithful to pray for the defenders, and he fixed the Feast of the Transfiguration on 6 August to mark the victory.

Callixtus ordered a new trial for Joan of Arc, at which she was vindicated after her death. He canonised four saints and appointed nine cardinals in two consistories in 1456, among them his nephew Rodrigo de Borgia, later Pope Alexander VI. A story first found in a biography of 1475 holds that he excommunicated Halley's Comet; no known primary source supports it, and his bull of 29 June 1456 does not mention the comet. He died on 6 August 1458 and in his will left 5000 ducats to found a hospital. The Catholic historian Ludwig von Pastor judged that, except for his nepotism, he deserved high praise for his energy in defending Europe against Turkish power.
pope-clement-ii: Suidger was born in Hornburg in the Duchy of Saxony, the son of Count Konrad von Morsleben-Horneburg and his wife Amulrad von Meyendorf. In 1040 he became Bishop of Bamberg. In 1046 he accompanied King Henry III of Germany to Italy, where Henry went at the request of the laity and clergy of Rome to restore order and receive the imperial crown.

In the autumn of 1046 three rivals claimed the papacy: Benedict IX and Sylvester III, backed by rival noble factions, and Gregory VI, who had paid Benedict to resign in order to free the city from the House of Tusculum. The transaction looked like simony, and doubts about any of them could undermine Henry's coronation. The Council of Sutri deposed Benedict and Sylvester and accepted Gregory's resignation. Henry then proposed Suidger, who was elected as Clement II and became the first pope placed on the throne by the power of the German emperors.

He kept the see of Bamberg and governed both it and Rome. His election was criticised by the reform party in the curia because of the royal involvement and because he already held a diocese. His first act was to crown Henry and Agnes of Poitou, and he gave Henry the title and diadem of a Roman patrician, understood to carry the right to indicate who should be pope. His Roman synod of 1047 passed decrees against simony, and a dispute among Ravenna, Milan and Aquileia over precedence was settled for Ravenna.

Clement went with Henry through southern Italy and laid Benevento under an interdict for refusing to open its gates. He canonised Wiborada, a nun of St Gall martyred by the Hungarians in 925. He died near Pesaro on 9 October 1047, and his body was taken to Bamberg Cathedral, where it lies in the western choir; it is the only tomb of a pope north of the Alps. A toxicological examination in the mid-20th century found lead sugar in his remains, which confirmed old rumours of poisoning, though it is not clear whether he was murdered or whether the substance was used as medicine.
pope-clement-iii: Paolo Scolari was born in Rome, in the rione of the Pigna, into a family of high social standing but not noble. He was the son of Giovanni and Maria, and according to some scholars was related to the mother of Pope Innocent III. Pope Alexander III made him archpriest of the Liberian Basilica and cardinal-deacon of Sergio e Bacco, and in December 1180 cardinal bishop of Palestrina.

He was elected on 19 December 1187, two days after the death of Gregory VIII. The cardinals' first choice, Theobald of Ostia, had refused, and Scolari had been passed over two months earlier because of poor health. Only eight cardinals voted, three of them Romans, and the electors may have hoped that a Roman pope would bring the curia back to the city.

That is what happened. He ended a conflict of half a century between the popes and the citizens of Rome by an agreement allowing the citizens to elect their magistrates while the pope kept the nomination of the governor. A treaty of 31 May 1188 settled the old grievances, and the papacy returned to Rome after an exile of six years. He found a depleted College of cardinals, no more than twenty, and created thirty-one cardinals in three promotions, most of them Romans.

He sent Josias, Archbishop of Tyre, to persuade King Henry II of England and King Philip II of France to undertake the Third Crusade. He urged the Christian kings of Spain to unite against the Muslims, comparing the Reconquista to the crusades in the Holy Land, and called for a full trade embargo with the Islamic world. In March 1188 he made the Scottish church independent of the Archbishop of York, subject only to Rome.

In April 1189 Clement ended the conflict with Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa. He agreed to crown Henry VI as emperor but angered him by giving Sicily to Tancred, a son of Roger III, Duke of Apulia, and the dispute was acute when the pope died in 1191. The cardinals unanimously elected the 85-year-old Celestine III the same day, a man who belonged to neither the imperial nor the Sicilian faction.
pope-clement-iv: Gui Foucois, also called Guy le Gros, was born in Saint-Gilles-du-Gard in the County of Toulouse, the son of a lawyer, Pierre Foucois. At nineteen he enlisted as a soldier to fight the Moors in Spain, then studied law in Toulouse, Bourges and Orleans and became a noted advocate in Paris, where he acted as secretary to King Louis IX. He married and had two daughters, and after his wife's death entered the Church.

His rise was rapid. He became pastor of Saint-Gilles in 1255, Bishop of Le Puy in 1257 and Archbishop of Narbonne in 1259. In December 1261 he became the first cardinal created by Pope Urban IV, for the see of Sabina, and from 1262 to 1264 he was papal legate in England.

His election followed a four-month conclave at Perugia, during which the cardinals argued over whether to call in Charles I of Anjou, the youngest brother of Louis IX, to carry on the papal war against the Hohenstaufen. Clement was in France when elected and had to enter Italy in disguise. He settled at Viterbo, since the Ghibelline party controlled Rome. Charles recognised him as feudal overlord, and with papal money and supplies marched on Naples, defeating and killing Manfred at the Battle of Benevento. At the Battle of Tagliacozzo Conradin, the last of the Hohenstaufen, was taken prisoner and later beheaded at Naples. Clement is said to have disapproved of Charles's cruelties, though Gregorovius's charge that he was an accomplice is contested.

In 1264 he renewed the prohibition of the Talmud, ordering that the Jews of the Crown of Aragon submit their books to Dominican censors, without condemning those who kept copies to death. In February 1265 he summoned Thomas Aquinas to Rome as papal theologian. In 1267 and 1268 he corresponded with the Mongol Ilkhanate ruler Abaqa, who proposed a Franco-Mongol alliance, and answered non-committally.

Clement died on 29 November 1268 and was buried at the Dominican convent of Santa Maria in Gradi outside Viterbo; in 1885 his remains were moved to the church of San Francesco alla Rocca there. Divisions among the cardinals left the papal throne vacant for nearly three years. Contemporaries praised his asceticism and his refusal to enrich his relatives. He ordered the Franciscan scholar Roger Bacon to write the Opus Majus, which is addressed to him and includes treatises on optics and the scientific method.
pope-clement-vi: Pierre Roger was born in the château of Maumont in Limousin, the son of the lord of Maumont-Rosiers-d'Égletons. He entered the Benedictine order as a boy in 1301, at the Abbey of La Chaise-Dieu, and in 1307 went to Paris to study theology and canon law. In 1323 Pope John XXII ordered the Chancellor of Paris to confer on him the doctorate in theology. He lectured on Peter Lombard's Sententiae, promoted the works of Thomas Aquinas, and in 1325 wrote a treatise condemning the Defensor Pacis of Marsilius of Padua.

Church office followed quickly. He became Abbot of Fécamp in 1326, Bishop of Arras in 1328, Archbishop of Sens in 1329 and Archbishop of Rouen in 1330, serving King Philip VI of France as a councillor. Pope Benedict XII made him a cardinal priest on 18 December 1338.

The cardinals, fourteen of the nineteen of them French, elected him on 7 May 1342, and he was crowned on 19 May. He chose to stay in Avignon, refusing invitations to return to Rome from its people and from the poet Petrarch. To placate the Romans he issued the bull Unigenitus in 1343, reducing the interval between one Great Jubilee and the next from a hundred years to fifty. He enlarged the papal palace, kept composers of the Ars Nova style at court, and filled the College of Cardinals with Frenchmen, among them several nephews.

During the Black Death he stayed in Avignon, supervised the care of the sick and the burial of the dead, and granted remission of sins to all who died of the plague. In two bulls of 1348 he condemned the violence against Jews and rejected the claim that they caused the plague, noting that it afflicted Jews too.

He excommunicated the emperor Louis IV on 13 April 1346 and directed the election of Charles IV. He also removed Cola di Rienzo from Rome by a legate in December 1347 and made Prague an archbishopric in 1344.

Clement had suffered from kidney stones for years, and a tumour caused an abscess and fever in his last week. He died on 6 December 1352. His body was taken in procession to the abbey of La Chaise-Dieu, where a tomb begun in 1346 and completed in 1351 stands in the choir. Huguenots attacked it in 1562 and destroyed its forty-four statues of his relatives.

He left the reputation of a fine gentleman, a prince munificent to profusion and a patron of the arts and learning, but no saint. He is said to have remarked that he had lived as a sinner among sinners.
pope-clement-vii: Giulio de' Medici was born illegitimately in Florence on 26 May 1478, one month after his father, Giuliano de' Medici, brother of Lorenzo de' Medici, was murdered in Florence Cathedral in the Pazzi conspiracy. He spent his first seven years with his godfather, the architect Antonio da Sangallo the Elder, and was then raised by Lorenzo alongside the future Pope Leo X. When Leo was elected in March 1513, Giulio became Archbishop of Florence within three months, and a papal dispensation recognised his birth as legitimate. Leo made him a cardinal on 23 September 1513. He governed Florence from 1519 to 1523.

After Adrian VI's death Giulio was elected on 19 November 1523 as Clement VII, with a reputation as a statesman, though contemporaries thought him worldly and indifferent to the Reformation. Charles V and Francis I each demanded that he take a side. After Francis conquered Milan in 1524 Clement joined France and Venice in a treaty of January 1525, but Francis was crushed and imprisoned at Pavia and Clement turned back to Charles.

His wavering led to the Sack of Rome in 1527, during which he was imprisoned. In 1527 Henry VIII asked him to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, the emperor's aunt; Clement refused, possibly under pressure from Charles, whose effective prisoner he was. In 1533 he married his cousin's granddaughter, Catherine de' Medici, to the future Henry II of France at Marseille.

Clement was a patron in the Medici tradition. He commissioned or supervised Michelangelo's Last Judgment in the Sistine Chapel, the Medici Chapel and the Laurentian Library, and Raphael's Villa Madama, and he appointed Benvenuto Cellini head of the Papal Mint. In 1533 he approved Copernicus's heliocentric theory.

He died on 25 September 1534 after months of illness, having reigned ten years, and was buried in St Peter's. Contemporaries blamed poison, but his symptoms do not support that. He has been called the most unfortunate of the popes. The historian Paul Strathern writes that without his guidance the Medici could not have reached the heights they later did.
pope-clement-viii: Ippolito Aldobrandini was born in Fano in the Papal States on 24 February 1536, the son of Silvestro Aldobrandini and Lesa Deti, from a Florentine family. Like his father he became a canon lawyer and an Auditor of the Roman Rota, the highest ecclesiastical court of the Holy See. He was ordained a priest only on 31 December 1580, at forty-five. Sixtus V made him Cardinal-Priest of S. Pancrazio in 1585 and in 1588 sent him as legate to Poland, where he won the gratitude of the Habsburgs by securing the release of Archduke Maximilian. His confessor for thirty years was Saint Philip Neri.

Elected on 30 January 1592 after a stormy conclave in which a minority of Italian cardinals refused to be dictated to by Philip II of Spain, he took the name Clement VIII and aimed to free the papacy from dependence on Spain. In November 1592 he published the Clementine Vulgate, which remained the official Bible of the Catholic Church until the Nova Vulgata replaced it in 1979.

Henry IV of France embraced Catholicism on 25 July 1593, and in the autumn of 1595 Clement solemnly absolved him despite Spanish displeasure, ending the thirty years of religious war in France. When Alfonso II d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, died childless on 27 October 1597, Clement resolved to attach Ferrara to the Papal States; Henry IV's threats deterred Spain and the emperor from helping Cesare d'Este, and a papal army entered Ferrara almost unopposed. In 1594 he began an alliance of Christian powers for the Long War against the Ottoman Empire.

Clement was severe in matters of order and belief. He had several noble troublemakers put to death, including Beatrice Cenci, who had murdered her father, probably after his repeated abuses, and he rejected many pleas for clemency. In 1599 the miller Menocchio was burned after trial by the Inquisition, and in 1600 Giordano Bruno was burned at the stake, Clement taking part in the final phase of the trial. The bull Caeca et Obdurata of 1593 banned Jews from living in the Papal States outside Rome, Ancona and Avignon.

The jubilee of 1600 brought three million pilgrims. Crippled by gout in his last years, Clement died on 3 March 1605 and was buried in St Peter's; his remains were moved in 1646 to Santa Maria Maggiore. He left a reputation for prudence, munificence, ruthlessness and capacity for business.
pope-clement-xiii: Carlo della Torre di Rezzonico was born on 7 March 1693 into a recently ennobled patrician family of Venice. His father bought and finished the palace on the Grand Canal now called Ca' Rezzonico. He received a Jesuit education in Bologna, took a doctorate in canon and civil law at the University of Padua, and attended the Pontifical Academy of Ecclesiastical Nobles in Rome. He became Governor of Fano in 1721, was ordained priest on 23 December 1731, and was made a cardinal by Pope Clement XII in 1737. As Bishop of Padua from 1743 he visited his diocese often and reformed its running.

After Pope Benedict XIV died in 1758, negotiations between rival factions led to Rezzonico's election on 6 July 1758 with 31 votes of 44. He was crowned on 16 July. Modest in character and generous with his private fortune, he permitted vernacular translations of the Bible in Catholic countries and placed the Encyclopédie of D'Alembert and Diderot on the Index. He favoured dialogue with Protestants without compromise on doctrine, and recognised the Hanoverians as kings of Great Britain, refusing to recognise Charles Edward Stuart as Charles III after the death of James Francis Edward Stuart in 1766.

His pontificate was dominated by pressure to suppress the Society of Jesus. In 1758 the Marquis of Pombal expelled the Jesuits from Portugal. The Parlement of Paris suppressed them in France by the arrêt of 2 August 1762, which Clement annulled, and Louis XV expelled them in November 1764. The bull Apostolicum pascendi of 7 January 1765 praised the order but was largely ignored. On the night of 2–3 April 1767 Charles III of Spain had every Jesuit house in Spain surrounded and the Jesuits shipped to Civitavecchia.

In 1768 Clement issued a monitorium against the government of Philip, Duke of Parma, and the question of Parma's investiture, technically a papal fief, worsened the dispute. The Bourbon kings seized Avignon, Benevento and Pontecorvo and in January 1769 demanded the total suppression of the Jesuits. Clement agreed to call a consistory, but died on the eve of its meeting. Poison was suspected, but there appears to be no conclusive evidence.

He collapsed on the night of 2 February 1769 after a day of audiences and died quickly; an aneurysm near the heart is generally believed to have been the cause. He was buried in the Vatican on 8 February, and in 1774 his remains were moved to a monument sculpted by Antonio Canova.
pope-cornelius: Emperor Decius, who ruled from 249 to 251, persecuted Christians rather sporadically and locally, but in January 250 he ordered all citizens to perform a religious sacrifice before commissioners or face death. Many Christians refused and were martyred, including Pope Fabian on 20 January 250, while others took part in the sacrifices to save their lives. During the persecution it proved impossible to elect a successor, and the papal seat stayed vacant for a year, with the church governed by several priests, including Novatian. When Decius left Rome to fight the Goths, the Roman clergy chose a new bishop. The more moderate Cornelius was unwillingly elected over Novatian and others in March 251.

Cornelius held, with Cyprian of Carthage, that Christians who had lapsed could be restored to communion through repentance shown in a period of penance. Novatian held that idolatry was unpardonable and that the Church had no authority to forgive apostates. Supporters of the stricter position had Novatian consecrated bishop and refused to recognise Cornelius. Both sides wrote to other bishops. Cornelius had the support of Cyprian, Dionysius and most African and Eastern bishops, while Novatian had a minority of the Roman clergy and laity. Cornelius convened a synod of 60 bishops that confirmed him as the rightful pope and excommunicated Novatian and his followers.

His letters give a picture of the Roman church. It had forty-six priests, seven deacons, seven sub-deacons, forty-two acolytes, fifty-two ostiarii and over 1,500 widows and persons in distress, and it fed over 1,500 people daily. From these numbers it has been estimated that there were at least 50,000 Christians in Rome in his time.

Decius was killed in battle with the Goths in June 251, and persecution resumed under his successor, Trebonianus Gallus. Cornelius was exiled to Centumcellae, where he died in June 253. The Liberian catalogue ascribes his death to the hardships of banishment, while later sources say he was beheaded. He was buried in a catacomb behind a Latin inscription reading Cornelius Martyr. One of his letters mentions the office of exorcist in the church for the first time.

His head was claimed by Kornelimünster Abbey near Aachen, and in the Rhineland he was venerated as one of the Four Holy Marshals in the late Middle Ages. His feast day is 16 September, shared with Cyprian; it was originally 14 September, the date on which, according to Jerome, both were martyred.
pope-eugene-iv: Gabriele Condulmer was born in Venice to a rich merchant family; his father was Angelo Condulmer and his mother Bariola Correr. His sister Polissena was the mother of the future Pope Paul II, and he was a nephew of Pope Gregory XII. On 30 December 1407, at twenty-four, he was made Bishop of Siena by his uncle, with a dispensation for his age. Siena's political leaders objected to a young foreigner and he resigned in 1408, the year Gregory made him a cardinal. He served as papal legate in the March of Ancona and at Bologna, and was elected pope unanimously on 3 March 1431.

His first quarrel was with the Colonna, relatives of his predecessor Martin V. The main struggle of his pontificate was with the Council of Basel, opened on 23 July 1431. On 18 December 1431 he dissolved it, but it refused to disband and renewed the Council of Constance's resolutions that a council stands above the pope. Under a compromise arranged by the emperor Sigismund he recognised the council in 1433.

Troops from Milan invaded the Papal States and a republic controlled by the Colonna was set up in Rome. On 4 June 1434 Eugene escaped down the Tiber disguised as a monk, pelted with stones, and reached Florence in October. In 1438 he convened a rival council at Ferrara; Basel deposed him on 25 June 1439 and elected Duke Amadeus VIII of Savoy as the antipope Felix V. On 6 July 1439 the bull Laetentur caeli proclaimed a union with the Eastern Orthodox Church, which proved temporary. Eugene entered Rome on 28 September 1443 after nearly ten years away.

In the bull Creator Omnium of 17 December 1434 he rescinded Portugal's right to conquer the Canary Islands, and he excommunicated anyone who enslaved newly converted Christians there, though he later tempered this at the king of Portugal's request. He first protected Jews, then in 1442 issued Dudum ad nostram, which restricted Jewish life but was not enforced in his lifetime.

Eugene died in Rome on 23 February 1447. His victory over Basel contributed to the collapse of the conciliar movement, though it was won by concessions to princes, so the papacy relied more on the Papal States for revenue. He re-established the University of Rome in 1431 and consecrated Florence Cathedral on 25 March 1436.
pope-francis: Jorge Mario Bergoglio was born on 17 December 1936 in Flores, a neighbourhood of Buenos Aires, the eldest of five children. His father, Mario José Bergoglio, was an accountant and an Italian immigrant from Piedmont; his mother, Regina María Sívori, was a housewife born in Buenos Aires to a family of northern Italian origin. The family left Italy in 1929 to escape the fascist rule of Benito Mussolini. At 21, after life-threatening pneumonia and three cysts, he had part of a lung removed.

Bergoglio entered the Society of Jesus as a novice on 11 March 1958, after three years at the archdiocesan seminary in Villa Devoto, and studied the humanities in Santiago, Chile. He took perpetual vows on 12 March 1960 and taught literature and psychology in Santa Fe and Buenos Aires. He was ordained in 1969 and was Jesuit provincial superior in Argentina from 1973 to 1979. In 1976 the Argentine Navy kidnapped two Jesuit priests, Orlando Yorio and Franz Jalics, during the Dirty War. Bergoglio is widely reported to have failed to protect them; a criminal complaint filed in 2005 was dismissed, but the debate over his conduct has continued.

He became archbishop of Buenos Aires on the death of his predecessor, Quarracino, on 28 February 1998, and was created a cardinal in 2001 by Pope John Paul II. He doubled the number of priests working in the city's shantytowns, which earned him the name villero bishop, and put the archdiocese's finances on a stricter footing. After the resignation of Pope Benedict XVI, the conclave elected him pope on 13 March 2013. He took the name Francis in honour of Francis of Assisi, and was the first Jesuit pope, the first from Latin America and the first from the Southern Hemisphere.

As pope Francis called for decentralised, synodal governance, made women full members of dicasteries of the Roman Curia and convened the Synod on Synodality. He was a behind-the-scenes broker, with the Government of Canada, of the restoration of diplomatic relations between the United States and Cuba announced on 17 December 2014.

His last public appearance was on Easter Sunday, 20 April 2025. He died on Easter Monday, 21 April 2025, aged 88, of a cerebral stroke. His funeral took place on 26 April, and on 8 May the conclave elected Robert Francis Prevost as Pope Leo XIV. Francis had appointed more than 80 per cent of the cardinals who elected his successor, and he formalised the Church's opposition to the death penalty in all cases.
pope-gregory-i: Gregory was born around 540 in Rome, recently reconquered by the Eastern Roman Empire from the Ostrogoths, into a wealthy noble family with close ties to the church. His father, Gordianus, was a patrician and senator who served for a time as Prefect of the City of Rome, and his great-great-grandfather had been Pope Felix III. Gregory was himself prefect of Rome at 30. On his father's death he turned the family villa into a monastery dedicated to Andrew the Apostle, later rededicated as San Gregorio Magno al Celio.

In 579 Pope Pelagius II chose Gregory as apocrisiarius, his ambassador to the imperial court in Constantinople, and he held the post until 586. The Roman delegation had gone to ask the emperor for military aid against the Lombards. Emperor Maurice had long decided to limit his efforts against them to intrigue and diplomacy, and the empire was occupied with the Persians in the East and the Avars and Slavs to the north. There is no evidence that Gregory's tenure accomplished much for the objectives of Pelagius.

He returned to his monastery in 585 and was elected by acclamation in 590, when Pelagius II died of the plague then spreading through Rome. Gregory wrote letters disavowing any ambition for the papacy, and one to Maurice asking him not to confirm his election, though the prefect of Rome intercepted it. He built a system of charitable relief for the poor of Rome, most of them refugees from Lombard incursions, holding that the wealth belonged to the poor and the church was only its steward. He sent missionaries to England, among them Augustine of Canterbury and Paulinus of York, and died on 12 March 604.

Gregory is the only pope between the fifth and the eleventh centuries whose correspondence and writings survive in enough quantity to form a comprehensive body. His Moralia in Job is one of the longest patristic works, based on talks on the Book of Job. His Pastoral Care became the definitive statement of the nature of the episcopal office. The Dialogues are four books on the miracles of holy men of sixth-century Italy, with the second devoted to a life of Saint Benedict.

John the Deacon wrote that Gregory revised the liturgy of the Mass, removing many things, changing a few and adding some. In his own letters Gregory says he moved the Pater Noster to just after the Roman Canon, where it still stands in the Roman Liturgy, and he established the nine Kyries at the beginning of Mass. He is honoured with Augustine, Jerome and Ambrose as one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers.
pope-gregory-ii: Gregory was born into a noble Roman family in 669, the son of Marcellus and Honesta. As a young man he was placed in the papal court and made a subdeacon under Pope Sergius I, later a deacon in charge of the library of the Roman Church and then a papal secretary. In 711 he accompanied Pope Constantine to Constantinople to deal with Rome's rejection of the canons of the Quinisext Council. Gregory handled the negotiations, and Emperor Justinian II agreed that the papacy could disregard whichever of the council's decisions it wished. He was consecrated on 19 May 715.

Gregory began by repairing Rome's Aurelian Walls, a task interrupted in October 716 when the Tiber flooded the city for eight days. He took a close interest in missions. In 716 Duke Theodo of Bavaria visited him, and Gregory sent delegates to help establish a church hierarchy there. In 718 the Anglo-Saxon missionary Winfrid approached him; he took the name Boniface and was commissioned in May 719 to preach in Germany. Gregory made him a bishop in November 722. He also restored Monte Cassino in 718.

He tried to keep on good terms with the Lombard king Liutprand. Around 721 he appealed to Charles Martel to drive the Lombards out, but Charles did not respond. Gregory and Liutprand later met at Sutri and reached the agreement known as the Donation of Sutri, by which Sutri and some hill towns in Latium were given to the papacy, the first extension of papal territory beyond the Duchy of Rome.

From about 722 Gregory was at odds with Emperor Leo III, who tried to raise taxes on the papal patrimonies in Italy to pay for an ongoing war. Gregory refused, and the people of Rome drove out the imperial governor. When Leo issued an iconoclast edict in 726, Gregory rejected it, and the Exarchate of Ravenna rose in revolt; Gregory dissuaded the armies from marching on Constantinople. Greek sources say he excommunicated Leo, but no western source confirms it.
Gregory died on 11 February 731 and was buried in St Peter's Basilica. His defiance of Leo prepared the way for the temporal power of the popes, and he is commemorated as a saint.
pope-gregory-ix: Ugolino dei Conti was born in Anagni, near Rome. Sources give his birth between about 1145 and 1170, and he is said to have been in his nineties, if not nearly a hundred, at his death. He studied at the Universities of Paris and Bologna. His cousin Innocent III made him Cardinal-Deacon of Sant'Eustachio in December 1198, and in 1206 he became Cardinal Bishop of Ostia and Velletri. He was Dean of the Sacred College of Cardinals by 1218 or 1219. At the request of Francis of Assisi, Pope Honorius III appointed him Cardinal Protector of the Franciscans in 1220.

Elected pope in 1227, he took the name Gregory because he assumed the office at the monastery of Saint Gregory ad Septem Solia. He continued the policy of papal supremacy of Gregory VII and Innocent III. In 1231 his bull Parens scientiarum, issued after the University of Paris strike of 1229, settled differences between the scholars and the local authorities by extending papal patronage; it has been called the university's magna carta. He also proclaimed a crusade against the Stedinger in October 1232 and endorsed the Northern Crusades.

Gregory began his pontificate by suspending Emperor Frederick II for delay in carrying out the promised Sixth Crusade, and excommunication followed. Frederick took Jerusalem, but Gregory distrusted him, and the war of 1228 to 1230 is known as the War of the Keys. After a truce, Frederick's defeat of the Lombard League in 1239 raised the prospect that he would dominate all Italy, and Gregory excommunicated him again and denounced him as a heretic. The struggle ended only with Gregory's death on 22 August 1241; his successor Innocent IV declared a crusade against the Hohenstaufen in 1245.

Gregory had Nova Compilatio decretalium, the Decretals, prepared and promulgated in 1234, completing the systematising of papal pronouncements begun with Gratian's Decretum of 1140. It gave papal legal theory its foundation. It also gave the doctrine of the perpetual servitude of the Jews the force of canon law. In 1239 he ordered all copies of the Talmud confiscated, after the intervention of the convert Nicholas Donin.

He appointed papal inquisitors, mostly Dominicans and Franciscans, from 1231. Thomas Madden holds that the aim was to bring due process to the haphazard episcopal inquisitions; Walter Ullmann judged the procedure a systematic perversion of justice. Gregory supported the mendicant orders, befriended Dominic and Clare of Assisi, and canonised Elisabeth of Hungary, Dominic, Anthony of Padua and Francis of Assisi.
pope-gregory-vii: Hildebrand was born in Sovana, in what is now southern Tuscany, the son of a blacksmith. He studied in Rome at the monastery of St Mary on the Aventine, where one of his masters was the future Pope Gregory VI. When Gregory VI was deposed at the Council of Sutri in December 1046, Hildebrand followed him to Cologne. He later accompanied Abbot Bruno of Toul to Rome, where Bruno was elected pope as Leo IX and made him a deacon and papal administrator.

Hildebrand later served as legate and became archdeacon of the Roman church between 1058 and 1059. He was a main force behind the election of Pope Alexander II in 1061 and behind the law giving the cardinals exclusive rights to elect a pope. On 21 April 1073, during Alexander's funeral, the clergy and people cried out for Hildebrand to be pope. He fled and hid, but he was elected and took the name Gregory.

In 1074 Gregory summoned a council at the Lateran that condemned simony and confirmed clerical celibacy, and in 1075 he decreed that only the pope could appoint or depose bishops. This led to the Investiture Controversy with Henry IV. In 1076 a synod at Worms declared Gregory deposed, and on 22 February 1076 he excommunicated Henry and absolved his subjects of their oaths. German princes then turned against the king, who travelled to Canossa and knelt barefoot in the snow to beg forgiveness.

The absolution settled nothing about investiture. In March 1077 the German nobles elected Rudolf of Swabia as rival king, and in 1080 Gregory again excommunicated Henry, who had thirty bishops declare Gregory deposed and elect Archbishop Guibert of Ravenna. Henry entered Rome in March 1084, and Guibert, enthroned as Clement III, crowned him emperor. Gregory's ally Robert Guiscard then marched on the city, and his Normans' excesses so angered the Romans that Gregory withdrew from Rome.

Gregory withdrew to Monte Cassino and then to Salerno, where he died on 25 May 1085, probably as a prisoner of the Normans. Three days earlier he had withdrawn all his excommunications except those against Henry and Guibert. He is venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church.

His claims reached beyond Germany. He asserted that Corsica and Sardinia belonged to the Roman Church, and he claimed Spain, Hungary and Croatia as its property. He planned an expedition to help eastern Christians, which foreshadowed the First Crusade. Opponents such as Beno of Santi Martino e Silvestro accused him of necromancy and tyranny.
pope-gregory-x: Teobaldo Visconti was born around 1210 in Piacenza. He began his career in the household of the Cistercian Cardinal Giacomo di Pecorari, Bishop of Palestrina, whom he served as majordomo and accompanied on legations, and he became a canon of Piacenza and of the Cathedral of Lyons. After the cardinal's death in 1244 he settled in Lyons and helped organise the council that met there in 1245, where he met Bonaventure and Thomas Aquinas.

In 1246 he was appointed Archdeacon in the diocese of Liège and was told to preach a crusade. His time there was unhappy, and he left Liège, spending years in Paris, where he became a friend of King Louis IX. Pope Clement IV later sent him to England, where he befriended Prince Edward, the future Edward I, and went with him on crusade.

The cardinals, divided between French and Italian parties at Viterbo, chose him on 1 September 1271 after he was proposed by a committee of six. He was at Acre on the Ninth Crusade when the news came. Not yet a priest, he was ordained on 19 March 1272 and crowned on 27 March at St Peter's Basilica. At his last sermon in Acre he quoted Psalm 137: if I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning.

The Second Council of Lyon met on 1 May 1274 to consider the schism between East and West, the condition of the Holy Land and abuses in the Church. To finance a crusade he imposed on all clerics a tax of 10 per cent of income for six years. In the constitution Ubi periculum, ratified on 16 July 1274, he laid down the rules of the conclave: the cardinals shut in together, two thirds of votes needed, and one dish a day if no pope was chosen after three days. The rules were briefly annulled by Adrian V and John XXI but stood until the 20th century.

On 7 October 1272 he issued the bull Vineam Sorec, which condemned violence against Jews and forced baptism and rejected the blood libel. He also received Kublai Khan's letter carried by the Polos and an embassy of the Mongol Ilkhanate leader Abaqa, but plans for a crusade ended with his death.
Ill with a hernia, he died at Arezzo on 10 January 1276 on his way back to Rome and is buried in its cathedral. Pope Clement XI beatified him in 1713.
pope-gregory-xi: Pierre Roger de Beaufort was born at Maumont in France. His uncle, Pierre Cardinal Roger, Archbishop of Rouen, was elected pope in 1342 as Clement VI. Clement gave his nephew a number of benefices and in 1348 made the eighteen-year-old a cardinal deacon. He studied at the University of Perugia, where he became a skilled canonist and theologian.

After the death of Pope Urban V in December 1370, eighteen cardinals entered the conclave at Avignon on 29 December. Cardinal Roger was unanimously elected the next day. He first opposed his own election but accepted and took the name Gregory XI. He was ordained priest on 4 January 1371, consecrated and crowned the following day in the cathedral of Notre Dame des Doms.

Gregory tried at once to reconcile the kings of France and England and failed. On 20 August 1372 he confirmed a treaty between Sicily and Naples at Villeneuve-lès-Avignon that settled the dispute between those two papal fiefs. He also tried to reform corrupt practices in the monastic orders, such as fees charged to visitors at holy sites and the display of false relics, and in 1376, at the urging of Catherine of Siena, he tried to organise a crusade.

Like earlier Avignon popes he appointed Frenchmen as legates and governors in Italy, whom the Italians hated. Bernabò Visconti of Milan seized Reggio and other papal fiefs in 1371, and Gregory excommunicated him. A Florentine-led coalition of Italian cities then fought the papacy in the War of the Eight Saints (1375–1378); on 31 March 1376 Gregory excommunicated Florence and placed it under interdict. Catherine of Siena pleaded for peace on Florence's behalf, but the war ended only after his death, with a peace concluded at Tivoli in July 1378.

Catherine also wrote him 14 letters between 1375 and 1378 urging reform, peace and a return to Rome. Despite the protests of the French king and most of the cardinals, Gregory left Avignon on 13 September 1376, sailed from Marseille on 2 October, reached Corneto on 6 December and entered Rome on 17 January 1377, ending about 68 years of papal rule from France.

Gregory XI died on 27 March 1378, aged 48 or 49, and was succeeded by the Italian Urban VI. Most of Europe then supported Clement VII, now considered an antipope, and the Western Schism that followed forced Europe into a dilemma of allegiance. It was not fully resolved until the Council of Constance (1414–1418) and the election of Pope Martin V.
pope-gregory-xiii: Ugo Boncompagni was born in Bologna, where he studied law and graduated in 1530. He taught jurisprudence for some years, and his students included the future cardinals Alexander Farnese, Reginald Pole and Charles Borromeo. At 36 he was summoned to Rome by Pope Paul III, under whom he held several appointments. Pope Pius IV made him Cardinal-Priest of San Sisto Vecchio and sent him to the Council of Trent.

He also served as a legate to Philip II of Spain, forming a close relationship with the king. After the death of Pope Pius V, the conclave of less than 24 hours chose him on 13 May 1572. He took the name Gregory XIII in homage to Gregory the Great, and many historians attribute the speed of the election to Spanish backing.

As pope he set out to reform the Church by carrying out the recommendations of the Council of Trent. He required cardinals to reside in their sees, appointed a committee to update the Index of Forbidden Books and sponsored a new edition of the Corpus juris canonici. The power of the papacy grew under him while that of the cardinals declined. He recognised the Discalced Carmelites as a distinct province in 1580 and gave official status to the Congregation of the Oratory in 1575. He was a generous patron of the Jesuit colleges in Rome and founded seminaries, beginning with the German College.

In foreign policy he was more concerned with the Protestants than with the Turks. He backed Philip II's plans against Elizabeth I of England, and in 1579 a papal expedition of about 50 soldiers landed in Ireland and took part in the Second Desmond Rebellion, ending in the Smerwick Massacre. After the St Bartholomew's Day Massacres of Huguenots in 1572 he held a Te Deum. He received the Tenshō embassy from Japan, the first pope to do so.

Gregory is best known for the Gregorian calendar, devised by the physician and astronomer Aloysius Lilius and finally modified by the Jesuit Christopher Clavius. The Julian year of 365 days and 6 hours was slightly too long, and over 13 centuries the vernal equinox had slipped to 10 March. By the bull Inter gravissimas of 24 February 1582, the day after Thursday 4 October 1582 became 15 October. Catholic states followed at once or within a year or two, but Protestant Europe took more than a century; Great Britain and its colonies adopted it in 1752.

He died on 10 April 1585. To raise funds he had confiscated properties across the Papal States, which enriched his treasury for a time but alienated much of the nobility and caused economic and social disorder.
pope-honorius-iii: Cencio Savelli was born in Rome, a son of Aimerico of the Savelli family. He was a canon at Santa Maria Maggiore and became Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church on 5 December 1189 and Cardinal Deacon of Santa Lucia in Silice on 20 February 1193. Under Pope Clement III and Pope Celestine III he was treasurer of the Roman Church and compiled the Liber Censuum, and from 1194 to 1198 he acted as Vice-Chancellor. In 1197 he became tutor to the young Frederick, the Sicilian king and future emperor, who had been made a ward of Pope Innocent III. Innocent made him a cardinal priest in 1200.

Innocent III died on 16 July 1216, and seventeen cardinals met two days later. Troubled affairs in Italy and fear of a schism led them to elect by compromise, empowering Ugolino of Ostia and Guido Papareschi to choose. They named Cencio Savelli, who accepted reluctantly and took the name Honorius III. He was crowned at Rome on 31 August 1216.

He worked to carry out the Fifth Crusade, endorsed by the Lateran Council of 1215, taxing the pope's and cardinals' incomes by a tenth for three years and other clergy by a twentieth. In April 1217 he crowned Peter II of Courtenay Latin Emperor of Constantinople, but Peter was captured by Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus and died in confinement. Frederick II repeatedly delayed his vow to go; the Egyptian campaign failed with the loss of Damietta on 8 September 1221, after quarrels between the crusaders and the papal legate Pelagius.

Honorius arranged Frederick's marriage to Isabella II of Jerusalem, but Frederick had still not sailed when the pope died. He also continued Innocent III's campaign against the Cathar heresy, drawing the royal house of France into it.

He approved the Dominican Order in 1216, the Franciscan Order in 1223 and the Carmelite rule in 1226, and in 1219 invited Saint Dominic to Santa Sabina. In 1217 he gave the title of King of Serbia to Stefan the First-Crowned. He insisted on a well-educated clergy and favoured the universities of Paris and Bologna.

Honorius III died in Rome on 18 March 1227, and the crusade he had planned was left to his successor Gregory IX. His writings include the Liber censuum Romanae ecclesiae, a record of the Apostolic See's revenues, donations and agreements, lives of Celestine III and Gregory VII, an Ordo Romanus and thirty-four sermons. The Grimoire of Pope Honorius, attributed to him, was probably forged some four hundred years after his death.
pope-innocent-ii: Gregorio Papareschi came from a Roman family, probably of the rione Trastevere. A former Cluniac monk, he was made cardinal deacon of Sant'Angelo in 1116 by Pope Paschal II. Pope Callixtus II used him on difficult missions, among them to Worms for the Concordat of Worms, the peace made with Emperor Henry V in 1122, and to make peace with King Louis VI of France in 1123. In 1124 he became a close adviser to Pope Honorius II.

Honorius II died on the evening of 13 February 1130 and a commission of six cardinals led by the chancellor Haimeric hastily elected Gregorio, who was consecrated the next day. The other cardinals declared the election uncanonical and chose Anacletus II, a Roman whose family were enemies of Haimeric's supporters, the Frangipani. Anacletus took control of Rome, and Innocent fled by sea to Pisa and then to France, where Bernard of Clairvaux secured his recognition. In October 1130 King Lothair III of Germany acknowledged him at Würzburg, and in January 1131 he met Henry I of England at Chartres.

Lothair's expedition to Italy in 1132 had Anacletus set aside as a goal, but achieved little more than Lothair's coronation by Innocent in the Lateran Basilica on 4 June 1133, since Anacletus held St Peter's. The council of Pisa of May 1135 excommunicated Anacletus and his supporters, and the schism ended only with Anacletus's death on 25 January 1138.

At the Second Lateran Council of April 1139 Roger II of Sicily, Innocent's most uncompromising foe, was excommunicated, and a canon banned crossbows, slings and bows against Christians. On 22 July 1139 Roger's son Roger III of Apulia ambushed the papal troops at Galluccio and captured the pope, who on 25 July acknowledged Roger's kingship in the Treaty of Mignano. In March 1139 he declared that the Knights Templar should answer only to the papacy.

In his last years Innocent rebuilt the church of Santa Maria in Trastevere, which has Ionic capitals taken from the Baths of Caracalla. A quarrel with Louis VII of France over the archbishop of Bourges, which brought an interdict on the kingdom, and a struggle with the town of Tivoli turned Roman factions against him. As he lay dying in 1143 the Commune of Rome began the deliberations that reinstated the Roman Senate the following year. He died on 24 September 1143 and was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus said by tradition to have been the emperor Hadrian's.
pope-innocent-iii: Lotario de' Conti was born at Gavignano, near Anagni, to Trasimondo de' Conti di Segni, of the Conti family that eventually produced nine cardinals and four popes. He studied theology in Paris and possibly law in Bologna, and became a Cardinal-Priest in 1191. As a cardinal he wrote De Miseria Condicionis Humane, On the Misery of the Human Condition, which survives in more than 700 manuscripts. On 8 January 1198, the day Celestine III died, he was elected pope after only two ballots, at the age of thirty-seven, and took the name Innocent III.

Innocent began with a wide sense of his authority and claimed supremacy over Europe's kings, though he respected their temporal authority. He excommunicated Alfonso IX of León for marrying a near relative, and received Aragon in vassalage from Peter II, whom he crowned in Rome in 1204. In the contest for the Holy Roman Empire after the death of Emperor Henry VI, he declared for Otto IV in 1201, and later backed Henry's son Frederick, whose guardian he had become. Otto's defeat at the Battle of Bouvines on 27 July 1214 settled the matter. At King John's request he declared Magna Carta annulled, which led to a rebellion by the English barons.

He greatly extended the crusades. He proclaimed the Fourth Crusade in 1198 and imposed on the clergy a tax of one-fortieth of their income, the first time a pope taxed the clergy directly. When the crusaders could not pay the Venetians, they diverted first to Zadar and then to Constantinople, against his orders, and he excommunicated them. He also sanctioned the military order of the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1204 and called the Albigensian Crusade after the murder of his legate Peter of Castelnau in 1208. That crusade led to about 200,000 deaths and brought the region under the French crown. In 1209 he reluctantly admitted Francis of Assisi and his followers.

On 15 November 1215 he convened the Fourth Lateran Council, regarded as the most important Church council of the Middle Ages, which issued seventy reforming decrees. Among them, canon 18 forbade clergymen to take part in judicial ordeals, and other canons required Jews and Muslims to wear distinguishing dress. The council set the Fifth Crusade for 1217. In 1216 Innocent moved to northern Italy to reconcile Pisa and Genoa, and he died suddenly at Perugia on 16 July 1216. His body lay in the cathedral there until Pope Leo XIII moved it to the Lateran in December 1891. He considerably refined Western canon law through his decretals and the Lateran Council.
pope-innocent-iv: Sinibaldo Fieschi was born in Genoa, the son of Beatrice Grillo and Ugo Fieschi, Count of Lavagna, of a noble merchant family of Liguria. He studied at the universities of Parma and Bologna and was a canon of the Cathedral of Parma from 1216 to 1227. Regarded as one of the best canonists of his time, he wrote a commentary on papal decrees. Called to the Roman Curia by Pope Honorius III, he rose quickly, and Pope Gregory IX made him Cardinal-Priest of San Lorenzo in Lucina on 18 September 1227. He was papal governor of the March of Ancona from 1235 to 1240.

After a year and a half of contentious debate, the conclave elected Fieschi on 25 June 1243. He accepted reluctantly, having been on friendly terms with Emperor Frederick II. Negotiations failed over the return of Lombardy to the Patrimony of St Peter. Finding himself unsafe in Rome, Innocent fled on 7 June 1244 by way of Genoa to Lyon, where he arrived on 29 November.

The First Council of Lyon met in three public sessions in June and July 1245, with about 150 bishops, mostly from France and Spain. It ended on 17 July with the solemn deposition and excommunication of Frederick, and the release of his subjects from their allegiance. The conflict eased only with Frederick's death in December 1250. Innocent left Lyon in April 1251 and returned to Rome in October 1253. On 15 May 1252 he issued the bull Ad extirpanda, which advised civil authorities to treat heretics as criminals and authorised torture to compel confessions.

He saw himself as Vicar of Christ, with power above earthly kings. In 1245 he sent Giovanni da Pian del Carpine to the Mongols; the Khan Güyük replied in 1246 demanding the submission of the Pope and of Europe's rulers. On 23 September 1243 the bull Qui iustis causis authorised crusades in Livonia and Prussia for the Teutonic Order. In 1247 he ordered that the Talmud be censored rather than burned. He is often credited with developing the idea of legal personality, persona ficta.

In his last years Innocent worked to overthrow Manfred of Sicily, Frederick's natural son. On 14 May 1254 he invested Edmund Crouchback, the nine-year-old son of Henry III of England, with the kingdom of Sicily. He entered Naples on 27 October 1254, and learned there of Manfred's victory at Foggia on 2 December over papal forces. He died in Naples on 7 December 1254 and was succeeded by Alexander IV.
pope-innocent-x: Giovanni Battista Pamphili was born in Rome on 7 May 1574, the son of Camillo Pamphili, of a family originally from Gubbio. He graduated from the Roman College in 1594, served as a consistorial lawyer in 1601, and in 1604 succeeded his uncle, Cardinal Girolamo Pamphili, as auditor of the Roman Rota. In 1623 Pope Gregory XV sent him as nuncio to Naples. In 1625 he accompanied Francesco Barberini to France and Spain, and in May 1626 he became nuncio to the court of Philip IV of Spain, which began a lifelong association with the Spaniards.

The conclave of 1644 lasted from 9 August to 15 September. A French faction led by the nephews of Urban VIII objected to the Spanish candidate, and Pamphili was accepted as a compromise, although he had served as legate to Spain; Cardinal Mazarin arrived with the French veto too late. As Innocent X he soon began legal action against the Barberini for misappropriation of public funds. Francesco, Antonio and Taddeo Barberini fled to Paris, where Mazarin protected them. Innocent confiscated their property and did not yield until Mazarin prepared to send troops to Italy. The Barberini were later rehabilitated.

Hostilities with the Duchy of Parma resumed in 1649, and papal forces destroyed the city of Castro on 2 September 1649. Innocent objected to the Peace of Westphalia. In 1650 he issued the brief Zelo Domus Dei against it, backdated to 1648 to preserve possible claims to confiscated property, and the European powers ignored it. In 1653 the bull Cum occasione condemned five propositions of Jansenius's Augustinus, which led to the formulary controversy, Blaise Pascal's Lettres Provinciales, and finally the razing of the convent of Port-Royal.

In 1650 Innocent held a Jubilee. He had Gian Lorenzo Bernini's Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi built in Piazza Navona, and raised the Colegio de Santo Tomás in Manila to the rank of a university. Diego Velázquez painted his portrait. His sister-in-law Olimpia Maidalchini had great influence over him; Leopold von Ranke concluded that she was not his lover.

Innocent suffered from gout in his later years, and his health declined from August 1654. He died on the night of 6 January 1655, with Secretary of State Chigi among those present. His tomb is in the Church of Sant'Agnese in Agone, which he had built in 1652 beside the family palace. He was succeeded by Pope Alexander VII.
pope-innocent-xii: Antonio Pignatelli was born on 13 March 1615 in Spinazzola, now in Apulia, the fourth of five children of Francesco Pignatelli, 4th Marquess of Spinazzola, and Porzia Carafa, 1st Princess of Minervino. His family was among the most aristocratic of the Kingdom of Naples and had produced several viceroys and ministers of the crown. His mother was related to Pope Paul IV. He studied at the Collegio Romano in Rome and took a doctorate in both canon and civil law.

At the age of 20 he became an official at the court of Pope Urban VIII, and later served as governor of Fano and Viterbo. He was inquisitor in Malta from 1646 to 1649 and then governor of Perugia, after which he was ordained priest. He became Titular Archbishop of Larissa in 1652, was Apostolic Nuncio to Poland from 1660 to 1668 and to Austria from 1668 to 1671, and then held the sees of Lecce, Faenza and, from 1686, Naples.

When Pope Alexander VIII died in 1691, factions loyal to France, Spain and the Holy Roman Empire could not agree on a candidate. After five months Pignatelli emerged as a compromise between the French and imperial cardinals, receiving 53 of 61 votes. He took the name Innocent XII in honour of Innocent XI and was crowned on 15 July 1691.

He declared his opposition to nepotism at once. In 1692 the bull Romanum decet Pontificem abolished the office of Cardinal-Nephew and forbade popes to grant estates, offices or revenues to relatives; only one relative, and only if otherwise suitable, could be made a cardinal. He said that the poor were his nephews.

He also tried to check simony in the Apostolic Chamber, simplified life at his court, and introduced the Forum Innocentianum to improve the administration of justice in the Papal States. In 1693 he compelled French bishops to retract the four propositions on Gallican Liberties drawn up by the assembly of 1682, and in 1699 he decided for Jacques-Benigne Bossuet against Fénelon in their controversy. He invited the physician Marcello Malpighi to Rome in 1692.

Ill with gout, Innocent XII could not attend the opening of the Holy Door at Saint Peter's Basilica on 25 December 1699 for the Jubilee of 1700, and Cardinal Emmanuel-Théodose de La Tour d'Auvergne represented him. He nevertheless blessed the crowds at Easter and named three cardinals in June 1700. He died on 27 September 1700 and was succeeded by Pope Clement XI. His tomb in Saint Peter's Basilica is by Filippo della Valle. He appears as a narrator in Robert Browning's poem The Ring and the Book (1869).
pope-john-paul-ii: Karol Józef Wojtyła was the youngest of three children of Karol Wojtyła, an ethnic Pole, and Emilia Kaczorowska, a schoolteacher. His mother died in 1929, when he was eight. In his youth he worked occasionally as a stage actor, and during the Second World War he took work in a quarry to avoid being sent to a German forced labour camp. Adam Stefan Sapieha, the Archbishop of Kraków, encouraged him to study theology and ordained him on 1 November 1946. On 4 July 1958 Pope Pius XII appointed him auxiliary bishop of Kraków, and at 38 he became the youngest bishop in Poland.

After Pope John Paul I died following only 33 days as pope, a second conclave opened on 14 October 1978, split between Cardinal Giuseppe Siri and Cardinal Giovanni Benelli. Cardinal Franz König suggested Wojtyła as a compromise, and he won on the eighth ballot on 16 October, taking his predecessor's name. He wrote 14 encyclicals, completed a reform of the Church's legal system and the Roman Curia, and saw the 1983 Code of Canon Law and the Catechism of the Catholic Church promulgated. He beatified 1,344 people and canonised 483 saints.

On 13 May 1981 he was shot in the abdomen in St. Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Ağca, lost nearly three-quarters of his blood and underwent five hours of surgery. As pope he made public apologies for more than 100 wrongdoings, among them the trial of Galileo Galilei (31 October 1992) and the silence of many Catholics during the Holocaust (1998).

He died on 2 April 2005 and was succeeded by Pope Benedict XVI. He was beatified on 1 May 2011 and canonised on 27 April 2014 by Pope Francis, alongside Pope John XXIII. He has been credited with helping to end communist rule in Poland and the rest of Europe, and under him the Church greatly expanded its influence in Africa and Latin America. He has also been criticised for allegedly not acting against, or being insufficiently harsh with, the sexual abuse of children by priests, both as archbishop in the Polish People's Republic and as pope.
pope-john-xii: Octavian was the son of Alberic II of Spoleto, patrician and self-styled prince of Rome. His mother is believed to have been Alda of Vienne, daughter of King Hugh of Italy, though there is some doubt, and Benedict of Soracte recorded him as the son of a concubine. Before Alberic's death in 954 he made the Roman nobles swear that the next papal vacancy would go to his son. Octavian succeeded his father as prince of the Romans and, after the death of Agapetus II, was elected pope on 16 December 955, adopting the name John XII. He issued secular directives as Octavian and church documents as John.

Around 960 John led an attack on the Lombard duchies of Beneventum and Capua, but retreated and made a treaty with Gisulf I of Salerno at Terracina. Attacked by King Berengar II of Italy and unable to control the Roman nobility, he appealed to King Otto I of Germany. Otto entered Rome on 31 January 962, and John crowned him emperor, the first in the West since the death of Berengar I almost 40 years before. Eleven days later they ratified the Diploma Ottonianum, which made the emperor guarantor of the independence of the Papal States and confirmed the freedom of papal elections, while the emperor kept the right to agree to an election before consecration.

In 960 he confirmed Saint Dunstan as archbishop of Canterbury, and at a synod on 12 February 962 he agreed to found the Archbishopric of Magdeburg. After Otto left Rome, John sent envoys to the Magyars and the Byzantine Empire to form a league against him and negotiated with Adalbert, the son of Berengar. Otto besieged Rome in the summer of 963. John fled to Tibur with the papal treasury, and a council summoned by Otto deposed him and elected Leo VIII.

When Otto left, John returned in February 964, and a synod he summoned declared his deposition uncanonical. He died on 14 May 964. Liudprand of Cremona, a partisan of Otto, recorded the charges brought at the Synod of Rome in 963, among them simony, ordaining a ten-year-old bishop, and adultery, and much of the later condemnation of John rests on them. Ratherius of Verona also wrote of immoral conduct. The historian Ferdinand Gregorovius judged him leniently, pointing to his youth and the anomalous position of prince and pope at once, and his enemies used the accusations to obscure the political side of his deposition.
pope-john-xix: Romanus was born in Rome, the third son of Count Gregory I of Tusculum and his wife, Mary. While his brother Benedict VIII was pope, Romanus held temporal power in the city as consul and senator, so that the family controlled both the papacy and the government of Rome.

When Benedict died, Romanus, who was still a layman, was elected to succeed him. He was ordained in all the orders in succession and consecrated bishop so that he could take the papal chair, and he took the name John. He was closely related to five other popes of the 10th and 11th centuries, as well as to some of the most powerful rulers of Italy at the time.

John XIX supported Emperor Conrad II after the death of Emperor Henry II in 1024. Conrad and his wife, Gisela of Swabia, were crowned with great pomp at St. Peter's Basilica at Easter 1027. Two kings, Rudolph III of Burgundy and Cnut the Great of Denmark and England, took part in the journey to Rome. Cnut went to repent for his sins, to pray, and to improve conditions for pilgrims and merchants on the road to Rome, and negotiations over the toll gates Rudolph controlled were successful. In 1025 John sent a crown to Poland and blessed the coronation of the Polish king Bolesław I the Brave.

His relations with Constantinople worsened. He rejected a proposal by Patriarch Eustathius of Constantinople to recognise that patriarchate's sphere of interest in the east, and he is also reported to have agreed, for a large bribe, to recognise the patriarch's claim to the title of ecumenical bishop; general indignation in the Church forced him to withdraw. He also invited the musician Guido of Arezzo to Rome to explain his musical notation and encouraged him to instruct the Roman clergy in music.

John placed Cluny Abbey under his protection and renewed its privileges despite the protests of Goslin, bishop of Macon. He offered Odilo of Cluny the archbishopric of Lyons, which Odilo refused, and the pope then chided him for disobedience. John died in October 1032. He was said to have been killed by a mob of angry peasants, but there is no direct evidence for this. His nephew Benedict IX succeeded him while still young; some sources give his age as 12, though he was more likely about 18 or 20.
pope-john-xxii: Jacques Duèze was the son of Arnaud Duèze, probably a merchant or banker of Cahors. He studied canon law at Montpellier and theology in Paris, taught civil law at Cahors and canon law at Toulouse, and became Bishop of Fréjus in 1300 on the recommendation of Charles II of Naples. In 1307 a knight and a priest tried to kill him; both were sentenced to death in 1309. He served as chancellor to Charles II, became Bishop of Avignon on 18 March 1310, and was made Cardinal-Bishop of Porto-Santa Rufina by Clement V on 23 December 1312.

After Clement V died in 1314 the cardinals, split into three factions, could not agree for two years. Philip, Count of Poitiers, summoned 23 cardinals to Lyon in August 1316 and forbade them to leave until they had chosen a pope. They elected Jacques on 7 August 1316, and he took the name John XXII.

John was an effective administrator who reorganised the Church and favoured heavily regulated government, living in Avignon rather than Rome. He canonized Louis of Toulouse in 1317 and, after a long inquiry that heard 111 witnesses, Thomas Aquinas on 18 July 1323. In 1329 he condemned writings of Meister Eckhart as heretical. His bull Super illius specula of 1326 treated witchcraft as heresy open to the Inquisition. In 1332 he announced a move to Bologna, but a revolt there in 1334 destroyed the papal palace built for him.

He quarrelled with the Holy Roman Emperor Louis IV the Bavarian, whom he excommunicated on 23 March 1324 and deposed on 11 July. Louis entered Rome on 17 January 1328, was crowned there, and in May had Pietro Rainalducci made Antipope Nicholas V, who submitted in 1330. John also opposed the Spiritual Franciscans, who held that Christ and his apostles had owned nothing: by the bull Quum inter nonnullos of 12 November 1323 he declared that doctrine erroneous and heretical. Michael of Cesena and William of Ockham fled Avignon and wrote against him.

Between November 1331 and March 1332 John preached four sermons arguing that the faithful dead do not see God until the Last Judgment. The Sorbonne's theologians opposed this in January 1334, and on the day before his death he agreed that those who die in grace enjoy the beatific vision at once. He died in Avignon on 4 December 1334, at about the age of 90, and was buried in the cathedral of Notre-Dame-des-Doms.
pope-julius-ii: Giuliano della Rovere was born at Albisola near Savona, in the Republic of Genoa, into a noble but impoverished family. He was educated by his uncle Francesco della Rovere among the Franciscans and studied at Perugia. When his uncle was elected Pope Sixtus IV in 1471, Giuliano became Bishop of Carpentras and, in an act of open nepotism, a cardinal within two months. He held several bishoprics at once and from 1475 was the first Archbishop of Avignon. He was a rival of Rodrigo Borgia, who won the conclave of 1492 as Alexander VI, and in 1494 della Rovere took refuge in France and urged Charles VIII to invade Italy.

Della Rovere was elected on 1 November 1503, in a few hours, after winning over Cesare Borgia with promises of money and continued support in the Romagna. Historians such as Ludwig von Pastor say that bribery and promises played a part. He took the name Julius, used by only one earlier pope. Early in his reign he worked to end the power of the Borgia family and forbade anyone to speak or think of Alexander VI. He aimed to centralise the Papal States and to free Italy from the barbarians.

Julius led troops in person on at least two occasions: against Giovanni Bentivoglio at Bologna in 1506–07 and against the Duchy of Ferrara in 1510–12. In 1508 he joined Louis XII of France, Emperor Maximilian I and Ferdinand II of Aragon in the League of Cambrai against Venice, which he placed under an interdict in 1509. He convened the Fifth Council of the Lateran, which met from May 1512, after Louis XII and Maximilian had backed a rival council at Pisa to threaten him. In 1506 he founded the Vatican Museums and organised the Swiss Guard for his protection.

Julius was seriously ill from 1512, and on 4 February 1513 he discussed his funeral arrangements; he died on 21 February. He was one of the most powerful popes and a central figure of the High Renaissance, and under him the Papal States gained power and centralisation. He revived the plan to replace the old basilica of St Peter's, though Giuliano da Sangallo's proposal was not accepted. Erasmus satirised him after his death in Julius Excluded from Heaven, which shows him drunk and refused entry by St Peter. His character was violent and gruff, and his Master of Ceremonies, Paris de Grassis, said he hardly ever jested.
pope-leo-iii: According to the Liber Pontificalis, Leo was of the Roman nation, the son of Atzuppius. He is usually considered to have been of Greek origin, and his father's name may suggest an Arab background. He seems to have known Greek. Pope Adrian I made him cardinal-priest of Santa Susanna and, it seems, vestiarius, chief of the pontifical treasury. He was elected on 26 December 795, the day Adrian was buried, and consecrated the next day, perhaps in haste to prevent Frankish interference. He sent Charlemagne the keys of the confession of St Peter and the standard of the city, showing that he regarded the Frankish king as protector of the Holy See.

On 25 April 799, during the procession of the Greater Litanies, Leo was attacked by armed men, among them relatives of Adrian I, who tried to root out his tongue and tear out his eyes. Two of Charlemagne's missi dominici rescued him, and he went to Charlemagne's camp at Paderborn. His enemies accused him of adultery and perjury. Charlemagne came to Rome in November 800 and held a council on 1 December; on 23 December Leo took an oath of purgation, and his opponents were exiled.

Two days later, on Christmas Day 800, Leo crowned Charlemagne as Emperor of the Romans. Einhard says the king had no suspicion of what was to happen. Yet the elevation had probably been discussed for some time, not least because a woman, Irene of Athens, occupied the imperial throne in Constantinople. The coronation offended Constantinople, but Irene was too weak to oppose it.

Leo helped restore King Eardwulf of Northumbria and settled disputes between the archbishops of York and Canterbury; in 803 Lichfield was again a regular diocese. He supported the Western teaching that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both the Father and the Son, yet refused to change the creed, and placed two silver shields in Rome bearing it in Greek and Latin. In 808 he committed Corsica to Charlemagne against Muslim raids.
Leo died on 12 June 816 and was later moved to a tomb holding the first four popes named Leo. In 1673 Clement X entered his name in the Roman Martyrology.
pope-leo-iv: Leo was a Roman by birth and was educated at the monastery of St. Martin near St. Peter's. Pope Gregory IV noticed him and made him a subdeacon, and Pope Sergius II created him cardinal-priest of Santi Quattro Coronati. In April 847 he was unanimously chosen to succeed Sergius. Because the Saracen attack on Rome in 846 had left the people fearful for the city, he was consecrated on 10 April 847 without waiting for the consent of the emperor.

Leo began at once to repair the damage the Arab raid had done to the churches of Rome. He restored the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls and St. Peter's Basilica, whose altar again received its gold covering, weighing 206 pounds and studded with gems after the original had been stolen. He then appealed to the Christian kingdoms to confront the raiders.

He also put the city's walls in repair, rebuilding fifteen of the great towers, and was the first to enclose the Vatican hill with a wall. The new line enclosed the suburb on the right bank of the Tiber, including St. Peter's, which had been undefended. The district is still known as the Leonine City and corresponds to the later rione of Borgo. The work took four years and was paid for with money from the emperor and help from the cities and agricultural colonies of the Duchy of Rome.

In 849, when a Saracen fleet from Sardinia approached Portus, Leo summoned Naples, Gaeta and Amalfi to form a league under Cesarius, son of Duke Sergius I of Naples. Aided by a fierce storm, the league destroyed the Saracen fleet off Ostia. Raphael and his pupils painted the Battle of Ostia in the Vatican Palace. Leo held three synods, one in 850 attended by Emperor Louis II, and in 853 went to Ravenna to settle a dispute with its archbishop, with little success. Shortly before his death he welcomed Aethelwulf, King of Wessex, and his sons, including the seven-year-old Alfred the Great, as pilgrims.
