Leo IV died on 17 July 855 and was succeeded by Benedict III; a legend that Pope Joan followed him is regarded by scholars as fictional. He was first buried in his own monument in St. Peter's Basilica and later moved to a tomb holding the first four popes named Leo. He is also credited with placing a rooster, the emblem of St Peter, on Old St. Peter's, and his deacon Nicholas I later decreed that one be placed on every church.
pope-leo-ix: Bruno was the youngest son of Count Hugh IV of Nordgau and Hedwig of Dagsburg and was born at Egisheim in Upper Alsace. His father was a first cousin of the Emperor Conrad II. At the age of five he was placed with Berthold, Bishop of Toul, who ran a school for the sons of the nobility, and in 1017 he became a canon at St. Stephen's in Toul.

In 1026, as a deacon, he led the contingent of the aged Bishop Herimann of Toul on Conrad's expedition to Italy; Herimann died, and Bruno was elected to succeed him. He was consecrated in 1027 and administered the diocese for over twenty years through famine and war. He did political service for Conrad II and Henry III and spread the rule of Cluny.

After the death of Pope Damasus II in 1048, an assembly at Worms chose Bruno in December, with the agreement of the emperor and the Roman delegates. He insisted on being freely elected at Rome, set out shortly after Christmas, met Abbot Hugh of Cluny at Besançon, where the young monk Hildebrand joined him, and arrived in pilgrim's dress in February. He took the name Leo IX. His Easter synod of 1049 again required celibacy of the clergy down to the rank of subdeacon and set him against simony. He travelled through Italy, Germany and France, holding councils at Pavia, Reims and Mainz.

Patriarch Michael I Cerularius of Constantinople objected to the Latin use of unleavened bread and fasting days. In 1054 Leo wrote to him, citing the Donation of Constantine, which he believed genuine. His legate Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida delivered a bull excommunicating the patriarch, an act legally invalid since the pope had died, and the patriarch excommunicated Humbert in turn. This is popularly considered the official split between the Eastern and Western churches.

In the south, fearing the Normans, the Byzantines appealed to the pope. Leo led an army of Italians and Swabian mercenaries against them and was totally defeated at the Battle of Civitate on 15 June 1053. The Normans received him with submission, but he was held in honourable captivity at Benevento from June 1053 to March 1054, until he acknowledged their conquests in Calabria and Apulia.

Leo IX died in Rome on 19 April 1054, not long after his return. The Catholic Church regards him as a saint, with a feast day on 19 April. He is considered one of the most historically significant popes of the Middle Ages, because he was instrumental in bringing about the Great Schism of 1054.
pope-leo-x: Giovanni de' Medici was born in Florence on 11 December 1475, the second son of Lorenzo de' Medici and Clarice Orsini. He was destined for a Church career and received the tonsure at seven; by ten he held dozens of benefices. He was educated at his father's humanist court by men such as Angelo Poliziano, Pico della Mirandola and Marsilio Ficino, and studied theology and canon law at Pisa. He was admitted to the College of Cardinals in 1492, and took part in the conclave of 1492 that elected Alexander VI.
He was elected pope on 9 March 1513, when French cardinals were absent, with the support of the younger and noble members of the college. He was not yet a priest, and was ordained on 15 March.

Leo oversaw the closing sessions of the Fifth Council of the Lateran, but did not carry out its reforms. He tried to carve out a state for his brother Giuliano in central Italy, and after Giuliano's death in 1516 turned to his nephew Lorenzo, declaring the Duchy of Urbino forfeit and giving it to him. Francesco Maria della Rovere's attempt to retake it led to an eight-month war in 1517. After a plot by several cardinals to poison him, Leo executed Alfonso Petrucci and on 3 July 1517 named 31 new cardinals, almost without precedent.

In 1517 Martin Luther wrote his Ninety-five Theses on indulgences. Leo at first did not grasp the importance of the movement. Luther met Cardinal Cajetan at Augsburg in October 1518 but would not retract, and Leo's bull of 1520, Exsurge Domine, condemned him. He remained a patron of the arts and learning: Raphael decorated the Vatican rooms, work on St Peter's went forward, and he reorganised the Roman university in 1513.

Leo died suddenly of pneumonia on 1 December 1521, aged 45, and was buried in Santa Maria sopra Minerva. He spent lavishly on the arts, charity, benefices, dynastic wars and his own luxury: within two years he had spent the treasure left by Julius II, and the papal treasury was 400,000 ducats in debt by 1521. Many link his name with the Reformation, because his pontificate did not enforce the Lateran reforms, and the sale of indulgences to fund St Peter's precipitated Protestantism. His court included musicians from France, Germany and Spain. He also permitted a Hebrew printing press in Rome.
pope-leo-xiii: Gioacchino Pecci was born on 2 March 1810 at Carpineto Romano, near Rome, the sixth of seven children of Count Domenico Ludovico Pecci, a colonel in Napoleon's French army, and Anna Francesca Prosperi-Buzzi. He studied at the Jesuit College in Viterbo until 1824. In 1837 Pope Gregory XVI appointed him a prelate, and he was ordained a priest on 31 December that year. He then served as papal legate to Benevento, and in 1843, aged 33, as nuncio to Belgium, where he was made an archbishop and developed excellent relations with the royal family.

From 1846 Pecci was Archbishop of Perugia. In 1849 he called a provincial council to reform religious life, enlarged the seminary and hired Thomist professors and founded shelters and soup kitchens. He became a cardinal in the consistory of 19 December 1853. When Pope Pius IX died on 7 February 1878, the conclave assembled on 18 February, and Pecci was elected on the third ballot and took the name Leo XIII. He was crowned on 3 March 1878.

The Holy See had lost the Papal States, and under Leo it sought to regain international standing by acting as an arbiter of disputes. He opened the Vatican Archives to qualified researchers, among them the historian Ludwig von Pastor,. He created 147 cardinals in 27 consistories, among them John Henry Newman.

Leo wrote 86 encyclicals. In Aeterni Patris of 4 August 1879 he made the revival of the theology of Thomas Aquinas the charter of Catholic teaching, to be followed in the training of priests and in universities. Humanum genus of 1884 reaffirmed condemnations of Freemasonry, arguing that its principles were incompatible with Catholic doctrine. He issued eleven encyclicals on the rosary and was called the Rosary Pope.

His encyclical Rerum novarum of 1891 addressed social inequality for the first time with papal authority, discussing the rights and duties of capital and labour. It affirmed workers' rights to a fair wage, safe conditions and trade unions, and the rights to property and free enterprise, and it rejected both atheistic communism and laissez-faire capitalism. It is thought to have laid the foundations of modern Catholic social teaching, and Leo was called the Pope of the Workers.

Leo XIII died on 20 July 1903, aged 93, of pneumonia followed by hemorrhagic pleurisy. He was buried in the Vatican Grottoes, and in 1924 his remains were moved to the Archbasilica of Saint John Lateran. He had the fourth-longest reign of any pope.
pope-martin-v: Oddone Colonna was born at Genazzano, between 26 January and 20 February in 1368 or 1369, the son of Agapito Colonna and Caterina Conti. He studied law at the University of Pavia, became apostolic protonotary under Pope Urban VI, and was created Cardinal-Deacon of San Giorgio in Velabro by Pope Innocent VII in 1405. In 1409 he took part in the Council of Pisa and supported Antipope Alexander V and then John XXIII. He followed John in his flight to Schaffhausen on 21 March 1415, but returned to Constance and took part in the proceedings that deposed him.

The Council of Constance was long divided by the rival claims of Pope Gregory XII and Antipope Benedict XIII, until Gregory resigned and Benedict was deposed. Oddone was elected on 11 November 1417 by 23 cardinals and 30 delegates of the council, and took the name Martin from Martin of Tours, whose feast fell that day. He was ordained priest on 13 November and consecrated bishop the next day. The election effectively ended the Western Schism.

Martin left Constance in May 1418 and travelled slowly, lingering at Florence, and entered Rome only in September 1420. The pope then ruled little more than Rome and its surroundings, since Braccio da Montone held Umbria and local vicars held much of Romagna and the Marche. In Rome he restored churches, palaces and bridges, engaged masters of the Tuscan school, and helped start the Roman Renaissance. From 1423 his main concern was war with Braccio, who was defeated at the Battle of L'Aquila on 2 June 1424 and died a few days later.

In 1420 he issued a bull calling for a crusade against the Wycliffites, Hussites and other heretics, and in 1428 he ordered the remains of John Wycliffe dug up and burned. The crusades against the Lollards ultimately failed. He summoned a council in 1423 that met at Pavia and then Siena, was poorly attended, and was dissolved; the Council of Basel opened in February 1431. On 9 December 1425 he founded the University of Louvain, at the request of Duke John IV of Brabant.

Martin V died in Rome of a stroke on 20 February 1431, aged 63, and is buried at St. John Lateran. In 1423 he ruled that annuities redeemable at the seller's option were lawful, which allowed them to be widely used in commerce as a way round the ban on interest. He also confirmed the privileges of the Jews in bulls of 1418 and 1422, although he later repealed several of his ordinances.
pope-paul-ii: Pietro Barbo was born in Venice on 23 February 1417, the son of Niccolò Barbo and Polissena Condulmer, a sister of Pope Eugene IV. He was trained as a merchant, but his uncle's election as pope turned him to a religious career, and his rise was rapid. He became Archdeacon of Bologna, Bishop of Cervia and of Vicenza, and in 1440 a cardinal-deacon. In 1445 he became archpriest of the Vatican Basilica.

He was elected on 30 August 1464, on the first ballot, by fourteen of the nineteen cardinals present. The terms agreed at the conclave required him to convene an ecumenical council within three years, but he modified them at his own discretion, which cost him the confidence of the College of Cardinals. He became withdrawn and inaccessible, granting audiences only at night.

Paul built the Palazzo San Marco, now the Palazzo Venezia, lived in it as pope and amassed a great collection of art and antiquities. On 18 September 1467 he created eight cardinals at once, five of them candidates pressed by kings. His attempt to remove redundant offices led him to abolish the college of Abbreviators, which formulated papal documents and employed humanists, and a storm of indignation followed. He also moved against the Roman Academy. Bartolomeo Platina, a member of both, wrote a pamphlet demanding that the restrictions be reversed and was imprisoned in the winter of 1464 for four months.

In February 1468 Paul arrested Platina and other members of the Academy on charges of irreligion, immorality and an alleged conspiracy to assassinate him. They were interrogated under torture and later released. Platina's history of the pontiffs, written in 1479, drew an unfavourable portrait of Paul that influenced opinion for centuries, until critical research showed otherwise. The affair convinced men of letters that cultural conformity would be enforced in Rome. Paul also rejected King George of Poděbrady of Bohemia for upholding the Utraquists. He summoned George to Rome in August 1465 and in December 1466 pronounced excommunication and a sentence of deposition against him.

Paul approved the introduction of printing into the Papal States, first at Subiaco in 1464 and at Rome in 1467, although books produced there were largely limited to Latin classics and church texts. In 1466 he allowed the Carnival horse race to be run along the Via Lata, which became known as the Via del Corso. He died suddenly on 26 July 1471, of a heart attack, though reports of the death varied.
pope-paul-iii: Alessandro Farnese was born at Canino, in the Papal States, the second son of Pier Luigi I Farnese. He received a humanist education at the University of Pisa and at the court of Lorenzo de' Medici, joined the Roman Curia in 1491 and in 1493 was made Cardinal-Deacon by Alexander VI. His sister Giulia was reputedly Alexander's mistress, and he was mockingly called the Borgia brother-in-law. As a young cleric he lived dissolutely and had at least four children by Silvia Ruffini, among them Pier Luigi, whom Julius II legitimated in 1505.

He became Bishop of Parma in 1509 but was ordained priest only in 1519. Under the influence of his vicar-general he broke off the relationship and committed himself to reform. He was elected pope on 13 October 1534, in a conclave that thought his poor health meant a short reign.

Paul III was the first pope to take active reform measures in response to Protestantism. In 1537 a committee of nine prelates produced the Consilium de emendenda ecclesia, which exposed abuses in the Curia. It led to no result, though the report was widely printed. He recognised the Society of Jesus on 27 September 1540 and reorganised the Holy Office of the Inquisition in 1542. A council planned for Mantua failed, and the Council of Trent was convoked on 15 March 1545 under the bull Laetare Hierusalem. In 1538 he formed the Holy League against the Ottoman Empire with Charles V and Venice, which dissolved after its fleet was routed at Preveza, and he excommunicated Henry VIII in December 1538.

He was a major patron of the arts. He renewed the commission for Michelangelo's Last Judgement, completed in 1541, and in 1546 made Michelangelo supervisor of the building of St Peter's. He continued the Palazzo Farnese, and Titian painted his portrait in 1543. In 1537 he issued the bull Sublimis Deus, declaring that the peoples of the Americas were human beings who were not to be robbed of their freedom or possessions.

Paul advanced his family. He made his grandsons cardinals at 14 and 16, and planned to acquire the duchies of Parma and Piacenza for his son Pier Luigi, who was assassinated at Piacenza in 1547. Charles V refused to give up Piacenza, and the pope's quarrel over the inheritance with his grandson Cardinal Alessandro Farnese is said to have brought on the illness from which he died on 10 November 1549, aged 81. He had failed to suppress the Reformation, but his pontificate laid the foundation of the Counter-Reformation. His bronze tomb, by Guglielmo della Porta, is in St Peter's Basilica.
pope-paul-iv: Gian Pietro Carafa was born at Capriglia Irpina, near Avellino, into the prominent Carafa family of Naples. His relative Cardinal Oliviero Carafa resigned the see of Chieti in his favour. Under Pope Leo X he was ambassador to England and then nuncio in Spain, where he conceived a violent detestation of Spanish rule that affected his later policies. In 1524 Pope Clement VII allowed him to resign his benefices and join the Theatines. He was made a cardinal in December 1536 and Archbishop of Naples. After the Regensburg Colloquy of 1541 failed, he persuaded Pope Paul III to set up a Roman Inquisition, with himself as one of its Inquisitors-General.

Carafa was a surprise choice to succeed Pope Marcellus II. He was elected on 23 May 1555 and crowned on 26 May, accepting apparently because Emperor Charles V opposed his election. Austere and authoritarian, he used the Holy Office against the Spirituali and imprisoned Cardinal Giovanni Morone, whom he suspected of being a hidden Protestant.

His bull Cum nimis absurdum of 17 July 1555 aimed to lead the Jews to convert. It restricted their trades, forbade them Christian servants, required yellow hats, and allowed one synagogue per city, so that seven were destroyed in Rome. It also ordered a walled ghetto in Rome, near the Rione Sant'Angelo, with a single gate locked at sundown; the Jews paid the costs. In 1556 about a hundred Marranos of Ancona were imprisoned and 25 Conversos who had reverted to Judaism were burned. The Roman ghetto lasted until the end of the Papal States in 1870.

Displeased by the five-year truce between France and Spain of February 1556, Paul urged Henry II of France to invade Spanish Naples. On 1 September 1556 Philip II of Spain invaded the Papal States with 12,000 men under the Duke of Alba. After French forces were defeated at Civitella del Tronto in August 1557, Paul agreed to neutrality in the Peace of Cave-Palestrina of 12 September 1557. After scandals he banished his nephews from Rome in 1559.

Paul IV died on 18 August 1559. Crowds rioted even before his death. They decapitated his statue on the Campidoglio and threw it into the Tiber, freed over 400 prisoners from the city jails, killed the Inquisitor Tommaso Scotti, burned the Inquisition's offices and removed the Carafa arms from buildings across the city. His nephew had him buried without ceremony, and in 1566 Pius V moved his remains to Santa Maria sopra Minerva.
pope-pius-ii: Enea Silvio Piccolomini was born on 18 October 1405 in Corsignano, in Sienese territory, to a noble but impoverished family. His father Silvio was a soldier. He worked in the fields with his father before leaving in 1423 to study the humanities and civil law at Siena, and then at Florence under Francesco Filelfo.

In 1431 he became secretary to Domenico Capranica, bishop of Fermo, and went with him to the Council of Basel. He later served the antipope Felix V, Emperor Frederick III and Pope Eugenius IV. He was ordained priest in Vienna on 4 March 1446, became Bishop of Trieste in 1447 and Bishop of Siena in 1450, and was made a cardinal in 1456.

He was elected pope on 19 August 1458, and his first priority was to free Europe from the threat of the Turks through a great crusade. He convened a congress of Christian princes at Mantua, setting out on 22 January 1459, but it made little progress. He allied himself with the Aragonese claimant Ferdinand to the throne of Naples and for much of his reign waged what looked like a personal war on Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta, Lord of Rimini, who was almost wholly subdued. In October 1461 he persuaded Louis XI of France to abolish the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges, but Louis soon restored it in effect.

In 1462 he wrote to Mehmed II urging him to become a Christian. In November 1463 he again called for a crusade, and Skanderbeg declared war on the Ottomans. Despite a fever, he left Rome for Ancona on 18 June 1464 to lead the crusade in person, but the army melted away for want of transport and from pestilence. He could only watch the Venetian fleet arrive from a window, and he died on 14 August 1464. He also rebuilt his birthplace as Pienza, perhaps the first city-planning project of modern Europe.

Piccolomini was named imperial poet laureate in 1442 and wrote in Latin. His Tale of Two Lovers is an erotic novel, and he also wrote comedies, of which Chrysis survives, and erotic poems, all before his election. In 1463 he published the bull In Minoribus Agentes, withdrawing his earlier writing for the Council of Basel and against Eugenius IV, with the words to reject Aeneas and accept Pius. His longest, the Commentaries, is a third-person autobiography first published in 1584.
pope-pius-iv: Giovanni Angelo Medici was born in Milan on 31 March 1499, the second of eleven children of Bernardino Medici and Clelia Serbelloni. He studied philosophy and medicine at Pavia and then at Bologna, where he took his doctorate in canon and civil law on 11 May 1525. His family considered itself a branch of the House of Medici and used the same coat of arms; modern historians have found no proof of the connection. He went to Rome in 1527 and, as a favourite of Pope Paul III, rose to be Archbishop of Ragusa from 1545 to 1553 and vice-legate of Bologna.

Paul III made him a cardinal on 8 April 1549 and sent him on diplomatic missions to the Holy Roman Empire and Hungary. He was elected pope on 25 December 1559 and installed on 6 January 1560. He brought the nephews of Paul IV to trial: Cardinal Carlo Carafa was strangled and Duke Giovanni Carafa of Paliano beheaded.

On 18 January 1562 Pius convened the Council of Trent for the third and final time. With the help of Giovanni Morone and Charles Borromeo he brought it to a close by management and concession, and the bull Benedictus Deus of 26 January 1564 confirmed its decrees. His bull Dominici Gregis Custodiae of 24 March 1564 set rules for forbidding books. He relaxed the laws of Paul IV on the Roman Ghetto, allowing Jews to own property up to 1500 ducats.

Pius had a strong passion for building. He had the Porta Pia and the Via Pia laid out, improved Rome's water supply and had Michelangelo rebuild Santa Maria degli Angeli. Giorgio Vasari lamented the austere Roman culture of his reign. He created 46 cardinals in four consistories, among them three nephews, including Borromeo. A conspiracy led by Benedetto Accolti, partly provoked by tax increases, was discovered in 1565.
Pius, who suffered from gout, died on 9 December 1565, with Borromeo and Philip Neri at his side. He was buried in Santa Maria degli Angeli in 1583. His successor was Pius V.
pope-pius-ix: Giovanni Maria Mastai-Ferretti was born on 13 May 1792 in Senigallia, the ninth child of a noble family, and was educated at the Piarist College in Volterra and in Rome. The conclave of 1846, after the death of Pope Gregory XVI, met in an unsettled political climate and divided between right and left. Conservatives backed Luigi Lambruschini, the late pope's Cardinal Secretary of State, while liberals supported Tommaso Pasquale Gizzi and the 54-year-old Mastai-Ferretti, who was elected and took the name Pius IX.

He entered the papacy amid widespread expectations that he would champion reform in the Papal States, which he ruled directly, and in the whole Church. At first he eased restrictions on Jewish movement, granted an amnesty to revolutionaries and appointed an enlightened minister, Pellegrino Rossi; Italian patriots hailed him as a coming redeemer of Italy. His course changed radically after the Revolutions of 1848.

Rossi was assassinated, Pius was made prisoner in his own palace and fled Rome, and he excommunicated all participants in the short-lived Roman Republic. After the French army suppressed it and he returned in 1850, his policies and pronouncements became increasingly conservative. In 1854 he promulgated the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, and his Syllabus of Errors of 1864 condemned liberalism, secularization and the separation of church and state.

The First Vatican Council, which he convened and which met in 1869–1870, defined the dogma of papal infallibility, and Pius led the worldwide Church toward ever greater centralization in Rome. The end of the Papal States was the most notable event of his pontificate. When France withdrew the troops that protected them during the Franco-Prussian War, the Kingdom of Italy captured Rome on 20 September 1870; Pius refused to leave the Vatican and declared himself a prisoner there. He created 122 cardinals and canonized 52 saints.

Pius IX died on 7 February 1878. The Mortara case, in which a six-year-old Jewish boy was taken by force from his family, remains one of the controversies of his reign. His appeal for financial support revived the donations known as Peter's Pence, and he strengthened the central power of the Holy See and the Roman Curia over the Catholic Church. Pope John Paul II beatified him in 2000.
pope-pius-v: Antonio Ghislieri was born on 17 January 1504 in Bosco, in the Duchy of Milan, to Paolo Ghislieri and Domenica Augeri. At fourteen he entered the Dominican Order, taking the name Michele, and he was ordained a priest at Genoa in 1528. He lectured for sixteen years at Pavia, and in 1550 he was recalled to Rome for inquisitorial work.

Pope Paul IV made him Bishop of Sutri in 1556 and inquisitor in Milan and Lombardy, and in 1557 he became a cardinal and inquisitor general. As a cardinal he prosecuted eight French bishops for heresy and rebuked Pope Pius IV for wishing to make a thirteen-year-old relative a cardinal. He was elected pope on 8 January 1566, with the support of Cardinal Charles Borromeo, and crowned ten days later.

Pius V reduced the cost of the papal court, dismissed the court jester, forbade horse racing in St Peter's Square and imposed severe sanctions against blasphemy and adultery, which made him disliked in Rome. In day-to-day life he was ascetic, wearing a hair shirt beneath his Dominican habit. Enforcing the decrees of the Council of Trent took precedence over other aims. He promulgated the 1570 edition of the Roman Missal, which was made mandatory throughout the Latin Church except where a Mass dating from before 1370 was in use.

He opposed the Huguenots in France and urged Mary, Queen of Scots, to restore Catholicism in Scotland. After the failure of the Rising of the North he issued the bull Regnans in Excelsis, dated 27 April 1570, declaring Elizabeth I of England a heretic and releasing her subjects from their allegiance, after which Elizabeth began to persecute English Catholics for treason. He arranged the Holy League against the Ottoman Empire, whose combined fleet under Don John of Austria won the Battle of Lepanto on 7 October 1571.

Pius V died on 1 May 1572, having suffered from bladder stones for which he would not undergo an operation. He had declared Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church in 1567 and commissioned the first complete edition of Aquinas's works. He was beatified by Pope Clement X in 1672 and canonised by Pope Clement XI on 22 May 1712. The Missal of 1570 remained essentially unchanged for about four centuries, until the revision under Pope Paul VI in 1969.
pope-pius-vi: Giovanni Angelo Braschi was born in Cesena on Christmas Day 1717, the eldest of eight children of Count Marco Aurelio Tommaso Braschi and Anna Teresa. He studied at the Jesuit college of Cesena, took a doctorate in canon and civil law in 1734 and continued at the University of Ferrara. He became private secretary to Cardinal Tommaso Ruffo, and his skill in a mission to the court of Naples won him the esteem of Pope Benedict XIV, who made him a secretary in 1753.

He was ordained priest in 1758, ending an engagement to be married, and in 1766 Clement XIII appointed him treasurer of the camera apostolica. As a conscientious administrator he made enemies, and Pope Clement XIV made him Cardinal-Priest of Sant'Onofrio on 26 April 1773, which for a time left him without a specific task. He retired to the Abbey of Saint Scholastica at Subiaco.

Elected on 15 February 1775, he took the name Pius VI. His early acts promised reform in the Papal States: he tackled corruption, reduced expenditure and encouraged agriculture. He restored the Via Appia, expanded the Pio-Clementine Museum and was a great patron of the arts. In November 1789 he erected the first American see, the Diocese of Baltimore.

The French Revolution dominated the later years. Pius condemned the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen and the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and in 1791 diplomatic relations with France ended when revolutionaries seized the Comtat Venaissin, ending 516 years of papal rule in Avignon. French troops under Napoleon Bonaparte defeated the papal army in 1796, and peace was granted at Tolentino on 19 February 1797.

After the killing of General Duphot in Rome on 28 December 1797, General Louis-Alexandre Berthier entered the city on 10 February 1798, proclaimed a Roman Republic and demanded that Pius renounce his temporal authority. He refused, and was taken prisoner and escorted to Siena, then to the Certosa near Florence, and finally to the citadel of Valence, where he died on 29 August 1799. His reign of more than twenty-four years is the fifth-longest in papal history.

His body was not buried until 30 January 1800, since Napoleon saw advantage in burying him as part of efforts to restore the Church in France. In 1802 he was buried in Rome with a Catholic funeral attended by his successor, Pius VII.
pope-pius-vii: Barnaba Chiaramonti was born in Cesena in 1742, the youngest son of Count Scipione Chiaramonti, in a noble but not wealthy family. At 14 he became a novice of the Order of Saint Benedict, and he was ordained a priest in 1765 after teaching at Benedictine colleges in Parma and Rome. His fortunes rose when his relative Giovanni Angelo Braschi became Pope Pius VI. He became Bishop of Tivoli in 1782, Cardinal-Priest of San Callisto and Bishop of Imola in 1785. When French armies invaded Italy in 1797, he counselled submission to the new Cisalpine Republic, and in a Christmas homily said that Christian virtue makes men good democrats.

After Pius VI died in French custody in 1799, a conclave met in Venice and, after several months, elected Chiaramonti as a compromise candidate proposed by Ercole Consalvi, on 14 March 1800. He took the name Pius VII and was crowned with a papier-mâché tiara, since the French had seized the papal tiaras. Consalvi, whom he made Cardinal Secretary of State, negotiated the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon, which acknowledged Catholicism as the religion of the majority of French citizens, but not as the official religion. Pius VII attended Napoleon's coronation in 1804.

In 1809, after Pius refused to join the Continental System, France annexed the Papal States and exiled him, first to Savona and then to France. He called Napoleon a stubborn son, but still a son. He signed the Concordat of Fontainebleau in 1813, then began to revoke its concessions in March 1814. After Napoleon abdicated he returned to Rome in May 1814 and was welcomed as a hero. He restored the Society of Jesus in 1814 and, through Consalvi at the Congress of Vienna, urged an end to the Atlantic slave trade.

Pius VII also revived the Inquisition and the Index of Condemned Books, and, after the restoration of papal rule, reinstituted the confinement of Jews to the Roman Ghetto, with its doors closed at night. He condemned Freemasonry and the Carbonari in 1821. He restored the Arch of Titus, supported archaeological excavations at Ostia and enriched the Vatican Library. He created new dioceses in the United States, among them Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Bardstown in 1808. He fractured his hip on 6 July 1823 and died on 20 August 1823. His beatification cause was opened in 2007, and he holds the title Servant of God.
pope-pius-xi: Ambrogio Damiano Achille Ratti was born in Desio, in the province of Milan, in 1857, the son of the owner of a silk factory. He was ordained a priest in 1879 and selected for a life of academic study, obtaining three doctorates in philosophy, canon law and theology at the Gregorian University in Rome. From 1882 to 1888 he was a professor at a seminary in Padua, with expert paleography as his speciality, and from 1888 to 1911 he worked at the Ambrosian Library in Milan.

In 1918 Pope Benedict XV appointed him apostolic visitor in Poland, and in 1919 papal nuncio and titular archbishop. During the Bolshevik advance on Warsaw in August 1920 he was the only foreign diplomat who refused to flee the city. Benedict created him cardinal and Archbishop of Milan on 3 June 1921, and Benedict XV died on 22 January 1922.

Ratti was elected pope and headed the Catholic Church from 6 February 1922. His first encyclical, Ubi arcano, of December 1922 inaugurated the Catholic Action movement, aimed at Christianizing increasingly secular societies. Divini illius Magistri (1929) asserted the need for Christian influence over education, and Casti connubii (31 December 1930) praised Christian marriage and prohibited contraception. Quadragesimo anno (1931) restated Leo XIII's warnings against both socialism and unrestrained capitalism and called international capitalism materially and spiritually exploitative. He also wrote Quas primas, establishing the feast of Christ the King.

He was the first sovereign of Vatican City, created on 11 February 1929, when the Lateran Treaty ended the long hostility with the Italian government. Pius XI took a pragmatic approach to forms of government, stating that the Church is never bound to one form more than another, and concluded a record number of concordats, including the Reichskonkordat with Nazi Germany, whose betrayals he condemned four years later in the encyclical Mit brennender Sorge. He canonised Thomas More, Peter Canisius, Bernadette of Lourdes and Don Bosco.

The end of his pontificate was dominated by his speaking out against Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini and by his defence of the Church against outside interference. Pius XI died on 10 February 1939 in the Apostolic Palace and was buried in the Papal Grotto of Saint Peter's Basilica. He took a strong interest in fostering the participation of laypeople in the Church, especially through Catholic Action.
pope-siricius: Siricius was a native of Rome; his father's name was Tiburtius. He entered the service of the Church early and, according to the inscription on his grave, was a lector and then a deacon of the Roman Church under Pope Liberius. After the death of Damasus I he was elected pope unanimously, despite attempts by Ursinus to promote himself. Emperor Valentinian II confirmed the election, which ended any further objection.

Siricius was an active pope, involved in the administration of the Church and in handling the factions and viewpoints within it. In reply to a letter from Bishop Himerius of Tarragona he issued the Directa decretal, with decisions on fifteen points concerning baptism, penance, church discipline and the celibacy of the clergy. These are the oldest completely preserved papal decretals.

He helped to mend the Meletian schism at Antioch, which began when the Arian emperors repeatedly exiled Meletius of Antioch. Meletius died during the First Council of Constantinople in 381 and his followers objected to his successor. Through the mediation of John Chrysostom and Theophilus of Alexandria, an embassy led by Bishop Acacius of Beroea persuaded Siricius to recognise Flavian and readmit him to communion.

When the Spanish bishop Priscillian, accused of heresy by his fellow bishops, was executed by Emperor Magnus Maximus on a charge of magic, Siricius, with Ambrose of Milan and Martin of Tours, protested to the emperor. Older sources claim he acted against the Manichaeans in Rome, but this is likely a mistake, since Augustine does not mention it and the measures probably belong to Pope Leo I.

Siricius is sometimes said to be the first bishop of Rome to style himself pope. Other authorities note that pope was from the early 3rd century an honorific for any bishop in the West, and that Marcellinus, who died in 304, is the first bishop of Rome shown with the title; it was confined to the bishop of Rome in the West from the early 6th century. Siricius died on 26 November 399 and was succeeded by Anastasius I. He is buried in the basilica of San Silvestro, and his feast day is 26 November.
pope-sixtus-iv: Francesco della Rovere was born in Celle Ligure, near Savona, the son of Leonardo Beltramo di Savona della Rovere and Luchina Monteleoni. Accounts of his family differ: Mandell Creighton holds that his origin was so lowly that he lacked a surname and took the name from a Turin family he tutored. At the age of nine he joined the Franciscan Order. He studied at Bologna and Padua, received his doctorate at Padua in 1444 and lectured at several Italian universities. In 1464 he was elected Minister General of the Franciscan order, and in 1467 Pope Paul II made him a cardinal.

His reputation for piety helped the cardinals to choose him as pope on the unexpected death of Paul II, and he took the name Sixtus on 9 August 1471. He declared a crusade against the Ottoman Turks, but the fleet disbanded after the conquest of Smyrna, and he turned to temporal and dynastic matters. Six of the 34 cardinals he created were nephews. Pietro Riario rose to be a cardinal and the effective ruler of Rome until his death in 1474. Sixtus was personally involved in the Pazzi conspiracy of 1478 against Lorenzo de' Medici and his brother Giuliano, and answered its failure with an interdict and two years of war with Florence.

On 1 November 1478 he issued the bull establishing the Spanish Inquisition in Castile, under pressure from Ferdinand of Aragon, and in 1482 he condemned its worst abuses. In Rome he restored the aqueduct of the Acqua Vergine, rebuilt or restored over 30 churches, sponsored the Sistine Chapel and the Ponte Sisto, and began the first paving since antiquity. He donated Roman sculptures that founded a papal art collection, refounded and enlarged the Vatican Library, and in 1477 authorised the creation of Uppsala University.

Sixtus fell ill on 8 August 1484 and died on the evening of 12 August. The Medici envoy announced it with the words 'may God forgive him'. His tomb was destroyed in the Sack of Rome in 1527. His bronze funerary monument by Antonio del Pollaiuolo, completed by 1493, is now in the Treasury of St Peter's Basilica. Even the hostile chronicler Stefano Infessura agreed that his work in Rome deserved admiration.
pope-sixtus-v: Felice Piergentile was born on 13 December 1521 at Grottammare, in the Papal States, the son of Francesco Piergentile, a gardener who had taken refuge there from the oppression of the duke of Urbino. At the age of twelve he became a novice of the Franciscan Order, taking the name Fra Felice in 1535, and he finished his studies at the Franciscan Magna Domus of Bologna in September 1544.

He served as inquisitor general of the Venetian Holy Inquisition, but his severity and high-handed conduct led to quarrels, and in 1560 the Venetian government asked for his recall. Pius V made him a cardinal in 1570. Under Gregory XIII, whom he disliked, Cardinal Montalto lived in retirement at the Villa Montalto on the Esquiline Hill.

He was elected pope on 24 April 1585, taking the name Sixtus V in honour of Sixtus IV, also a Franciscan, and was crowned on 1 May 1585. He moved against lawlessness in the Papal States with severity. About 5,000 bandits were executed in the five years before his death, although 27,000 more were reputedly still at liberty in central Italy. To repair the finances he sold offices, established a new Monti and levied new taxes, storing a large surplus against emergencies such as a crusade.

Sixtus spent heavily on public works. The Acqua Felice aqueduct fed twenty-seven new fountains, new streets connected the great basilicas, four obelisks were erected, including the one in Saint Peter's Square, and the dome of St. Peter's was completed. Antiquities served as raw material: Trajan's Column and the Column of Marcus Aurelius became pedestals for statues of Peter and Paul, and the Septizodium of Septimius Severus was demolished for building materials. Reclamation of the Pontine Marshes reached more than 9,500 acres before it was abandoned on his death.

In 1588 the bull Immensa Aeterni Dei reorganised the Roman Curia, and he limited the College of Cardinals to seventy. In the same year the bull Effraenatam extended excommunication to contraception and to abortion at any stage. He renewed the excommunication of Queen Elizabeth I of England and promised a subsidy to the Armada of Philip II, payable only once the expedition had landed.

Sixtus fell ill with a fever on 24 August 1590 and died on 27 August. He was loathed by his political subjects as he lay dying, but later writers count him among the most important popes: impulsive, obstinate, severe and autocratic, yet open to large ideas and energetic in carrying them out.
pope-stephen-ii: Stephen was born in Rome, then part of the Exarchate of Italy within the Eastern Roman Empire, in 714. He was a Roman aristocrat. In 751 the Lombard king Aistulf captured the Exarchate of Ravenna and turned his attention to the Duchy of Rome. Stephen was selected on 26 March 752 to succeed Pope Zachary, following the recent death of the pope-elect, also named Stephen.

Relations between the papacy and the Eastern Roman emperors were strained in the mid-8th century because of the Isaurian dynasty's support for iconoclasm. Constantinople, itself beset by the Abbasid Caliphate to the south and the Bulgars to the north-west, could send no troops. Emperor Constantine V answered Stephen's repeated requests for help only with the advice to follow the ancient policy of Rome and set another Germanic people against the Lombards.

Stephen turned instead to Pepin the Short, king of the Franks, who had recently defeated an Umayyad invasion of Gaul. He travelled to Paris to plead in person against the Lombard and Muslim threats. On 6 January 754 he re-consecrated Pepin as king, and he anointed him at Saint-Denis in a ceremony that was evoked in the coronation rites of French kings until 1789. Pepin in return assumed the role of ordained protector of the Church.

At Quiercy the Frankish nobles consented to a campaign in Lombardy. Catholic tradition holds that Pepin there promised in writing to give the Church territories to be taken from the Lombards. This Donation of Pepin has not survived as a document, though later 8th-century sources quote from it. Pepin invaded Italy twice, and in 756 his army forced the Lombard king to surrender his conquests. Pepin conferred on the pope the territories of Ravenna, with cities such as Forlì, and the Pentapolis in the Marche, but left the Lombard kings their kingdom.

The Donation made the pope for the first time a temporal ruler over a strip of territory running diagonally across Italy from the Tyrrhenian to the Adriatic. The medieval popes could not exercise effective sovereignty over these mountainous lands, and the new Papal States kept the Lombard pattern of many small counties and marquisates, each centred on a fortified rocca. Charlemagne confirmed his father's donation in 774. Stephen II died on 26 April 757 and was succeeded by his brother Paul I. His pontificate marks the division between the Byzantine Papacy and the Frankish Papacy.
pope-sylvester-ii: Gerbert was born about 946, or at any rate between 945 and 950, in what was then the Duchy of Aquitaine. His exact birthplace is unknown. His parents took him to a nearby Benedictine abbey for instruction, and around 963 he entered the Monastery of St. Gerald of Aurillac. In 967 Count Borrell II of Barcelona took him to Catalonia to study mathematics. He studied under Bishop Atto of Vich and probably at Santa Maria de Ripoll, whose manuscripts came from Muslim Spain, especially Córdoba. In 973 Archbishop Adalberon appointed him a teacher at the cathedral school of Rheims.

Gerbert learned of Hindu–Arabic digits and applied them to the abacus, probably without the numeral zero. His pupil Richer recorded that he could calculate with it far faster than others using Roman numerals. He used an armillary sphere to teach astronomy, built a hydraulic organ with brass pipes at Rheims, and in 984 wrote to Abbot Eberhard of Tours about founding a large scientific library. His writings on arithmetic, geometry and astronomy were mainly teaching texts for his students.

After Adalberon died in 989, King Hugh appointed Arnulf as archbishop of Rheims. Arnulf was deposed in 991 for alleged treason and Gerbert succeeded him, but a synod in 995 declared the deposition invalid. Gerbert then taught Otto III, and in 998 Pope Gregory V made him archbishop of Ravenna. With imperial support he was elected pope in 999 and took the name Sylvester II, after Sylvester I, the adviser of Emperor Constantine I. He confirmed Arnulf at Rheims and acted against simony and concubinage among the clergy. In 1001 the Roman populace revolted and forced Otto III and Sylvester to flee to Ravenna. Otto died in 1002 on a third expedition to regain Rome.

Sylvester returned to Rome soon after the emperor's death, though the rebellious nobility remained in power. He died on 12 May 1003 and is buried in St. John Lateran. He was the first French pope. Later legends, found in William of Malmesbury and in a pamphlet by Cardinal Beno, a partisan of Emperor Henry IV, said that he stole a book of the dark arts from a Saracen philosopher, built a brazen head that answered yes or no, and made a pact with a demon.
pope-urban-ii: Urban II was baptised Eudes, or Odo, and was born into a noble family of Châtillon-sur-Marne in France. In 1050 he began his studies at the cathedral school of Reims. He became prior of the abbey of Cluny, and Pope Gregory VII named him cardinal-bishop of Ostia in about 1080. He was a prominent supporter of the Gregorian reforms, especially as legate in the Holy Roman Empire in 1084. Odo was elected by acclamation at a small meeting of cardinals and other prelates at Terracina in March 1088, after the short reign of Victor III.

From the start Urban faced Guibert, the former bishop of Ravenna, who held Rome as the antipope Clement III after the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV took the city in 1084. Urban continued Gregory's policies with more flexibility and diplomacy. Kept away from Rome, he toured northern Italy and France, and synods renewed condemnations of simony, lay investiture and clerical marriage. He upheld the excommunication of King Philip I of France over his marriage to Bertrade de Montfort.

At the Council of Piacenza in March 1095 he received an ambassador from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos asking for help against the Turkish tribes in Anatolia. At the end of the Council of Clermont, on 27 November 1095, he preached in the open air to a large crowd and called on them to take the Holy Land and the eastern churches from the Seljuks. He promised remission of sins to those who went, and the same indulgence applied to fighting the Moors in Spain.

No exact record of the Clermont speech exists. Five versions survive, written later and differing widely; Fulcher of Chartres, who was present, wrote his in about 1101. Urban's own letters speak more of liberating the eastern churches than of Jerusalem. Historians disagree about his motives: some point to reunion with the Eastern Church after the schism of 1054, others to his need for legitimacy against Clement III, others to fear of the Seljuks.

French armies removed Clement III from Rome in 1097. Urban died on 29 July 1099, fourteen days after Jerusalem fell but before the news reached Italy, and Paschal II succeeded him. Pope Leo XIII beatified him on 14 July 1881.
pope-urban-iv: Jacques Pantaléon was the son of a cobbler of Troyes. He studied theology and common law in Paris and became a canon of Laon and then Archdeacon of Liège. At the First Council of Lyon in 1245 he attracted the attention of Pope Innocent IV, who sent him twice on missions to Germany. On one of them he negotiated the Treaty of Christburg between the pagan Prussians and the Teutonic Knights. He became Bishop of Verdun in 1253, and in 1255 Pope Alexander IV made him Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem.

Pantaléon was at Viterbo seeking help for the Christians of the East when Alexander IV died. After a three-month vacancy, the eight cardinals chose him on 29 August 1261, and he was crowned on 4 September. He was the first pope elected without being a cardinal. A month before his election the Latin Empire of Constantinople had fallen to the Byzantines under Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos, and Urban tried without success to stir up a crusade to restore it.

He took up the quarrel in Denmark between Jakob Erlandsen, Archbishop of Lund, and King Christopher I. After the king's death the regent Margaret Sambiria released the archbishop, and Urban agreed to a dispensation allowing women to inherit the Danish throne. The main questions were still open when he died.

His attention was chiefly on Italy, where Ghibelline cities favouring the Hohenstaufen faced Guelf cities favouring the pope. His captain was the condottiere Azzo d'Este. To counter Manfred, the heir of Frederick II, he supported Charles of Anjou, Count of Provence, in seizing the Kingdom of Sicily. Charles promised not to claim imperial lands in northern Italy or the Papal States and to pay an annual tribute of some 10,000 ounces of gold, while the pope would work to block the election of Conradin as King of the Germans.

Urban died in Perugia on 2 October 1264, before Charles reached Italy, and his successor Pope Clement IV kept to his agreements. He issued the bull Transiturus on 11 August 1264 and asked Thomas Aquinas to write the texts for the Mass and Office of Corpus Christi, which included the hymns Pange lingua, Tantum ergo and Panis angelicus. Two centuries after his death he became a character in the legend of the Minnesänger Tannhäuser, first attested in 1430, in which he said that forgiving the knight was as impossible as his staff growing leaves.
pope-urban-viii: Maffeo Vincenzo Barberini was born in April 1568 at Barberino Val d'Elsa, the son of the Florentine nobleman Antonio Barberini and Camilla Barbadoro. His father died when he was three, and his mother took him to Rome, where his uncle Francesco Barberini, an apostolic protonotary, took charge of him. He was educated by the Jesuits and received a doctorate of law from the University of Pisa in 1589. He served as papal legate to King Henry IV of France from 1601, became Archbishop of Nazareth in 1604, and was made a cardinal by Pope Paul V in 1606.

Barberini was elected pope on 6 August 1623 after the death of Gregory XV and took the name Urban VIII. His papacy covered 21 years of the Thirty Years' War. His military policy aimed less at restoring Catholicism than at securing his independence in Italy. The Duchy of Urbino was incorporated into the papal dominions in 1626, and in 1641 he began the Wars of Castro against Odoardo Farnese, Duke of Parma and Piacenza, whom he excommunicated. Castro was destroyed and its duchy joined the Papal States; he was the last pope to extend papal territory.

He opposed Copernican heliocentrism and ordered the trial of Galileo after the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems appeared, in which the character Simplicio argues Urban's view. Galileo was summoned to Rome in 1633. Urban created 74 cardinals, among them his brother and two nephews, and his family amassed great wealth; Leopold von Ranke estimated 105 million scudi. His 1638 bull Commissum Nobis forbade the enslavement of natives living in the Jesuit Reductions of South America.

Urban was a patron of the arts and favoured the sculptor and architect Gian Lorenzo Bernini, who worked on the Palazzo Barberini, the baldacchino in St Peter's Basilica and the Fontana del Tritone. Bronze taken from the portico of the Pantheon prompted the saying that what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.

The papal debt rose from 16 million scudi at his election to 28 million by 1635 and 35 million by 1640. The cost of the Wars of Castro made him unpopular in Rome, and a crowd destroyed his bust on the Capitoline Hill after his death on 29 July 1644. His death is said to have been hastened by distress at the war's outcome. Giovanni Battista Pamphili succeeded him as Innocent X.
pope-zachary: Zachary was born in 679 into a family of Greek origin in the Calabrian town of Santa Severina. He was most probably a deacon of the Roman Church and as such signed the decrees of the Roman council of 732. He was chosen to succeed Gregory III on 3 or 5 December 741, and he was the last pope of the Byzantine Papacy.

Gregory III's alliance with the Lombard Duchy of Spoleto had put papal cities at risk when the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento rebelled. Zachary turned to King Liutprand the Lombard directly, and out of respect for him the king restored the territory the Lombards had seized and sent back captives without ransom. At the request of the Exarchate of Ravenna he persuaded Liutprand to abandon a planned attack on the city. The Liber pontificalis stresses his personal influence with Liutprand and with his successor Ratchis.

He corresponded with Archbishop Boniface of Mainz, confirmed the new bishoprics of Würzburg, Büraburg and Erfurt, and in 742 made Boniface papal legate to the Concilium Germanicum. In 745 he convened a synod in Rome to discourage the worship of angels. Asked by the Frankish Mayor of the Palace Pepin the Short whether it was better that the man with the royal power or the man without it should be king, he answered that it was better for the one who held the power, and soon afterwards the Frankish nobles abandoned the last Merovingian king, Childeric III. He also protested to the Byzantine emperor Constantine V about his iconoclastic policy.

Zachary built the original church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva near the Pantheon, over an ancient temple of Minerva, and restored the Lateran Palace. After Venetian merchants bought many slaves in Rome to sell to the Muslims of Africa, he forbade the traffic and paid the merchants their price, so that the slaves were freed.

He died on 15 March 752 and was buried in St Peter's Basilica. His elected successor, Stephen, died within days, so that Stephen II followed. The church historian Johann Peter Kirsch called him an excellent, capable, vigorous and charitable successor of Peter, and Peter Partner called him a skilled diplomat in a dark corridor of history.
popocatepetl: Popocatépetl is a stratovolcano in the eastern half of the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt, 70 kilometres south-east of Mexico City, from which it can be seen depending on atmospheric conditions. A high saddle, the Paso de Cortés, links it to its twin volcano Iztaccíhuatl to the north, and the two lie within the Izta-Popo Zoquiapan National Park. The cone is about 25 kilometres across at its base and has a steep-walled elliptical crater. Paleomagnetic studies put its age at about 730,000 years. Its glaciers shrank greatly in the 1990s, partly through warmer temperatures and largely through volcanic activity, and were gone by early 2001.

About 23,000 years ago a lateral eruption destroyed the volcano's ancient cone and sent an avalanche up to 70 kilometres from the summit. Since the mid-Holocene there have been three major Plinian eruptions, about 3,000, 2,150 and 1,200 years ago. The latter two buried the village of Tetimpa and preserved evidence of its preclassical culture. DNA analysis of teeth and bones suggests that a violent eruption in the mid to late first century CE may have caused the large migrations that settled Teotihuacan.

An expedition led by Diego de Ordaz made the first recorded European ascent in 1519, and the early sixteenth-century monasteries on its slopes are a World Heritage Site. More than fifteen major eruptions have been recorded since the Spanish arrived in 1519. After about half a century of dormancy, activity increased in 1991, and smoke has risen constantly from the crater since 1993.

The name comes from the Nahuatl words popōca, 'it smokes', and tepētl, 'mountain'. Mexicans call it El Popo, and in local lore it is Don Goyo, a spirit said to have met a villager of Santiago Xalitzina as an old man called Gregorio Chino Popocatépetl. He is held to warn the locals of eruptions, and on 12 March, the day of San Gregorio, they bring flowers and food to the volcano. In Tlaxcaltecan mythology Iztaccíhuatl was a princess who died of grief when she was falsely told that the warrior Popocatépetl had been killed in battle. The gods turned them into mountains, and Popocatépetl became a volcano.
popol-vuh: The Popol Vuh is a foundational sacred narrative of the Kʼicheʼ people of Guatemala, one of the Maya peoples. Its name is translated as Book of the Community or Book of Counsel, literally the book that pertains to the mat, because a woven mat served as a royal throne in ancient Kʼicheʼ society and symbolised the unity of the community. The story was preserved by oral tradition until about 1550, when it was written down.

Ximénez is generally thought to have borrowed a phonetic manuscript from a parishioner, a rendering of an oral recitation made near Santa Cruz del Quiché soon after Pedro de Alvarado's conquest of 1524. Adrián Recinos and Dennis Tedlock, comparing the genealogy at the end with dated colonial records, suggest a date between 1554 and 1558. The preamble states that it is written under the Law of God and Christianity because the old Popol Vuh can no longer be seen.

The text has no divisions in its manuscript, but popular editions follow the arrangement of Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg in 1861: a preamble and four books. Book One tells of the creation of animals and then humans; the first humans, made of earth and mud, crumbled, and the second, made of wood, were washed away in a flood, and the survivors became monkeys. The Hero Twins Hunahpú and Xbalanqué kill Vucub-Caquix and his sons in Book Two.

In Book Three their father Hun-Hunahpú and uncle Vucub-Hunahpú are killed at a ballgame in the underworld Xibalba. The twins, conceived after their father's death, defeat the Lords of Xibalba and become the sun and the moon. In Book Four humans are made successfully from maize, and the book follows the movement of the Kʼicheʼ. Depictions of the Hero Twins and other episodes appear on Maya ceramics, and a stucco frieze at El Mirador may show them.

In 1701 the Dominican priest Francisco Ximénez came to Santo Tomás Chichicastenango and transcribed the work, setting out the Kʼicheʼ and a Spanish translation in parallel columns. His manuscript passed to the University of San Carlos after the clerics were expelled from Guatemala in 1829–30. Carl Scherzer copied part of it in 1854, and in 1855 Charles Étienne Brasseur de Bourbourg took the volume to France. It reached the Newberry Library in Chicago through the collection of Edward E. Ayer, where Adrián Recinos rediscovered it in 1941. Translators include Delia Goetz, Munro Edmonson and Dennis Tedlock. In 2012 the text was declared intangible cultural heritage of Guatemala.
porcelain: Porcelain, also called china, is a ceramic material made by heating raw materials, generally including kaolinite, in a kiln to temperatures between 1,200 and 1,400 °C. Its strength and translucence, greater than those of other pottery, come mainly from vitrification and the formation of the mineral mullite at these temperatures. It is often regarded as the most prestigious type of pottery for its delicacy, strength and whiteness, and it is frequently glazed and decorated. It can be divided into three main categories: hard-paste, soft-paste and bone china. The term has no universal definition.

Porcelain was invented in China over centuries of experiment, starting with proto-porcelain wares of the Shang dynasty (1600–1046 BCE). By the Eastern Han dynasty (25–220 CE) glazed ceramics had developed into porcelain as the Chinese defined it, and by the late Sui and early Tang dynasties the requirements of whiteness and translucency had been met, in types such as Ding ware. Such wares were already exported to the Islamic world. Under the Song dynasty (960–1279) production became highly organised, and Jingdezhen has been the largest centre since the Yuan dynasty.

Portuguese merchants began direct sea trade with Ming China in 1517 and Dutch merchants in 1598, and blue-and-white wares reached Europe. Japan could not make its own porcelain until Korean potters, captured during the Japanese invasions of Korea (1592–1598), found clay near Arita. Japanese exports to Europe began around 1660.

Chinese porcelain was held in such esteem in Europe that china became a synonym for the Italian-derived word porcelain. In Saxony, Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus and Johann Friedrich Böttger produced the first hard, white European porcelain in 1708, and the Meissen factory was established in 1710. In 1712 the Jesuit François Xavier d'Entrecolles revealed many Chinese manufacturing secrets in letters published in Europe.

Factories followed at Vincennes, moved to Sèvres in 1756, and in England at Chelsea in 1743 and elsewhere. Thomas Frye patented a porcelain containing bone ash in 1749, the first bone china. The Imperial Porcelain Factory in Saint Petersburg was founded under an agreement of 1744 signed by Elizabeth of Russia. Porcelain is also used for electrical insulators, laboratory ware and tiles.
porfirio-diaz: Porfirio Díaz was baptized on 15 September 1830 in the city of Oaxaca, the sixth of seven children; his exact birth date is unknown. His father, José Faustino Díaz Orozco, was an illiterate workman employed by a firm of merchants, and his mother's mother was Mixtec. In 1845 he entered the seminary of Oaxaca to study for the priesthood, but he later changed to law, with the future president Benito Juárez among his mentors. He fought for the Liberals in the Reform War.

In the second French intervention Díaz fought at the Battle of Puebla in 1862. He was captured after the second siege of the city in 1863 and escaped. As commander in southern Mexico he resisted the French until Oaxaca City fell in 1865, and after a second escape he won the Battle of Miahuatlán on 3 October 1866 and retook Oaxaca City. In June 1867 he commanded the forces that took Mexico City.

When Juárez won the election of 1871 against Díaz, Díaz's supporters alleged fraud and rose in the Plan de la Noria, proclaimed on 8 November 1871. The Plan of Tuxtepec of 15 January 1876 opposed the re-election of President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, and Díaz took leadership of that rising. He took formal control of the presidency at the start of 1877 and won the election that year. In 1880 he stepped down in favour of his ally Manuel González, but in 1884 he abandoned the principle and held office continuously until 1911.

Díaz kept power by co-opting and coercing rival interests, and foreign investors from the United States, Britain, Germany and France were an important support of his regime. Railways financed from abroad opened remote regions to markets. Land surveys gave investors secure title, but they often wiped out the claims of communities that could not prove title, and survey companies kept one-third of the land they measured. Rural communities and small farmers lost their holdings. In 1910 Díaz allowed Francisco I. Madero to stand against him, then had him jailed during the election. Madero issued the Plan of San Luis Potosí calling for armed rebellion, and in May 1911, after the Federal Army suffered defeats, Díaz resigned in the Treaty of Ciudad Juárez.

Díaz went into exile in Paris, where he died of heart failure on 2 July 1915, aged 84. He was buried in the Cimetière du Montparnasse. Before his fall, an adulatory literature called Porfirismo portrayed him internationally as the statesman who had brought stability to Mexico. His legacy has been revised since the 1990s.
porrentruy: Porrentruy lies on both sides of the Allaine River in Ajoie, the bulge in the north-western corner of Switzerland that extends into France, at the foot of the Jura Mountains. It is the seat of the district of Porrentruy. The first trace of human presence is a Mesolithic tool, and the first known settlement dates from the Roman era. Ruins of a Gallo-Roman temple were found in 1983, and a kilometre of the Roman road from Augst to Mandeure lies nearby.

The name first appears in 1136 as Purrentru and presumably comes from the Latin pons Ragentrudis, the bridge of Ragentrud, wife of the Frankish king Dagobert I. The Counts of Pfirt built a castle on a defensible hill and made it the capital of Ajoie. In 1281 they sold the territory to the Bishop of Basel, but the Counts of Montbéliard refused to hand over the town.

Bishop Henry of Isny asked King Rudolph I of Habsburg for support, and after six weeks under siege the count gave way. On 20 April 1283 the king asked the bishop to grant the town a charter. The bishop sold Ajoie back to Montbéliard in 1386, but the town was again subject to the bishop from 1461.

The Reformation in Basel led the bishopric to move its headquarters to Porrentruy in 1527. Under Bishop Jakob Christoph Blarer von Wartensee, who reigned from 1575 to 1608, the town reached the height of its importance, with the castle enlarged and a Jesuit college built, and this prosperity ended with the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War in 1618, when the town was repeatedly occupied, besieged and plundered. On 27 April 1792 French Revolutionary troops drove out the bishop.

Porrentruy became the capital of a dependent republic, which France incorporated in 1793 as the Département du Mont-Terrible. In 1815 the town was given to the Canton of Bern. In the 19th century politics was marked by conflict between Liberal-Radicals and Catholic Conservatives, and the Radicals held the mayor's office from 1860 until 1972. The Canton of Jura, created on 1 January 1979, chose Delémont rather than Porrentruy as its capital.

Porrentruy had 6,675 inhabitants in 2018, most of whom speak French. It houses the cantonal courts, the archives of the former episcopal see of Basel and the cantonal library. The old town, with Gothic, Baroque and neoclassical buildings, is part of the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the castle, the Jesuit church and college and the Church of Saint-Pierre are listed as sites of national significance. The Porte de France, built in 1563, is the only medieval city gate left. In 1988 the town won the Wakker Prize for its architectural heritage.
port-au-prince: Port-au-Prince lies on the Gulf of Gonâve, whose bay acts as a natural harbour and has sustained economic activity since the Taíno. The city's layout resembles an amphitheatre, with commercial districts near the water and residential neighbourhoods on the hills above. The name means 'Prince's Port', but it is unclear which prince was meant: one theory points to Le Prince, a ship that arrived in 1706, though the islets in the bay were called les îlets du Prince as early as 1680.

The area was part of the Taíno chiefdom of Xaragua. Under Spanish rule the governor Nicolas Ovando, from 1503, had Taíno leaders killed at a feast, and violence and disease decimated the native population. The Spanish administration abandoned the region in 1606, and French filibusters arrived around 1650, setting up a hospital that gave the region the name Hôpital. Spain renounced its claims in 1697. Petit-Goâve was too malarial and Léogâne hard to defend, so Port-au-Prince was built in 1749, and in 1770 it replaced Cap-Français as capital of Saint-Domingue.

In 1804 it became the capital of independent Haiti. After the assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines in 1806 it was capital of the southern republic under Alexandre Pétion, and it became capital of all Haiti when the country was unified in 1820. American forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. On 12 January 2010 a magnitude 7.0 earthquake destroyed most of the central historic area, including the cathedral and the National Palace; Haiti's government estimated the death toll at 230,000.

Port-au-Prince is the capital and most populous city of Haiti, with a population estimated at 1,200,000 in 2022. It is the seat of the State University of Haiti, established in 1920, and the Presidential Palace stands on the Champ de Mars. Its cultural sites include the National Museum, founded in 1938, the National Archives and the National Library. Each November the national cemetery fills with people celebrating Fet Gede, a Vodou festival of the dead.
port-louis: Dutch settlers used the site as a harbour from 1606 and called the area the Harbour of Tortoises. Under French government it became the administrative centre of Mauritius, then called Ile de France, and a major reprovisioning halt for French ships passing between Asia and Europe around the Cape of Good Hope. The port is named in honour of King Louis XV, and the French governor Bertrand-François Mahé de La Bourdonnais contributed to the development of the city. Because the Moka Mountain Range shelters it from cyclone winds, it was chosen to house both the main harbour and the fort.

The port kept its value during the British occupation of the island in the Napoleonic Wars, when it helped Britain control the Indian Ocean. Port calls fell drastically after the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, but rose during the canal's seven-year closure from 1967. Modernisation in the late 1970s helped it remain the central point for all imports and exports of Mauritius.

Port Louis is the capital and most populous city of Mauritius, with 147,066 inhabitants at the 2018 census. The main harbour is the only official port of entry and exit for sea vessels in the country, and ships must be cleared there before visiting any other anchorage. It is the biggest port facility in the Indian Ocean region, with specialised terminals for sugar, fish and containers.

Many buildings reflect the city's colonial history, among them French colonial buildings of the 18th century such as Government House, the Jummah Mosque, Saint James Cathedral, a Tamil temple and the five-tier Port Louis Theatre. The Aapravasi Ghat is the remains of the immigration depot built by the British government to import labourers from India, Eastern Africa, Madagascar, China and Southeast Asia to work on the island's sugar estates. The Intercontinental Slavery Museum deals with slavery and indentured labour.
port-moresby: Port Moresby lies on the shores of the Coral Sea, on the south-western coast of the Papuan Peninsula of the island of New Guinea. The place where the city was founded has been inhabited by the Motu-Koitabu people for centuries. When Europeans first came, the largest settlement, Hanuabada, consisted of five villages of Motu and Koita people, who were organised into units called iduhu, somewhat like clans. Port Moresby was already an important centre of trade, visited by distant tribes of New Guinea.

In February 1873 the crew of HMS Basilisk, surveying the southern shore of New Guinea, reached the harbour. Captain John Moresby named it for his father, Admiral of the Fleet Sir Fairfax Moresby. Missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1873 and 1874. In 1883 the Premier of Queensland ordered the police magistrate Henry Chester to take possession of the eastern half of New Guinea, and on 4 April the Union Jack was raised at Port Moresby. A protectorate over the south-eastern coast was proclaimed in October 1884, and Special Commissioner Peter Scratchley chose the site as the colonial capital.

In 1906 the Papua Act transferred Papua, with Port Moresby as capital, to direct Australian rule. In the Second World War it was a prime objective of Imperial Japanese forces in 1942 and 1943, and by September 1942 it was an important Allied complex of bases. General Douglas MacArthur had his headquarters there from November 1942 to October 1944. It was granted city status in 1972 and became the capital of independent Papua New Guinea in September 1975.

Port Moresby is the capital and largest city of Papua New Guinea, with 756,754 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Although surrounded by Central Province, it forms its own National Capital District, and the Motu and Koitabu landowners are represented by the Motu Koita Assembly. The National Parliament Building, opened in 1984, and the National Museum and National Library stand in the suburb of Waigani.
port-of-spain: Port of Spain measures about 10.4 square kilometres and lies in the north-west of the island of Trinidad, between the Gulf of Paria, the Northern Range and the Caroni Swamp. The Laventille Hills form its eastern boundary. The climate is tropical monsoon, with little seasonal variation, a wet season from May to December and a dry season from January to April. The city proper is small. It forms the western end of a continuous built-up area, the East-West Corridor, which runs about 24 kilometres east to Arima.

The Spanish founded the town as Puerto España. The first settlement stood near an Amerindian fishing village called Cumucurapo, meaning place of the silk cotton trees, in the area now known as Mucurapo. The name Conquerabia is also recorded for an Amerindian settlement here. It may have been a separate village, another name for Cumucurapo, or the result of a misunderstanding by early Spanish settlers, who set up a port called Puerto de los Españoles, later Puerto de España. In 1560 a Spanish garrison was posted near the foot of the Laventille Hills.

Queen's Park Savannah, once sugar land, was bought by the town council in 1817 from the Peschier family. After an election in 1887 Michel Maxwell Philip became mayor, a post previously held only by white men, which the historian Bridget Brereton wrote perhaps marked the emergence of the coloured man as a political force in Trinidad. The city was also the de facto capital of the short-lived West Indies Federation.

Port of Spain is the capital and chief port of Trinidad and Tobago, with a municipal population of 49,867 in 2017. It is a retail and administrative centre, with most government offices, and a financial centre for the Caribbean. The Trinidad and Tobago Stock Exchange, the Central Bank, the Red House and Independence Square are in the downtown district. Queen's Park Savannah, about 110 hectares, is the largest open space. The pre-Lenten Carnival is the city's main annual festival, and the city was among the hosts of the 2007 Cricket World Cup.
port-vila: Port Vila lies on the west coast of the island of Efate, in Shefa Province, and is the capital and largest city of Vanuatu. Locally it is called simply Vila. The name of the area is Efil in the native South Efate language and Ifira in the neighbouring Mele-Fila language, of which Vila is a variant. Ifira is a small island in Vila Harbour where many traditional landowners live. The climate is tropical and maritime, with nearly constant trade winds, a wettest month in March and a driest in September.

Port Vila is the most important harbour and the centre of trade of Vanuatu. It is home to many languages: the daily lingua franca is Bislama, English and French are widely spoken, and many of Vanuatu's 138 indigenous languages are heard as people from rural areas move to the city.

Melanesian people have occupied the area for thousands of years. In 2004 an archaeological expedition at Teouma found a burial site of 25 tombs holding about three dozen skeletons of members of the Lapita culture; ceramics from the site were dated to the 13th century BCE. James Cook charted Efate in 1774 and named it Sandwich Island. His expedition did not land, but noted the good harbours and land suitable for European settlement.

In the late 19th century, when the islands were known as the New Hebrides, the economic balance began to favour the French by the 1890s, and they established large plantations. The French citizen Ferdinand Chevillard bought and cleared land around Port Vila for what was to be the largest French plantation on the island; it became instead the municipality of Franceville, which declared independence on 9 August 1889 and lasted only until June of the following year. After 1887 the territory was jointly administered by the French and the British, formalised in 1906 as an Anglo-French Condominium. During the Second World War Port Vila was an American and Australian airbase.

Port Vila had 49,034 inhabitants at the 2020 census, 16.3 per cent of the population of Vanuatu. The people are predominantly Melanesian, with small Polynesian, Asian, Australian and European populations. Christianity is the main religion in Vanuatu, and the city has a Roman Catholic cathedral, the Cathédrale du Sacré-Cœur, seat of the Diocese of Port Vila.

The Vanuatu Cultural Centre, which hosts the Vanuatu National Museum and the National Audiovisual Archives, stands at Saralana Park in front of the National Parliament. The city is one location of the University of the South Pacific, and is served by Bauerfield International Airport. It has been damaged by cyclones: Cyclone Uma in 1987 and Cyclone Pam on 13 March 2015, whose eye wall passed just east of the town.
porto: Porto stands on the Douro River estuary in northern Portugal, about 280 kilometres north of Lisbon, and its western part reaches the Atlantic coast. It is the capital of the Porto District. Its historic core, with the Luiz I Bridge and the Monastery of Serra do Pilar, was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, and has been a National Monument since 2001.

Before the Roman conquest the region was inhabited by the Gallaeci, a Celtic people, and findings suggest settlement at the mouth of the Douro as early as the eighth century BCE. As Portus Cale the town became a significant commercial hub under the Roman Empire, and its combined Celtic-Latin name has been cited as the origin of the name Portugal. In the Suebian and Visigothic periods it was a key centre for the spread of Christianity.

The Methuen Treaty of 1703 strengthened ties with England, and by 1717 English firms dominated the port wine trade. The Marquis of Pombal created a state-controlled wine company and demarcated the Douro, Europe's first protected wine region, which led in 1757 to the Revolta dos Borrachos, suppressed brutally by the authorities.

On 29 March 1809, during the Peninsular War, the Ponte das Barcas, a pontoon bridge, collapsed as civilians fled French forces, with an estimated 4,000 deaths. Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, then retook the city, crossing the Douro in wine barges. On 19 January 1919 monarchists declared the Monarchy of the North in Porto, which briefly served as the capital of the restored monarchy.

Porto is the second-largest city in Portugal, after Lisbon, with a metropolitan area of about 1.9 million people. Port wine takes its name from the city, since the cellars of Vila Nova de Gaia packaged and exported the fortified wine. In 2001 it shared the title of European Capital of Culture with Rotterdam.
porto-novo: Porto-Novo lies in the south of Benin on an inlet of the Gulf of Guinea, 13 kilometres from the Atlantic, from which it is separated by a lagoon. It stands about 30 kilometres east of Cotonou and 12 kilometres from the Nigerian border. Its commune covers 52 square kilometres. The city sits at the edge of the Dahomey Gap, which makes its climate drier than its nearness to the equator would suggest.

Porto-Novo was once a tributary of the Yoruba Oyo Empire, which offered it protection from the neighbouring Fon, who were expanding their power. The Yoruba called the city Ajashe, and the Gun called it Hogbonu. The first inhabitants were Yoruba-speaking, but a wave of migration from the region of Allada in the 1600s brought Te-Agbalin and his group to Ajashe in the late 16th century. In 1730 the Portuguese Eucaristo de Campos named the city Porto-Novo, because it resembled the city of Porto. It developed as a port for the transatlantic slave trade led by the Portuguese Empire.

In 1861 the British, who were active in nearby Nigeria, bombarded the city, and in 1863 the Kingdom of Porto-Novo accepted a French offer of protection. The neighbouring Kingdom of Dahomey objected to French involvement, and war broke out between the two states.
