In 1883 Porto-Novo was incorporated into the French colony of Dahomey and its dependencies, and in 1900 it became Dahomey's capital. The French sought to impose their language in every sphere of life and to stamp out the indigenous languages. Kings continued to rule in the city, officially and unofficially, until the death of the last, Alohinto Gbeffa, in 1976; from 1908 the king held the title of Chef supérieur.

Many Afro-Brazilians settled in Porto-Novo after returning to Africa following emancipation in Brazil, and Brazilian architecture and foods remain important to its cultural life. Under French rule, people often fled across the new border into British-ruled Nigeria to avoid harsh taxation, military service and forced labour. The border cuts through contiguous Yoruba- and Egun-speaking areas.

Porto-Novo is the official capital of Benin and the second-largest city, with 264,320 people at the census of 2013. The national parliament sits there, while the presidency and most other government institutions are in Cotonou. Its residents are mostly Yoruba and Gun. King Toffa's Palace, now a museum, and its surrounding district were added to UNESCO's Tentative List in 1996. The Da Silva Museum tells of the returning Afro-Brazilians, and the Alexandre Sènou Adandé Ethnographic Museum holds a large collection of Yoruba masks.
porto-torres: Porto Torres lies on the north-west coast of Sardinia, in the centre of the Gulf of Asinara, about 25 kilometres east of Cape Falcone and 15 kilometres from Sassari. It is a comune in the Metropolitan City of Sassari. The municipality is split into two parts of almost equal size: the town, with its industrial area and Roman ruins, on the flat Nurra plain, and the islands of Asinara and Isola Piana, which since 1997 form the Asinara National Park. Its full Latin name was Colonia Iulia Turris Libisonis, where Turris, tower, probably refers to a nuraghe or to Monte d'Accoddi.

Traces of human presence include the altar of Monte d'Accoddi, necropolises and, from the Bronze and Nuragic ages, the necropolis of Su Crucifissu Mannu, where two skulls show signs of surgery, possibly for relieving migraines and tumours or for religious reasons.

The town was founded in the 1st century BCE as Colonia Iulia Turris Libisonis, apparently by Julius Caesar, and was the first Roman colony on the whole island. Pliny calls it the only colony on Sardinia in his time, which suggests that there had been merely a fort before. The main road across the island ran from Caralis, Cagliari, to Turris, and a second road ran along the west coast. Remains include a temple dedicated to Fortune, baths, a basilica, an aqueduct and a bridge. It was an episcopal see in the early Middle Ages. The Romanesque basilica of San Gavino, built between 1065 and 1080, honours three saints said to have been beheaded in 303 under Diocletian and Maximian.

The city was inhabited until the 11th century, when most people moved to Sassari. In the Judicate of Logudoro its name became Torres. It was partly under Genoese hands until the early 15th century, when the Aragonese took it, and later it became part of the Kingdom of Sardinia. Torres was separated from Sassari in 1842, when the area around the basilica joined the fishermen's community by the port to form Porto Torres. It was bombed by the Allies on 18 April 1943.

Porto Torres is the second biggest seaport on the island after Olbia. The basilica of San Gavino, the largest Romanesque church in Sardinia, has two apses instead of the usual western facade and eastern apse, and its crypt holds several Roman sarcophagi; it was the main cathedral of the archdiocese of Sassari until 1441.
portoferraio: Portoferraio is a town and comune on the edge of the harbour of the island of Elba, in the province of Livorno in Tuscany, and is the island's largest municipality. Many of its buildings stand on the slopes of a tiny hill bordered on three sides by the sea, and the town centre is crowded around the small marina in a natural cove. The name has changed over time: Ferraia in Etruscan times, Fabricia under the Romans and Ferraio under the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, founded the town in 1548 as Cosmopoli, meaning Cosimo's City, to balance the presence of the Spanish citadel at Porto Azzurro. It had three forts, Forte Stella, Forte Falcone and Forte Inglese, and a massive line of walls, all still visible today. An edict of 1556 gave special privileges to all who settled in Cosmopoli, and the first Jews arrived at the beginning of the 17th century. A synagogue was built in 1631-1632, and in 1702 the Grand Duke ordered the Jews to live on a designated street, a small ghetto they could not leave after one in the morning.

The town remained with the Grand Duchy of Tuscany until the late 18th century, when its strategic position brought it into contention with France, Great Britain and Austria. A British garrison withstood the Siege of Porto Ferrajo in 1801, but the Treaty of Amiens in 1802 transferred the town to France. In 1814 it was handed over to Napoleon Bonaparte as the seat of his first exile. It grew quickly in the 19th century as the main port for shipping iron ore from Rio Marina to the mainland, whence its present name, meaning Iron Port. In 1860 it became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

In the Second World War German forces occupied Elba, and in late June 1944 an Allied force composed mainly of Free French troops liberated the island in a fight that lasted two days; Portoferraio was damaged by the fighting and bombing. Mining ended from the 1970s, and the town became an internationally known seaside destination. Its main sights are the three forts, an archaeological museum and Napoleon's house.
portoviejo: The Spanish captain Francisco Pacheco founded the town on 12 March 1535 near the coast as Villa Nueva de San Gregorio de Portoviejo. In 1628 it was moved inland to its present site because of Indian attacks. It is still known as the city of the Royal Tamarind Trees, after the tamarind plantations that once stood around it. Its Spanish name, San Gregorio de Portoviejo, survives in the private university that bears it.
An earthquake of magnitude 7.8 struck the region on 16 and 17 April 2016, and Portoviejo suffered over 300 deaths and heavy damage to buildings. The airport served as a shelter for those affected.

Portoviejo is the capital of Manabí Province, about 30 kilometres from the Pacific coast. It is the political and economic centre of the valley of the Portoviejo River, which also takes in the cantons of Santa Ana and Rocafuerte. About 110 square kilometres of that valley are cultivated every year. The city is important for coffee, cattle and fishing, has an agricultural-processing industry and has good road connections to Quito and Guayaquil.

Its cooking uses peanuts, bananas, cheese, corn and yucca, with dishes such as biche de pescado, corviche and bolón de verde. Ecuador has declared its gastronomy intangible heritage, and UNESCO has admitted the city to its Creative Cities Network in the category of gastronomy. Among its sights are the Mamey Ecological Park, a botanical garden of 50 hectares owned by the Technical University of Manabí, founded in 1952, the Metropolitan Cathedral of Jesus the Good Shepherd and the archaeological park of Cerro Jaboncillo outside the city.
portsmouth-new-hampshire: The Piscataqua River is a tidal estuary with a swift current, but it forms a good natural harbour, and it is the boundary between New Hampshire and Maine. The first European to explore and write about the area was Martin Pring in 1603. Colonists settled the west bank in 1630 and named the place Strawbery Banke after the wild strawberries growing there. Fort William and Mary, on what is now New Castle Island, protected the village. Fishing, lumber and shipbuilding were the principal businesses, and the port prospered as a link between upstream industries and merchants abroad.

Enslaved Africans were imported as labourers as early as 1645 and were integral to the city's prosperity, and Portsmouth took part in the Triangle Trade. The town was incorporated in 1653 and named after the colony's founder, John Mason, who had been captain of the English port of Portsmouth in Hampshire. Its shipyard completed its first ship for the Royal Navy, HMS Falkland, in 1696. After Queen Anne's War, Governor Joseph Dudley chose the town to host the negotiations for the 1713 Treaty of Portsmouth, which temporarily ended hostilities between the Abenaki and the colonies of Massachusetts Bay and New Hampshire.

In 1774 Paul Revere rode to Portsmouth to warn that the Royal Navy was coming to capture the port, and the Patriot government later moved the capital inland to Exeter. In 1779 nineteen enslaved African Americans of Portsmouth petitioned the state legislature for the abolition of slavery, citing the principles of the Revolution; the legislature tabled it, and New Hampshire abolished slavery in 1857. Portsmouth was incorporated as a city in 1849. A fire in 1813 burned 244 buildings, and the fire district created afterwards required brick walls and slate roofs, which gave the downtown its distinctive look. As mill towns grew on river power, Portsmouth's port declined.

Portsmouth is a city in Rockingham County, New Hampshire, with a population of 21,956 at the 2020 census. It keeps many Colonial, Georgian and Federal style houses, some now museums, and a Historic District Commission protects its architecture. The Captain Gregory Purcell house, where John Paul Jones boarded in 1781–1782 while his ship Ranger was built on Badger's Island in Kittery, is the only surviving property in the United States associated with him. The Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, founded in 1800 as the first federal navy yard, stands on Seavey's Island in Kittery, Maine, and was where the 1905 treaty ending the Russo-Japanese War was signed.
portuguese-empire: The Kingdom of Portugal arose from the Reconquista, the gradual reconquest of the Iberian Peninsula from the Moors. It became a separate kingdom in 1139, completed its reconquest of Moorish territory by reaching the Algarve in 1249, and was freed from the threat of Castile by the Treaty of Ayllón in 1411. Portuguese attention then turned overseas, first to the Marinid Sultanate in North Africa. Historians point to the chance to continue the crusade against Islam, the promise of glory and spoils for the military class, and the hope of expanding trade and addressing Portugal's economic decline.

Ceuta proved a disappointment, but Portugal held it and explored the Atlantic coast of Africa under Infante Henry the Navigator, who led and financed exploration until his death in 1460. Gil Eanes rounded Cape Bojador in 1434. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 divided the world outside Europe between Portugal and Spain along a meridian 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in May 1498 and in 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral made landfall on the Brazilian coast. Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate in 1510 and made it the capital of the East Indies.

In 1580 Philip II of Spain seized the Portuguese crown, beginning the Iberian Union, and the colonies were attacked by the Dutch Republic, England and France. Portugal had a smaller population and could not defend its overstretched trading posts, and the empire began a slow decline. After the Restoration War began in 1640, the gold of Minas Gerais, discovered in 1693, became the economic focus of the empire. In 1808, after a French invasion, John VI moved the royal court to Brazil, which became independent in the 1820s. The remaining colonies were forts and plantations on the African coast, Portuguese Timor and enclaves in India and Macau; the British Ultimatum of 1890 ended Portugal's Pink Map project to join Angola and Mozambique.

Under António de Oliveira Salazar the Estado Novo resisted decolonisation and renamed the colonies overseas provinces. Macau was returned to China on 20 December 1999. Eight former colonies have Portuguese as their official language, and with Portugal they belong to the Community of Portuguese Language Countries, which is the cultural and intergovernmental successor of the empire. Portuguese remains co-official with Cantonese in Macau. The Azores and Madeira are the only overseas territories still politically linked to Portugal.
portuguese-language: Portuguese belongs to the Ibero-Romance group, which evolved from several dialects of Vulgar Latin in the medieval Kingdom of Galicia and the County of Portugal. Before the Roman conquest the territory of modern Portugal was inhabited by the Gallaeci, Lusitanians, Celts, Iberians, Phoenicians, Greeks and Ligurians, whose languages were gradually replaced but left words behind, many of them about nature, agriculture and material culture. The Roman presence began in 218 BCE and full consolidation came in 19 BCE under Augustus. Latin spread outward from the cities and was tied to Roman citizenship. In the 5th century the Suebi and Visigoths conquered the peninsula and contributed about 500 Germanic words, many to do with warfare.

Portuguese has a rich system of nasal vowels, and its spelling is largely phonemic but shaped by etymology and tradition. Its verbs have kept more inflections from classical Latin than any other major Romance language, and it has features that other Romance languages, except Galician and Fala, lack, among them the future subjunctive and the personal infinitive. Its lexicon of around 228,500 entries comes largely from Latin, with more than 3,000 words traced to pre-Roman Celtic sources and loanwords from Germanic, Arabic, African, Amerindian and Asian languages. It is fully mutually intelligible with Galician, with which it shares its origin in the medieval language Galician-Portuguese. Two standard varieties are used for learning, European and Brazilian Portuguese.

Colonial expansion carried Portuguese across the world. It is the official language of eight countries: Portugal, Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, São Tomé and Príncipe and Timor-Leste, and shares official status in Macau and Equatorial Guinea. There are about 267 million speakers in all, some 200 million of them in South America and 30 million in Africa. In Cape Verde and Guinea-Bissau a Portuguese-based creole is also widely spoken. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries unites all the officially Lusophone nations, and recent spelling agreements have tried to give the language one spelling everywhere.
porus: Porus is known only from Greek sources. His kingdom lay between the Hydaspes (Jhelum) and Acesines (Chenab) rivers, and Strabo noted that it held almost 300 cities. Scholars differ on who he was. Michael Witzel conjectures that he was a king of the Pūrus, a Vedic tribe, and Hem Chandra Raychaudhuri largely agreed. Ishwari Prasad and others argue that he was a Shurasena, because Quintus Curtius Rufus says his vanguard carried a banner of Herakles.

Porus was hostile to the neighbouring polity of Taxila, whose earlier ruler Ambhiraj, his maternal uncle, he had assassinated. When Alexander the Great crossed the Indus, Omphis, the ruler of Taxila and son of Ambhiraj, greeted him and hoped to use his forces to bring Porus and Abisares to submission. Abisares offered submission, but Porus refused.

At the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BCE, Alexander crossed the river on a stormy night just before dawn, while the rest of his forces were spread along the bank to distract Porus. Porus took a defensive position on the plain, with infantry and elephants in front and cavalry and chariots on the wings. Alexander's cavalry charged his left wing, and his cavalry was driven back into the infantry lines, causing confusion.

The mahouts were killed with sarissas and the elephants pushed back into Porus' own columns. Porus refused to surrender and wandered on an elephant until he was wounded and his force routed. The exact site and strengths are unknown because the sources differ widely, and A. B. Bosworth warns that they are highly exaggerated. Alexander founded Nicaea at the site of the victory and Bucephalous in memory of his horse.

Alexander, impressed by Porus, did not depose him. He restored and enlarged his territory, annexing that of Glausaes, and Omphis was reconciled with him. Porus joined a campaign east of the Acesines against a cousin of his and took part in the siege of Sangala. When Alexander turned back at the Hyphasis, Porus was left as de facto ruler of the entire territory east of the Hydaspes, with no European satrap beside him.

After Alexander died in 323 BCE and Perdiccas was murdered in 321 BCE, the regent Antipater, according to Diodorus, recognised Porus' authority over the territories along the Indus. Eudemus, who had been Alexander's satrap in the Punjab, killed him. Porus reportedly died sometime between 321 and 315 BCE. In the medieval Alexander Romance he is defeated by Alexander in single combat, and he has appeared in many later films, series and games.
poseidon: The earliest attested form of the god's name is written in Linear B as Po-se-da-o and Po-se-da-wo-ne. If the surviving tablets can be trusted, these names occur more often than that of Zeus. A feminine variant, po-se-de-ia, suggests a lost consort goddess, in effect the precursor of Amphitrite.

Poseidon was the chief god at Pylos and Thebes, and carried the title wanax, meaning king or protector, and the title Earth-shaker. He had a chthonic aspect, being called Lord of the Underworld, and in the Mycenaean period his cult was probably tied to protecting the palace. In a culture that depended heavily on the sea, there is not enough evidence that he was then linked with it.

Poseidon is one of the twelve Olympians. In the standard myth he was born to the Titans Cronus and Rhea and swallowed by his father, then freed when Zeus gave Cronus an emetic. According to Homer and Apollodorus, Zeus, Poseidon and Hades divided the world by lot: Zeus received the sky, Poseidon the sea and Hades the Underworld.

His weapon was a trident forged by the Cyclopes. In Arcadia he was related to Demeter and Despoina and worshipped as a horse and a god of waters, and most Greeks saw him as tamer or father of horses who struck the ground with his trident to create springs.

Several myths tell of his contests for cities. Athena became patron of Athens after a competition in which Poseidon struck the Acropolis with his trident and raised a salt spring, while he remained present there through his surrogate Erechtheus. He fathered Theseus with Aethra, and in the Odyssey he punished Odysseus for blinding his son Polyphemus, delaying his return by ten years.

His worship spread over Greece and southern Italy, and he was specially honoured in the Peloponnese and the Ionic cities. The city names Poteidaia in the Chalkidiki peninsula and Poseidonia, a Greek colony in Italy later known as Paestum, show the weight of his cult. The Panhellenic Isthmian Games at Corinth were held in his honour and included athletic and musical contests and horseracing.

At Mycale in Ionia, representatives of twelve cities held the Panionia, a festival of Poseidon Helikonios that became the meeting place of the Ionian League. Athens had a month named Poseidaon in its calendar. A Homeric Hymn addresses him as tamer of horses and saviour of ships. His Roman equivalent is Neptune.
posidonius: Posidonius, nicknamed the Athlete, was born around 135 BCE into a Greek family in Apamea, a Hellenistic city on the Orontes River in northern Syria. As a young man he moved to Athens and studied under Panaetius, the leading Stoic philosopher of the age. After Panaetius died in 110 BCE he settled in Rhodes, gained citizenship, and kept a school there that became the leading institution of its time.

From about the 90s BCE he made voyages round the Mediterranean to gather scientific data and observe peoples. At Gades on the Atlantic coast of Hispania he saw tides much higher than in the Mediterranean and held that daily tides follow the Moon's orbit. In Gaul he studied the Celts and noted that they honoured the Druids, whom he saw as philosophers.

On Rhodes Posidonius held office as one of the Prytaneis, the most important political office there. He was chosen for at least one embassy to Rome, in 87–86 BCE, during the First Mithridatic War. Under him Rhodes eclipsed Athens as the centre of Stoic philosophy, drawing Greek and Roman students.

Pompey attended a lecture in 66 BCE and again in 62 BCE, when Posidonius, suffering from gout, answered his pain by declaring that it would never persuade him it was an evil. Cicero attended his lectures in his twenties and called him 'my teacher'; Posidonius politely declined to write on Cicero's consulship. His grandson Jason of Nysa succeeded him as head of the school.

His works survive only in fragments, though the titles of more than twenty are known. He wrote on physics, astronomy, geography, history, ethics and mathematics, and held that philosophy was the master art that alone could explain the cosmos. A Stoic who also drew on Plato and Aristotle, he saw the universe as an interconnected whole. He estimated the Sun's distance at 9,893 times the Earth's radius and reasoned that the Moon causes the tides.

In his Histories he continued Polybius's account of Roman expansion, covering 146–88 BCE in 52 volumes. His lost geography of the Celts was a main source for Diodorus Siculus, Strabo, Caesar and Tacitus. Strabo called him the most learned of the philosophers of his time.
positivism: Positivism holds that all genuine knowledge is either true by definition or positive, meaning facts derived by reason and logic from sensory experience. It rejects other ways of knowing, such as intuition, introspection or religious faith. Although the approach has recurred in Western thought, modern positivism was first set out in the early nineteenth century by Auguste Comte. Massive advances in the natural sciences then encouraged thinkers such as Henri de Saint-Simon, Pierre-Simon Laplace and Comte to believe that the scientific method should replace metaphysics.

Comte first described the outlook in The Course in Positive Philosophy, published between 1830 and 1842, and followed it in 1844 with A General View of Positivism. The first three volumes of the Course dealt with the existing physical sciences, and the last two stressed the coming of a science of society. For Comte the physical sciences had to arrive first, before humanity could turn to the complex science of society itself.

Comte's sociological positivism holds that society, like the physical world, operates according to scientific laws. Fabien Magnin, the first working-class adherent, led a movement called Proletarian Positivism, and Comte named him his successor as president of the Positive Society. Eugène Sémérie described positivism as a political party that aimed to reconcile order with progress.

Émile Durkheim rejected much of Comte's philosophy but kept its method, holding that the social sciences continue the natural sciences into human conduct. He set up the first European department of sociology, at the University of Bordeaux in 1895, and published Suicide in 1897, in which he compared suicide rates among Catholic and Protestant populations. Logical positivism grew from the Vienna Circle, whose doctrines Otto Neurath, Hans Hahn and Rudolf Carnap summarised in a pamphlet of 1929.

Positivism has been criticised for reductionism. Giambattista Vico asserted in 1725 the superiority of the science of the human mind, and Wilhelm Dilthey argued that only humanistic knowledge gives insight into thoughts, feelings and desires. At the turn of the twentieth century German sociologists, among them Max Weber, introduced methodological antipositivism, which concentrates on cultural norms and values seen from a subjective perspective. In 1934 Karl Popper argued in The Logic of Scientific Discovery against verificationism, holding that an observation can at best falsify a statement. It remains popular, but it has declined since the turn of the twentieth century under criticism from antipositivists and critical theorists.
potala-palace: The palace is named after Mount Potalaka, regarded in Buddhist tradition as the abode of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. It stands on Marpo Ri, the Red Hill, in the centre of the Lhasa Valley, on the site of an earlier palace attributed to Songtsen Gampo and traditionally dated to 637. Two chapels at its northwest corner, the Phakpa Lhakhang and the Chogyel Drupuk, preserve parts of that palace; the second is a cavern identified as Songtsen Gampo's meditation cave.

Ngawang Lozang Gyatso, the Fifth Dalai Lama, began the present building in 1645 after his adviser Konchog Chophel, Thirty-fifth Ganden Tripa of the Gelug school, pointed out that the site lay between Drepung and Sera monasteries and the old city of Lhasa and suited a seat of government. The outer structure took three years, the interior and its furnishings 45. The Dalai Lama and his government moved into the White Palace in 1649, and the Red Palace was added between 1690 and 1694.

The Potala is built in the dzong style at about 3,700 metres and measures 400 metres from east to west and 350 from north to south. Its sloping stone walls average 3 metres thick and 5 at the base, and copper was poured into the foundations as protection against earthquakes. The complex rises thirteen stories and holds more than 1,000 rooms, 10,000 shrines and some 200,000 statues. The crimson Red Palace contains the principal halls, chapels and shrines of past Dalai Lamas, and a Kalachakra Mandala was made there in the 1690s.

From 1649 until 1959 the palace was the residence of the Dalai Lamas. It was damaged in the Tibetan uprising of 1959, when Chinese shells were fired into its windows, and it became a museum complex after the annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China. It escaped damage in the Cultural Revolution in 1966 through the intervention of Zhou Enlai. The Potala Palace was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994, after a restoration in 1989–1994.
potato: The potato is the underground stem tuber of Solanum tuberosum, a perennial in the nightshade family. Its tubers are not roots but stems that form from thickened rhizomes at the tips of long thin stolons. Wild potato species occur from the southern United States to southern Chile. Genetic studies show that the cultivated potato has a single origin, in the area of present-day southern Peru and extreme northwestern Bolivia, around Lake Titicaca, where pre-Columbian farmers domesticated it about 7,000 to 10,000 years ago from a species in the Solanum brevicaule complex.

The earliest archaeologically verified tuber remains come from the coastal site of Ancon in central Peru and date to 2500 BCE. The most widely cultivated variety, Solanum tuberosum tuberosum, is indigenous to the Chiloé Archipelago and has been grown by the local indigenous people since before the Spanish conquest.

The English word potato comes from the Spanish patata, in turn from the Taíno batata, which meant sweet potato and not the plant now called simply the potato. The name spud comes from spudde, a short and stout knife or dagger in the 15th century, and was transferred to the tuber from around 1840.

The Spanish introduced potatoes to Europe in the second half of the 16th century. Selective breeding has since produced over 5,000 varieties, about 3,000 of them in the Andes, mainly in Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Chile and Colombia. Over 100 cultivars might be found in a single valley, and a dozen or more might be maintained by a single agricultural household. Most potatoes are self-incompatible and bear no useful fruit when self-pollinated, which makes crop breeding difficult, since all sexually produced plants must be hybrids.

The potato has been an essential crop in the Andes since the pre-Columbian era. The Moche culture of northern Peru represented it in ceramics, both naturally and as human figures. In Inca mythology Axomamma, a daughter of the earth mother Pachamama, is the goddess of potatoes, who ensured the fertility of the soil and the growth of the tubers. In Haudenosaunee mythology the first potatoes grew out of the feet of Earth Woman after she died giving birth to her twin sons, Sapling and Flint. Chuño, a freeze-dried potato product, is traditionally made by Quechua and Aymara communities of Peru and Bolivia.

In Europe the potato became an essential crop, especially in Northern and Eastern Europe. In the late 19th century numerous images of potato harvesting appeared in European art, including the works of Willem Witsen and Anton Mauve. Raw potatoes contain toxic glycoalkaloids, chiefly solanine and chaconine, and tubers exposed to light can become toxic.
potomac-river: The Potomac has two sources. The North Branch rises at the Fairfax Stone in West Virginia and the South Branch near Hightown in Highland County, Virginia, and the two meet just east of Green Spring in Hampshire County, West Virginia. From there the river flows towards Washington, D.C. and the Chesapeake Bay, passing through five geological provinces: the Appalachian Plateau, the Ridge and Valley, the Blue Ridge, the Piedmont Plateau and the Atlantic coastal plain.

At Little Falls the river drops from the Piedmont to the coastal plain at the Atlantic Seaboard fall line, and below it the tides reach the river. The estuary widens until it is 11 statute miles wide at its mouth between Point Lookout, Maryland, and Smith Point, Virginia. The river's drainage area is about 14,700 square miles, and it forms the boundary between Maryland and Washington, D.C. on one bank and West Virginia and Virginia on the other.

The Potomac has long been inhabited by Native Americans. Before European contact the region was governed by the Algonquian Piscataway confederacy and its allies, under a leader called the Tayac, until power shifted south to the Powhatan confederacy. The name is a European spelling of Patawomeck, the name of a village on the southern bank. Captain John Smith explored the river in 1608, and his map was published in London in 1612.

George Washington was born in, surveyed and spent most of his life within the Potomac basin. He intended the Patowmack Canal to link the Tidewater region near Georgetown with Cumberland, Maryland. It was begun in 1785, completed in 1802 and closed in 1830. The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal then ran along the Maryland bank from 1831 to 1924. The First United States Congress stated by an act of 16 July 1790 that the capital should be on the river.

In the American Civil War the river was a boundary between the Union and the Confederacy, and the Union's largest army was named the Army of the Potomac. Robert E. Lee crossed it twice to invade the North, in the campaigns that ended at Antietam on 17 September 1862 and Gettysburg on 1 to 3 July 1863. Maryland and Virginia long disputed control of the river; the 1877 Black-Jenkins Award gave Maryland the river as far as the low-water mark on the Virginia side.

Washington, D.C. lies entirely on its banks, as does Mount Vernon, the home of George Washington, and the river is nicknamed the Nation's River. The Washington Aqueduct began drawing the capital's drinking water from the Potomac in 1864, and the river supplies about 78 per cent of the water used in the Washington area. Its navigable parts were designated a National Recreation Trail in 2006.
potosi: Potosí lies at a nominal 4,067 metres above sea level, one of the highest cities in the world, at the foot of the Cerro de Potosí, also called the Cerro Rico or rich mountain, whose peak reaches 4,824 metres. The mountain is a dacite volcanic dome with silver-bearing veins and is honeycombed by workings that reach depths of 1,150 metres. At peak production in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries the ore contained up to 40 per cent silver.

The city was founded in 1545 as a mining town, and the indigenous prospector Diego Huallpa is traditionally credited with discovering the Cerro Rico. In the second half of the 16th century the mountain produced an estimated 60 per cent of all silver mined in the world. The easily smelted ore was exhausted by 1565, and output recovered through mercury amalgamation, first the patio process of Bartolomé de Medina and from 1609 a pan process invented at Potosí. The crown licensed private miners and taxed them, with a 20 per cent levy called the quinto. By about 1603 there were roughly 6,000 Europeans, 5,000 Africans and at least 120,000 native Andeans in the city, the second largest in the world after London.

Indigenous workers were drafted into the mines under the mita, based on an older Andean system of labour for public works. Thirteen thousand men a year were conscripted, about one in seven adult men of the indigenous population in the area covered. They carried ore up ladders in shafts lit by candles and died from falls and pneumonia, while mercury poisoned many in refining. Historians differ on the mita's weight: Noble David Cook notes that in 1603 only 5,100 of 58,800 indigenous workers were mitayos, whereas Peter Bakewell stresses that many other workers were former mitayos or mitayos in their off weeks.

Potosí is the capital of the Department of Potosí in Bolivia. Its historic centre, with a large amount of preserved colonial architecture, forms with the Cerro Rico a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Mining changed from silver to tin in 1891 and continued in tin until 1985, and the city is still a mining centre.
potsdam: Potsdam lies on the River Havel, a tributary of the Elbe, about 25 kilometres south-west of Berlin's city centre. The area was formed from a series of large moraines left after the last glacial period, and the hilly landscape holds about 20 lakes and rivers in and around the city, among them the Griebnitzsee, Templiner See and Jungfernsee. Only a quarter of the city is built up, the rest remaining green space. The highest point is the Kleiner Ravensberg, at 114 metres. The name of the city and of many of its boroughs is of Slavic origin; it seems originally to have been Poztupimi, perhaps from a West Slavonic term meaning beneath the oaks.

The area shows signs of occupation since the Bronze Age. After the migrations of the Germanic peoples, Slavs moved in, and Potsdam was probably founded after the 7th century as a settlement of the Hevelli tribe centred on a castle. It was first mentioned in 993, when Emperor Otto III gave the territory to Quedlinburg Abbey, and it received its town charter in 1345. In 1573 it was still a small market town of about 2,000 people, and the Thirty Years' War cost it nearly half its population. It had been a Hohenzollern possession since 1415, and in 1660 the Elector of Brandenburg chose it as a hunting residence.

The Edict of Potsdam of 1685 offered religious freedom and made the city a centre of European immigration, drawing Huguenots and settlers from Russia, the Netherlands and Bohemia. The royal residences were built mainly under Frederick the Great, including Sanssouci, by Georg Wenzeslaus von Knobelsdorff, in 1744.

When Berlin was capital of Prussia and then of the German Empire, the court remained in Potsdam, and in 1914 Emperor Wilhelm II signed the Declaration of War in the New Palace. The city lost its status as a second capital in 1918. On 21 March 1933 Paul von Hindenburg and Adolf Hitler shook hands in Potsdam's Garrison Church in the ceremony known as the Day of Potsdam. Allied bombing raids, notably on the Old Town on 14 April 1945, severely damaged the city.

Potsdam is the capital and largest city of the German state of Brandenburg and part of the Berlin/Brandenburg Metropolitan Region. Its parks and palaces, among them Sanssouci and Cecilienhof Palace, form Germany's largest World Heritage Site. Babelsberg in the south-east has a film studio founded in 1912, the oldest large-scale film studio in the world, and Potsdam was named a UNESCO City of Film in 2019. The city became a centre of science in the 19th century, and it has the University of Potsdam and more than 30 research institutes.
potsdam-declaration: At the start of the Potsdam Conference the United States delegation considered a proclamation demanding Japan's unconditional surrender in the name of the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union and China. The text went through many drafts. Joseph Stalin declined to endorse it, since the Soviet Union was not yet at war with Japan, and committed instead to subscribing once it entered the war. On 24 July President Harry S. Truman gave Winston Churchill a draft, and the American delegation adopted all the British amendments.

Chiang Kai-shek was not at the conference, so China was asked by telegram. He agreed to one amendment, listing the President of the National Government of the Republic of China before the British prime minister. Churchill authorised the text on 26 July before submitting his resignation that evening, after his unexpected election defeat. The signatures of Chiang and Churchill were in fact in Truman's handwriting.

The declaration demanded the elimination for all time of the authority of those who had misled the Japanese people into world conquest, the occupation of points in Japanese territory to be designated by the Allies, and the limiting of Japanese sovereignty to Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, Shikoku and minor islands. Japanese forces were to be disarmed and sent home. It stated that the Allies did not intend the Japanese to be enslaved as a race or destroyed as a nation, but that war criminals would receive stern justice.

It also offered the revival of democratic tendencies, freedom of speech, religion and thought, industries that would sustain the economy but not rearmament, and the withdrawal of occupying forces once a peaceful and responsible government had been established. It never mentioned the emperor, and left unstated the number of occupation points, the fate of the minor islands and the form of Allied control. The warning of prompt and utter destruction has been read as a veiled reference to the atomic bomb, which was not named.

The declaration was broadcast to Japan and more than 3 million leaflets describing it were dropped, but it was never sent through diplomatic channels. In Tokyo, Foreign Minister Shigenori Tōgō and others felt it must be accepted, but the war minister and the chiefs of staff opposed it. Prime Minister Kantarō Suzuki described the policy as mokusatsu, which the United States took as rejection. Hiroshima was bombed on 6 August and Nagasaki on 9 August, the day the Soviet Union declared war on Japan.

The emperor announced acceptance in a radio broadcast, and surrender documents were signed on the USS Missouri on 2 September 1945. The declaration then served as the legal basis for the occupation's reforms. Historians still debate whether the demand for unconditional surrender stalled possible peace negotiations.
pound-sterling: The basic unit of currency in medieval England was the silver penny, or sterling, weighing about one 240th of a tower pound. Two hundred and forty of these coins made a pound of sterlings, a term later shortened to pound sterling and kept in accounting even after the sterling had ceased to circulate. The earliest known instances occur in Orderic Vitalis's 12th-century Historia Ecclesiastica, which mentions librae sterilensium. The sign £ derives from the capital L for the Roman libra, the pound weight, which became an English unit defined as the tower pound. A pound sterling was literally a tower pound of sterling silver.
The pound emerged after the adoption of the Carolingian monetary system in England about 800, and by the ninth century it was a unit of account equal to 240 silver pence.

In 1158 King Henry II introduced a new coinage, the Tealby penny, in which a tower pound of 92.5 per cent silver was minted into 240 pennies. This alloy, called sterling silver, is harder than the 99.9 per cent fine silver traditionally used, and its coins wore down less quickly. Under Edward III the introduction of gold coins received from Flanders as payment for English wool brought economic and trade opportunities but also unsettled the currency for the next 200 years, and the first changes of 1344 reduced the penny to about 20 grains of sterling silver. The demands of the Hundred Years' War led to further debasements towards the end of the reign of Henry IV.

Before decimalisation in 1971 the pound was divided into 20 shillings and each shilling into 12 pence, making 240 pence to the pound. The abbreviations £sd, for pounds, shillings and pence, recall the Roman libra, solidus and denarius. Coins had special names, among them florin, crown, farthing, sovereign and guinea. On Decimal Day in 1971 the pound was divided into 100 pence.

Sterling is the currency of the United Kingdom and of nine of its dependent territories, and it was formerly the currency of the Kingdom of England. It is the world's oldest currency in continuous use since its inception. The Bank of England is its central bank. Sterling was historically also used to varying degrees by the colonies and territories of the British Empire, and the currency of the Crown Dependencies and of a third of the British Overseas Territories is either sterling or pegged to it at par. In wholesale foreign exchange markets the sterling and US dollar rate is called cable, from the mid-19th century, when it was transmitted by transatlantic cable.
pozega-croatia: Požega lies at an elevation of 152 m in the south-western part of the Požega basin, a fertile valley formed by the Slavonian mountains of Požeška Gora, Psunj, Papuk, Krndija and Dilj. The valley has been important since antiquity, and its Roman name was Vallis Aurea, 'golden valley'. The Latin name of the town was Incerum. Between 1921 and 1991 the town was called Slavonska Požega. Its main occupations include farming, viticulture, livestock breeding, metal-processing, food, textile, timber and printing industries.

The first mention of Požega is in the Gesta Hungarorum, which names it among three forts of Slavonia that were conquered. The fortress, on a hill in the present town centre, was probably built in the 11th century, and the town is documented in a charter of Andrew II of 11 January 1227. It was the residential estate of the Croatian-Hungarian queen, and its citizens enjoyed privileges that matched those of a free royal city. From the late 14th century Ottoman raids caused economic decline, and the town walls built in the 15th century did not prevent the Turks from seizing Požega in 1537.

In about 150 years of Ottoman rule Požega was the seat of a sanjak. The town was liberated by citizens led by the friar Luka Ibrišimović on 12 March, a day the city now observes as its own; the Ottomans retook it in 1690 and held it for a year. Under Habsburg rule from the 1690s the town grew. A grammar school opened in 1699, Jesuits built a theatre in 1727, and the Academia Posegana, with faculties of philosophy and theology, ran from the early 1760s. In 1765 Empress Maria Theresa gave the town a royal free city charter. In 1847 it was the first city in Croatia to use the Croatian language officially, and it was nicknamed the Slavonian Athens.

Požega is a city in western Slavonia and the administrative centre of Požega-Slavonia County, with a population of 22,364 at the 2021 census. Its central square, with the Church of the Holy Spirit, the Franciscan monastery, the Town House and a plague column, is considered one of the most beautiful in Croatia. The Cathedral of St. Teresa of Ávila was built with Maria Theresa's support. The Gymnasium, founded in 1699, is one of Croatia's oldest educational institutions, and Požega has been a diocesan see since 1997.
poznan: Poznań lies on the River Warta in west Poland, within the Greater Poland region. Its highest point, at 157 metres, is the summit of Morasko hill in the north, within the Morasko meteorite nature reserve, and its lowest, at 60 metres, lies in the Warta valley. The name probably derives from the Polish verb poznać, 'to meet' or 'to know', marking the area as a meeting place. The earliest references are in the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg, which mentions a bishop of Poznań in 970 and the city in 1005.

For centuries before the Christianization of Poland, Poznań was an important cultural and political centre of the Western Polans. A fortified stronghold stood between the Warta and Cybina rivers on what is now Ostrów Tumski, and Mieszko I built one of his main gords there. His baptism in 966, seen as a defining moment in the Christianization of the Polish state, may have taken place in Poznań.

After the baptism construction began of Poznań's cathedral, the first in Poland, and the city was the main seat of Bishop Jordan, the first missionary bishop sent to Poland. The Congress of Gniezno in 1000 established the country's first permanent archbishopric at Gniezno, though Poznań kept bishops of its own. The cathedral was the burial place of early Piast monarchs, among them Mieszko I, Bolesław I the Brave, Casimir I, Przemysł I and Przemysł II. The Town Hall was rebuilt in Renaissance style after a fire in 1536 and finished in 1560.

In the later 17th and most of the 18th century wars and occupations devastated the city. Prussian authorities later merged the walled city with its suburbs and took down the old walls in the early 19th century. The Treaty of Versailles awarded Posen to the new Poland. From 1939 to 1945 Poznań was the capital of the Reichsgau Wartheland, part of Nazi Germany, and many Polish inhabitants were executed, arrested, expelled or used as forced labour.

Poznań is the administrative capital of the Greater Poland Voivodeship and the seat of the oldest Polish diocese. It is home to Adam Mickiewicz University and hosts the Poznań International Fair. Its Old Town, Town Hall, cathedral and the Baroque Fara church are among its main heritage sites.
pozzuoli: Pozzuoli is the main city of the Phlegrean Peninsula in the Metropolitan City of Naples, in Campania, and has 74,665 inhabitants. The local volcanic sand, pozzolana, called pulvis puteolanus in Latin, reacted chemically with water and turned a mix of sand and lime into a mortar strong enough to bind aggregate into a load-bearing unit. It was the basis of Roman concrete and made possible the dome of the Pantheon, which is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

The Samnites occupied Dicaearchia in 421 BCE after conquering Cumae, and the Roman occupation of Campania from 341 BCE began its Romanisation. In the Second Punic War Rome reinforced the defences and placed a garrison there, and Hannibal failed to capture it in 215 BCE. After the Roman conquest of the east it became the Mediterranean port of Rome, though it lay some 150 miles away. It became the great emporium for the Alexandrian grain ships, and Lucilius wrote in about 125 BCE that it was second only to Delos in importance. Its exports from Campania included blown glass, mosaics, wrought iron and marble.

Inscriptions show a polyglot population of Greeks, Jews, later Christians, Nabataeans and Tyrians, who formed trading stations and guilds. The apostle Paul landed there on his way to Rome and stayed seven days. In 37 CE Emperor Caligula had a floating bridge of trading vessels built from the town to Baiae and rode across it on horseback. The development of the port of Ostia, begun under Claudius in 42 CE and enlarged by Trajan between 100 and 106, brought the decline of Puteoli. The city was plundered by Alaric I in 410, by Genseric in 455 and by Totila in 545, and took centuries to recover.

Pozzuoli's sights include the Flavian Amphitheatre, the third largest in Italy after the Colosseum and the Capuan Amphitheatre. The Macellum, also called the Temple of Serapis, is considered the city's symbol, though it was a marketplace and takes its name from a mistaken reading after a statue of Serapis was found in 1750. Its three marble columns bear marks of marine molluscs from a time when bradyseism had lowered the ground and let sea water in. From August 1982 to December 1984 hundreds of tremors damaged 8,000 buildings, displaced 36,000 people and raised the sea bottom by almost two metres.
prague: Prague is situated on the Vltava River, into which the Berounka flows in the suburb of Lahovice. Most of the city lies on the Prague Plateau. Its highest point is the hill Teleček on the western border, at 399 metres, and its lowest is the Vltava at Suchdol, at 172 metres. The city grew from a settlement stretching from Prague Castle in the north to the fort of Vyšehrad in the south. Its archaeological deposits are over 10 metres deep. The name Praha has been explained in several ways, among them as meaning a threshold, a ford or rapid, or a burned forest cleared for settlement.

The region was settled as early as the Paleolithic. Around the fifth and fourth centuries BCE a Celtic tribe, the Boii, appeared there and gave Bohemia its name, meaning home of the Boii. They built the largest Celtic oppidum in Bohemia, at Závist, and in the last century BCE Germanic tribes slowly drove them out. The 2nd-century map of Ptolemaios mentions a Germanic city called Casurgis near the site of present-day Prague.

Prague became the capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia and the residence of several Holy Roman Emperors, most notably Charles IV, who reigned from 1346 to 1378, and Rudolf II, who reigned from 1575 to 1611. Charles University, founded in 1348, is the oldest university in Central Europe. The city played major roles in the Bohemian and Protestant Reformations and in the Thirty Years' War. It was an important city to the Habsburg monarchy and to Austria-Hungary, and the capital of Czechoslovakia in the interwar period and in the Communist era after World War II.

Prague suffered considerably less damage in World War II than some other major cities in the region, which allowed most of its historic architecture to stay true to form. The city contains buildings in many styles, from Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque to Art Nouveau and Cubist. The Estates Theatre was the venue of the premieres of Mozart's Don Giovanni and La clemenza di Tito.

Prague is the capital and largest city of the Czech Republic and the historical capital of Bohemia, with a population of about 1.4 million. It has had the status of a statutory city again since 24 November 1990. The historic centre has been on the UNESCO list of World Heritage Sites since 1992. Among its landmarks are Prague Castle, Charles Bridge, the Old Town Square with the astronomical clock, the Jewish Quarter and Vyšehrad. It has been nicknamed the City of a Hundred Spires.
prague-castle: Prague Castle occupies an area of almost 70,000 square metres, about 570 metres in length and an average of about 130 metres wide, and is recorded by the Guinness Book of Records as the largest ancient castle in the world. Its architecture blends the styles of the last millennium. It includes the Gothic St Vitus Cathedral, the Romanesque Basilica of St George, a monastery, several palaces, gardens and defensive towers. The neighbourhood around it is called Hradčany.

The first walled building, the Church of the Virgin Mary, was built in 870. The basilicas of St George and St Vitus were founded in the first half of the 10th century under Duke Vratislaus I of Bohemia and his son Wenceslaus I. King Ottokar II of Bohemia improved the fortifications, and under Charles IV the royal palace was rebuilt in Gothic style and work began on the vast Gothic church that replaced the rotunda and basilica of St Vitus; it was completed almost six centuries later.

The castle stood uninhabited during the Hussite Wars and the decades after. In 1485 King Vladislaus II Jagiellon began to rebuild it. A large fire in 1541 destroyed much of it, and under the Habsburgs Renaissance buildings followed. Rudolph II made the castle his main residence and housed his art collections in the Spanish Hall. The Third Defenestration of Prague in 1618 took place at the castle and set off the Bohemian Revolt. In 1648 invading forces looted many works of Rudolph's collection in the Battle of Prague, the last act of the Thirty Years' War. Empress Maria Theresa carried out the last major rebuilding in the second half of the 18th century.

In 1918 the castle became the seat of Tomáš Masaryk, president of the new Czechoslovak Republic. The Slovenian architect Jože Plečnik renovated the New Royal Palace and the gardens, and St Vitus Cathedral was finished on 28 September 1929. During the Nazi occupation the castle was the headquarters of Reinhard Heydrich, the Reich Protector, who was ambushed in Operation Anthropoid on 27 May 1942 on his way to it and died of his wounds a week later. After 1948 it housed the offices of the communist government, and since 1993 it has been the seat of the head of state of the Czech Republic.
prague-spring: De-Stalinization in Czechoslovakia began under Antonín Novotný in the late 1950s and early 1960s but moved more slowly than in most other countries of the Eastern Bloc. In the early 1960s the economy declined, and Novotný's New Economic Model of 1965 increased the demand for political reform. In May 1963 the Liblice Conference on Franz Kafka marked the beginning of a cultural opening, and at the Writers' Congress of June 1967 speeches by Ludvík Vaculík, Milan Kundera and Antonín Liehm broke with the regime. Alexander Dubček, First Secretary of the Communist Party of Slovakia, and the economist Ota Šik challenged Novotný in the Central Committee, and Leonid Brezhnev supported his removal.

Dubček replaced Novotný as First Secretary on 5 January 1968, and on 22 March Ludvík Svoboda became president. The writers' weekly became Literární listy and appeared without censorship on 29 February. In April the party launched an Action Programme that promised more freedom of the press, speech and movement, a limit on the power of the secret police, a federation of two equal nations and a ten-year transition towards democratic elections, under the slogan socialism with a human face. Reform was to proceed under the party's direction. Soviet and other leaders were alarmed: at Dresden on 23 March the leaders of the USSR, Hungary, Poland, Bulgaria and East Germany questioned the Czechoslovak delegation.

On the night of 20–21 August 1968 armies of Warsaw Pact countries invaded Czechoslovakia, and by the morning of 21 August the country was occupied. During the invasion 72 Czechs and Slovaks were killed. Dubček called on his people not to resist, but there was widespread nonviolent resistance: road signs were removed or painted over, except those pointing to Moscow. Dubček was arrested and taken to Moscow, where he and the other leaders except František Kriegel signed the Moscow Protocol.

In April 1969 Gustáv Husák replaced Dubček as First Secretary, and a period called normalization began. Husák reversed the reforms, purged liberals from the party and re-centralised the economy. The only significant change to survive was the federalization of the country into the Czech Socialist Republic and the Slovak Socialist Republic in 1969. On 16 January 1969 the student Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square in protest. Czechoslovakia remained a Soviet satellite state until the Velvet Revolution of 1989, and the last Soviet troops left in 1991.
praia: The island of Santiago was discovered by António da Noli in 1460, and its first settlement was Ribeira Grande, now called Cidade Velha. A village named Praia de Santa Maria was first mentioned around 1615 and grew beside the natural harbour. The ports of Santiago were calls for ships sailing between Portugal and its colonies in Africa and South America. Between the end of the 16th century and the end of the 18th, both Ribeira Grande and Praia were attacked by privateers several times, among them Sir Francis Drake in 1585 and Jacques Cassard in 1712.

Praia's position on a plateau gave it better protection against such raids, and it gradually overtook Ribeira Grande. A naval battle was fought in Praia harbour on 16 April 1781 between Great Britain and France, while Portugal was neutral; it ended in a tactical draw and a French strategic victory. Charles Darwin's voyage with HMS Beagle made Praia its first stop in 1832. In the 19th century the Plateau was rebuilt on a grid plan, lined with colonial buildings and mansions, and Praia officially became a city in 1858.

Resistance to Portuguese rule rose in the 1950s, but there was no open independence war as in Guinea-Bissau. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 in Portugal, Cape Verde declared independence in July 1975, and Praia then grew quickly as people moved in from all the islands.

Praia is a set of plateaus and the valleys around them. The plateaus are generally called achada, a Portuguese word for a volcanic plateau, and the central one is simply the Plateau. For a long time only the Plateau counted as the city, with the paved streets and services, while the other neighbourhoods were treated as outlying suburbs and grew in a more haphazard way. After independence they merged with it into the city as it is understood now. The climate is arid, with about 210 millimetres of rain a year, most of it in August, September and October.

Praia is the capital and largest city of Cape Verde and its political, economic and cultural centre, the seat of Praia Municipality, which holds some 29 per cent of the country's population. The city's own population was estimated at 151,436 in 2015. Landmarks of the old centre include Albuquerque Square, the Presidential Palace, built at the end of the 19th century to house the Portuguese governor, and the Monumento de Diogo Gomes. The Museu Etnográfico was founded in 1997, and since 2016 the historic centre has been on the tentative list of World Heritage Sites.
prajadhipok: Prajadhipok was born on 8 November 1893 in Bangkok, the youngest son of King Chulalongkorn and Queen Saovabha Phongsri. Unlikely to succeed to the throne, he chose a military career and was sent abroad to Eton College in 1906 and then to the Woolwich Military Academy, from which he graduated in 1913, taking a commission in the Royal Horse Artillery. In 1918 he married his cousin Rambai Barni; the couple had no children. His brothers died within a short period, and when King Vajiravudh died in 1925 he became king at thirty-two. He was crowned on 25 February 1926.

Prajadhipok inherited a budget in heavy deficit and royal accounts in disorder, and the world was soon in the Great Depression. He created a Supreme Council of State of five senior princes, who gradually took the main ministerial posts for themselves and their relatives, signalling a return to royal oligarchy. In 1927 he formed a Committee of the Privy Council of 40 members as a possible forerunner of a parliament, but it remained unimportant. In a 1926 memorandum he doubted that Siam was ready for representative government.

In October 1931 he ordered a constitution to be prepared, but Prince Damrong and other royal members of the Supreme Council opposed it, and the planned announcement of April 1932 was not made. On the morning of 24 June 1932, while he was at Hua Hin, the Khana Ratsadon took control of the Ananda Samakhom Throne Hall in Bangkok and demanded a constitution. He accepted at once, and the first permanent constitution was promulgated on 10 December. In October 1933 Prince Boworadej led an armed revolt, the Boworadet Rebellion, which failed and diminished the king's prestige.

Relations with the Khana Ratsadon deteriorated over royal powers, such as a veto, and over royal assets. While in England for medical treatment he announced that he would abdicate unless his requests were met. The People's Party rejected the ultimatum, and he abdicated on 2 March 1935 in favour of Ananda Mahidol. He lived in Surrey and Kent, and died of heart failure on 30 May 1941 at Compton House in Surrey. His ashes were taken to Siam in 1949.

The historian David K. Wyatt describes him as a hard-working executor who underestimated the Bangkok elite's growing nationalism. A royalist view calls him the father of Thai democracy, citing his abdication statement, but later historians have challenged it as a myth, arguing that his manoeuvres aimed at preserving the power of a declining monarchy.
prakrit: Prakrit is a group of vernacular classical Middle Indo-Aryan languages used in the Indian subcontinent from about the 5th century BCE to the 12th century CE. Western linguists usually hold that Prakrit was the speech of ordinary people, while Sanskrit was a prestige register alongside it. Most modern Prakrit grammarians hold instead that the Prakrits descend from Sanskrit, and the Prākṛta Prakāśa says that Sanskrit is the source and the language that comes from it is therefore called prākṛta.

The oldest stage of Middle Indo-Aryan is attested in the inscriptions of Ashoka, about 260 BCE. The most prominent form is Ardhamāgadhı̄, associated with the kingdom of Magadha, where Mahāvīra, the last Tīrthaṅkara of Jainism, was born; the earliest Jain texts were composed in it. Regional Prakrits such as Maharashtri appear by about 200 CE and the late stage called Apabhramsha by about 900 CE.

The term is used in different ways. Some scholars apply it to every Middle Indo-Aryan language that departs from Sanskrit, though not all of these were called Prakrit in ancient times. Others, such as Richard Pischel and Oskar von Hinüber, use it for a smaller set of literary languages. Among the dramatic Prakrits, Shauraseni, Magadhi and Maharashtri are the most prominent, and in plays characters spoke different Prakrits according to role: Shauraseni for the heroine and her friends, Dramili for forest-dwellers and Avanti for cheats and rogues.

Under the Mauryan Empire various Prakrits had the status of royal language, and Ashoka used Prakrit. For much of the first millennium it was the preferred language for fictional romance, and Jains used it for commentaries, stories and hymns. Literary Prakrit is often wrongly taken for common speech: in the market scene of Uddyotana's Kuvalaya-mala of 779 the narrator speaks a few words in 18 languages, none of which resembles the Prakrit he uses for the narration. In Sanskrit plays such as Kalidasa's Shakuntala, lead characters speak Sanskrit while minor characters and most women speak Prakrit. The local forms of Apabhramsha evolved into the modern Indo-Aryan vernaculars. Prakrit literature has received less attention than Sanskrit, and most surviving manuscripts were copied between 1300 and 1800.
praxiteles: Praxiteles of Athens was the son of Cephisodotus the Elder and the most admired of the Attic sculptors of the 4th century BCE. Some writers have held that there were two sculptors of the name, one a contemporary of Pheidias and the other his better-known grandson, but there is no certain evidence for either view. Accurate dates for him are elusive. He was probably no longer working in the time of Alexander the Great, since there is no evidence that Alexander employed him. Pliny's date of 364 BCE is probably that of one of his most noted works.

Praxiteles chose human beings or dignified, less elderly deities such as Apollo, Hermes and Aphrodite, rather than Zeus or Poseidon. He probably invented the S-curve. He and his school worked almost entirely in Parian marble, and some statues were coloured by the painter Nicias. No sculpture can be attributed to him beyond doubt, but many copies survive, and coins carry silhouettes of his best-known types.

His Aphrodite of Cnidus was his best-known statue and the first full-scale female nude in Greek art. According to Pliny, the people of Cnidus valued it so highly that they refused to sell it to King Nicomedes in return for discharging the city's large debt. The Colonna Venus in the Vatican Museums is often thought the most faithful copy. The Apollo Sauroktonos, a youth leaning on a tree and striking at a lizard, is known from Roman copies.

The Hermes and the Infant Dionysus was found in 1877 at Olympia, in the Temple of Hera, where Pausanias had seen a statue of Hermes and Dionysus that he attributed to Praxiteles. Scholars have identified it with this one, but whether it is his work has long been debated. The Encyclopædia Britannica of 1911 called it a masterpiece, while the sculptor Aristide Maillol called it kitsch. Some argue that it is a Roman copy or a Hellenistic work, but no argument from its unfinished back, drapery or hair is conclusive. It is in the Archaeological Museum of Olympia.

His supposed relationship with his model, the Thespian courtesan Phryne, has inspired painters and composers. The ancient reports that he worked on the Mausoleum of Maussollos and the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus are widely considered dubious.
prayagraj: Prayagraj lies in the south of Uttar Pradesh, at the Triveni Sangam, the confluence of the Ganges, the Yamuna and the mythical Sarasvati, which according to Hindu legend wells up from underground. The place was known in ancient times as Prayāga, meaning place of a sacrifice in Sanskrit, since the god Brahma was believed to have performed the first sacrifice there.

The name Prayag alone is still used for the city. Geographically it is part of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, at the mouth of the Yamuna. The Prayag Kumbh Mela is held at the Sangam every 12 years, and the ashes of several national leaders, among them Mahatma Gandhi in 1948, have been immersed there.

The earliest mention of Prayāga as a pilgrimage is in the Rigveda Pariśiṣṭa, a supplement of about 1200 to 1000 BCE. The Pali canon records the Buddha saying that bathing there cannot wash away cruel deeds, and the Mahabharata describes a bathing pilgrimage at Prayag as atonement for past wrongs. The city is also sacred to Jains, who believe their first Tirthankara, Rishabhanatha, attained kevala jnana there.

Some recent studies trace the Gupta dynasty to the Prayaga region, where the Allahabad Pillar Inscription indicates its early centre of power. In 644 the Chinese traveller Xuanzang described Prayaga as a great city with hundreds of temples, two Buddhist institutions to its south, and a Grand Place of Almsgiving where wealthy people and kings gave alms.

Abul Fazal records in the Ain-i-Akbari that on 13 November 1583 the Mughal emperor Akbar reached the spot where the rivers meet, laid the foundations of a city and planned four forts. It was called Ilahabas or Ilahabad, later Allahabad. British troops were first stationed in the fort in 1765 under the Treaty of Allahabad, signed by Robert Clive, the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and Shuja-ud-Daula, Nawab of Awadh. The East India Company acquired the city in 1801.

In 1857 Maulvi Liaquat Ali raised the banner of revolt there, and Allahabad was the scene of a massacre of European troops. It became the capital of the North-Western Provinces in 1858, and for a day the capital of India, and was capital of the United Provinces from 1902 to 1920. The Civil Lines quarter, built in 1857, was the largest town-planning project in India before New Delhi.

The city is the judicial capital of Uttar Pradesh, with the Allahabad High Court, and the administrative headquarters of Prayagraj district. Hindi is the most widely spoken language. Its landmarks include the Triveni Sangam, Allahabad University, All Saints Cathedral and Anand Bhavan, and it has buildings in Indo-Islamic and Indo-Saracenic styles. The Kumbh Mela held there is among the largest peaceful gatherings in the world.
pre-columbian-era: The term, also called the pre-contact, pre-Hispanic or, in Brazil, pre-Cabraline era, spans the history of the Americas from the initial peopling in the Upper Paleolithic to the onset of European colonisation. It covers Indigenous cultures before significant European influence, which in some cases did not come until decades or even centuries after 1492. Many of these societies developed permanent settlements, cities, agriculture, monumental architecture, major earthworks and complex hierarchies. Some had declined by the time of the first permanent European colonies and are known mainly through archaeology and oral histories.

Before archaeology developed in the 19th century, historians relied on the records of the conquerors and early European travellers. The Maya kept written records, many of which were destroyed by Christian Europeans such as Diego de Landa, though a few survive and others were transcribed or translated into Spanish.

Asian Paleo-Indians are thought to have entered the Americas by the Bering Land Bridge and possibly along the coast, and spread south through an ice-free corridor and along the Pacific coast. Genetic evidence supports several migrations from Asia. In North America, the Woodland period lasted from roughly 1000 BCE to 1000 CE, and the Adena and Hopewell traditions built monumental earthworks and wide trade networks. The Mississippian culture appeared around 1000 CE and built great mound complexes; Cahokia may have reached a population of over 20,000, and its Monks Mound remains the largest earthen construction of the prehistoric Americas. In the Southwest the Ancestral Puebloans built the Cliff Palace of Mesa Verde and the great houses of Chaco Canyon.

Mesoamerica produced a series of related civilisations over about 3,000 years. The Olmec, the earliest known, consolidated power at San Lorenzo between 1600 and 1500 BCE. Teotihuacan, first settled about 300 BCE, had become a metropolis by 150 CE, while the Maya flourished between 250 and 650 CE and developed a script, mathematics and a calendar. The Mexica later led the Aztec Triple Alliance with Tetxcoco and Tlacopan.

In South America the Norte Chico or Caral-Supe civilisation emerged around 3200 BCE on the coast of Peru, and is regarded as the oldest known civilisation in the Americas. Later states included the Moche, Wari and Tiwanaku. The Inca dominated the Andes from 1438 to 1533, ruling some 9 to 14 million people connected by a 40,000-kilometre road system. Early inhabitants also bred wild teosinte into maize, and over two-thirds of the food crops grown worldwide are native to the Americas.
premier-league: Despite major European success in the 1970s and early 1980s, the mid and late 1980s were a low point for English football. Stadiums were ageing with poor facilities, hooliganism was rife, and after the Heysel Stadium disaster of 1985 all English clubs faced a five-year ban from European competition, with Liverpool given an extra year. The Football League First Division, the top level since 1888, lagged behind Italy's Serie A and Spain's La Liga in attendance and revenue, and several top English players had moved abroad.

At the close of the 1990-91 season a proposal was tabled for a new league that would bring more money into the game. The Founder Members Agreement, signed on 17 July 1991 by the top-flight clubs, set the principles of the FA Premier League, which was founded on 20 February 1992.

The league began with 22 clubs, a number the top flight had reached only at the start of 1991-92, and was reduced to 20 in 1995, when four teams were relegated and only two promoted. In the 2000s Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool and Manchester United dominated and were called the Big Four; from 1999-2000 to 2008-09 three of them finished in the top four every season. Manchester United won six titles in the decade, Arsenal two and Chelsea two under José Mourinho. Arsenal's unbeaten 2003-04 season earned them the nickname the Invincibles, the only such season of the Premier League era.

After 2009 Tottenham Hotspur and Manchester City regularly reached the top four, forming what came to be called the Big Six. Manchester City's title in 2011-12 was the first by a club outside the Big Four since Blackburn Rovers in 1994-95. Video assistant referees were introduced from the 2019-20 season, the season in which Liverpool won their first Premier League title, ending a 30-year wait for a top-flight championship. In October 2020 Manchester United and Liverpool announced Project Big Picture, a proposal for closer alignment between top clubs and the English Football League, which the league's leadership and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport criticised.

The Football Association Premier League Limited is a corporation owned by its member clubs, each a shareholder with one vote on rule changes and contracts. The clubs choose a chairman, a chief executive and a board. The Football Association is not involved in daily operations but holds a veto as a special shareholder over the choice of chairman and chief executive and over new rules. Each club plays the others twice, home and away, for 38 games, with three points for a win and one for a draw, and the lowest-placed teams are relegated to the EFL Championship.
preslav: Preslav lies in what is now north-eastern Bulgaria, some 20 kilometres south-west of the regional capital, Shumen, and its ruins are a national archaeological reserve. The name is of Slavic origin, and the place apparently began as a Slavic settlement until it was fortified at the beginning of the ninth century. Its closeness to the then Bulgarian capital of Pliska led to fast growth under the khans Krum and Omurtag. By the coronation of Boris I in 852 it had become an important strategic military centre and the seat of the Ichirgu-boil, and many churches were built after the conversion of the Bulgarians to Christianity in 864.

A pagan revolt of the Pliska nobility led by Prince Vladimir in 892 decided the city's future. In 893 Vladimir was dethroned, and at the Council of Preslav Boris I appointed Simeon the Great his successor and moved the capital from the still somewhat pagan Pliska to Preslav. In the following eighty years it became a centre of Bulgarian politics and diplomacy and of Slavic culture, literature and fine arts. A chronicler records that it took Simeon 28 years to build his capital, and excavations show that it kept growing in the 930s and 940s, reaching its peak in the middle of the rule of Peter I.

With its town planning, its economy and buildings such as the Round Church and the Royal Palace, it rivalled the largest centres in the west. The Preslav Literary School, founded in Pliska in 886, moved to Preslav with the court in 893.

John Exarch, Constantine of Preslav and Chernorizets Hrabar, the leading Old Bulgarian writers, worked there, and the Cyrillic script probably developed around the school in the tenth century. The city also had large ceramic workshops producing glazed tiles, art ceramics and ceramic icons.

The city's fortunes turned at the end of the 960s, when it was occupied by Prince Sviatoslav of Kiev. The ensuing war between the Rus' and the Byzantines left it burnt and ravaged by the army of Emperor John I Tzimisces, who took away the treasury, the Bulgarian tsar's regalia and much of Simeon's library. He renamed it Ioannoupolis, a name that did not last. The city kept some importance for three hundred years, and Tatar raids in the 1270s drove away its last citizens. Survivors founded a village of the same name two kilometres north, which took the name of the medieval capital in 1878 and became the present town of Veliki Preslav, with a museum and archaeological reserve.
presov: Prešov lies in eastern Slovakia at the confluence of the rivers Torysa and Sekčov, in the Košice Basin, at an altitude of 296 metres. The Slanské vrchy rise to the east and the Šarišská vrchovina to the west, and Košice lies about 34 kilometres to the south. In the Middle Ages the town stood at a crossroads of trade routes and was part of the defence system of the emerging Hungarian state. Several authors derive the name from the Hungarian eper, meaning strawberry, and people of Prešov are traditionally called koňare, horse keepers.

The area was inhabited as far back as the Paleolithic period, and the oldest tools and mammoth bones found there are 28,000 years old. Continuous settlement dates from the 8th century, and Slavs arrived between the 4th and 5th centuries. The first written mention is from 1247, in the form Theutonici de Epuryes. After the Mongol invasion of 1241, King Béla IV of Hungary invited German colonists to fill gaps in the population, and Prešov became a German-speaking settlement. King Andrew III of Hungary granted it city rights in 1299, and Louis the Great raised it to a royal free town in 1347.

Prešov later belonged to the Pentapolitana, a community of five royal cities with Košice, Bardejov, Levoča and Sabinov. A town school is first mentioned in 1429 and the first coat of arms dates from 1453. The Prešov Greek Catholic Archeparchy was founded on 3 November 1815 by Emperor Francis II. After the Second World War the Prešov Orthodox Diocese was created by dividing the Mukachevo-Prešov Orthodox Diocese, and the Cathedral of St Prince Alexander Nevsky was built between 1946 and 1950 in the traditional Russian style. In the past Prešov was a typical multiethnic town in which Slovak, Hungarian, German and Yiddish were spoken.

Prešov is the seat of the Prešov Region and of Šariš, with a population of about 85,000. The old town has Baroque, Rococo and Gothic buildings, while housing estates of concrete panel buildings on the outskirts show Soviet influence. The city is the seat of the Roman Catholic Co-Cathedral of St Nicholas, the Slovak Greek Catholic metropolis and a diocese of the Evangelical Church of the Augsburg Confession. The University of Prešov includes Greek Catholic and Orthodox theological faculties. Its museums include the Museum of Ruthenian Culture and a collection of Judaica in the Prešov Synagogue, and its lively music scene has earned it the nickname Slovak Seattle.
prester-john: Prester John, in Latin Presbyter Ioannes, was imagined as a Nestorian patriarch and king who ruled a Christian nation lost among pagans and Muslims in the Orient, and who was said to descend from the Three Magi. The title Prester comes from the Greek presbyteros, meaning elder. The legend drew on reports of Saint Thomas the Apostle preaching in India, recorded in the third-century Acts of Thomas, and on embellished reports of the Church of the East in Asia. René Grousset suggested that it may have begun with the Kerait clan, thousands of whom joined that church shortly after the year 1000.

The narrative began in earnest in 1145, when the chronicler Otto of Freising reported meeting Hugh, bishop of Jabala, at the court of Pope Eugene III in Viterbo. He said that Prester John had recently won a great battle against the rulers of Media and Persia. Robert Silverberg links this to the victory of the Qara Khitai under Yelü Dashi over the Seljuks at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141.

About 1165 copies of a Letter of Prester John, probably forged, began to spread through Europe. It claimed to be addressed to the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos by a Christian sovereign and King of India, who lived in a palace of gems and gold and ruled from Persia to China. It was translated into many languages, including Hebrew, and circulated in ever more embellished form for centuries. Textual study of the Hebrew versions points to an origin among the Jews of northern Italy or Languedoc, and its author was most likely a Westerner. Pope Alexander III wrote to Prester John on 27 September 1177 through his physician Philip, of whom nothing more is recorded.
