After 1221, when Jacques de Vitry reported a King David of India advancing against the Saracens, the legend was linked to the Mongols. Genghis Khan's foster father Toghrul, a Nestorian ruler of the Keraites defeated in 1203, was identified with the Prester, and Franciscan envoys such as Giovanni da Pian del Carpine and William of Rubruck travelled to the Mongols partly in hope of an eastern ally. As the Mongol Empire collapsed, Europeans placed the kingdom elsewhere, and from about 1250 it was increasingly located in Ethiopia. By 1520 Europeans knew the Ethiopian emperor as Prester John, though Ethiopians never used the name. In the 17th century Hiob Ludolf showed there was no native connection.
pretoria: Pretoria stands about 56 kilometres north-northeast of Johannesburg, at an altitude of about 1,339 metres. It lies in a warm, sheltered, fertile valley in the transitional belt between the plateau of the Highveld to the south and the lower-lying Bushveld to the north, surrounded by the hills of the Magaliesberg range, and straddles the Apies River. It is called the Jacaranda City for the roughly 60,000 to 70,000 jacaranda trees along its streets.

Pretoria was founded in 1855 by Marthinus Pretorius, a leader of the Voortrekkers, who named it after his father Andries Pretorius and chose a spot on the banks of the Apies as the new capital of the South African Republic. The elder Pretorius had become a national hero of the Voortrekkers after his victory over Dingane and the Zulus in the Battle of Blood River in 1838, and had negotiated the Sand River Convention of 1852, in which the United Kingdom acknowledged the independence of the Transvaal. Pretoria became the capital of the republic on 1 May 1860, superseding Potchefstroom.

In the First Boer War, Republican forces besieged the city in December 1880 and March 1881, and the peace treaty was signed in Pretoria on 3 August 1881 at the Pretoria Convention. In the Second Boer War the city surrendered to British forces under Frederick Roberts on 5 June 1900, and the conflict ended in Pretoria with the Peace of Vereeniging, signed on 31 May 1902 at Melrose House. That war ended the Transvaal Republic and began British hegemony in South Africa.

In 1910 the Boer republics of the South African Republic and the Orange River Colony were united with the Cape Colony and Natal Colony as the Union of South Africa. Pretoria became the administrative capital of the whole country, with Cape Town as the legislative capital and Bloemfontein as the judicial capital, and from 1910 to 1994 it was also the capital of the province of Transvaal. It achieved official city status on 14 October 1931 and remained the administrative capital when South Africa became a republic in 1961.

Pretoria is the executive capital of South Africa, seat of the executive branch and home to all foreign embassies. It forms the central part of the City of Tshwane Metropolitan Municipality. It is an academic and research centre, with the University of Pretoria, the University of South Africa and the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research. The Voortrekker Monument and Kruger House, residence of the president of the South African Republic, are among its museums and monuments.
pribor: Příbor lies on the Lubina River in the Moravian-Silesian Foothills, about 10 kilometres east of Nový Jičín and 20 kilometres south-west of Ostrava. Its highest point is 370 metres above sea level. The town has about 8,300 inhabitants. Its name means cutlery in modern Czech, but this is only a coincidence. If the Czech name is older, it probably comes from při boru or při zboru, meaning at a pine forest or at a ruin. If the German name Freiberg came first, it was originally rendered Vriburch or Freiburg and means free castle or castle with free access.

Count Frank von Hückeswagen founded the town in 1251, as a deed of the Moravian margrave Ottokar II confirmed in the same year, where it was called Vriburch. Its square was laid out on an old trade route to Poland, and the count built a solid castle. His descendants held the town until 1359, when it passed to the Bishops of Olomouc, who favoured it. Franz von Dietrichstein in particular granted it a number of privileges.

During the Thirty Years' War the town burned down three times, most destructively in the Swedish invasion of 1643, and it recovered in the second half of the 17th century. In 1694 Karl II von Liechtenstein-Kastelkorn founded a Piarist monastery and gymnasium, which also made education available to poorer people and made Příbor an important centre of education. From 1875 to 1938 the Czech Teacher Institute operated there and trained a number of significant teachers and figures of culture.

Příbor is one of the oldest towns in the region, and its historic centre is protected as an urban monument reservation. A regular square is lined with burgher houses, mostly Renaissance with Baroque alterations. The Baroque Piarist monastery now houses the town museum, a library and a primary art school. The most important of the town's four churches is the Church of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, founded with the town, whose present brick building dates from the 14th century and has a tall slender tower. Sigmund Freud's birthplace is a museum with an exhibition about his life and work.
pridi-banomyong: Pridi was born in Ayutthaya province on 11 May 1900 into a family of farmers, the second of five children. He became one of the country's youngest barristers in 1919, at nineteen, and in 1920 won a scholarship to study in France. There he began to assemble a group of fifty civil servants who wanted to turn Thailand's absolute monarchy into a constitutional one. He received a doctorate from the University of Paris in 1927, the year he co-founded Khana Ratsadon with like-minded Siamese students, and he returned to Siam to work in the Ministry of Justice.

On 24 June 1932 Khana Ratsadon, the People's Party, with Pridi leading its civilian faction, carried out a coup that ended 150 years of absolute monarchy under the Chakri dynasty. In 1933 his Draft National Economic Plan, calling for the nationalisation of land, public employment and social security, was rejected by royalists, who shut down parliament, and he was accused of being a communist and went into exile. He returned in 1934, founded Thammasat University and served as minister of the interior, of foreign affairs and of finance. As foreign minister he signed treaties revoking the extraterritorial rights of twelve countries.

As regent from 1941 to 1945 he refused to sign Plaek Phibunsongkhram's declaration of war on Britain and the United States and built the Free Thai Movement against the Japanese, though Nigel Brailey argues that his stance sprang mainly from hostility to Phibun. He became prime minister in 1946. On 9 June 1946 King Ananda Mahidol was found dead of a gunshot wound; a commission ruled that neither suicide nor murder was proved, and Pridi's opponents blamed him.

On 8 November 1947 a coup returned Phibun to power and Pridi was taken to Singapore. A counter-coup he attempted in 1949 failed, and he left for China, never to return to Thailand. In 1970 he went to France, and he died near Paris on 2 May 1983. His ashes were brought back to Thailand three years later. The charge that he was the mastermind of the king's death has since been regarded as politically motivated, and he won every libel suit he brought over it. UNESCO recognised the centenary of his birth, and Thammasat University has a library and an international college named for him.
prilep: Prilep lies in the northern part of the Pelagonia plain, in the south of North Macedonia, 74 kilometres from Skopje and 44 from Bitola. In antiquity the region belonged to Pelagonia and was annexed to the Macedonian kingdom during the 4th century BCE. Near the village of Čepigovo are the ruins of the ancient city of Styberra, which the Goths razed in 268 though it remained partly inhabited. The name first appears in Greek as Prilapos in 1014, and derives from Old Slavic words meaning stuck on the rock, after the hilltop above the town.

In 1014 Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria was said to have had a heart attack at Prilep on seeing thousands of his soldiers blinded by the Byzantines after the Battle of Kleidion. In 1041 the Byzantine emperor Michael IV defeated Petar Delyan's rebellion in the region. Byzantium lost the town to the Second Bulgarian Empire, but retook it. Serbian King Dušan took Prilep in 1334, and after 1365 it belonged to King Vukašin, co-ruler with Dušan's son Stefan Uroš V. After Vukašin's death in 1371 his son Marko ruled it, and rebuilt the citadel into an important stronghold.

Prilep became part of the Ottoman Empire in 1395 and stayed so until 1913, when the Kingdom of Serbia annexed it. Its bazaar began to develop in the 18th century, and one of the largest annual fairs in Macedonia was held there in the middle of the 19th. Bulgaria occupied the town from 17 November 1915 to 25 September 1918. It then joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and, from 1929, the Vardar Banovina. In the Second World War it was occupied by the German Army on 8 April 1941 and by the Bulgarian Army on 26 April 1941, and local partisans attacked the police station on 11 October 1941. Communist partisans retook it definitively on 3 November 1944.

Prilep is a regional centre of tobacco growing and also produces white marble. The Markovi Kuli, the ruins of the fortress above the town, are among its medieval sites, along with the Treskavec Monastery, built in the 12th century in the mountains north of the town, which has frescoes of the 14th and 15th centuries. The dialect of Prilep, with those of Veles, Bitola and Ohrid, was chosen as a basis of the standard Macedonian language after the Socialist Republic of Macedonia was formed within Yugoslavia.
primary-chronicle: The Primary Chronicle, in Old East Slavic the Povest vremennykh let, takes its title from the opening line of the Laurentian text: these are the narratives of bygone years regarding the origin of the land of Rus', the first princes of Kiev, and the source from which the land of Rus' had its beginning. It covers the period from about 850 to 1110 and was compiled in Kiev in the 1110s. Medieval tradition credited the monk Nestor the Chronicler. Modern scholars consider it an anonymous compilation by several editors, because the internal evidence and Nestor's known works often contradict one another.

In 1116 the hegumen Sylvester of Kiev extensively edited the text and signed it; the new edition glorified Vladimir II Monomakh, patron of his monastery's village. A third edition followed two years later, centred on Monomakh's son Mstislav the Great. The authors drew on oral tradition, Rus'–Byzantine treaties, Norse sagas, and Byzantine chronicles such as those of John Malalas and George Hamartolos.

The narrative traces the Slavs back to a son of Noah and tells the founding of Kiev by Kyi, Shchek, Khoryv and Lybid. It relates the calling of the Varangians and the rise of the Rurik dynasty, Oleg the Wise's conquest of Kiev after the murder of Askold and Dir, and Olga's vengeance on the Drevlians, who had murdered her husband Igor. It describes the siege of Kiev by the Pechenegs in 968, the conversion of Vladimir the Great, and the succession crisis after his death, in which Yaroslav rose to power.

Christian themes run through the text, which is usually taken to reflect its monastic authors. In the Korsun legend, Vladimir captures the Greek city of Korsun in Crimea and demands the emperor's sister Anna in marriage; he is baptised before the marriage.

The original manuscript has not survived. The text is known from later copies, chiefly the Laurentian Codex of 1377, written at Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal for Prince Dmitry Konstantinovich, and the Hypatian Codex of the 15th century. Because the manuscripts contain chronological errors, folklore and political revisions, historians treat its accuracy critically; Aleksey Shakhmatov showed in 1908 that it combines earlier accounts and documents.

It remains the main written source for the early history of the East Slavs, with corrections from the Novgorod First Chronicle. Samuel Hazzard Cross published an influential English translation of the Laurentian text in 1930, completed in a revised edition by Olgerd P. Sherbowitz-Wetzor in 1953, and by the early 21st century Primary Chronicle had become the common English name for the text shared by the main surviving manuscripts.
prince-edward-island: Prince Edward Island lies in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, about ten kilometres across the Northumberland Strait from both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. It has a land area of 5,686 square kilometres and is the only Canadian province consisting entirely of islands. Its bedrock is sedimentary. When the Pleistocene glaciers receded about 15,000 years ago a strip of land still joined the area to the mainland, and rising seas flooded it and formed the island. The Mi'kmaq call it Abegweit or Epekwitk, roughly land cradled on the waves.

The Mi'kmaq are the Indigenous inhabitants, and the island formed part of Mi'kma'ki, their homeland. Jacques Cartier was the first known European to see it, in 1543. In 1604 France claimed the Maritimes as the colony of Acadia and named the island Île Saint-Jean. The Mi'kmaq never recognised the claim but welcomed the French as trading partners and allies. It passed to Britain in 1763 and became a separate colony in 1769.

In the mid-1760s a survey led by Samuel Holland divided the island into 67 lots, allocated by lottery on 1 July 1767 to supporters of King George III. Ownership stayed with landlords in England, which angered settlers who could not gain title to the land they worked. Islanders spent decades trying to persuade the Crown to confiscate the lots. The Charlottetown Conference was held from 1 to 7 September 1864, but the island stayed out of Confederation in 1867. Facing railway debts, it joined Canada on 1 July 1873, and Canada financed a buy-out of the last absentee landlords.

Prince Edward Island is the smallest Canadian province by area and population but has the highest population density. Its capital and largest city is Charlottetown, and it is one of the three Maritime provinces. Farming is central to the economy, and the island produces about a quarter of Canada's potatoes. Surnames of its earliest settlers are still mostly Acadian, Scottish, Irish and English. Its nicknames include Birthplace of Confederation. A law of 1982 limits non-resident ownership of land, a legacy of the colonial land question.
prince-elector: The German practice of electing monarchs began when ancient Germanic tribes formed ad hoc coalitions and elected their leaders. While all free men originally voted, suffrage came to be limited to the leading men of the realm. At the election of Lothar III in 1125 a small number of eminent nobles chose the monarch and then submitted him to the remaining magnates for approval, and soon the right to choose was settled on an exclusive group of princes. A letter of Pope Urban IV in 1265 suggests that by immemorial custom seven princes held the right, namely those who had voted in the disputed election of 1257, which produced two kings.

Disputes followed over who held the Wittelsbach seat, the Count Palatine or the Duke of Bavaria, and over the right of the King of Bohemia to take part. The Golden Bull of 1356 settled the disputes. The composition then remained unchanged until the 17th century, except that in 1547, after the Schmalkaldic War, the Saxon electorate passed from the Ernestine to the Albertine branch of the Wettin family.

In 1623 Frederick V, the Elector Palatine, came under the imperial ban after the Bohemian Revolt and his seat went to the Duke of Bavaria. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 created a new post for the Count Palatine, raising the number to eight. A further post, for the Elector of Hanover, was created in 1692. In 1777 the number fell back to eight when the Elector Palatine inherited Bavaria. In 1803 new electorates were created for Württemberg, Baden, Hesse-Kassel and Salzburg, but the Holy Roman Empire was abolished in 1806 before any of the new electors could vote.

Electors ranked behind only the emperor, kings and the highest dukes, and held privileges not shared with other princes; the Golden Bull gave them the Privilegium de non appellando, barring their subjects from appeal to a higher imperial court. Each held a high office of the Empire: the Archbishop of Mainz was Archchancellor of Germany, the Archbishop of Cologne of Italy and the Archbishop of Trier of Burgundy.

Under the Golden Bull a majority sufficed, each elector had one vote, and elections were held regularly at Frankfurt from the 14th century. From the 16th century electors drafted a Wahlkapitulation, a contract that the king-elect swore to keep. All kings elected from 1438 to 1740 were from the Habsburg dynasty. After 1806 the former electors kept their lands, many taking the titles of king or grand duke, and Hesse-Kassel remained an electorate until 1866.
prince-eugene-of-savoy: Eugene was born at the Hôtel de Soissons in Paris on 18 October 1663, the youngest of five sons of Eugene Maurice, Count of Soissons, a French general officer, and Olympia Mancini, a niece of Cardinal Mazarin. From the age of ten he was brought up for a career in the church, but at 19 he chose a military career. Because of his poor physique and possibly a scandal involving his mother, Louis XIV refused him a commission in the French army and forbade him to enlist elsewhere. Embittered, he left France and entered the service of Emperor Leopold I, in whose army his elder brother Louis Julius had just fallen.

Eugene arrived at Leopold's camp in mid-August 1683, when the Ottoman army was besieging Vienna, and distinguished himself there at the age of 20. He commanded troops at Buda in 1686 and at Belgrade in 1688 and was a field marshal by 25. As commander-in-chief in Hungary he won the Battle of Zenta in 1697, which ended the Ottoman threat for nearly twenty years. In the War of the Spanish Succession he won victories in Italy, including Turin in 1706, and with the Duke of Marlborough won at Blenheim in 1704, Oudenaarde in 1708 and Malplaquet in 1709.

In 1716 Charles VI sent him to Hungary against the Turks. With about 70,000 men he attacked the Grand Vizier Damat Ali Pasha's army of some 200,000 on 5 August at Petrovaradin; the Vizier died of wounds. Eugene took Belgrade in 1717 and secured peace in 1718. As president of the Imperial War Council he later led a defensive campaign in the War of the Polish Succession, hampered by poor troops and a shortage of funds.

Eugene returned to Vienna in October 1735, weak and unwell, and died in his sleep in the night of 20-21 April 1736. His heart was buried with his ancestors in the Basilica of Superga in Turin and his body in St Stephen's Cathedral. He never married. A patron of the arts, he built the Stadtpalais in Vienna and, with the architect Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt, Baroque palaces including the Belvedere. Napoleon counted him among the eight great commanders of history, though later military critics have disagreed. An equestrian statue in Vienna calls him the wise counsellor of three emperors.
prince-henry-the-navigator: Henry was born on 4 March 1394, the third surviving son of King John I of Portugal, founder of the House of Aviz, and of Philippa, sister of King Henry IV of England. He may have been born in Porto. As early as 1410 or 1412 he had commissioned captains to explore the coasts beyond Cape Non. In 1415, at 21, he took part in the capture of the Moorish port of Ceuta, where he was knighted with his brothers Edward and Peter and made Duke of Viseu, the first time the title duke was used in Portugal. He relieved Ceuta again in 1418, and the two expeditions let him gather intelligence about the lands to the south from Muslim prisoners.

In 1419 Henry became governor of the Algarve, and in 1420 administrator of the Order of Christ, which funded his plans. His brother King Edward granted him all profits from trade in areas he discovered and the sole right to authorise expeditions beyond Cape Bojador. He was the main organiser of the disastrous expedition to Tangier in 1437, after which his younger brother Ferdinand stayed a hostage until his death. Henry promoted the colonisation of the Azores during Peter's regency.

Henry directed the development of the caravel, a lighter ship that could sail farther, and sponsored voyages, taking a 20 per cent tax on their profits. João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira found Porto Santo in 1418 and settlers reached Madeira in 1420. After fifteen failed expeditions in ten years, Gil Eanes passed Cape Bojador in 1434. The Portuguese reached the Bay of Arguin in 1443 and the Senegal River in 1444. Gold and slaves began arriving in Portugal, and by 1452 the gold allowed the minting of the first cruzado coins.

Henry died on 13 November 1460 and was buried in the Monastery of Batalha. No one called him Henry the Navigator in his lifetime or for three centuries: two nineteenth-century German historians coined the name, and British biographers popularised it. The idea of a school of navigators at Sagres is regarded by modern historians as a misconception, created in the 18th century. He employed some cartographers, but there was no organised centre of navigation science. By 1462 the Portuguese had explored the African coast as far as Sierra Leone.
prince-maximilian-of-baden: Maximilian was born in Baden-Baden on 10 July 1867, the son of Prince Wilhelm Max of Baden and Princess Maria Maximilianovna of Leuchtenberg, a granddaughter of Eugène de Beauharnais. He studied law and cameralism at Leipzig University and trained as an officer in the Prussian Army. After the death of his uncle Grand Duke Frederick I of Baden in 1907 he became heir to the grand-ducal throne of his cousin Frederick II, whose marriage remained childless, and he became president of the upper house of Baden's parliament.

He married Princess Marie Louise of Hanover and Cumberland in 1900. In 1914 he became honorary president of the Baden section of the German Red Cross, working for prisoners of war, and he spoke against the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917.

After the Supreme Army Command told the government in late September 1918 that the front was about to collapse, Chancellor Georg von Hertling's cabinet resigned and Max was appointed Imperial Chancellor and minister-president of Prussia on 3 October 1918. He had reservations about the plan and said openly that he was no politician, but Wilhelm II convinced him to take the post. His government rested on the majority parties of the Reichstag, and for the first time included Social Democrats, among them Philipp Scheidemann and Gustav Bauer. He sought an armistice on the basis of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, and when Erich Ludendorff turned to continued fighting, Max had him dismissed.

A political amnesty was passed, and in late October the constitution was amended so that the chancellor answered to the Reichstag. As revolution spread in early November, Max urged Wilhelm II to abdicate. At noon on 9 November 1918 he announced the abdication of the emperor and the renunciation of the crown prince without waiting for their consent. He then resigned and handed the chancellorship to Friedrich Ebert in an unconstitutional move, and refused Ebert's request to stay on as regent.

Max returned to Baden and spent the rest of his life in retirement. He rejected a mandate to the Weimar National Assembly of 1919 and in 1920 founded the Schule Schloss Salem boarding school with Kurt Hahn. He published Völkerbund und Rechtsfriede, Die moralische Offensive and Erinnerungen und Dokumente. In 1928 he became head of the House of Zähringen as Margrave of Baden, and he died at Salem on 6 November 1929. Although regarded as a weak chancellor, he is seen as having played a vital role in the transition to a government based on the Reichstag majority, which made Ebert's government acceptable to some conservative forces in the bureaucracy and military.
prince-of-wales: The first known use of the title Prince of Wales was in the 1160s, by Owain Gwynedd, ruler of Gwynedd, in a letter to Louis VII of France. Owain probably meant to claim pre-eminence over the other Welsh rulers of Deheubarth, Powys and Gwynedd. After his death in 1170 only Rhys ap Gruffydd of Deheubarth is known to have used it, in two charters of the 1180s. Gwynedd's rulers preferred styles such as Prince of North Wales, until Dafydd ap Llywelyn revived the title in 1245.

Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Dafydd's nephew, used no other style from 1262 until his death in 1282: Prince of Wales and Lord of Snowdon. By 1263 he had induced the remaining native rulers to do him homage, and he built governing structures that made his authority effective across the Principality of Wales. Henry III of England recognised his title and authority in the Treaty of Montgomery of 1267.

Edward I of England conquered Wales between 1277 and 1283. Llywelyn was killed in 1282, and his brother Dafydd, who took up his title, was defeated and executed in 1283, after which the principality was permanently annexed. To finalise the conquest, on 7 February 1301 Edward invested his Welsh-born son Edward of Caernarfon as Prince of Wales, beginning the custom of granting the title to the heir apparent.

The title is neither automatic nor heritable. It merges with the Crown when its holder becomes king, and reverts to the Crown if he dies first, leaving the sovereign free to grant it to the new heir. Since 1301 the heir has generally also been made Earl of Chester, and the prince is typically Duke of Cornwall, a duchy created in 1337 by Edward III for his son Edward of Woodstock, the Black Prince.

Two later claimants tried to revive the Welsh title. Owain Lawgoch made an abortive invasion attempt in 1372. Owain Glyndŵr's supporters proclaimed him Prince of Wales at the start of his revolt in 1400, and in 1404 he had himself crowned and planned state institutions for a new principality. The rebellion began to fail by 1406, and he died in obscurity, probably around 1415. Henry Tudor, the future Henry VIII, received the title in 1504 after the death of his brother Arthur in 1502, and Charles Stuart, later Charles I, received it in 1616 after the death of his brother Henry Frederick in 1612. Edward, later Edward VIII, was invested at Caernarfon Castle in July 1911, the first such public investiture for centuries.
prince-vijaya: The Mahavamsa gives Vijaya a marvellous ancestry. His grandmother Suppadevi, daughter of the king of Vanga and a princess of Kalinga, was carried off by Sinha, the lion, whom some modern interpreters take to have been an outlaw living in the forest. Their son Sinhabahu escaped with his mother and sister, killed his father, founded the city of Sinhapura in the Lala country and married his sister Sinhasivali. Vijaya was the eldest of their thirty-two sons. Where Sinhapura lay is uncertain: it has been placed in Bengal, Odisha, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh, among other places.

Made prince regent by his father, Vijaya became notorious with his followers for violent deeds, and prominent citizens demanded his death. Sinhabahu instead expelled them: their heads were half shaved and they were put on a ship, their wives and children being sent off on separate ships.

In the Mahavamsa's telling the kingdom was named Tambapanni, copper-red hands, because the red soil coloured the hands of Vijaya's men, and his people were called Sinhala after Sinhabahu. His ministers founded villages, among them Upatissagama. To be crowned he needed a queen of noble house, and the Pandya king of Madhura, identified with Madurai, sent his daughter with a hundred noble maidens, craftsmen and a thousand families of eighteen guilds, who landed at the port of Mahatittha.

Vijaya then sent Kuveni away, since his people feared supernatural beings. She went with their two children, Jivahatta and Disala, to the Yakkha city of Lankapura, where she was killed as a traitor. The children fled to Sumanakuta, and from them the chronicle derives the Pulinda, identified with the Vedda people. Vijaya, crowned, is said to have given up his evil ways and ruled in peace and justice.

Having no heir, Vijaya in old age sent for his twin brother Sumitta, but died before a reply came. His ministers governed for a year until Panduvasudeva, Sumitta's youngest son, arrived from Sinhapura to rule. The older Dipavamsa tells a similar story without Kuveni or the South Indian princess, and two other versions of the legend, one recorded by Xuanzang and one a Jataka painted at Ajanta, give the founding prince other names.

There is no archaeological evidence for the story. In Sri Lanka it is often treated as history and used in political argument: Sinhalese scholars such as K. M. de Silva have cited it for the Indo-Aryan origins of the Sinhalese, while Tamil authors such as Satchi Ponnambalam have dismissed it as fiction serving Sinhalese territorial claims.
princely-state: The princely states were the traditional monarchical states of India that had formed, under various degrees of pressure, subsidiary alliances with the East India Company. The British Raj took over these relationships after 1858. Some dynasties, especially those of Rajput princes, were long established, while others dated from the turbulent disintegration of the Mughal Empire in the 18th century. Some, mainly with Muslim ruling families, were of foreign origin: the rulers of Hyderabad were Turco-Persians and those of Bhopal Afghans. Only the Rajput states, Manipur and a scattering of South Indian kingdoms could trace their lineage to the period before the Mughal Empire.

India under the Raj consisted of British India and the princely states. By treaty the British controlled the external affairs of the states absolutely, while the states kept control of their internal affairs, subject to substantial British influence. Rulers bore titles such as Maharaja, Nawab, Nizam and Wadiyar, all of which the British translated as prince. Precedence was set by gun salutes of an odd number from three to 21; about 120 states were salute states, though more than 500 existed in all. The Chamber of Princes, established in 1920, gave the rulers a forum to voice their needs until 1947.

The doctrine of lapse, pursued most vigorously by the Governor-General the Marquess of Dalhousie, placed under Company control any state whose ruler died without a male biological heir. Dalhousie annexed seven states, among them Awadh, Nagpur, Jhansi and Satara. Resentment of these annexations contributed to the discontent behind the rebellion of 1857, and the doctrine ended with Company rule in 1858.

In 1920 the Indian National Congress asked the princes to establish responsible government. At independence on 15 August 1947, 565 princely states were officially recognised, covering 40% of the area of pre-independence India and 23% of its population. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V. P. Menon persuaded the rulers of almost all of them to accede to India, and most others joined Pakistan. Hyderabad was annexed. Kalat declared independence and acceded to Pakistan on 27 March 1948, after which the Khan's brother revolted against the accession.
princess-alice-of-the-united-kingdom: Alice Maud Mary was born at Buckingham Palace on 25 April 1843, the third child and second daughter of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. Her sex was greeted with mixed feelings, and the Privy Council sent Albert a message of congratulation and condolence. Her education was devised by Albert's friend Baron Stockmar and included needlework, woodwork, French and German. She nursed her grandmother the Duchess of Kent in 1861, and when her father fell fatally ill in December 1861 she nursed him until his death, then spent six months as her mother's unofficial secretary. Her mother's search for a husband produced only two suitable princes, and Alice found neither acceptable.

Alice was engaged to Prince Louis of Hesse on 30 April 1861. Parliament granted her a dowry of 30,000 pounds, which Albert thought would not allow her to do great things in the little realm of Hesse. They married on 1 July 1862 in a private ceremony at Osborne House, which the Queen called more of a funeral than a wedding. Her life in Darmstadt was unhappy because of impoverishment, family tragedy and worsening relations with her husband and mother. She became friends with the theologian David Friedrich Strauss, whose views on the Bible she shared, which led Empress Augusta to call her a complete atheist.

Alice took an interest in nursing, especially the work of Florence Nightingale. When Hesse sided with Austria in the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, she managed field hospitals while heavily pregnant. Her Princess Alice Women's Guild took over much of the running of the state's military hospitals. She founded the Alice-Hospital in Darmstadt in 1869 and the Alice Society for Women's Training and Industry. Her husband became Grand Duke Louis IV in 1877, and she became grand duchess, with greater duties that strained her health.

Her youngest son Friedrich, who had haemophilia, died on 29 May 1873 after falling from a window, and Alice never recovered from the loss. In November 1878 diphtheria struck the Hessian court. She nursed her family for over a month before falling ill herself, and died on 14 December 1878, the first of Queen Victoria's nine children to die.

Her daughter Alix married Tsar Nicholas II and passed on the gene for haemophilia to the Tsarevich Alexei; Alix and her family were killed by the Bolsheviks at Ekaterinburg in 1918. Her daughter Elisabeth, who had married Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich, was killed the day after. Her grandson Louis Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of India. The Alice-Hospital continued to flourish long after her death.
princeton-university: The institution began in Elizabeth, New Jersey, in 1746 as the College of New Jersey, one of the nine colonial colleges established before the American Revolution. Its formative years were shaped by the Log College, a seminary founded by the Reverend William Tennent at Neshaminy, Pennsylvania, in about 1726. No legal connection existed, but many of its pupils and adherents later supported the college; Princeton historians reject the older view that it was the college's predecessor.

After the death of President Jonathan Dickinson the college moved in 1747 to Newark, where the parsonage of his successor Aaron Burr Sr. stood. Governor Jonathan Belcher granted a second charter on 14 September 1748 after the first was disputed by Anglicans, and gave the college his library of 474 volumes.

Nassau Hall, begun in 1754 and finished in 1756, was the first seat of the New Jersey Legislature in 1776 and was involved in the Battle of Princeton in 1777. The Congress of the Confederation met there from 30 June to 4 November 1783. A fire gutted its interior in 1802, and a large student riot in 1807 led to the resignation of President Samuel Stanhope Smith.

Woodrow Wilson, an alumnus and professor, became the 13th president and introduced the preceptorial system in 1905, adding small-group teaching to lectures. In 1906 the university became nonsectarian. Wilson kept the college closed to Black students. The college had officially become a university in 1896. After 1945 it desegregated and expanded its research, and it explicitly prohibited the admission of women from its founding until 1969.

Undergraduates complete independent work, including a senior thesis, and first- and second-year students live in one of seven residential colleges. Customs include the Reunions parade of alumni, called the P-rade, and the belief that a student who leaves through the FitzRandolph Gates before graduating will not graduate. Alumni include the presidents James Madison and Woodrow Wilson and the vice presidents Aaron Burr, George M. Dallas and John Breckinridge. Albert Einstein, who belonged to the Institute for Advanced Study, lectured and visited often and became associated with the university.
principate: The term comes from the position of princeps senatus, the most influential member of the Roman Senate in the Republic, which Sulla abolished and Augustus revived in 28 BCE. Princeps, meaning leading or first citizen, had applied to nobles who distinguished themselves in service to the Republic. After the Battle of Actium and the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra, Octavian gained power step by step while courting the Senate and the people and presenting himself as a restorer of the Republic.

On 13 January 27 BCE he made a show of returning power to the Senate. On 16 January the Senate gave him the title augustus and asked him to take command of the provinces again, which he accepted for ten years, and with them control of most of the legions.

Historians Werner Eck and Sarolta Takács trace the authority Augustus created to three sources: powers of office delegated by the Senate and people, his immense private fortune, and the patron-client relationships he built across the empire. Together these formed his auctoritas. After a second settlement in 23 BCE, when he gave up the consulship, he held a proconsular imperium greater than that of all other proconsuls throughout the empire and the power of a tribune for life, which let him convene the Senate and people and veto their actions. In 12 BCE he became pontifex maximus, a title that emperors kept until 476 CE.

The forms of oligarchic self-rule inherited from the Republic, under the motto of the Senate and People of Rome, masked the reality of autocratic rule. After the fall of the Julio-Claudian dynasty in 68 CE, Vespasian gave the position a legal basis in the lex quae dicitur de imperio Vespasiani, and the military role of the imperator gradually overshadowed the civilian ideal of the princeps.

The nineteenth-century German scholar Theodor Mommsen proposed the periodisation of Principate and Dominate. He saw the Principate as a constitutional system, a diarchy in which power was shared between the princeps and the Senate, that broke down in the third century under Diocletian. Since the early twentieth century scholars have increasingly rejected this view.

Historians following Ronald Syme regard the Principate as a variant of monarchy, and they no longer find diarchy a useful concept. Jochen Bleicken considers the scheme unsuitable because its legal basis is flawed and it suggests that the earlier imperial period was freer. The term is nonetheless still used for the first phase of the Roman Empire, from Augustus to the end of the Crisis of the Third Century.
principia-mathematica-newton: In January 1684 Edmond Halley, Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke discussed the inverse-square law. Hooke claimed to have derived it and all the laws of planetary motion but produced no derivation, and Halley, who could derive the law only for the circular case, resolved to ask Isaac Newton. The first book was presented to the Royal Society at the close of April 1686. Hooke made priority claims, and Newton, who hated disputes, threatened to suppress the third book; Halley tactfully persuaded him to go on. The Society had just spent its book budget, so Halley paid for the publication himself, and the book appeared in summer 1687.

The Principia is written in Latin in three books. Book 1, De motu corporum, concerns motion without a resisting medium and begins with lemmas on the method of first and last ratios, a geometrical form of infinitesimal calculus. Book 2 largely concerns motion through resisting mediums, and Newton was a pioneer of fluid mechanics there. Book 3, De mundi systemate, applies universal gravitation to the Solar System. It shows by stages that the inverse-square law holds for the satellites of Jupiter and then for all bodies, treats the irregularities of the Moon's motion and the motion of comets, offers the first theory of the precession of the equinoxes and estimates the share of the Sun and Moon in the tides.

Newton published two further editions: in 1713, edited by Roger Cotes for Richard Bentley, and in 1726, under Henry Pemberton. The later editions added four Rules of Reasoning in Philosophy and a General Scholium. Andrew Motte made the first English translation in 1729. Alexis Clairaut wrote in 1747 that the book marked the epoch of a great revolution in physics, and Joseph-Louis Lagrange and Pierre-Simon Laplace gave it extreme praise. It is generally considered one of the most important works in the history of science. A picture of a page of the book was carried by the Voyager spacecraft in 1977.
printing-press: A printing press applies pressure to transfer ink onto paper, cloth or a similar surface. Johannes Gutenberg, a German goldsmith, invented the movable-type press around 1440 by combining four existing technologies: the screw press, movable type, the codex book and mechanised paper production. The Chinese artisan Bi Sheng made the first movable type in the 11th century, in baked clay, and the oldest surviving book with metal movable type is the Jikji of 1377, from the Korean state of Goryeo. None of these East Asian methods spread widely, because a Chinese text needed thousands of characters, whereas Gutenberg's press used the Latin alphabet with a small set. Gutenberg added a hand mold for casting type and an oil-based ink suited to metal type.

A compositor set individual metal letters into lines, which were arranged in a frame called a galley and then in a forme resting on the bed. The type was inked with leather pads called ink balls, a dampened sheet was laid over it, and a long lever, the bar, drove a screw that pressed the platen onto the paper. All of this was done by hand, and the basic design of the wooden handpress stayed largely the same for over three centuries. Lord Stanhope built an iron press by 1800 that printed a sheet in one pull. In 1814 The Times began printing on steam-driven presses built by Friedrich Koenig.

By the end of the 15th century around 270 European cities had printers, and by 1500 presses in Western Europe had produced over 20 million copies. Between 1518 and 1520 printers in Germany distributed 300,000 copies of Martin Luther's works. The press spread rapidly because it was portable and printers could move to a neighbouring city when one authority tried to curb them. Jesuit missionaries set up a press at Goa in 1556, and Juan Pablos set one up in Mexico City in 1539.

The historian Elizabeth Eisenstein described the press as an agent of change. Books became cheaper, authors came to be more closely associated with their works, and books increasingly appeared in vernacular languages rather than Latin. Church and secular authorities introduced licensing and banned books, with limited success. The press is now generally treated as one of several causes of the Reformation rather than the only one.
pristina: Pristina lies on an alluvial plain in the regions of Llap and Kosovo, across the Gollak Hills in central and eastern Kosovo. The area has been inhabited since the Neolithic, and the earliest recognised traces were found at Gračanica, Matiçan and Ulpiana. In antiquity it belonged to the Dardanian Kingdom, and the nearby settlement of Ulpiana represents the heritage of the classical era. The origin of the city's name is unknown; Eric P. Hamp connected it with an Indo-European word for a ford and a word cognate with English stone.

After the division of the Roman Empire the area stayed within the Byzantine Empire between the 5th and 9th centuries. It was ceded to the First Bulgarian Empire in the middle of the 9th century, fell again to the Byzantine Empire in the early 11th century, when it was part of a theme called Bulgaria, and passed several times to the Second Bulgarian Empire. The Kingdom, later Empire, of Serbia held it through the 13th and 14th centuries. King Stefan Milutin founded the nearby Gračanica monastery in 1315, and Pristina is first recorded in 1342, as a village, in the reign of Stefan Dušan.

In 1455 it had a small population of 300 households. In the following century it became an important mining and trading centre because of its position near Novo Brdo, known for its trade fairs and for goatskin, goat hair and gunpowder. During the Austro-Turkish War of the late 17th century, townspeople under the Catholic Albanian priest Pjetër Bogdani pledged loyalty to the Austrian army, and he supplied a force of 6,000 Albanian soldiers. According to Noel Malcolm the town then had a majority of about 15,000 Muslims, probably Albanian.

Albanians pillaged and partly burned Pristina in May 1901. Serb forces took it on 22 October 1912, and Bulgaria occupied it in 1915. In 1948 it was chosen as the capital of the province of SAP Kosovo within Yugoslavia, and it remained the capital after Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008.

Pristina is the capital and largest city of Kosovo, with 227,466 residents at the census of 2024, most of them Albanians. It holds the Parliament, the courts and the residences of the president and prime minister. The University of Pristina, founded in the 20th century, is the largest and oldest in the city, and the National Theatre of Kosovo dates from 1946. Of 426 protected monuments in Kosovo, 21 are in Pristina, many of them from the Byzantine and Ottoman periods.
prizren: Prizren lies on the banks of the Prizren River in the foothills of the Šar Mountains in southern Kosovo, and its municipality borders Albania and North Macedonia. Excavations in the Prizren Fortress show that the site was inhabited from the Middle Bronze Age, around 2000 BCE, to the late Iron Age. The city has traditionally been identified with Theranda in Roman Dardania, although recent research suggests that Theranda may have stood at present-day Suva Reka. The fort was rebuilt under the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian.

The present town is first mentioned in 1019, in the time of Basil II, as Prisdriana. Byzantine rule ended there when the Serbian Nemanjić dynasty took the fort and the town, and in 1219 Prizren's church separated from the Patriarchate of Constantinople. The old town grew below the fortress, where Ragusan traders were based. Stefan Dušan founded the Monastery of the Holy Archangels and was buried in it; the city briefly served as capital of the Serbian Empire under him.

From 1371 regional feudal rulers held it, among them the Mrnjavčević, Balšić and Branković families. The Ottomans took Prizren on 21 June 1455 and made it the capital of the Sanjak of Prizren, later part of Rumelia Eyalet and a larger city of the Kosovo vilayet. The League of Prizren was created there in 1878 to seek the national unification and autonomy of Albanians within the Ottoman Empire.

Serbian forces captured the city in the First Balkan War in 1912, and it passed into the Kingdom of Serbia. The takeover was bloody, with 400 people dead in the first few days, and reports later emerged of widespread killings of Albanians. In 1946 it became part of the Autonomous Region of Kosovo and Metohija within the People's Republic of Serbia.

Prizren is the second most populous city and municipality of Kosovo, and the constitution designates it the country's historical capital. Albanian, Bosnian and Turkish are used as official languages of the municipality, as well as the two official languages of Kosovo. It is regarded as the most culturally and ethnically varied city in Kosovo, with Albanian, Bosniak, Turkish and Romani communities.

The city is known for its heritage of mosques, churches and old buildings, among them the Sinan Pasha Mosque, the Monastery of the Holy Archangels and Our Lady of Ljeviš, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Dokufest film festival is held there.
probus-emperor: Probus was born in Sirmium in Pannonia Inferior, the son of Dalmatius. The Historia Augusta gives his father's name as Maximus and says his personal wealth was modest. He entered the army around the age of 25 and rose rapidly. The emperor Valerian appointed him a military tribune at a very young age, and he justified the choice with a victory over the Sarmatians on the Illyrian frontier.

He became one of Aurelian's highest-placed lieutenants and reconquered Egypt from Zenobia in 273. In 275 Tacitus made him supreme chief of the east with extraordinary powers, and after Tacitus died in 276 the troops in Asia Minor elected Probus emperor in his camp.

Florian, the half-brother of Tacitus, had also proclaimed himself emperor, but he was killed by his own soldiers after an indecisive campaign against Probus in Cilicia. Probus referred his claim to the Senate in a respectful dispatch, and it ratified it. In 277 he defeated the Goths on the lower Danube. In 278 he campaigned in Gaul against the Alemanni and Lugii, while his generals cleared the province of Frankish and Burgundian raiders. He then crossed the Rhine, repaired the fortifications of Hadrian between the Rhine and Danube, and accepted the submission of nine major tribes, which pledged recruits for his army.

By demanding a tribute of manpower he set a precedent for bringing foreign soldiers into the empire as auxiliaries on a large scale. In peacetime he set soldiers to useful works, such as planting vineyards in Gaul and Pannonia. In 280 and 281 he put down three usurpers, Julius Saturninus, Proculus and Bonosus, and in the winter of 281 he held a triumph in Rome. He left Rome in 282 to prepare a campaign against Persia.

Accounts of his death differ. According to Joannes Zonaras, the commander of the Praetorian Guard, Marcus Aurelius Carus, was proclaimed emperor by his troops; troops Probus sent against him changed sides, and his remaining soldiers killed him at Sirmium in September or October 282. Other sources say soldiers who objected to civic work such as draining marshes rebelled against him. Carus became emperor and had the killers put to death.

Edward Gibbon, drawing largely on the Historia Augusta, treated Probus as the last of the benevolent constitutional emperors of Rome. His successor Carus did not seek the Senate's confirmation of his title, and Diocletian later undermined its authority. Probus's victories continued the line of soldier emperors from Illyria begun by Claudius Gothicus.
procopius: Apart from his own writings, the main source for Procopius's life is an entry in the Suda, a Byzantine encyclopaedia written after 975. He was a native of Caesarea in Palestine and would have received a conventional upper-class education in Greek classics and rhetoric, perhaps at the school at Gaza. He may have studied law, possibly at Berytus or Constantinople, and became a lawyer. He knew Latin, as was natural for a man with legal training.

In 527, the first year of Justinian's reign, Procopius became legal adviser to the general Belisarius. He served with Belisarius on the eastern front until the defeat at the Battle of Callinicum in 531, and he witnessed the Nika riots of January 532, which Belisarius and Mundus put down with a massacre in the Hippodrome. In 533 he went with Belisarius against the Vandal kingdom in North Africa and took part in the capture of Carthage. He then rejoined him for the war in Italy, lived through the Gothic siege of Rome, which lasted a year and nine days, and saw Belisarius enter Ravenna in 540.

His relations with Belisarius appear to have cooled after that, and when Belisarius returned to Italy in 544 Procopius appears no longer to have been on his staff. The date of his death is not certain. Many historians place it in 554, but an urban prefect of Constantinople named Procopius is recorded in 562, and some scholars think he may be the historian.

His History of the Wars, in eight books, is his most important work. The first two books cover the conflict with Sassanid Persia, including the war of Khosrau I in 540 and the great plague from 542. The next two cover Belisarius's campaign against the Vandal kingdom, and the final four the war in Italy against the Ostrogoths. The eighth book brings the history to 553.

The Secret History claims to report the scandals Procopius could not include in his official history for fear of angering the emperor, the empress and the generals. It portrays Justinian as cruel, venal and incompetent. It was discovered in 1623 in the Vatican Library, and scholars differ on how far it shows his real feelings. On Buildings, in contrast, is a panegyric on Justinian's public works, probably written at his behest.
prohibition-in-the-united-states: Drinking had been contested in America since the colonial period. The American Temperance Society, formed in 1826, had reached 1.5 million members by 1835. The dry crusade continued from the 1840s, led by Protestant denominations, and in the late 19th century it linked saloons with political corruption. Maine's law of 1851 banned the manufacture and sale of liquor, and twelve states followed before its repeal in 1856. The Woman's Christian Temperance Union gave the movement a national grassroots base, and after 1900 the Anti-Saloon League coordinated it.

The Senate proposed the Eighteenth Amendment on 18 December 1917, and it became part of the Constitution when a 36th state approved it on 16 January 1919; the country went dry on 17 January 1920. The Volstead Act set the rules for enforcement and defined the banned drinks. Religious use of wine was permitted, and private possession and consumption were not illegal under federal law, though many local laws were stricter. Enforcement lacked a central authority, some states such as Maryland and New York refused to enforce the amendment, and the terrain, ports and long borders with Canada and Mexico made smuggling hard to stop.

Many of the wealthy stockpiled liquor before 1920, while small portable stills were on sale within a week of the ban. Within six months over 15,000 doctors and 57,000 pharmacists held licences to prescribe or sell medicinal alcohol. A black market grew up, and organised crime has been argued to have gained a financial basis from it. In Cicero, Illinois, the gang leader Al Capone operated despite the police.

Before the Volstead Act about 14% of federal, state and local tax revenue came from alcohol, and when the Great Depression struck, governments wanted that income. Captain William H. Stayton's Association Against the Prohibition Amendment, founded in 1918, was the largest of nearly forty groups working for repeal. The Twenty-first Amendment repealed the Eighteenth on 5 December 1933, the only time in American history that an amendment was passed to repeal another. It lets states restrict or ban alcohol, and dry counties remain.

Its effects are disputed. One review concluded that Prohibition probably reduced per capita alcohol use and harm at first, but that the benefits eroded as a black market grew. Rates of cirrhosis fell, while another study found consumption fell to about 30 percent of its earlier level and later rose to 60–70 percent. The historian Lisa McGirr argues that it expanded the powers of the federal state and fell hardest on African Americans, immigrants and poor whites.
proletariat: The word comes from the Latin proletarius, a social class of Roman citizens who owned little or no property. The name presumably originated with the census held every five years, which registered citizens and their property and fixed their military duties and voting privileges. Those who owned 11,000 assēs or fewer fell below the lowest category for military service, and their children, called prōlēs, were listed instead of property, hence proletarius, a producer of offspring. Their only contribution to the commonwealth was their children, the future citizens who could colonise conquered territories.

The proletarii were the lowest class in the Comitia Centuriata, largely deprived of voting rights. Voting began with the highest social ranks, so a majority could be reached early and their votes never taken.

In the early 19th century liberal scholars in Western Europe noted the similarities between the growing industrial working class and the Roman proletarians. In 1839 the French philosopher Felicité Robert de Lamennais compared workers to the slaves of Rome in De l'esclavage moderne, published in English as Modern Slavery. The Swiss economist Jean Charles Léonard de Sismondi was the first to apply the term to the working class created by capitalism, and Karl Marx most likely met it in his writings.

Marx used the term for a class with no significant ownership of the means of production, whose only means of subsistence is to sell its labour power for a wage. In his theory capitalism rests on the exploitation of the proletariat by the bourgeoisie: the goods the workers produce belong to the capitalist, who sells them, and wages absorb only part of the price. Marx argued that the conflict of interest between the two classes gives workers common interests across national boundaries, and that the proletariat would displace capitalism through a dictatorship of the proletariat, leading to a communist society.

Marxist theory defines the borders of the proletariat only vaguely. Above it lie the lower petty bourgeoisie, such as small shopkeepers, and below it the lumpenproletariat, a class Marx considered retrograde, made up of the poorest outcasts living outside legal employment.

During the Chinese Communist Revolution the concept stressed a proletarian class consciousness, developed through political education by the Chinese Communist Party, rather than social attributes such as being an industrial worker. This allowed the revolution to address the relative weakness of China's industrial working class. The socialist states that followed the Russian Revolution championed an official version of proletarian culture.
prosthesis: The word prosthesis comes from the Ancient Greek prosthesis, meaning "addition, application, attachment". Prostheses originate in the ancient Near East around 3000 BCE, with the earliest evidence in ancient Egypt and Iran. The earliest recorded mention of eye prostheses is the Egyptian story of the Eye of Horus, in which Thoth restores the plucked-out left eye of Horus. The earliest archaeological evidence, from about 3000 to 2800 BCE, is an eye prosthesis buried with a woman at Shahr-i Shōkhta in Iran, probably of bitumen paste covered with a thin layer of gold.

A prosthesis may restore the function of a missing body part or serve a cosmetic purpose. The part may be lost through injury, disease or a condition present at birth. Limb prostheses replace arms or legs at various levels of amputation, and organ prostheses include artificial hearts and kidneys. Cosmetic prostheses have long been used to disguise injuries and disfigurements. A prosthetist prescribes, designs and manages the device, usually beginning with a plaster cast of the affected limb.

The Egyptians were early makers of foot prostheses, as a wooden toe found on a mummy shows. In South Asia the Rigveda, about 1200 BCE, tells of the warrior queen Vishpala. Roman bronze crowns have also been found, but their use may have been more aesthetic than medical.

An Italian surgeon recorded an amputee whose artificial arm allowed him to remove his hat, open his purse and sign his name. Ambroise Paré, considered the father of modern prosthetics, improved both amputation surgery and design; among his inventions was an above-knee device, a kneeling peg leg and foot with a fixed position, an adjustable harness and a knee lock. Pieter Verduyn made the first non-locking below-knee prosthesis. After the Second World War the National Academy of Sciences urged more research, and government funding set up programmes in the armed forces and the Veterans Administration. Elaine Scarry argues that every artifact extends the body, as chairs supplement the skeleton and tools the hands.
protagoras: Protagoras was born in Abdera, in Thrace, opposite the island of Thasos, around 490 BCE. According to Aulus Gellius he first made his living as a porter, until the philosopher Democritus saw him carrying a load of small pieces of wood tied with a short cord so accurately that Democritus took him for a mathematical prodigy, and took him into his household to teach him philosophy. Protagoras became well known in Athens and a friend of Pericles.

His dates are not recorded but are worked out from surviving writings. In Plato's Protagoras he says he is old enough to be the father of Socrates, Prodicus or Hippias, and in the Meno he is said to have died at about 70, after forty years as a practising sophist. His death is therefore placed about 420 BCE, though the story of his trial for impiety on which assumptions rest appears to be fake.

Plato credits Protagoras with inventing the role of the professional sophist. He taught subjects related to virtue and political life, and above all whether virtue could be taught. Plato has him claim to teach the proper management of one's own household and of public affairs. The titles of his books, such as Technique of Eristics, show that he also taught rhetoric and argument. Aristotle records that he was criticised for claiming to make the weaker argument stronger.

His best-known statement, from his lost work Truth, is that of all things the measure is Man. Plato took it to mean that there is no objective truth. Protagoras seems to have meant that each person's experience shapes their judgments, so that two people may truly find the same weather cold and hot, but he held that views are not of equal worth: a sophist teaches students to tell the useful from the harmful. Plato and Aristotle both argued against him.

Of his lost work On the Gods, Protagoras is reported to have written that he had no means of knowing whether the gods existed, because of the obscurity of the subject and the brevity of human life. According to Diogenes Laërtius this angered the Athenians, who expelled him and burned his books in the marketplace; Cicero also mentions the destruction. The classicist John Burnet doubts the account, since both writers lived centuries later and contemporaries do not mention such persecution. Very few fragments of his writing survive.
protestant-reformation: Europe suffered a series of calamities from the early 14th century, culminating in the Black Death, which killed about a third of its population. Humanism, with its slogan ad fontes, back to the sources, brought enthusiasm for textual criticism: Lorenzo Valla showed that the Donation of Constantine, a basic document of papal authority, was a medieval forgery. Many of Luther's ideas were anticipated by Wycliff, Hus, Erasmus and others, and scholars now see the Reformation as in important respects a continuation of trends within late medieval Catholicism.

Pope Leo X announced a new plenary indulgence in 1515 to finance the building of St Peter's Basilica, and the friar Johann Tetzel sold indulgences in Germany with unusually aggressive methods. The Reformation is usually dated from Martin Luther's publication of the Ninety-five Theses in 1517.

Printing carried the new ideas quickly: Luther was responsible for about one fifth of all works printed in Germany in the first third of the 16th century. Huldrych Zwingli led reform in Zürich from 1522, and John Calvin shaped the Continental Reformed tradition. Radical reformers such as the Swiss Brethren demanded believers' baptism and a church free of the state. The Peasants' War of 1524 and 1525 drew on the new excitement against authority. In April 1525 Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach turned the Teutonic Order's Prussia into a hereditary duchy, and the Reformation was introduced in Electoral Saxony on Christmas Day 1525. At the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 the Protestants presented the Augsburg Confession, written by Melanchthon.

Elsewhere the kings of Denmark and Sweden took the lead in Scandinavia. In England, William Tyndale's New Testament had more than 15,000 copies in secret circulation by about 1535, and under Edward VI Thomas Cranmer's Book of Common Prayer replaced the Mass with a vernacular liturgy. Disputes in Germany led to the Schmalkaldic War, and later came the French Wars of Religion and the revolt in the Netherlands, where more Protestants were persecuted between 1523 and 1555 than in any other country.

The Catholic response, the Counter-Reformation, included new orders, above all the Jesuits, whose establishment Paul III sanctioned in 1540. The Council of Trent met from December 1545 to 1563, reaffirmed that apostolic tradition was as authentic a source of faith as the Bible, and stressed good works in salvation, rejecting two important elements of Luther's theology. Historians often use the plural to stress that the movement was not uniform but the result of parallel movements: Lutheranism, Calvinism, the Radical Reformation and the Catholic Reformation. It is considered one of the events that signified the end of the Middle Ages, and the end of the Reformation era is disputed among scholars.
protestantism: Protestantism follows the theology of the Protestant Reformation, a movement that began in the 16th century with the aim of reforming the Catholic Church of perceived errors and abuses. It began in the Holy Roman Empire in 1517, when Martin Luther published his Ninety-five Theses in reaction to abuses in the sale of indulgences. Luther argued against buying or earning forgiveness and claimed instead that salvation is a gift God gives to those who have faith.

The name comes from a protest. Six princes of the Holy Roman Empire and the rulers of fourteen Imperial Free Cities issued a protest against the edict of the Diet of Speyer in 1529 and were the first to be called Protestants. Lutheranism spread into Denmark–Norway, Sweden, Finland, Livonia and Iceland, and Calvinist churches spread in Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Scotland, Switzerland, France, Poland and Lithuania. The separation of the Church of England from the Catholic Church under King Henry VIII began Anglicanism.

Protestants hold to justification by faith alone, the priesthood of all believers, and the Bible as the highest authority for faith and practice. They reject papal supremacy, and early Protestants rejected transubstantiation. Lutherans affirmed a corporeal presence of Christ in Holy Communion, along with Catholics, while the Reformed affirmed a real spiritual presence.

The movement soon divided into branches: Lutheranism, Anglicanism, Calvinism or Reformed Christianity, and later Methodism, which grew from a revival within the 18th-century Church of England under John Wesley, and the Baptists, who hold that baptism should be given only to professing believers. The Radical Reformation, which had no state sponsorship and faced intense persecution from both Catholics and mainstream Protestants, gave rise to Anabaptism, whose descendants include the Amish, Hutterites and Mennonites.

The Reformation affected marriage and family, education, the political and social order, the economy and the arts. Protestant churches reject a celibate priesthood and allow their clergy to marry. Freedom of conscience gained priority after Luther refused to recant at the Diet of Worms in 1521, and Rhode Island, Connecticut and Pennsylvania combined democratic constitutions with freedom of religion. Protestants founded hospitals, schools and aid organisations, and in the 19th century many took part in the abolition of slavery, prison reform and woman suffrage. Estimates of the number of Protestants worldwide range from 600 million to 1 billion, because scholars disagree on which denominations count.
providence-rhode-island: Providence lies at the head of Narragansett Bay, at the mouth of the Providence River, which is formed in the middle of the city by the confluence of the Moshassuck and Woonasquatucket rivers. Its limits enclose a small area of about 20.5 square miles, of which roughly a tenth is water. Like Rome, it is one of many cities claimed to stand on seven hills. The city grew up before the automobile, and its streets run irregularly, radiating from old gathering places such as Market Square.

Roger Williams settled Providence in June 1636. As a minister in the Massachusetts Bay Colony he had advocated the separation of church and state and condemned the colonists' confiscation of land from the Indians, and for these and other opinions described as diverse, new and dangerous he was convicted of sedition and heresy and banished. He and his companions first settled at Rumford, then moved down the Seekonk River, around Fox Point and up the Providence River to the meeting of the Moshassuck and Woonasquatucket. They named the settlement after God's merciful Providence. It grew into one of the original Thirteen Colonies.

Williams founded the First Baptist Church in America there in 1638, and the Old State House served as the state's capitol from 1762 to 1904. Providence developed as a busy port and was one of the first cities in the country to industrialise, becoming noted for textile manufacturing and then for machine tools, jewellery and silverware. Its population peaked in the 1940s, just before the nationwide movement to the suburbs.

Providence is the capital and largest city of Rhode Island and the county seat of Providence County; its population was 190,934 at the 2020 census. The State House houses the General Assembly and the offices of the governor. The East Side has the largest contiguous area of buildings on the National Register of Historic Places in the U.S., many of them from before the Revolution. The city has Italian, Portuguese and Irish neighbourhoods, and is home to Brown University, the Rhode Island School of Design, Providence College and other institutions of higher education.
province-of-albacete: The Province of Albacete lies in central Spain, in the southern part of Castile–La Mancha, in the southeast of the Central Plateau. Its capital, the city of Albacete, is 262 kilometres by road southeast of Madrid. The province borders the provinces of Granada, Murcia, Alicante, Valencia, Cuenca, Ciudad Real and Jaén. Its main river is the Júcar, which crosses the northeast and is known for its deep gorges and trees. The highest point is La Atalaya, at 2,083 metres in the Sierra de las Cabras.

The territory has been inhabited since ancient times, as cave paintings in the Cueva del Niño and the Cueva de la Vieja show. In Roman times it was divided among Carpetania, Celtiberia, Contestania, Bastetania and Oretania. The Romans built a significant settlement at Libisosa, and under the Visigoths Tolmo de Minateda grew in prominence. In the Muslim period numerous farmhouses, castles and watchtowers were built to fight off invaders. On 25 April 1707 the Battle of Almansa was fought near Albacete, in which Philip V triumphed and established the House of Bourbon on the Spanish throne.

In 1822 the short-lived Province of Chinchilla was created from municipalities of La Mancha, Cuenca and the Kingdom of Murcia, with its capital at Chinchilla de Monte-Aragón, very close to Albacete. It became the basis on which Javier de Burgos created the Province of Albacete in 1833. After the Constitution of 1978 the province left the Murcia region and joined Castile–La Mancha, whose Statute of Autonomy was approved in 1982.

The province covers 14,931.74 square kilometres and has 87 municipalities and seven judicial districts, with a population of 390,751. Besides the capital, towns of more than 10,000 inhabitants are Hellín, Villarrobledo, Almansa, La Roda and Caudete.
province-of-castellon: The province is bordered by the provinces of Valencia to the south, Teruel to the west and Tarragona to the north, and by the Mediterranean Sea to the east. Its western side lies in the mountainous Sistema Ibérico area. Penyagolosa, the highest mountain of the province and the second highest in the Valencian Community, is regarded as one of the most emblematic Valencian mountains.

The Greenwich Meridian passes through the province, and commemorative monuments mark it at La Pobla Tornesa, Castellón and Almassora. At Castellón it crosses the 40th parallel, and the exact point can be visited at the Meridian Park. The province is divided into 135 municipalities and, historically, into eight comarques: Alcalatén, Alt Maestrat, Alto Mijares, Alto Palancia, Baix Maestrat, Plana Alta, Plana Baixa and Ports.

Besides Castellón de la Plana, the major cities are Vila-real, Borriana, La Vall d'Uixó and Vinaròs. Traditionally the economy rested on citrus fruit and vegetables, notably at Nules and Benicarló. From the 17th century the province developed a ceramic and tile industry, centred on Onda, L'Alcora, Nules, Castellón de la Plana and Vila-real, and most Spanish tile producers are now concentrated there. Furniture and chemical industries are also present, and there is a large oil refinery at Castellón de la Plana.

Older industries such as footwear at La Vall d'Uixó, fishing at Castellón and Vinaròs, and textiles at Vilafranca and Morella have given way to services and tourism. Seaside resorts include Benicàssim, Orpesa, Vinaròs, Borriana and Peníscola. Inland, the monumental towns of Morella, Vilafamés, Sant Mateu and Segorbe draw visitors, as do mineral springs at Montanejos, Benassal and Catí.
provins: There are signs of human occupation in the area as early as the Paleolithic. In Roman Gaul Provins stood at the crossroads of two regional corridors, one from Soissons to Troyes and one running south towards Sens. By the 9th century the town was minting its own coin, the denier provinois, and Charlemagne had sent his missi dominici there.

Under the protection of the Counts of Champagne, Provins hosted one of the largest Champagne fairs, crucial to the medieval economy. In the upper town the fair was held twice a year, in May and November, while the lower town had a yearly market in September. The town also became a banking centre, and the denier was widely accepted throughout Europe. The fairs continued from 1120 until 1320.

King Philip IV visited several times in the late 13th century and devastated the town with harsh taxes, which ended its prosperity and caused residents to flee. The town was besieged repeatedly and changed hands frequently from the 14th to the 16th centuries, and this instability reduced its importance. On 3 August 1429 the recently crowned Charles VII attended Mass at Saint-Quiriace there with his court and Joan of Arc. Largely untouched by the Industrial Revolution, Provins remained a small market town in the 19th century.

Provins lies in the Seine-et-Marne department in the Île-de-France region and is the sous-préfecture of its arrondissement. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001. Its 12th-century fortifications survive, including the Caesar Tower and the city walls, and many buildings of the upper town date from the 12th century, when they housed merchants' residences, shops and counting houses. Of the fair towns of the County of Champagne, Provins is the only one that has kept much of its medieval character.

The collegiate church of Saint-Quiriace was built by Henry I of Champagne to display the head of Judas Cyriacus, brought from Jerusalem, and its 12th-century construction was never completed. Two sets of caves lie under parts of the town: one probably used in the Middle Ages to store food and extract fuller's earth, the other deeper, with Bronze Age and Iron Age graffiti. Provins is a centre of cultivation of the Provins rose, Rosa gallica, from which jam, honey and sweets are made.
prudentius: Aurelius Prudentius Clemens was born in 348 in the Roman province of Tarraconensis, the northern part of the Iberian Peninsula. He practised law with some success and was twice a provincial governor, perhaps in his native country, before the emperor Theodosius I summoned him to court.

Towards the end of his life, possibly around 392, he retired from public life to become an ascetic. He fasted until evening, abstained entirely from animal food, and wrote poems, hymns and controversial works in defence of Christianity. He later collected the Christian poems written in this period and added a preface, which he himself dated 405.

His poetry was influenced by early Christian authors such as Tertullian and Ambrose, as well as by the Bible and the acts of the martyrs. The Cathemerinon, or Book in Accordance with the Hours, has twelve lyric poems on times of the day and church festivals. The Peristephanon, or Crowns of Martyrdom, has fourteen on Iberian and Roman martyrs, some suggested to him by sacred images in churches or by the inscriptions of Pope Damasus I. Two hymns from the Cathemerinon, including Corde natus ex parentis, are still in use today.

His other works include the Apotheosis, which attacks those who deny the Trinity and the divinity of Jesus, and the Hamartigenia, which attacks the dualism of Marcion. The Books Against Symmachus oppose the pagan senator Symmachus, who asked that the altar of Victory, removed by Gratian, be restored to the Senate house. The Dittochæon has 49 quatrains meant as captions for the murals of a basilica in Rome.

The Psychomachia, or Battle of Souls, describes the struggle of faith, supported by the cardinal virtues, against idolatry and the corresponding vices. It joined elements of Hellenic epic with inner psychological conflict, and became the inspiration of medieval allegorical literature; C. S. Lewis judged its influence greater than its artistic merit. By joining Christianity with classical culture, Prudentius remained one of the most popular medieval authors, and as late as the 13th century Henri d'Andeli set him beside Horace and Statius.
prut: The Prut rises on the eastern slope of Mount Hoverla in the Carpathian Mountains, in Ukraine's Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. It first flows north, turns north-east near Yaremche and south-east near Kolomyia, and after reaching the border between Moldova and Romania bends further south-east and then south. Its upper reaches, as far as Delyatyn, are mountainous, and near Yaremche it drops over the waterfall of Probiy. The lowest part of its basin is strongly marshy, and ships can travel from the mouth up to Leova. The basin covers 27,540 square kilometres, and Chernivtsi is the largest city on its banks.
Herodotus lists the river, as Porata or Pyretus, among the five rivers of the Scythian country that swell the Danube. In 1538 the army of Suleiman crossed it during the campaign of Karaboğdan.

In the Russo-Turkish War of 1710-1711 the army of Peter the Great, allied with Dimitrie Cantemir, the ruler of Moldova, met the Ottoman army under Grand Vizier Baltaci Mehmed Pasha. The Russian camp between Stănilești and the river was completely surrounded. Talks began on 21 July 1711 and the Treaty of the Prut was signed on 23 July. Cantemir went into exile in Moscow, and Greek Phanariotes from Istanbul came to rule Moldova. On 1 August 1770 Pyotr Rumyantsev defeated a larger Ottoman army at the Battle of Kagul on the river, and in 1821 Alexander Ypsilantis crossed it at Sculeni to start a rebellion in the Danubian Principalities, which set off the Greek War of Independence.

The river has been a frontier several times. Before the First World War it divided Romania from the Russian Empire, between 1918 and 1939 it ran partly through Poland and Greater Romania, and after the Second World War it marked the border between Romania and the Soviet Union. Today it forms 31 kilometres of the border between Romania and Ukraine and 711 kilometres of that between Romania and Moldova.
